docs.title: Welcome
docs.text: Welcome to Health Education, an interactive, intelligent textbook designed to empower K-12 students with knowledge and skills for lifelong health.

docs.title: About This Textbook
docs.text: This comprehensive health education resource is organized by grade level, from Kindergarten through Grade 12, to ensure age-appropriate content and learning progression. Each grade band features carefully sequenced chapters that build foundational knowledge and critical health literacy skills.

docs.title: Explore by Grade Level
docs.text:
Start with your grade level to access courses, chapters, and interactive learning experiences:

  • Kindergarten — Health and safety fundamentals
  • Grade 1 — Foundations of health and safe habits
  • Grade 2 — Health basics, friendships, and feelings
  • Grade 3 — Wellness, safety, and trusted adults
  • Grade 4 — Nutrition, growth, and emotional health
  • Grade 5 — Personal health, wellness, and safety skills
  • Grades 6-8 — Health equity, relationships, and substance awareness
  • Grades 9-12 — Advanced health decision-making and advocacy

docs.title: 📚 Chapters
docs.text: Each grade level includes chapters organized around core health topics like nutrition, relationships, mental health, safety, and disease prevention. Browse all textbooks by grade.

docs.title: 🎮 Interactive MicroSims
docs.text: Learn by doing! Explore hundreds of interactive simulations that bring health concepts to life — from decision-making scenarios to visual concept maps to tracking tools.

docs.title: 🎨 Posters

docs.title: 🗺️ Learning Graph Viewer

docs.title: Welcome from Scout
docs.text:
Welcome, friend!

Hi there — I'm Scout, and I'll be with you in every chapter of this book. Health is really about the choices we make every day: what we eat, how we move, how we handle big feelings, and how we keep ourselves and our friends safe. We'll take it one small step at a time, and you don't have to get everything right on the first try. Let's think it through together — healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Why Health Education Matters
docs.text:
Every child on Earth grows up making health decisions — about food, sleep, friendships, screens, risk, and their own changing bodies. Those decisions shape outcomes that last a lifetime, yet health is one of the most unevenly taught subjects in the world. Where a strong, age-appropriate health curriculum exists, students gain skills — evaluating information, communicating, making decisions, setting goals, asking for help — that carry far beyond any single lesson.

Worldwide:

  • About one in seven adolescents aged 10–19 (roughly 14%) lives with a mental health condition, and most cases go unrecognized and untreated.1
  • Half of all mental health conditions begin by age 14, which makes the school years the single most important window for prevention and early support.1
  • In 2022, more than 390 million children and adolescents aged 5–19 were overweight — including about 160 million living with obesity — a figure that has risen on every continent.2
  • Suicide is the third leading cause of death among older adolescents (ages 15–19) globally, a reminder that mental and emotional health belongs in the curriculum, not in the margins.1

In response, the World Health Organization and UNESCO have called on every country to make every school a health-promoting school, with health skills taught deliberately rather than left to chance.3

These numbers are not abstractions — they are the students sitting in classrooms in Nairobi, Helsinki, São Paulo, and Minneapolis alike. This book exists to give any teacher, in any country, a complete and ready-to-use way to teach health well.

What makes this different from a traditional textbook. This is an intelligent textbook: it is built on validated learning graphs of more than 600 interconnected concepts, so each idea is introduced only after its prerequisites are in place. Throughout, students don't just read — they manipulate interactive MicroSims, work through infographic posters, and build intuition by experimenting rather than memorizing. And the entire work is open source and free: no paywalls, no access codes, no per-seat licensing, and no expiring annual edition. Any school, anywhere, can adopt it tomorrow.

docs.title: Eight Grade-Specific Textbooks in One
docs.text:
Health Education is not one book with a single reading level applied on the fly. It is eight complete, grade-specific textbooks published together as a single site — each one written and calibrated from scratch for its learners:

Textbook Audience Reading approach Kindergarten Ages ~5 Read-aloud; teacher-facing, game-first Grade 1 Ages ~6 Early elementary Grade 2 Ages ~7 Early elementary Grade 3 Ages ~8 Elementary Grade 4 Ages ~9 Elementary Grade 5 Ages ~10 Elementary Grades 6–8 Middle school Analyze influences, apply in scenarios Grades 9–12 High school Evaluate, synthesize, design

Six health strands run through the bands:

  1. Food and Nutrition
  2. Human Growth and Development (extending to Sexual Health in grades 6–12),
  3. Mental and Emotional Health
  4. Personal Health and Wellness
  5. Personal Safety and Violence Prevention
  6. Substance Use Awareness and Prevention (grades 6–12).

A third grader and a high schooler studying the same strand get genuinely different pages: different vocabulary, different examples, different MicroSim complexity, and different assessment difficulty — never the same page with the reading age swapped out.

For the youngest bands (K–3), where reading fluency is still developing, the teacher is the primary audience and interactive MicroSim "games" carry much of the student experience. By grades 9–12, students work directly with the text and reach capstone-level outcomes such as designing a personal health plan or a peer-support strategy.

docs.title: A Standalone Library of MicroSims and Infographics
docs.text:
The 370 interactive MicroSims and 86 infographic posters in this book are among the highest-quality assets in the entire project — and they are built to stand on their own. Each MicroSim is a self-contained, browser-based simulation focused on a single concept; each poster is a wide-format visual guide with interactive callouts plus explore and quiz modes.

You do not need to adopt the whole textbook to use them. Educators anywhere are welcome to:

  • Embed a single MicroSim or poster in a slide deck, worksheet, or learning management system.
  • Project a poster for a class discussion, a bell-ringer, or a family night.
  • Hand students one simulation as a station activity, independent of any chapter.
  • Remix them into an existing curriculum that is otherwise unrelated to this book.

Every MicroSim runs in any modern browser with no install, no account, and no tracking, and the source is openly licensed (see License). Browse the full collections on the MicroSims and Posters pages.

docs.title: How to Use This Book
docs.text:
Start with the grade band that matches your learners under Textbooks by Grade, then read within a strand in order — concepts are sequenced so each one builds on the ones before it. The book includes:

  • 8 grade-specific textbooks spanning Kindergarten through Grade 12
  • 68 chapters across the eight bands and six health strands
  • 370 interactive MicroSims — browser-based simulations students can manipulate to explore a concept
  • 86 interactive infographic posters — visual guides with explore and quiz modes
  • 8 learning graphs — one per band — visualizing how concepts depend on one another
  • Annotated references linking to authoritative public-health and educational sources

Use the search bar (top right) to jump straight to a term, and open a band's learning graph when you want to see how a topic fits into the larger picture.

docs.title: About the Author
docs.text:
Dan McCreary is a semi-retired AI researcher, solution architect, and educator who has spent more than three decades helping Fortune 100 organizations reason over massive datasets. At Optum he founded the Generative AI Center of Excellence and led the team that built one of the world's largest healthcare knowledge graphs — spanning over 25 billion vertices — to unify member, provider, and patient insights. Dan's deep background in knowledge representation and systems thinking underpins the precise learning graphs and intelligent-textbook workflows used throughout this project.

He is the co-author of Making Sense of NoSQL (Manning Publications), the founding chair of the NoSQL Now! conference, and a frequent keynote speaker on semantic search, ontology strategy, and AI hardware. Beyond industry, Dan has mentored students as a STEM volunteer since 2014 and now applies the same rigor to building open educational resources. You can visit the Intelligent Textbooks Case Studies to see the many textbooks Dan has created or co-created with other authors.

Selected Credentials

  • B.A. in Physics and Computer Science from Carleton College
  • M.S.E.E. from the University of Minnesota
  • MBA coursework at the University of St. Thomas
  • Patent holder in semantic search and ontology management techniques
  • Advocate for large-scale Enterprise Knowledge Graph adoption across healthcare and education
  • Long-time promoter of accessible, low-cost AI-powered learning experiences

docs.title: How to Cite This Book
docs.text:
If you reference this textbook in academic work, curriculum proposals, lesson plans, or other publications, please use one of the following formats.

APA (7th edition)

McCreary, D. (2026). Health Education. https://dmccreary.github.io/health-education/

Chicago (17th edition)

McCreary, Dan. 2026. Health Education. https://dmccreary.github.io/health-education/.

MLA (9th edition)

McCreary, Dan. Health Education. 2026, dmccreary.github.io/health-education/.

BibTeX

@book{mccreary2026healtheducation,
  title  = {Health Education},
  author = {McCreary, Dan},
  year   = {2026},
  url    = {https://dmccreary.github.io/health-education/},
  note   = {Interactive intelligent textbook; eight grade-specific editions, K-12}
}

To cite a specific band and chapter, append the band and chapter — for example:

McCreary, D. (2026). Grade 1, Chapter 3: Understanding and Talking About Feelings. In Health Education. https://dmccreary.github.io/health-education/bands/grade-1/chapters/03-feelings/

docs.title: Appendix: Minnesota Health Standards Background
docs.text:
The content above is written to be useful to schools anywhere in the world. This final section documents the specific state framework that shaped the scope and sequence of this particular project; readers outside Minnesota can safely skip it.

Minnesota is working to replace a patchwork of locally developed health standards with its first consistent statewide K-12 framework. The eight grade bands and six strands in this book mirror that proposed framework. Its key goals are:

  • Equity: Give students comparable health education regardless of their district or ZIP code.
  • Clear progression: Define age-appropriate benchmarks for grades K-5 and the grade bands 6-8 and 9-12.
  • Skills over memorization: Help students practice evaluating information, communicating, making decisions, setting goals, adopting healthy behaviors, and promoting health.
  • Comprehensive coverage: Address nutrition, human development and sexual health, mental and emotional health, personal wellness, safety and violence prevention, and substance-use prevention. State-required subjects include CPR, vaping, cannabis, sexually transmitted infection prevention, and mental health.
  • Continued local curriculum control: Establish what students should know and be able to do while allowing districts to choose curricula, teaching methods, and local assessments.
  • Accountability and graduation alignment: Once implemented, require districts to teach and locally assess the standards and require high-school credit sufficient to satisfy them.

As of July 2026, the standards have completed drafting, public comment, and an April administrative hearing, but final adoption and classroom implementation dates remain to be determined. Locally developed health standards continue to apply until the statewide standards are implemented.

Sources: Minnesota Department of Education overview, proposed standards, state rationale, and Minnesota Statutes, chapter 120B.

  1. World Health Organization. (2024). Mental health of adolescents (fact sheet). https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/adolescent-mental-health ↩↩↩

  2. World Health Organization. (2024). Obesity and overweight (fact sheet). https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/obesity-and-overweight ↩

  3. World Health Organization & UNESCO. (2021). Making every school a health-promoting school: Global standards and indicators. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240025059 ↩

docs.title: Course Description for Health Education Courses
docs.text: Title: Health Education

docs.title: Important: This Is Not a Single Course
docs.text:
This project is not a single linear course written for one age group. It is a collection of health education teaching resources spanning Minnesota's proposed K-12 Health Academic Standards (2025, Commissioner Approved — see references.md and the harvest log at logs/harvest-mn-health-standards.md in the project root), organized into 8 parallel grade bands:

  • Kindergarten
  • Grade 1
  • Grade 2
  • Grade 3
  • Grade 4
  • Grade 5
  • Grades 6-8
  • Grades 9-12

Every one of the 6 content strands below runs through all 8 bands. Each band gets its own section of the site, and each section carries the full set of resource types — chapter content, quizzes, MicroSims, infographics, and references — written and calibrated for that band. A grade-3 learner and a grades-9-12 learner studying the same strand (e.g., Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) get different pages, different reading level, different MicroSim complexity, and different quiz difficulty, not the same page with a different reading age applied on the fly.

Reading level scales with band. Content generators (chapter-content- generator, quiz-generator, microsim-generator, etc.) must target band-appropriate reading level and cognitive complexity:

Band Approx. reading level Cognitive demand (per MDE anchor standards) K Pre-reader / read-aloud Identify, recognize, name 1-2 Early elementary Identify, describe, recall with simple support 3-5 Elementary Explain, identify, connect to personal experience 6-8 Middle school Analyze, evaluate influences, apply in scenarios 9-12 High school Design, evaluate, synthesize, apply across contexts

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: K-12 classroom teachers, curriculum coordinators, and students, each accessing the section that matches their grade band. Also health-standards compliance staff cross-checking site content against MDE's proposed benchmarks.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: None assumed for the Kindergarten band. Each subsequent band assumes mastery of the benchmarks in the band(s) before it, per that strand's own progression — e.g., grade 3 Food and Nutrition benchmarks assume grade 1-2 Food and Nutrition benchmarks were covered. Prerequisite edges in the learning graph should generally flow band-to-band within the same strand, not across strands.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
The 6 strands from the MDE proposed standards are the primary topic axis; each spans some or all of the 8 grade bands noted:

  1. Food and Nutrition (K-12)
  2. Human Growth and Development (K-5), continuing as Human Growth and Development and Sexual Health (6-12)
  3. Mental and Emotional Health (K-12)
  4. Personal Health and Wellness (K-12)
  5. Personal Safety and Violence Prevention (K-12)
  6. Substance Use Awareness and Prevention (6-12 only — not taught below grade 6)

Cutting across all 6 strands, the standards also define 8 anchor standards that describe the skill/knowledge type of a given benchmark (functional health knowledge, analyzing influences, accessing valid information, interpersonal communication, decision-making, goal setting, healthy practices/behaviors, promoting health/safety/wellbeing of self and others). The learning-graph-generator should treat strand × band as the concept-grouping axis and anchor standard as a tag/category on each concept, not a separate topic.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
Because outcomes scale by band, these are expressed as the progression across bands rather than a single end-state. By the end of grades 9-12, a student who has moved through all 8 bands in a strand will be able to:

  • Remember: Recall core health vocabulary and facts introduced starting in Kindergarten (e.g., food groups, emotion names, safety rules).
  • Understand: Explain why a health practice, behavior, or resource matters, in age-appropriate terms that grow more nuanced band over band.
  • Apply: Use functional health knowledge and skills (communication, decision-making, goal setting) in realistic personal and social scenarios.
  • Analyze: Evaluate influences on health behavior — media, peers, culture, advertising — with sophistication that increases from simple recognition (elementary) to critical evaluation (middle/high school).
  • Evaluate: Assess the reliability of health information, products, and services, and judge trade-offs in personal health decisions.
  • Create: Design a personal health plan, advocacy action, or peer-support strategy appropriate to the student's own life circumstances (grades 9-12 capstone-level outcome).

Content generators should produce band-scoped versions of these outcomes per section rather than assuming every learner reaches the grades 9-12 outcome.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text: This FAQ covers the entire Health Education project — all eight grade-band textbooks, the MicroSims, the infographic posters, the learning graphs, and the standards behind them — in one place, rather than repeating the same questions eight times per grade band.

docs.title: What is Health Education?
docs.text: Health Education is a free, open-source, interactive intelligent textbook covering health topics for students from Kindergarten through Grade 12. It is not one book but eight parallel grade-band textbooks sharing a single site, each written and calibrated for its own age group. See the About page for the full project overview and the Home page for a quick tour.

docs.title: Who is this textbook for?
docs.text: Three audiences: K-12 classroom teachers and curriculum coordinators planning lessons, students working through age-appropriate chapters and MicroSims directly, and health-standards compliance staff checking content against state benchmarks. For Kindergarten through Grade 3, the teacher is the primary audience because students aren't yet expected to read independently; from Grade 4 up, students increasingly use the text directly. See the Teachers Guide for a full walkthrough.

docs.title: Why are there eight separate textbooks instead of one?
docs.text: Because health topics need genuinely different vocabulary, examples, MicroSim complexity, and assessment difficulty at every age — not the same page with the reading level swapped on the fly. A third grader and a high schooler studying "Personal Safety and Violence Prevention" get different pages entirely. See the List of Textbooks by Grade and the Course Description for the reasoning behind the grade-band structure.

docs.title: What grade bands are covered?
docs.text: Eight bands: Kindergarten, Grade 1, Grade 2, Grade 3, Grade 4, Grade 5, Grades 6-8, and Grades 9-12. Each band has its own course description, chapters, and learning graph. Browse them from the List of Textbooks by Grade.

docs.title: How do I find the textbook for my grade level?
docs.text: Open "Textbooks By Grade" in the left navigation and choose your band. Each band section contains that band's course description, its chapters in teaching order, and its own learning graph. See List of Textbooks by Grade to jump directly to any band.

docs.title: What is an intelligent textbook?
docs.text: An intelligent textbook is a digital textbook that goes beyond static text and images — it includes interactive simulations, a structured map of how concepts relate to one another (a learning graph), and, as the site matures, self-grading quizzes and this glossary and FAQ. This project is currently a "Level 2" intelligent textbook (interactive, but not yet adaptive or AI-tutored). See the Teachers Guide for the full five-level explanation.

docs.title: Do I need to create an account or pay to use this textbook?
docs.text: No. The entire textbook, including all MicroSims and posters, is free to use with no account, no login, and no per-seat licensing. It is released under a Creative Commons license — see License for the exact terms.

docs.title: What topics (strands) does the curriculum cover?
docs.text: Six health strands run through every grade band: Food and Nutrition; Human Growth and Development (extending to Sexual Health in grades 6-12); Mental and Emotional Health; Personal Health and Wellness; Personal Safety and Violence Prevention; and Substance Use Awareness and Prevention (grades 6-12 only). See Course Description for the full topic breakdown.

docs.title: Is this textbook aligned to any official standards?
docs.text: Yes. The grade bands, strands, and benchmark coverage are built from Minnesota's 2025 K-12 Health Academic Standards (Commissioner Approved, December 2025). Every concept in every band's learning graph traces back to a specific benchmark in that standards document. See References for the source documents, and the "Standards Alignment" section of the Teachers Guide for guidance on using this outside Minnesota.

docs.title: Who is Scout the Dog?
docs.text: Scout is the textbook's friendly mascot — a golden retriever "pedagogical agent" who appears in student-facing chapter content (never in instructor-facing pages like this FAQ or the Teachers Guide) to welcome students to a chapter, highlight key concepts, give tips, and offer encouragement. Scout's catchphrase is "Healthy choices, happy you!" Read more in the "Scout the Dog" section of the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: How much does it cost to use this textbook?
docs.text: Nothing. The whole project — chapters, MicroSims, posters, and this FAQ — is free and open source under a non-commercial Creative Commons license. See License.

docs.title: Where do I start if I'm a parent wanting to preview content?
docs.text: Open "Textbooks By Grade" in the left navigation, choose your child's grade band, and read that band's course description first — it lists the exact topics covered before you read any chapter. See List of Textbooks by Grade.

docs.title: What are the six health strands?
docs.text: Food and Nutrition; Human Growth and Development / Sexual Health; Mental and Emotional Health; Personal Health and Wellness; Personal Safety and Violence Prevention; and Substance Use Awareness and Prevention. Every strand runs through every grade band except Substance Use, which begins in Grade 6. See Course Description.

docs.title: What does the Food and Nutrition strand cover across grades?
docs.text: It runs Kindergarten through Grade 12, starting with recognizing food groups and healthy versus unhealthy choices in early grades, progressing to reading nutrition labels and understanding macronutrients in upper elementary, and reaching personal nutrition planning and evaluating food systems and chronic disease risk by high school. Compare, for example, the food-and-nutrition chapter in Kindergarten against the same strand in Grades 9-12.

docs.title: What does the Human Growth and Development / Sexual Health strand cover?
docs.text: Kindergarten through Grade 5 focuses on family structures, body ownership, puberty basics, and trusted adults. Starting in Grade 6, the strand extends to Sexual Health, covering healthcare access, consent, boundaries, and STI prevention appropriate to middle and high school. See Grade 3, Growth and Puberty and Grades 9-12, Consent and Boundaries.

docs.title: What does the Mental and Emotional Health strand cover?
docs.text: It runs K-12, starting with naming feelings and simple coping strategies in early grades and progressing to recognizing anxiety versus everyday nervousness, supporting a struggling friend, and understanding stigma and brain health by middle and high school. See Grade 1, Understanding and Talking About Feelings and Grades 9-12, Mental Health and Crisis Support.

docs.title: What does the Personal Health and Wellness strand cover?
docs.text: This strand covers daily habits, hygiene, sleep, physical activity, and disease prevention, scaling from "staying healthy every day" routines in Kindergarten to evaluating chronic-disease risk factors and designing a personal wellness plan in high school. See Kindergarten, Staying Healthy Every Day.

docs.title: What does the Personal Safety and Violence Prevention strand cover?
docs.text: It covers recognizing unsafe situations, trusted adults, body safety, and getting help, growing from simple safety rules in Kindergarten to consent, coercion, bystander action, and digital safety in later grades. Because every band has a dedicated chapter for this strand, you can follow how one topic deepens across bands — see Kindergarten, Staying Safe through Grades 9-12, Digital and School Safety.

docs.title: What does the Substance Use Awareness and Prevention strand cover, and why does it start in Grade 6?
docs.text: This strand covers the effects of substances on the developing brain, refusal skills, substance use disorder, recovery, and related policy. Per Minnesota's standards, it is not taught below Grade 6, since substance-use content requires a level of abstraction and scenario reasoning that matches middle-school cognitive development. See Grades 6-8, Substances and the Developing Brain.

docs.title: What are the 8 anchor standards?
docs.text: Anchor standards describe the type of skill or knowledge a benchmark targets, independent of strand: functional health knowledge, analyzing influences, accessing valid information, interpersonal communication, decision-making, goal setting, healthy practices/behaviors, and promoting the health/safety/wellbeing of self and others. Every concept in a band's learning graph is tagged with one of these. See References for the source standards document.

docs.title: How does content difficulty change between grade bands?
docs.text: Reading level and cognitive demand both scale with band: Kindergarten targets pre-reader, identify/recognize/name skills; Grades 1-2 add simple description and recall; Grades 3-5 add explaining and connecting to personal experience; Grades 6-8 add analyzing and evaluating influences; and Grades 9-12 add designing, evaluating, and synthesizing across contexts. See the "Understanding the Grade-Band Structure" section of the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: What is a learning graph?
docs.text: A learning graph is a visual map showing how concepts in a course depend on one another, structured as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) — a diagram where arrows show which concepts must be understood before others. Each grade band has its own learning graph rather than one graph for the whole site. See the "The Learning Graph" section of the Teachers Guide and try the Learning Graph Viewer.

docs.title: How many concepts are in the learning graphs?
docs.text: Across all eight bands, the site tracks roughly 600 concepts in total — ranging from about 45 in Kindergarten to about 135 in Grades 6-8 and Grades 9-12, reflecting the greater depth expected at older grades. See each band's Learning Graph section, for example Grade 5's Concept List.

docs.title: How do concepts build on each other across grade bands?
docs.text: Prerequisite edges generally flow band-to-band within the same strand, not across strands — for example, Grade 3 Food and Nutrition concepts assume mastery of Grade 1-2 Food and Nutrition concepts, not mastery of an unrelated strand like Personal Safety. See Course Description for the prerequisite policy.

docs.title: What is the difference between a strand and a chapter?
docs.text: A strand is one of the six recurring topic areas (like Food and Nutrition) that appears in every band. A chapter is the specific, band-written unit of content covering that strand (or a combination of strands) for one grade level. A strand spans all eight bands; a chapter belongs to exactly one band.

docs.title: How many chapters are in each grade band?
docs.text: Kindergarten has 6, Grade 1 has 7, Grade 2 has 7, Grade 3 has 8, Grade 4 has 6, Grade 5 has 7, Grades 6-8 has 12, and Grades 9-12 has 15 — 68 chapters in total across all eight bands. See each band's chapter list, starting from List of Textbooks by Grade.

docs.title: What is a benchmark?
docs.text: A benchmark is a specific, coded statement of what a student should know or be able to do at a given grade (for example, code 0.1.1.1 for a Kindergarten benchmark). Every concept in this textbook's learning graphs traces back to a benchmark in Minnesota's health standards document. See References.

docs.title: What cognitive skills does a student develop by the end of Grades 9-12?
docs.text: By completing all eight bands in a strand, a student should be able to recall core health vocabulary (Remember), explain why a practice matters (Understand), apply communication and decision-making skills in realistic scenarios (Apply), evaluate influences like media and peer pressure (Analyze), judge trade-offs in health information and decisions (Evaluate), and design a personal health plan or advocacy action (Create). See the "Learning Outcomes" section of Course Description.

docs.title: What is functional health knowledge?
docs.text: It is one of the eight anchor standards — the foundational, factual health knowledge a student needs before they can apply skills like decision-making or goal setting. Definitions, body systems, food groups, and safety rules are typical examples. See Glossary for specific terms.

docs.title: What is a MicroSim?
docs.text: A MicroSim (short for "micro-simulation") is a small, interactive simulation that runs directly in a web browser — no software installation required. Students manipulate variables using sliders, buttons, sorting activities, or drag-and-drop, and immediately see how the model responds. See "Using the MicroSims" in the Teachers Guide and browse the full catalog at MicroSims.

docs.title: What technologies are MicroSims built with?
docs.text: The textbook's 370+ MicroSims use p5.js for scenario sorters, timelines, and games; vis-network for concept maps and network diagrams; Chart.js for bar and line charts; and simple HTML/CSS for checklists and matching activities. See the MicroSim technology table in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: What is an infographic poster, and how is it different from a MicroSim?
docs.text: An infographic poster is a single, richly designed static image summarizing a health concept — a checklist, comparison, or labeled diagram — with interactive callouts plus explore and quiz modes online, but also easy to print or project. A MicroSim, by contrast, is a live simulation students manipulate. Browse the full collection at Posters.

docs.title: What is the Learning Graph Viewer?
docs.text: An interactive tool for exploring how concepts connect and depend on one another across the curriculum, built with the same vis-network technology used for concept-map MicroSims. Try it at Learning Graph Viewer.

docs.title: What's in the glossary?
docs.text: The Glossary defines the health vocabulary used throughout the textbook — each entry gives a plain-language definition, a concrete example, and which grade(s) the term is used in, so you can quickly check whether a term is introduced at your students' level.

docs.title: What is a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)?
docs.text: A DAG is a diagram made of nodes and one-directional arrows with no cycles — you can never follow the arrows back to where you started. This textbook's learning graphs use a DAG structure so that prerequisite concepts always come before the concepts that depend on them. See Glossary for related terms, and Learning Graph Viewer to see one in action.

docs.title: Can I embed a MicroSim on my own website?
docs.text: Yes. Every MicroSim can be embedded in any web page — a Google Site, WordPress blog, an LMS like Canvas or Schoology, or a plain HTML file — using a single <iframe> line pointing at that MicroSim's URL. See the "Tips for Using MicroSims in Class" section of the Teachers Guide for the exact embed code.

docs.title: Where can I find references and sources?
docs.text: The site-wide References page lists the state and national standards documents this textbook is built from, including Minnesota's 2025 K-12 Health Academic Standards and its supporting rulemaking documents. Chapter-level reference lists, where present, link back to this same page.

docs.title: What is FERPA/COPPA, and why does it matter here?
docs.text: FERPA (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act) and COPPA (Children's Online Privacy Protection Act) are U.S. federal laws protecting student education records and children's online privacy. Because this textbook covers sensitive strands like Personal Safety and Substance Use, and much of its audience is under 13, schools should use anonymous, aggregate analytics rather than individually identifying student-tracking tools unless their district's data privacy officer has approved it. See "Customizing Your Analytics" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: My students read below their assigned grade band. How should I use the text?
docs.text: For Kindergarten through Grade 3, the textbook is designed with the teacher as the primary reader — read chapters aloud and lean on the MicroSim "games," which carry much of the student experience at that age. This applies at any grade if your students need extra reading support. See "Understanding the Grade-Band Structure" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: How should I handle questions from parents or the community about sensitive topics like sexual health or substance use?
docs.text: Point them first to the relevant band's course description, which lists exactly what is covered before any chapter content, and to Course Description, which explains the strand structure and the standards this content is built from. The About page also documents why this content matters and the data behind it, which can help ground a conversation about scope.

docs.title: My state's standards differ from Minnesota's. Can I still use this?
docs.text: Yes. The underlying health content generalizes well even where specific benchmark codes differ. Use your band's learning graph to compare concept coverage against your own state's scope-and-sequence document, and adjust locally as needed. See "How Teachers Can Use the Learning Graph" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: A link to a state standards document is broken. What do I do?
docs.text: This is called link rot — when an external page moves, is renamed, or is deleted. Try searching the document title on the source site (for Minnesota, education.mn.gov), check the Wayback Machine for an archived copy, or report the broken link as described below. See "A Note About Link Rot" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: I found an error, a typo, or a MicroSim that won't load. How do I report it?
docs.text: Submit a GitHub Issue at the project's repository, dmccreary/health-education, describing which band, chapter, or MicroSim has the problem and what you expected versus what you saw. If you'd rather not create a GitHub account, use the Contact page instead. See "Reporting Issues and Suggestions" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: The Minnesota standards this book is based on aren't finalized yet. Can I still use the textbook today?
docs.text: Yes. As of mid-2026, Minnesota's proposed standards have completed drafting and public comment but final statewide adoption is still pending; locally developed standards remain in effect until then. The health content and grade-band structure in this textbook remain sound and usable regardless of that administrative timeline. See the "Appendix: Minnesota Health Standards Background" section of the About page.

docs.title: My class spans multiple grade levels. Which band should I use?
docs.text: Match the band to your students' developmental level rather than their nominal grade, and check the reading-level and cognitive-demand table in the Teachers Guide. For a strand you're concerned students haven't mastered yet, skim the same strand's chapter in the band below to confirm the prerequisite ground has been covered.

docs.title: Can I skip chapters or teach them out of order?
docs.text: Within a band, chapters are numbered in a suggested teaching order but are largely self-contained by strand, so reordering is generally safe. Skipping a chapter is riskier for strands that build across bands (like Personal Safety) — check that band's learning graph first to see whether later chapters depend on concepts from the one you'd skip. See "How Teachers Can Use the Learning Graph" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: How should I pace a chapter?
docs.text: Each chapter is designed for roughly 2-3 class periods; chapters with more MicroSims (common in Grades 6-12) may take longer. See "Suggested Classroom Use" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: How can I use the learning graph to check prerequisites or plan remediation?
docs.text: Before teaching a concept, open that band's Concept List and Concept Taxonomy to verify students have covered its prerequisites in an earlier band or chapter. If a student struggles, trace the concept's prerequisites backward in the graph to find the specific gap. See "How Teachers Can Use the Learning Graph" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: When should I use a MicroSim versus a poster in class?
docs.text: Use MicroSims when you want students to manipulate a variable and predict an outcome — project it and have students call out predictions before you interact with a control. Use posters for warm-up discussions, as printed classroom-wall references, or in contexts like health fairs and parent communications where a static, standalone visual works better. See "Using the MicroSims" and "Using the Infographic Posters" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: Should students read chapters independently, or should I lead as the teacher?
docs.text: For Grade 4 and up, assign chapters as reading homework and use class time for MicroSims and discussion. For Kindergarten through Grade 3, read chapters aloud yourself and treat MicroSims as guided games you run together. See "Suggested Classroom Use" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: How do I customize this textbook for my district's local needs?
docs.text: Fork or clone the project's GitHub repository, edit the Markdown chapter files under docs/bands/<band>/chapters/, and rebuild the site with MkDocs. You can swap in your own state's standards, add a district-specific chapter, or adjust the reading level of a single band. See "Customizing Your Own Textbook" in the Teachers Guide for the full step-by-step guide.

docs.title: How should I cross-check my curriculum against the standards this book is built from?
docs.text: Compare your district's scope-and-sequence document against a band's Concept List and Concept Taxonomy, which trace every concept back to a specific Minnesota health-standards benchmark. See References for the source standards documents and "How Teachers Can Use the Learning Graph" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: I teach a combined middle/high school class. Should I use Grades 6-8 or Grades 9-12?
docs.text: Base the choice on cognitive demand rather than literal age: Grades 6-8 targets analyzing influences and applying skills in scenarios, while Grades 9-12 targets designing, evaluating, and synthesizing across contexts. Skim both bands' course descriptions and pick whichever cognitive level matches your students, or use the lower band's chapters as a foundation before moving to the higher band's. See Course Description.

docs.title: How do I fork or clone my own version of this textbook?
docs.text: Create a free GitHub account, then either fork the repository (a copy that stays on GitHub) at dmccreary/health-education, or clone it to your own computer with git clone for full local control. See "Step 2: Fork or Clone the Repository" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: How do I set up my own analytics for a customized version of this site?
docs.text: Create a Google Analytics property, get a Measurement ID (G-XXXXXXXXXX), and add it to the extra.analytics section of your mkdocs.yml. Data appears within 24-48 hours after your next deploy. See "Customizing Your Analytics" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: What's the difference between basic analytics and xAPI/LRS tracking?
docs.text: Basic web analytics (like Google Analytics) tracks anonymous, aggregate page views — which pages get visited and for how long. xAPI (Experience API) is a more advanced standard for tracking granular individual interactions, stored in a Learning Record Store (LRS). Because this is health content and much of the audience is under 13, aggregate analytics is the safer default; individually identifying xAPI tracking should only be used after consulting your district's data privacy officer. See "xAPI Monitoring (Advanced)" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: How is this site technically built?
docs.text: The site is built with MkDocs and the Material for MkDocs theme, which converts Markdown files in the docs/ folder into a static website. Content authors only need to know basic Markdown formatting to edit chapters. See "Key Technical Terms" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: Can I contribute new content back to the project?
docs.text: Yes — this is an open-source project. Submit suggestions or corrections as a GitHub Issue at dmccreary/health-education, or fork the repository, make your change, and open a pull request. See "How to Submit Feedback" in the Teachers Guide.

docs.title: How would I add new concepts to a band's learning graph?
docs.text: Each band's learning graph is generated from that band's course description and tracked in a concept list with dependency edges. Adding a new concept means updating the band's course description with the new topic, then regenerating or manually extending its Concept List, Concept Taxonomy, and dependency edges so prerequisites stay consistent. See a band's Learning Graph section, for example Grade 4's learning graph introduction, for the current structure to extend.

docs.title: What's on the roadmap for this textbook?
docs.text: Quizzes are planned but not yet published across all bands; this Glossary and FAQ are newly published as of mid-2026. Check the Teachers Guide "What is an Intelligent Textbook?" section, which tracks the current feature level, for the latest status.

docs.title: How do I cite this textbook in academic or curriculum work?
docs.text: Use APA, Chicago, MLA, or BibTeX formats — for example, APA: McCreary, D. (2026). Health Education. https://dmccreary.github.io/health-education/. To cite a specific band and chapter, append the band and chapter title and URL. See "How to Cite This Book" in the About page for all four formats.

docs.title: Ability-Inclusive Kindness
docs.text:
Treating people with kindness and fairness regardless of any physical, sensory, or learning differences they have, and including them in activities and conversations.

Example: Inviting a classmate who uses a wheelchair to join a game and adjusting the rules so everyone can play.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Accessibility Of Health Resources
docs.text:
The degree to which health services, information, and supports are easy for people to reach, afford, and use, regardless of location, income, ability, or language.

Example: A community clinic that offers free interpreters and evening hours is more accessible to working families.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Active Listening
docs.text:
Paying full attention to a speaker, showing interest through eye contact and body language, and responding in ways that show understanding.

Example: Nodding and repeating back what a friend said before offering your own opinion.

Used in: Grade 2, Grade 3

docs.title: Adapting Health Behaviors
docs.text:
Changing personal habits or routines in response to new information, life changes, or health goals in order to maintain or improve well-being.

Example: Switching from sugary snacks to fruit after learning about the effects of sugar on energy levels.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Addressing Exclusion And Bullying
docs.text:
Recognizing when someone is being left out or bullied and taking direct action, such as speaking up, including them, or reporting the behavior.

Example: Telling a teacher after seeing a classmate repeatedly excluded from group activities.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Addressing Stereotyping And Discrimination
docs.text:
Identifying unfair generalizations or unequal treatment based on group identity and responding with actions or words that challenge them.

Example: Correcting a friend who assumes all members of a group share the same interests.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Adolescent Access To Health Care
docs.text:
The ability of teenagers to obtain medical services, including how factors like cost, transportation, and confidentiality affect whether they seek care.

Example: A teen clinic that lets students schedule appointments without a parent present makes care easier to access.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Adolescent Healthcare Access Rights
docs.text:
The legal protections that allow teenagers to seek certain health services, sometimes without parental consent, depending on state law.

Example: In some states, teens can receive confidential treatment for mental health or reproductive care.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: AED Use
docs.text:
The steps for operating an automated external defibrillator, a portable device that checks heart rhythm and can deliver a shock to restore a normal heartbeat.

Example: Following the AED's voice prompts to place pads on a person's chest during cardiac arrest.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Alcohol Effects On Developing Body And Brain
docs.text:
The ways alcohol can disrupt growth, judgment, memory, and brain development in children and teens, whose bodies are still maturing.

Example: Alcohol use during adolescence can interfere with the brain regions responsible for decision-making.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Alcohol Misuse Consequences
docs.text:
The physical, social, legal, and academic problems that can result from drinking alcohol in unsafe or underage ways.

Example: Getting suspended from a sports team after being caught drinking at a school event.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Alcohol Short- And Long-Term Effects
docs.text:
The immediate impacts of alcohol, such as impaired coordination and judgment, along with the lasting health effects of continued use, such as liver damage.

Example: A single night of heavy drinking can impair reaction time, while years of heavy drinking can damage the liver.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Allergic Reaction
docs.text:
The body's immune response to a substance it mistakenly treats as harmful, which can cause symptoms ranging from mild itching to severe swelling.

Example: A child's skin breaking out in hives after eating peanuts.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Allergic Reaction Signs
docs.text:
The warning symptoms that indicate someone is having an allergic reaction, such as hives, swelling, trouble breathing, or itching.

Example: Noticing a classmate's lips swelling after eating a snack and telling an adult right away.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Allergy
docs.text:
A condition in which the body reacts strongly to a normally harmless substance, such as certain foods, pollen, or insect stings.

Example: Some people sneeze and get watery eyes when they are near cats because of an allergy.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Allergy Prevention And Management
docs.text:
Steps taken to avoid allergy triggers and to respond safely when a reaction occurs, such as reading food labels or carrying medication.

Example: A student checking snack labels for peanuts and keeping an epinephrine auto-injector nearby.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Alzheimer's Disease
docs.text:
A brain disease that gradually destroys memory and thinking skills, most often affecting older adults.

Example: A grandparent with Alzheimer's disease may forget the names of close family members over time.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Alzheimer's Disease And Other Dementias
docs.text:
A group of brain conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, that cause a progressive decline in memory, reasoning, and the ability to perform daily tasks.

Example: Dementia can make it hard for a person to remember how to get home from a familiar place.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Anxiety Symptoms And Causes
docs.text:
The physical and emotional signs of excessive worry or fear, such as a racing heart or restlessness, along with the stressors or situations that can trigger them.

Example: A student may feel a tight chest and racing thoughts before a big exam due to test anxiety.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Asking A Trusted Adult
docs.text:
Going to a parent, teacher, or other reliable grown-up for help, guidance, or information when needed.

Example: Telling a teacher when you feel unsafe on the playground.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Asking For Help
docs.text:
Telling another person, especially an adult, that you need support or assistance with a problem.

Example: Raising your hand to ask a teacher for help when you don't understand an activity.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Asking For Help With Body Changes
docs.text:
Reaching out to a trusted adult with questions or concerns about the physical changes that happen as a child's body grows.

Example: Asking a parent why you are getting taller and your voice sounds different.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Asking For Help With Choices
docs.text:
Seeking guidance from a trusted adult when trying to decide what to do in a difficult or confusing situation.

Example: Asking a parent for advice before deciding whether to join a new after-school activity.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Balanced Meal Planning
docs.text:
Choosing foods from different food groups so a meal provides a healthy mix of nutrients the body needs.

Example: Planning a dinner with vegetables, whole grains, protein, and fruit instead of only dessert.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Behavioral And Environmental Factors In Disease Risk
docs.text:
The personal habits and surrounding conditions, such as diet, exercise, and pollution, that can raise or lower a person's chance of developing a disease.

Example: Living near heavy traffic pollution combined with smoking both raise the risk of lung disease.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Belonging
docs.text:
A feeling of being accepted, valued, and included as part of a group or community.

Example: Feeling like part of the class when teammates cheer for you during a game.

Used in: Grade 1, Grade 5

docs.title: Benefits Of Being Substance-Free
docs.text:
The physical, mental, and social advantages of not using tobacco, alcohol, or other drugs, such as better health and clearer thinking.

Example: Athletes who avoid substances often recover faster and perform more consistently.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Benefits Of Physical Activity
docs.text:
The positive effects that regular movement and exercise have on the body and mind, such as stronger muscles and better mood.

Example: Running at recess can make you feel more awake and happy for the rest of the day.

Used in: Grade 1, Grade 3

docs.title: Benefits Of Physical Activity On Mood
docs.text:
The way that exercise and movement can improve how a person feels emotionally, often by reducing stress and increasing happiness.

Example: Going for a bike ride after a stressful day can help someone feel calmer.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Beverage Choice Evaluation
docs.text:
The process of comparing drinks based on factors like sugar content, nutrients, and hydration to decide which is the healthiest option.

Example: Comparing the sugar content of soda, juice, and water before choosing what to drink with lunch.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Beverages For Physical Activity
docs.text:
Drinks, such as water, that are appropriate choices before, during, or after exercise to stay properly hydrated.

Example: Drinking water during a soccer game instead of a sugary sports drink.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Bias
docs.text:
An unfair preference or judgment about a person or group, often based on limited or inaccurate information.

Example: Assuming a new student isn't good at sports just because of where they are from.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Body Parts
docs.text:
The different sections and structures that make up the human body, such as the arms, legs, and head.

Example: Pointing to and naming your elbow, knee, and shoulder.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Body Safety
docs.text:
Rules and practices that help protect a person's body from harm, including knowing which touches are appropriate and telling a trusted adult about unsafe situations.

Example: Knowing that no one should touch the parts of your body covered by a swimsuit without a good reason.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Bone-Strengthening Activity
docs.text:
Physical activity that puts force on bones through impact or muscle tension, helping bones grow stronger.

Example: Jumping rope and playing basketball are both bone-strengthening activities.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Boundary
docs.text:
A personal limit that tells others what behavior is acceptable or not acceptable toward you.

Example: Telling a friend "please don't read my journal" sets a boundary.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Boundary-Setting
docs.text:
The act of clearly communicating your personal limits to others in a relationship or interaction.

Example: Saying "I need space right now" when a sibling is bothering you.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Boundary-Setting Strategies
docs.text:
Specific approaches, such as using clear language or body language, for communicating personal limits to others effectively.

Example: Using a firm voice and direct eye contact to say "stop" when someone crosses a line.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Brain-Healthy Habits
docs.text:
Daily behaviors, such as sleeping enough and limiting substance use, that support healthy brain function and development.

Example: Getting eight hours of sleep each night supports memory and focus.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Breakfast
docs.text:
The first meal of the day, typically eaten in the morning, that provides energy after a night without food.

Example: Eating oatmeal and fruit before school.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Bullying
docs.text:
Repeated, intentional aggressive behavior, physical or verbal, that involves a real or perceived imbalance of power between people.

Example: A student repeatedly calling a classmate names and encouraging others to exclude them.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Bullying Effects On Mental Health
docs.text:
The emotional and psychological harm, such as anxiety or low self-esteem, that can result from being bullied.

Example: A student who is bullied over time may start to feel anxious about coming to school.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Bystander
docs.text:
A person who witnesses a bullying incident, conflict, or unsafe situation without being directly involved as the target or the one causing harm.

Example: A student who sees another student being teased at lunch but isn't part of the teasing.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Bystander Action Against Bullying
docs.text:
Steps a witness can take when they see bullying occur, such as speaking up, getting help, or supporting the person being targeted.

Example: Walking over to sit with a student who is being excluded and telling a teacher afterward.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Caffeinated And Energy Drink Effects
docs.text:
The physical impacts of consuming caffeine and energy drinks, such as increased heart rate, disrupted sleep, and jitteriness.

Example: Drinking an energy drink before bed can make it harder to fall asleep.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Caffeine In Drinks
docs.text:
A natural stimulant found in some beverages, such as soda and tea, that can affect energy levels and sleep.

Example: Some sodas contain caffeine, which is why they can make you feel more awake.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Cannabis Effects On Developing Body And Brain
docs.text:
The ways cannabis use can interfere with memory, attention, and brain development in children and teens.

Example: Cannabis use during the teen years can make it harder to concentrate in school.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Cannabis Short- And Long-Term Effects
docs.text:
The immediate effects of cannabis use, such as impaired coordination, along with lasting effects on memory and lung health from repeated use.

Example: Smoking cannabis can immediately slow reaction time and, over years, can harm the lungs.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Carbohydrates
docs.text:
A nutrient found in foods like bread, rice, and fruit that the body breaks down into sugar for energy.

Example: Pasta is a food that is high in carbohydrates.

Used in: Grade 3, Grade 4

docs.title: Caring Relationships
docs.text:
Connections with family, friends, or other trusted people that involve kindness, support, and concern for one another's well-being.

Example: A grandparent who checks in on you and listens when you are upset shows a caring relationship.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Choosing The Healthier Food
docs.text:
The skill of comparing two food options and selecting the one that provides better nutrition for the body.

Example: Picking an apple instead of a candy bar for a snack.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Choosing The Healthiest Option
docs.text:
The process of comparing several choices, such as foods, activities, or behaviors, and selecting the one most likely to support good health.

Example: Choosing a salad with grilled chicken over fried food at a restaurant.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Chronic Condition
docs.text:
A health condition that lasts a long time, often a lifetime, and usually requires ongoing management rather than a quick cure.

Example: Diabetes is a chronic condition that a person manages every day.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Chronic Disease Prevention Strategies
docs.text:
Actions, such as regular exercise and healthy eating, that lower the risk of developing long-lasting illnesses like heart disease or diabetes.

Example: Eating more vegetables and walking daily can help prevent type 2 diabetes.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Coercion
docs.text:
Pressuring or forcing someone to do something against their will through threats, manipulation, or intimidation.

Example: Threatening to end a friendship unless someone shares a secret is a form of coercion.

Used in: Grade 5, Grades 6-8

docs.title: Collaborative Goal-Setting Process
docs.text:
A method of setting personal or group goals that involves input, feedback, and agreement from multiple people, such as a student and a mentor.

Example: A student and coach working together to set a realistic training goal for the season.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Commercial Tobacco Addiction
docs.text:
A dependence on manufactured tobacco products, driven by nicotine, that makes quitting difficult even when a person wants to stop.

Example: A person who feels irritable and anxious without a cigarette may be experiencing commercial tobacco addiction.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Commercial Tobacco Effects On Developing Body And Brain
docs.text:
The ways nicotine and other chemicals in manufactured tobacco products can harm growth, lung development, and brain function in young people.

Example: Nicotine use in adolescence can affect the parts of the brain that control attention and impulse control.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Commercial Tobacco Short- And Long-Term Effects
docs.text:
The immediate effects of using manufactured tobacco products, such as increased heart rate, along with lasting effects like lung disease from continued use.

Example: Smoking raises heart rate right away and, over years, can lead to lung cancer.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Common Illness Symptoms
docs.text:
The typical warning signs of frequent illnesses, such as fever, cough, or upset stomach, that signal a person may be sick.

Example: A runny nose and sore throat are common symptoms of a cold.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Communicating And Interpreting Consent
docs.text:
The skill of both clearly expressing agreement or refusal and correctly understanding another person's expressed agreement or refusal in a relationship.

Example: Recognizing that silence or hesitation is not the same as a clear "yes."

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Communicating Boundaries And Consent
docs.text:
Clearly expressing personal limits and checking for agreement before engaging in an activity with another person.

Example: Asking "is it okay if I hug you?" before doing so.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Communicating Feelings
docs.text:
Expressing emotions to others using words, tone of voice, or body language so they can understand how you feel.

Example: Telling a friend "I feel sad when you leave me out" instead of staying quiet.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Communicating Needs
docs.text:
Clearly telling others what you require, whether physical, emotional, or social, so they can understand and respond appropriately.

Example: Telling a teacher "I need a quiet space to focus."

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
The exchange of information, ideas, or feelings between people through speaking, writing, gestures, or listening.

Example: Talking with a friend about weekend plans is a form of communication.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Communication For Conflict Resolution
docs.text:
Using clear, respectful language and active listening to work through disagreements and reach a solution.

Example: Calmly explaining your point of view and listening to the other person before agreeing on a compromise.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Communication In Decision-Making
docs.text:
Using discussion, questions, and listening with others to gather information and consider different views before making a choice.

Example: Talking with a parent about the pros and cons before deciding which after-school club to join.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Community And Cultural Recovery Supports
docs.text:
Programs, traditions, and relationships within a community or culture that help people heal and recover from substance use or trauma.

Example: A talking circle led by tribal elders that supports people recovering from addiction.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Community Food Access Initiatives
docs.text:
Programs or efforts designed to make healthy food easier to obtain for people in a community, especially those with limited access.

Example: A mobile market that brings fresh produce to neighborhoods without a grocery store.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Community Health Practice
docs.text:
An activity or habit, often shared among neighbors or local groups, that supports the well-being of people in a community.

Example: A neighborhood group organizing a walking club to stay active together.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Community Integration Of Cultural Recovery Practices
docs.text:
The inclusion of traditional cultural healing methods alongside standard treatment approaches within community recovery programs.

Example: A treatment center that combines counseling with traditional smudging ceremonies requested by clients.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Community Laws On Substance Use
docs.text:
Local and state rules that regulate the sale, possession, and use of substances such as alcohol, tobacco, and other drugs.

Example: A city ordinance that sets the legal age for buying tobacco products.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Community Nutrition Initiatives
docs.text:
Organized community efforts aimed at improving access to healthy food and educating residents about nutrition.

Example: A school district partnering with local farms to provide fresh vegetables in cafeterias.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Community Safety Practice
docs.text:
An action or rule that helps keep people safe within a shared neighborhood or public space.

Example: Looking both ways before crossing the street at a crosswalk.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Community Societal And Environmental Factors In Health Practices
docs.text:
The broader conditions surrounding a person, including local resources, social norms, and physical surroundings, that shape health behaviors.

Example: Living in a neighborhood without sidewalks can make it harder to exercise outdoors.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Community Values
docs.text:
Shared beliefs or priorities held by the people living in a particular area that influence local behaviors and decisions.

Example: A town that highly values recycling often has strong local recycling programs.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Community-Based Sexual Health Programs
docs.text:
Local services and education efforts, outside of school, that provide information and resources related to sexual health.

Example: A community health center that offers free confidential counseling and testing for teens.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Comparing Drink Choices
docs.text:
The skill of looking at different beverage options and identifying differences in their ingredients or health effects.

Example: Comparing the sugar amounts listed on a soda label and a milk carton.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Comparing Water To Other Drinks
docs.text:
Evaluating how water differs from beverages like soda or juice in terms of sugar, calories, and hydration benefits.

Example: Noticing that water has no sugar while a can of soda has several teaspoons.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Comprehensive Health Care
docs.text:
A broad range of medical services, including prevention, treatment, and follow-up care, aimed at addressing a person's overall health.

Example: A clinic that provides checkups, vaccinations, and counseling under one roof offers comprehensive health care.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Conflict
docs.text:
A disagreement or clash between two or more people who have different needs, opinions, or goals.

Example: Two friends arguing over whose turn it is to choose a game.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Conflict Management
docs.text:
Skills and strategies used to handle disagreements in a calm and constructive way before they escalate.

Example: Taking a deep breath and talking it out instead of yelling during an argument.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Conflict Resolution
docs.text:
The process of resolving a disagreement between people in a way that is fair and respectful to everyone involved.

Example: Two classmates agreeing to take turns using the same art supplies after discussing the problem.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Conflict-Resolution Skill Evaluation
docs.text:
The process of assessing how well a particular approach to resolving a disagreement worked and what could be improved.

Example: Reflecting on whether compromising or apologizing led to a better outcome after an argument.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Conflict-Resolution Skills
docs.text:
Specific abilities, such as active listening and compromise, that help people resolve disagreements peacefully.

Example: Using "I" statements instead of blame during a disagreement.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Consent
docs.text:
A clear, voluntary, and informed agreement to participate in an activity or interaction with another person.

Example: Asking a friend if it's okay to borrow their pencil and waiting for them to say yes.

Used in: Grade 5, Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Consent In Healthy Relationships
docs.text:
The ongoing practice of asking for and respecting agreement between partners before any shared activity, as a foundation of respectful relationships.

Example: Checking in with a partner before making plans that affect both people.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Consent Versus Coercion
docs.text:
The difference between a freely given agreement and one that results from pressure, manipulation, or force.

Example: Saying yes because you want to is consent; saying yes because you're afraid of what will happen if you say no is coercion.

Used in: Grade 5, Grades 6-8

docs.title: Consequences Of Sharing Explicit Content
docs.text:
The social, emotional, and legal outcomes that can result from sending or forwarding sexual images or messages, especially involving minors.

Example: Forwarding a private photo without permission can lead to school discipline or legal charges.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Constructing A Health Position
docs.text:
The process of forming and supporting an opinion or stance on a health-related topic using evidence and reasoning.

Example: Writing a paragraph explaining why schools should offer more physical education time, backed by research.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Coping Strategies Without Substances
docs.text:
Healthy ways to manage stress or difficult emotions that do not involve using alcohol, tobacco, or other drugs.

Example: Going for a run or talking to a friend instead of using substances to deal with stress.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Coping Strategy
docs.text:
A method or action a person uses to deal with stress, difficult emotions, or challenging situations.

Example: Taking slow breaths when feeling frustrated.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Coping With Challenges
docs.text:
Using strategies to manage difficult or stressful situations in a healthy way.

Example: Talking to a parent about feeling overwhelmed by homework instead of giving up.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Correct Body Part Names
docs.text:
The accurate, proper terms for parts of the human body, including private body parts, rather than nicknames or slang.

Example: Using the word "stomach" instead of a made-up nickname when describing where it hurts.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Covering Coughs
docs.text:
The practice of blocking a cough with a tissue or the inside of your elbow to prevent spreading germs to others.

Example: Coughing into your elbow instead of your hand during class.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: CPR Techniques
docs.text:
The steps used to help restart blood circulation and breathing in a person whose heart has stopped, including chest compressions and rescue breaths.

Example: Pushing hard and fast on the center of the chest while waiting for emergency responders to arrive.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Cultural And Historical Influences On Relationships
docs.text:
The ways that a society's traditions, history, and shared experiences shape how people form and behave in relationships.

Example: Historical family structures in a culture can influence how respect between generations is expressed today.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Cultural And Peer Influence On Health Practices
docs.text:
The effect that a person's cultural background and friend group have on the health choices and habits they adopt.

Example: A teen may choose to eat certain traditional foods because both family culture and friends value them.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Cultural Coping Practice
docs.text:
A method of managing stress or hardship that is rooted in a specific cultural tradition, such as a ceremony or shared activity.

Example: A family gathering for a traditional meal after a difficult event to support one another.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Cultural Coping Practices
docs.text:
Traditional methods, rituals, or shared activities from a specific culture that help individuals manage stress, grief, or hardship.

Example: Drumming circles used by some Indigenous communities to support emotional healing.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Cultural Food Tradition
docs.text:
A food, meal, or way of eating that is passed down within a family or cultural group and holds special meaning.

Example: A family making a special dish every year during a holiday celebration.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Cultural Food Traditions
docs.text:
Practices around food preparation, sharing, and celebration that are passed down within cultural or ethnic groups.

Example: Many cultures have specific dishes prepared for harvest festivals or religious holidays.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Cultural Germ Prevention Practices
docs.text:
Traditional habits or customs from different cultures that help reduce the spread of illness, such as specific greetings or hygiene routines.

Example: Some cultures bow instead of shaking hands, which reduces the spread of germs.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Cultural Nutrient Approaches
docs.text:
Ways that different cultures combine foods to provide the nutrients people need, based on traditional cooking methods and ingredients.

Example: Combining rice and beans in many cultures provides a complete source of protein.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Cultural Physical Activity
docs.text:
A form of movement, dance, sport, or exercise that comes from and holds meaning within a specific cultural tradition.

Example: Traditional powwow dancing is a form of cultural physical activity.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Cultural Physical Activity Traditions
docs.text:
Long-standing movement practices, such as traditional dances or games, that are passed down within a culture and often tied to celebration or identity.

Example: Jump rope games passed down through generations in some communities.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Cultural Resilience Strategies
docs.text:
Approaches rooted in a community's cultural heritage that help its members recover from hardship and maintain well-being.

Example: Storytelling traditions that pass down lessons about overcoming difficult times.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Cultural Self-Regulation Practices
docs.text:
Techniques from a cultural tradition that help individuals manage their emotions and behavior, such as meditation or breathing exercises.

Example: A family practicing quiet reflection time rooted in their cultural or spiritual background.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Cultural Sleep Practices
docs.text:
Customs and routines related to sleep, such as bedtime rituals or sleeping arrangements, that vary across different cultures.

Example: Some families share a sleeping space as part of their cultural tradition.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Cultural Support Practices
docs.text:
Traditions or customs within a culture that provide comfort, help, or connection to people who need it.

Example: Neighbors bringing meals to a family after a difficult event, as is customary in some communities.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Cultural Teachings For Wellbeing
docs.text:
Lessons, values, or traditions passed down within a culture that guide people toward healthy, balanced living.

Example: Teachings about respecting elders and living in balance with nature that support overall wellbeing.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Cultural Teachings That Protect Youth
docs.text:
Traditional values, stories, or guidance passed down within a culture that help keep young people safe and healthy.

Example: Teachings that emphasize respect and responsibility can help guide teens away from risky behavior.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Cultural Values Of Respect And Balance
docs.text:
Shared beliefs within a culture that emphasize treating others and oneself with respect and maintaining harmony in life.

Example: A cultural teaching that stresses balance between work, rest, and community.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Cultural Wellness Perspectives
docs.text:
Different ways that cultures understand and define what it means to be healthy and well, beyond just physical health.

Example: Some cultures view wellness as a balance between mind, body, spirit, and community.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Culturally Appropriate Help
docs.text:
Support or assistance that respects and reflects a person's cultural background, values, and communication style.

Example: A counselor who understands and respects a family's cultural traditions when offering advice.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Culturally Safe Healthcare Providers
docs.text:
Medical professionals who understand, respect, and adapt their care to a patient's cultural background so patients feel comfortable and respected.

Example: A doctor who learns about a patient's cultural beliefs about medicine before recommending treatment.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Culturally Safe STI Care
docs.text:
Sexually transmitted infection testing and treatment services that are provided in a way that respects a patient's cultural identity and reduces stigma.

Example: A clinic that trains staff to discuss STI testing without judgment toward patients from different backgrounds.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Daily Active Play
docs.text:
Physical movement and games that children do regularly each day to stay active and healthy.

Example: Playing tag with friends after school every afternoon.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Daily Energy Needs
docs.text:
The amount of energy, measured in calories, that a person's body requires each day to function and grow.

Example: An active teenager typically needs more daily energy than someone who sits most of the day.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Daily Movement
docs.text:
Any physical activity done throughout the day, such as walking, playing, or stretching, that helps keep the body active.

Example: Walking to school and playing outside are both forms of daily movement.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Dairy Group
docs.text:
The category of foods made from milk, such as cheese and yogurt, that provide calcium and other nutrients for strong bones.

Example: A glass of milk and a slice of cheese both belong to the dairy group.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Decision Outcomes
docs.text:
The results or consequences that follow after a person makes a choice.

Example: Choosing to study led to a good grade on the test.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Decision Reflection
docs.text:
The process of thinking back on a choice you made to consider whether it was a good decision and what you might do differently.

Example: Thinking about why sharing a toy made a friend happy after the fact.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Decision-Making Process
docs.text:
A series of steps, such as identifying options and weighing consequences, used to reach a thoughtful choice.

Example: Listing the pros and cons of joining a club before deciding to sign up.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Delivering Health Messages To Audiences
docs.text:
The skill of communicating health information clearly and persuasively to a specific group of people.

Example: Creating a poster about handwashing designed to convince younger students to wash their hands.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Dementia
docs.text:
A general term for a decline in memory, thinking, and reasoning abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life, most common in older adults.
