Example: A person with dementia may repeat the same question several times because they forget they already asked it.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Demonstrating Boundary-Setting
docs.text:
Showing, through words or actions, how to clearly communicate a personal limit to another person.

Example: Role-playing how to tell a friend "please stop" in a firm, clear voice.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Demonstrating Conflict Resolution
docs.text:
Showing, through words or actions, the steps used to work through a disagreement fairly.

Example: Acting out a scene where two students calmly talk through a disagreement and reach an agreement.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Demonstrating Refusal Skills
docs.text:
Showing, through words or actions, how to say no to unwanted or unsafe pressure from others.

Example: Practicing saying "no thanks, I don't want to" firmly when offered something unsafe.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Depression Symptoms And Causes
docs.text:
The emotional and physical signs of depression, such as persistent sadness or low energy, along with the factors that can contribute to it.

Example: Losing interest in activities you used to enjoy can be a symptom of depression.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Determining Need For Assistance
docs.text:
Recognizing when a situation requires help from another person, rather than being handled alone.

Example: Realizing that a deep cut needs an adult's help rather than just a bandage from a backpack.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Dietary Guidelines Across Cultures
docs.text:
Recommendations for healthy eating that can differ between cultures based on traditional foods, values, and available ingredients.

Example: Recommended daily grain intake may be met with rice in one culture and bread in another.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Digital Communication Effects On Relationships
docs.text:
The ways that texting, social media, and other online communication can positively or negatively affect friendships and relationships.

Example: Misunderstanding a friend's tone in a text message can lead to an unnecessary argument.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Digital Content Effects On Relationships
docs.text:
The impact that photos, videos, and messages shared online can have on trust, reputation, and connection between people.

Example: Sharing a private conversation publicly online can damage trust between friends.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Dignity And Compassion For All People
docs.text:
The practice of treating every person with respect and care, recognizing their inherent worth regardless of differences.

Example: Speaking respectfully to a person experiencing homelessness instead of ignoring them.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Disease Prevention Strategies
docs.text:
Actions, such as washing hands or getting vaccinated, that help reduce the chance of becoming sick.

Example: Washing your hands before eating helps prevent the spread of germs that cause illness.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Dressing For Weather
docs.text:
Choosing clothing that matches outdoor conditions, such as wearing a coat in the cold, to stay safe and comfortable.

Example: Putting on a raincoat and boots before going outside on a rainy day.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Drink Types
docs.text:
The different categories of beverages people consume, such as water, milk, juice, and soda.

Example: Water, milk, and juice are all different drink types found at lunch.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Effects Of Bullying And Exclusion
docs.text:
The emotional and social harm that can result when someone is bullied or intentionally left out of a group.

Example: A student who is repeatedly excluded from games may start to feel lonely and sad.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Effects Of Mental Health Challenges
docs.text:
The ways that conditions affecting emotions and thinking, such as anxiety, can impact a person's daily life, school work, and relationships.

Example: A student dealing with anxiety may find it hard to concentrate on schoolwork.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Effects Of Salty Foods
docs.text:
The impact that eating too much salt can have on the body, such as raising blood pressure over time.

Example: Eating a lot of salty chips regularly can make a person feel more thirsty and, over time, affect blood pressure.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Effects Of Sugary And Salty Foods
docs.text:
The health impacts, such as tooth decay, weight gain, or higher blood pressure, that can result from regularly eating foods high in sugar or salt.

Example: Frequently eating sugary candy and salty snacks can contribute to cavities and raised blood pressure over time.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Effects Of Sugary Foods
docs.text:
The impact that eating a lot of sugar can have on the body, such as cavities or quick spikes and drops in energy.

Example: Eating too much candy can lead to a sugar rush followed by feeling tired.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Effects Of Teasing
docs.text:
The emotional impact, such as embarrassment or hurt feelings, that can result from being made fun of by others.

Example: Being teased about clothing choices can make a student feel embarrassed and want to avoid school.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Emergency
docs.text:
A sudden, serious situation that requires immediate action to protect health or safety.

Example: A fire in the kitchen is an emergency that requires calling for help right away.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Emergency Medication Use
docs.text:
The proper way to use medicine designed for urgent health situations, such as an inhaler for asthma or an auto-injector for severe allergies.

Example: Using an epinephrine auto-injector immediately after signs of a severe allergic reaction appear.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Emergency Risk Reduction
docs.text:
Steps taken ahead of time to lower the chance of an emergency happening or to lessen its impact if it does occur.

Example: Keeping a first aid kit and fire extinguisher at home in case of an emergency.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Emotion Management Strategies
docs.text:
Specific techniques, such as deep breathing or talking to someone, used to handle strong feelings in a healthy way.

Example: Counting to ten before responding when feeling angry.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Emotional Triggers
docs.text:
Specific situations, words, or events that cause a strong emotional reaction in a person.

Example: Being interrupted while speaking might be a trigger that makes someone feel frustrated.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Emotions Influence Behavior
docs.text:
The idea that how a person feels can affect the choices they make and how they act.

Example: Feeling nervous before a test might cause someone to avoid studying.

Used in: Grade 3, Grade 4

docs.title: Emotions Shape Behavior
docs.text:
The concept that feelings play a role in guiding a person's actions and reactions in different situations.

Example: Feeling excited about a game might make someone rush through their homework to play sooner.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Emotions Vocabulary
docs.text:
Words used to describe and name different feelings, such as happy, sad, angry, or scared.

Example: Using the word "frustrated" instead of just saying "bad" to describe a feeling.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Empathy
docs.text:
The ability to understand and share the feelings of another person.

Example: Feeling sad when you see a friend crying and wanting to comfort them.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Empathy In Friendships
docs.text:
Understanding and caring about a friend's feelings, and responding to them with kindness and support.

Example: Noticing a friend seems upset and asking if they want to talk about it.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Empathy In Relationships
docs.text:
The ongoing practice of understanding and responding to another person's emotions and perspective within a relationship.

Example: Comforting a partner who is stressed about school, even when you don't share the same worry.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Encouraging Safe Choices
docs.text:
Supporting or motivating others to make decisions that protect their health and safety.

Example: Reminding a friend to wear a helmet before biking.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Environmental Health Risk
docs.text:
A danger to health that comes from conditions in the surrounding environment, such as pollution or unsafe water.

Example: Breathing smoky air from a nearby fire is an environmental health risk.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Equity
docs.text:
Fairness in how resources, opportunities, and support are provided, taking into account that people may need different things to have equal outcomes.

Example: Giving a student who needs glasses a pair to see the board, even if other students don't need them, is equity.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Evaluating Barriers To Health Practices
docs.text:
Identifying and assessing the obstacles, such as cost or time, that make it difficult for people to engage in healthy behaviors.

Example: Recognizing that a lack of nearby grocery stores is a barrier to eating fresh vegetables.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Evaluating Boundary And Consent Communication
docs.text:
Assessing how clearly and effectively a person expressed or understood personal limits and agreement in an interaction.

Example: Reflecting on whether a "maybe" was mistakenly treated as a "yes" during a conversation.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Evaluating Consequences In Health Decisions
docs.text:
Weighing the possible positive and negative results of a health-related choice before or after making it.

Example: Considering both the short-term fun and long-term health risks before deciding to try vaping.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Evaluating Decision Consequences
docs.text:
Assessing the outcomes, good or bad, that followed a choice a person made.

Example: Reviewing whether skipping breakfast led to feeling tired and less focused at school.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Evaluating Goal Plan Outcomes
docs.text:
Reviewing whether the steps taken to reach a goal were effective and led to the desired result.

Example: Checking whether a weekly exercise plan actually helped improve endurance.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Evaluating Goal Strategy Outcomes
docs.text:
Assessing whether the specific strategies used to pursue a goal were successful and worth continuing.

Example: Determining whether studying in short daily sessions improved test scores compared to cramming.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Evaluating Health Decision Outcomes
docs.text:
Reviewing the results of a health-related choice to judge whether it led to a positive or negative effect.

Example: Looking back on whether choosing to see a doctor early helped an illness get better faster.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Evaluating Health Products And Services
docs.text:
Comparing health-related items or services, such as supplements or clinics, to judge their safety, cost, and effectiveness.

Example: Checking whether a supplement's claims are backed by scientific evidence before buying it.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Evaluating Health Promotion Effectiveness
docs.text:
Judging how well a health campaign or educational effort succeeded in changing behaviors or raising awareness.

Example: Measuring whether a school anti-smoking campaign actually reduced tobacco use among students.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Evaluating Impact Of Health Behaviors
docs.text:
Assessing how specific habits or actions affect a person's overall physical, mental, or social well-being.

Example: Considering how regular sleep habits have improved concentration and mood over several weeks.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Evaluating Options In Health Decisions
docs.text:
Comparing the available choices related to a health situation to determine which is most beneficial.

Example: Weighing whether to treat a minor injury at home or see a doctor.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Evaluating Safety Behaviors
docs.text:
Judging whether specific actions taken by yourself or others are effective at preventing injury or harm.

Example: Reviewing whether wearing a helmet actually reduced the risk of injury during a bike accident.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Evaluating Supports For Health Practices
docs.text:
Assessing the people, programs, or resources available that help a person maintain healthy behaviors.

Example: Determining whether a gym membership or a walking group better supports a person's exercise goals.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Evaluating Trusted Adults And Professionals
docs.text:
The process of determining which adults or professionals are reliable and appropriate sources of help for a given health concern.

Example: Deciding to talk to a school counselor rather than a friend about a serious personal problem.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Evaluating Validity Of Health Information
docs.text:
Determining whether a health claim or source of information is accurate, reliable, and based on evidence.

Example: Checking whether a health article was written by a medical expert before believing its claims.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Examining Health-Supporting Practices
docs.text:
Looking closely at habits and behaviors to understand how they contribute to a person's overall health.

Example: Discussing how regular hand washing and enough sleep both support staying healthy.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Exclusion
docs.text:
The act of leaving someone out of a group, activity, or conversation on purpose.

Example: Not inviting a classmate to sit at the lunch table because of how they look.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Exclusion And Bias Effects On Mental Health
docs.text:
The emotional harm, such as sadness or lowered self-worth, that can result from being left out or unfairly judged because of bias.

Example: Being repeatedly excluded because of an accent can lead a student to feel isolated and anxious.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Exiting Unsafe Situations
docs.text:
Recognizing danger and taking action to leave a location or interaction that threatens personal safety.

Example: Leaving a party immediately after noticing people using drugs.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Expressing Emotions
docs.text:
Sharing feelings with others through words, facial expressions, or actions.

Example: Telling a parent "I'm really excited about the field trip!"

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Family
docs.text:
A group of people, such as parents, guardians, siblings, and other relatives, who are connected by blood, marriage, or close bonds of care.

Example: Your family might include parents, a sibling, and grandparents.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Family And Cultural Influence On Health Behavior
docs.text:
The effect that a person's household and cultural background have on the health habits they develop, such as diet or exercise routines.

Example: A family that regularly cooks traditional vegetable-based meals may raise children who prefer those foods.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Family And School Influence
docs.text:
The impact that both home life and the school environment have on a child's attitudes, habits, and behaviors.

Example: A school that promotes recycling combined with a family that recycles at home reinforces the habit.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Family Influence On Decisions
docs.text:
The effect that a person's family values, advice, and expectations have on the choices they make.

Example: Choosing not to try a risky activity because a parent's advice comes to mind.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Family Member Roles
docs.text:
The different responsibilities and functions that people within a family take on, such as caregiver, provider, or sibling.

Example: An older sibling might have the role of helping a younger sibling with homework.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Family Structure
docs.text:
The way a family is organized, including who lives together and cares for one another, such as parents, grandparents, guardians, or siblings.

Example: One family might have two parents and a sibling, while another might have a grandparent as the main caregiver.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Fats
docs.text:
A nutrient found in foods like oils, butter, and nuts that gives the body energy and helps it absorb certain vitamins.

Example: Avocados and peanut butter contain fats that give you long-lasting energy.

Used in: Grade 3, Grade 4

docs.title: Feelings
docs.text:
Emotions a person experiences, such as happiness, sadness, anger, or fear, in response to what is happening around them.

Example: A child might feel excited before a birthday party and sad when a pet is sick.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1

docs.title: Financial And Social Costs Of Substance Use
docs.text:
The money, relationships, opportunities, and reputation a person can lose as a result of using alcohol, tobacco, or other drugs.

Example: Buying vaping products regularly can drain a teen's savings while also straining friendships and trust with family.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Fitness Component
docs.text:
One of the specific parts of physical fitness, such as strength, endurance, flexibility, or heart health, that together describe overall fitness.

Example: Running builds cardiovascular endurance, while stretching improves flexibility.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Food And Water Safety Practices
docs.text:
Actions taken to keep food and drinking water free of germs and contamination so they are safe to consume.

Example: Boiling untreated water before drinking it is a food and water safety practice.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Food Energy
docs.text:
The fuel that food provides to the body, measured in calories, which powers movement, growth, and daily activities.

Example: Eating breakfast gives a student food energy to focus and play at school.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Food Group
docs.text:
One of the categories that foods are sorted into based on the nutrients they provide, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, and dairy.

Example: An apple belongs to the fruits food group.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1

docs.title: Food Group Function
docs.text:
The specific way each food group helps the body, such as building muscles, giving energy, or supporting bone growth.

Example: The protein food group helps build and repair muscles.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Food Handling Safety
docs.text:
Practices used when preparing, touching, or serving food to prevent germs from spreading and making people sick.

Example: Washing hands before touching food is part of food handling safety.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Food Label Analysis
docs.text:
The process of reading and interpreting the information on a food package, such as ingredients, serving size, and nutrients, to make informed choices.

Example: Comparing the sugar content on two cereal labels is a form of food label analysis.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Food Preparation Methods
docs.text:
The different ways food can be made ready to eat, such as baking, boiling, grilling, or mixing raw ingredients.

Example: Steaming vegetables and frying them are two different food preparation methods.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Food Preparation Safety
docs.text:
Steps taken while making food to avoid injury or illness, such as using clean tools and cooking food to a safe temperature.

Example: Using a cutting board instead of holding food in your hand while slicing it supports food preparation safety.

Used in: Grade 1, Grade 2

docs.title: Food Safety
docs.text:
The practice of handling, cooking, and storing food in ways that prevent illness caused by germs or contamination.

Example: Keeping raw chicken away from other foods is an example of food safety.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Food Safety Practices
docs.text:
Specific habits and actions, such as washing hands or checking expiration dates, used to keep food safe to eat.

Example: Checking that milk has not expired before drinking it is a food safety practice.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Food Sovereignty
docs.text:
The right and ability of a community or group of people to grow, gather, or choose their own healthy and culturally meaningful food.

Example: A tribal nation growing traditional crops on its own land is an act of food sovereignty.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Food Storage
docs.text:
The way food is kept, such as in a refrigerator, freezer, or pantry, to keep it fresh and safe.

Example: Storing milk in the refrigerator instead of leaving it on the counter helps it stay fresh.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Food Storage Safety
docs.text:
Practices for keeping food at the right temperature and location to prevent it from spoiling or growing harmful germs.

Example: Placing leftovers in the refrigerator within two hours of cooking is a food storage safety practice.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Food Systems And Chronic Disease Risk
docs.text:
The ways food is grown, processed, sold, and marketed in a society, and how these factors can increase or decrease a population's chances of developing long-term illnesses like diabetes or heart disease.

Example: Communities with limited access to fresh produce may see higher rates of chronic disease linked to processed food consumption.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Food Temperature Safety
docs.text:
Keeping food at temperatures that are cold enough or hot enough to prevent harmful germs from growing.

Example: Keeping cold cuts refrigerated until just before serving supports food temperature safety.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Foodborne Illness
docs.text:
A sickness caused by eating food that contains harmful germs, toxins, or chemicals.

Example: Eating undercooked chicken can cause a foodborne illness with symptoms like stomach cramps and vomiting.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Formulating Goal Strategies
docs.text:
Creating specific steps and methods to help reach a personal health goal.

Example: A student formulates a goal strategy by scheduling three workouts a week to build fitness.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Formulating Health Messages
docs.text:
Creating clear, accurate statements meant to inform or persuade others about a health topic.

Example: Designing a poster slogan that encourages classmates to wear helmets is formulating a health message.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Fruits Group
docs.text:
The category of foods that includes apples, bananas, berries, and other fruit, which provide vitamins and fiber.

Example: Oranges and grapes both belong to the fruits group.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Germs
docs.text:
Tiny living things, too small to see, that can enter the body and sometimes cause sickness.

Example: Germs on unwashed hands can spread a cold to someone else.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1, Grade 2

docs.title: Getting Help For Tech Situations
docs.text:
Telling a trusted adult when something uncomfortable, confusing, or unsafe happens while using a computer, tablet, or phone.

Example: A student tells a parent after seeing a scary pop-up while playing an online game.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Goal Plan Construction
docs.text:
The process of building a detailed, step-by-step plan to achieve a health-related goal.

Example: Listing daily actions needed to improve sleep habits over a month is goal plan construction.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Goal Plan Development
docs.text:
Creating the specific steps, timeline, and resources needed to work toward a personal goal.

Example: Writing down when and how often to practice a new skill is part of goal plan development.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Goal Setting
docs.text:
The process of deciding on something a person wants to achieve and planning how to reach it.

Example: Deciding to read for twenty minutes each night is an act of goal setting.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Goal-Supporting Actions
docs.text:
Specific behaviors a person does regularly that help move them closer to achieving a goal.

Example: Packing gym shoes the night before is a goal-supporting action for a fitness goal.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Grains Group
docs.text:
The category of foods made from wheat, rice, oats, or corn, which provide energy and fiber.

Example: Bread and rice both belong to the grains group.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Guiding A Peer To Help
docs.text:
Directing a friend or classmate toward the right kind of help, such as a trusted adult, when someone is in trouble.

Example: Telling a friend to get the school nurse when another student is hurt is guiding a peer to help.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Handling Relationship Conflict And Pressure
docs.text:
Using skills such as communication and boundary-setting to manage disagreements or unwanted pressure within a relationship.

Example: Calmly explaining why you disagree with a partner's request shows skill in handling relationship conflict and pressure.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Handwashing
docs.text:
Cleaning the hands with soap and water to remove germs and dirt.

Example: Handwashing before eating lunch helps prevent getting sick.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Harmful Or Explicit Content Sharing
docs.text:
Sending or forwarding pictures, videos, or messages online that are inappropriate, dangerous, or hurtful to others.

Example: Forwarding an embarrassing photo of a classmate without permission is harmful content sharing.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Harmful Technology Behavior
docs.text:
Actions taken online or with digital devices that can hurt oneself or others, such as bullying or sharing private information.

Example: Posting a mean comment about a classmate's photo is a harmful technology behavior.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
The overall condition of a person's body, mind, and relationships, including physical, mental, and social well-being.

Example: Eating well, managing stress, and having good friendships all contribute to a person's health.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1, Grade 2, Grade 3, Grade 4, Grade 5, Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Health Behavior Influences
docs.text:
The people, environments, and messages that shape the choices a person makes about their health.

Example: A coach encouraging daily stretching is a health behavior influence.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Health Behavior Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Reflecting honestly on one's own habits and choices to judge how they affect personal health.

Example: A student reviews their sleep log and realizes they need to go to bed earlier.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Health Concern Reporting
docs.text:
Telling a trusted adult about a symptom, worry, or problem related to one's health or someone else's.

Example: Letting a school nurse know about a persistent headache is health concern reporting.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Health Decision
docs.text:
A choice a person makes that affects their physical, mental, or social well-being.

Example: Choosing to wear a bike helmet is a health decision.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1

docs.title: Health Decision Options
docs.text:
The different choices available to a person when facing a situation that affects their health.

Example: When feeling tired, health decision options include resting, drinking water, or talking to an adult.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Health Decision Options And Consequences
docs.text:
The possible choices available in a health-related situation along with the results, positive or negative, that could follow each choice.

Example: Choosing to skip breakfast may lead to the consequence of feeling tired and unfocused at school.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Health Decisions And Community Wellbeing
docs.text:
The connection between individual health choices and the overall health and well-being of a neighborhood or larger group of people.

Example: A community's choice to build safe walking paths supports better health decisions for everyone who lives there.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Health Decisions And Personal Wellbeing
docs.text:
The link between the choices a person makes and their own physical, mental, and social health outcomes.

Example: Consistently choosing to manage stress through exercise supports a person's overall wellbeing.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Health Disparities From Social Conditions
docs.text:
Differences in health outcomes between groups of people that result from unequal social factors such as income, housing, or access to care.

Example: A neighborhood without a nearby grocery store may show higher rates of diet-related illness, a health disparity linked to social conditions.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Health Goal Focus Area Evaluation
docs.text:
Reviewing and judging which areas of health, such as nutrition, sleep, or stress, most need attention when setting a personal goal.

Example: After reviewing several health habits, a student decides sleep is the focus area most in need of improvement.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Health Helper
docs.text:
A person, such as a school nurse, doctor, or trusted adult, whose job or role includes helping others with health needs.

Example: The school nurse is a health helper students can visit when they feel sick.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Health Message Delivery
docs.text:
The way health information is presented and communicated to an audience, such as through a poster, speech, or video.

Example: Presenting a short skit about handwashing to the class is a form of health message delivery.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Health Message Design
docs.text:
The process of planning the content, words, and images used to communicate a health idea effectively to an audience.

Example: Choosing bright colors and a short slogan for an anti-vaping poster is part of health message design.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Health Promotion Factors Across Levels
docs.text:
The individual, community, and societal elements that work together to support or improve people's health.

Example: A city building bike lanes while a school teaches nutrition class are health promotion factors acting at different levels.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Healthcare Access Barriers
docs.text:
Obstacles that make it harder for a person to get medical care, such as cost, transportation, or lack of nearby clinics.

Example: Living far from the nearest doctor's office is a healthcare access barrier.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Healthcare Services Supporting Sexual Health
docs.text:
Medical and counseling resources, such as clinics or health educators, that provide information, testing, and care related to sexual health.

Example: A community health clinic offering confidential testing is a healthcare service supporting sexual health.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Healthy Conflict Resolution
docs.text:
Working out a disagreement in a calm, respectful way that considers everyone's feelings.

Example: Taking turns talking and agreeing on a compromise are part of healthy conflict resolution.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Healthy Peer Traits
docs.text:
Qualities of classmates or friends that make relationships positive, such as honesty, kindness, and respect.

Example: A friend who keeps promises and listens well shows healthy peer traits.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Healthy Relationship Characteristics
docs.text:
The qualities, such as trust, honesty, and mutual respect, that make a relationship supportive and safe.

Example: Partners who communicate openly and support each other's goals show healthy relationship characteristics.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Healthy Relationships
docs.text:
Connections with others, such as friends or family, that are built on respect, trust, and kindness.

Example: Sharing toys and listening to a friend's ideas helps build a healthy relationship.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Healthy Stress Management Without Substances
docs.text:
Using safe strategies, such as exercise or talking to someone, to cope with stress instead of turning to alcohol or drugs.

Example: Going for a run after a hard day is a form of healthy stress management without substances.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Healthy Technology Use
docs.text:
Using computers, tablets, and phones in ways that are safe, balanced, and appropriate for one's age.

Example: Taking breaks from a video game to play outside is an example of healthy technology use.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1

docs.title: Heimlich Maneuver
docs.text:
A first-aid technique using abdominal thrusts to help someone who is choking clear their airway.

Example: A trained bystander performs the Heimlich maneuver on a person choking on food.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: HIV
docs.text:
A virus that attacks the body's immune system, spread through certain body fluids, and can lead to serious illness if untreated.

Example: Using proper precautions during medical procedures helps prevent the spread of HIV.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: How Germs Spread
docs.text:
The ways tiny disease-causing organisms move from one person or surface to another, such as through touch, coughing, or shared items.

Example: Sneezing without covering your mouth shows how germs spread through the air.

Used in: Grade 1, Grade 2, Grade 4

docs.title: Hunger And Fullness Signals
docs.text:
The body's internal cues that indicate when a person needs to eat or has eaten enough.

Example: A growling stomach is a hunger signal, while feeling comfortably satisfied is a fullness signal.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Hunger Signal
docs.text:
A feeling or body cue, such as a growling stomach, that tells a person it is time to eat.

Example: Feeling a rumble in your stomach before lunch is a hunger signal.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Hydration
docs.text:
Having enough water in the body to keep it working properly.

Example: Drinking water throughout the day helps maintain good hydration.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Hydration Sugar And Caffeine Evidence
docs.text:
Research findings about how drinking water, sugary drinks, and caffeinated beverages affect the body's hydration and overall health.

Example: Studies showing that sugary sports drinks can be less hydrating than water are part of the hydration, sugar, and caffeine evidence.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Hygiene
docs.text:
Habits and practices, such as washing hands or brushing teeth, that keep the body clean and help prevent illness.

Example: Brushing your teeth every morning and night is part of good hygiene.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Hygiene As Disease Prevention
docs.text:
The idea that clean habits, such as handwashing and bathing, reduce the spread of germs and lower the chance of getting sick.

Example: Washing hands after using the restroom is hygiene practiced specifically to prevent disease.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: I-Statement
docs.text:
A way of expressing a feeling or need by starting with "I" instead of blaming others, such as "I feel upset when..."

Example: Saying "I feel left out when I'm not invited" is an I-statement.

Used in: Grade 2, Grade 3

docs.title: Identifying Needed Trusted Resources
docs.text:
Recognizing which trusted adults, organizations, or services can provide help for a specific health concern.

Example: Knowing that a school counselor is the right resource for a worry about friendships is identifying a needed trusted resource.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Identifying Relevant Health Topics
docs.text:
Recognizing which health subjects are important or applicable to oneself or one's community.

Example: Noticing that many classmates skip breakfast might lead a student to identify nutrition as a relevant health topic.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Identifying Supports And Barriers
docs.text:
Recognizing the people, resources, or obstacles that help or hinder progress toward a personal goal.

Example: A student notes that a supportive coach helps their fitness goal, while a busy schedule is a barrier.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Identifying Trusted Adults
docs.text:
Recognizing specific grown-ups, such as parents, teachers, or relatives, who can be relied on for help and guidance.

Example: A student lists a parent, teacher, and grandparent as trusted adults they can talk to.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Illegal Drug Effects On Developing Body And Brain
docs.text:
The harmful physical and mental changes that illegal drugs can cause in a child's or teen's still-growing body and brain.

Example: Using an illegal drug during adolescence can disrupt brain development linked to memory and decision-making.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Illegal Substance Consequences
docs.text:
The negative results, such as legal trouble, health harm, or damaged relationships, that can come from using illegal drugs.

Example: Getting suspended from school is one possible consequence of illegal substance use.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Illness Prevention Action
docs.text:
A specific step, such as washing hands or getting vaccinated, taken to reduce the chance of becoming sick.

Example: Covering a cough with your elbow is an illness prevention action.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Illness Prevention Practice
docs.text:
A regular habit that helps keep a person from becoming sick.

Example: Getting enough sleep every night is an illness prevention practice.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Impaired Driving Risk
docs.text:
The increased danger of crashing or hurting someone while driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

Example: Reaction time slows significantly, raising impaired driving risk after drinking alcohol.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Including And Supporting Others
docs.text:
Welcoming people into activities and helping them feel valued and cared for.

Example: Inviting a classmate who is sitting alone to join a game shows including and supporting others.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Including Others
docs.text:
Inviting or welcoming people to take part in an activity or group.

Example: Asking a new student to join a game at recess is including others.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Inclusive Environment Design
docs.text:
Planning spaces, activities, or programs so that people of all abilities and backgrounds can fully participate.

Example: Adding ramps and sensory-friendly quiet spaces to a school event supports inclusive environment design.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Inclusive Environments
docs.text:
Settings where people of all backgrounds and abilities feel welcome and able to participate.

Example: A classroom with materials in multiple languages helps create an inclusive environment.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Indigenous And Traditional Healing Approaches
docs.text:
Methods of caring for health passed down within Indigenous or cultural communities, such as traditional medicines or ceremonies.

Example: Using a traditional herbal remedy passed down through generations is an Indigenous healing approach.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Indigenous Restorative Justice Approaches
docs.text:
Methods rooted in Indigenous traditions that focus on healing and repairing harm within a community rather than punishment alone.

Example: A talking circle that brings together the people affected by harm to reach understanding reflects Indigenous restorative justice.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Indigenous Views Of Health And Substance Use
docs.text:
Perspectives from Indigenous communities on wellness and substance use that often emphasize balance, connection to community, and cultural traditions.

Example: Viewing health as connected to community and land reflects an Indigenous view of health and substance use.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Individual And Interpersonal Factors In Health Practices
docs.text:
Personal traits and relationships with others that influence the health choices a person makes.

Example: A person's self-confidence and a supportive friend group are both individual and interpersonal factors shaping health practices.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Individual Goal-Setting Process
docs.text:
The steps a single person follows to define, plan, and work toward a personal health goal.

Example: Choosing a goal, writing a plan, and tracking progress make up the individual goal-setting process.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Individual Versus Collaborative Goal Setting
docs.text:
The difference between setting a health goal alone compared to setting one together with others, such as a team or family.

Example: Planning a personal running goal alone is individual goal setting, while planning a family walking challenge together is collaborative.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Infectious Disease
docs.text:
An illness caused by germs, such as bacteria or viruses, that can spread from person to person.

Example: The common cold is an infectious disease that can spread through coughing.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Infectious Disease Prevention Strategies
docs.text:
Methods used to reduce the spread of illnesses caused by germs, such as vaccination, handwashing, and isolation.

Example: Staying home when sick is an infectious disease prevention strategy.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Infectious Disease Transmission
docs.text:
The way a disease-causing germ moves from one person, animal, or surface to another person.

Example: Sharing a water bottle with someone who is sick can lead to infectious disease transmission.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Influence
docs.text:
A person, message, or experience that affects the way someone thinks, feels, or behaves.

Example: A television commercial can be an influence on what snack a child wants to eat.

Used in: Grade 1, Grade 2

docs.title: Influences On Health Behavior
docs.text:
The various people, environments, and messages that shape the health-related choices a person makes.

Example: Family habits and friends' opinions are both influences on health behavior.

Used in: Grade 3, Grade 4

docs.title: Injury Prevention
docs.text:
Actions taken to reduce the risk of getting hurt.

Example: Wearing a seatbelt in a car is a form of injury prevention.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 3

docs.title: Justifying Health Choices
docs.text:
Explaining the reasons behind a health-related decision using facts or evidence.

Example: Explaining that eating vegetables supports the immune system is justifying a health choice.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Justifying Health Messages With Facts
docs.text:
Supporting a health-related statement or message with accurate evidence or research.

Example: Citing a study on sleep and memory to support a message about bedtime is justifying a health message with facts.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Kind Behavior
docs.text:
An action that shows care, helpfulness, or consideration toward another person.

Example: Sharing crayons with a classmate is kind behavior.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Kindness
docs.text:
The quality of being caring, friendly, and generous toward others.

Example: Helping a classmate pick up dropped books shows kindness.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1

docs.title: Kindness And Belonging
docs.text:
The connection between treating others with care and helping everyone feel accepted as part of a group.

Example: Sitting with a new student at lunch shows kindness and helps them feel a sense of belonging.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Kindness And Respect For All Abilities
docs.text:
Treating people fairly and considerately regardless of physical, learning, or developmental differences.

Example: Including a classmate who uses a wheelchair in a game shows kindness and respect for all abilities.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Knowing When To Seek Help
docs.text:
Recognizing the signs that a situation requires the assistance of a trusted adult or professional.

Example: Realizing that a friend's sadness has lasted for weeks is knowing when to seek help.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Law And Consent
docs.text:
The legal rules that define when agreement to an activity, such as a sexual relationship, is considered valid and voluntary.

Example: Laws setting an age of consent are part of the relationship between law and consent.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Laws On Impaired Driving
docs.text:
Legal rules that set limits on driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs and establish penalties for breaking them.

Example: A law setting a blood alcohol limit for drivers is a law on impaired driving.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Limiting Caffeinated Drinks
docs.text:
Reducing how much soda, coffee, or energy drinks a person consumes.

Example: Choosing water instead of an energy drink after practice is limiting caffeinated drinks.

Used in: Grade 3, Grade 4

docs.title: Limiting Sugary Drinks
docs.text:
Reducing how much soda, juice, or other sweetened beverages a person consumes.

Example: Choosing milk instead of soda at lunch is limiting sugary drinks.

Used in: Grade 3, Grade 4

docs.title: Locating Health Helpers
docs.text:
Identifying where and how to find people, such as a school nurse or doctor, who can provide health assistance.

Example: Knowing the nurse's office is next to the main office is locating a health helper.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Macronutrient
docs.text:
One of the three main nutrients the body needs in large amounts for energy: carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.

Example: Protein is a macronutrient the body uses to build and repair muscle.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Maintaining Boundaries While Helping Others
docs.text:
Supporting someone in need while still protecting one's own time, energy, and emotional well-being.

Example: Offering to listen to a friend's problem but setting a time limit shows maintaining boundaries while helping others.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Managing Emotions
docs.text:
Recognizing feelings and using healthy strategies to handle them appropriately.

Example: Taking deep breaths when feeling angry is a way of managing emotions.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Managing Health Influences
docs.text:
Recognizing and responding to the people, media, or environments that affect health choices in order to make good decisions.

Example: Choosing to ignore an advertisement for sugary cereal shows managing health influences.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Managing Personal Growth
docs.text:
Taking an active role in tracking and supporting one's own physical, emotional, and social development.

Example: Setting new goals as interests and abilities change is managing personal growth.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Managing Relationships
docs.text:
Using communication and problem-solving skills to keep connections with others positive and healthy.

Example: Talking through a disagreement calmly with a friend is managing relationships.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Managing Strong Emotions
docs.text:
Using strategies to calm down and think clearly when feeling intense feelings like anger or frustration.

Example: Counting to ten before responding when upset is a way of managing strong emotions.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Marketing Claims Analysis
docs.text:
Examining advertising statements about a product to judge whether they are accurate or misleading.

Example: Checking whether a cereal box claim of being "healthy" matches its actual sugar content is marketing claims analysis.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Meal And Snack Evaluation
docs.text:
Judging whether a meal or snack provides balanced nutrition based on the foods and portions included.

Example: Reviewing a lunch tray to see if it includes fruits, vegetables, protein, and grains is meal and snack evaluation.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Meal And Snack Planning
docs.text:
Deciding ahead of time what foods to eat for meals and snacks to meet nutritional needs.

Example: Packing a lunch with a sandwich, fruit, and water bottle is meal and snack planning.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Media And Technology Influence
docs.text:
The effect that television, social media, advertising, and digital devices have on a person's thoughts, feelings, or choices.

Example: Seeing fitness influencers online can be a media and technology influence on exercise habits.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Media Influence
docs.text:
The effect that television, advertising, or online content has on a person's opinions or choices.

Example: A commercial for sugary cereal is an example of media influence on food choices.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Media Representation Of Mental Health
docs.text:
The way mental health conditions and experiences are portrayed in movies, television, and social media.

Example: A TV show that shows a character seeking counseling in a realistic way is a positive media representation of mental health.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Medication Interaction Risks
docs.text:
The dangers that can occur when two or more medicines are taken together and affect the body in unexpected or harmful ways.

Example: Mixing certain cold medicine with another prescription can create a medication interaction risk.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Medication Storage And Disposal Safety
docs.text:
Safe practices for keeping medicines out of reach of children and properly getting rid of unused or expired medication.

Example: Locking medicine in a cabinet and returning unused pills to a pharmacy drop box supports medication storage and disposal safety.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Mental Health Awareness Campaigns
docs.text:
Organized efforts, such as events or media messages, designed to educate people and reduce stigma about mental health.

Example: A school hosting a mental health awareness week with posters and speakers is a mental health awareness campaign.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Mental Health Benefits Of Culture
docs.text:
The positive effects that traditions, community practices, and cultural identity can have on a person's emotional well-being.

Example: Participating in a family cultural celebration can provide a sense of belonging that supports mental health.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Mental Health Challenge
docs.text:
A difficulty involving a person's emotions, thoughts, or behavior that affects their well-being, such as anxiety or depression.

Example: Feeling persistently worried about many things can be a sign of a mental health challenge.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Mental Health Changes Over Time
docs.text:
The way a person's emotional and psychological well-being can shift as they grow, face new experiences, or encounter stress.

Example: A student may feel more anxious during a big life change, showing how mental health changes over time.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Mental Health Stigma Reduction
docs.text:
Efforts to lessen the shame, silence, or negative judgment often associated with mental health conditions.

Example: Talking openly about therapy in class discussions supports mental health stigma reduction.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Mental Health Treatment Options
docs.text:
The different kinds of professional support available for mental health conditions, such as counseling, therapy, or medication.

Example: Meeting weekly with a licensed counselor is one mental health treatment option.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Misusing Over-The-Counter Medications
docs.text:
Taking non-prescription medicine in a way not intended, such as too much or for a purpose other than directed.

Example: Taking extra cold medicine to feel a certain way is misusing an over-the-counter medication.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Misusing Prescription Medications
docs.text:
Taking medicine prescribed to oneself or someone else in a way not directed by a doctor.

Example: Taking a sibling's prescribed medication without a doctor's approval is misusing prescription medication.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Modeling Positive Health Choices
docs.text:
Showing others, through one's own actions, examples of healthy behavior worth following.

Example: A student choosing water over soda at lunch in front of friends is modeling a positive health choice.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Moderate And Vigorous Activity
docs.text:
Physical activity levels ranging from moderate, which raises heart rate somewhat, to vigorous, which raises it significantly and increases breathing rate.

Example: A brisk walk is moderate activity, while running is vigorous activity.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Multiple Perspectives On Health Decisions
docs.text:
The recognition that different people, cultures, or experiences can lead to different valid viewpoints about a health choice.

Example: Two families may have different views on food choices based on their cultural traditions, showing multiple perspectives on health decisions.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Muscle-Strengthening Activity
docs.text:
Physical activity that works the muscles against resistance to build strength, such as lifting weights or doing push-ups.

Example: Doing push-ups twice a week is a muscle-strengthening activity.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Mutual Respect In Health Decisions
docs.text:
Both people involved in a decision valuing each other's opinions, needs, and boundaries equally.

Example: Two partners discussing a health choice and honoring each other's concerns shows mutual respect in health decisions.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Naming Feelings
docs.text:
Putting a word to an emotion a person is experiencing, such as saying "I feel scared" or "I feel happy."

Example: Saying "I feel proud" after finishing a puzzle is naming a feeling.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Negative Health Influence
docs.text:
A person, message, or situation that encourages an unhealthy choice or behavior.

Example: A friend who dares another child to skip washing their hands is a negative health influence.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Negative Influence
docs.text:
A person, message, or situation that pushes someone toward an unhealthy or unsafe choice.

Example: A classmate encouraging another student to be unkind is a negative influence.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Negotiation Skills
docs.text:
The ability to talk through a disagreement and reach an outcome that works for everyone involved.

Example: Suggesting a compromise so both people get a turn on the swing uses negotiation skills.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Nicotine Effects On Developing Body And Brain
docs.text:
The harmful physical and mental changes nicotine can cause in the still-growing bodies and brains of children and teens.

Example: Nicotine use during adolescence can affect areas of the brain involved in attention and learning.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Nicotine Short- And Long-Term Effects
docs.text:
The immediate and lasting physical changes that nicotine use causes in the body.

Example: A short-term effect of nicotine is an increased heart rate, while a long-term effect can be addiction.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Non-Infectious Disease
docs.text:
An illness that is not caused by germs and cannot spread from person to person, such as diabetes or asthma.

Example: Asthma is a non-infectious disease that affects breathing but cannot be caught from someone else.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Nonverbal Communication
docs.text:
Sharing thoughts or feelings without words, using facial expressions, gestures, posture, or tone of voice.

Example: Crossing your arms and frowning is a form of nonverbal communication that can show frustration.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Nonviolent Conflict Resolution
docs.text:
Settling a disagreement using calm, respectful methods rather than physical or verbal aggression.

Example: Talking through a disagreement instead of yelling is nonviolent conflict resolution.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Nutrient Value Evaluation
docs.text:
Assessing how much of each important nutrient a food or meal provides compared to the body's needs.

Example: Comparing the vitamin and mineral content of two snacks is a nutrient value evaluation.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Nutrition Label
docs.text:
The printed information on packaged food that lists ingredients, serving size, calories, and nutrients.

Example: Checking the nutrition label shows how much sugar is in a granola bar.

Used in: Grade 3, Grade 4

docs.title: Nutrition Label Comparison
docs.text:
Looking at the nutrition labels of two or more foods to decide which is the healthier choice.

Example: Comparing the fiber content on two bread labels is a nutrition label comparison.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Nutrition Plan Design
docs.text:
Creating a structured approach to eating that meets a person's nutritional needs and health goals.

Example: Building a weekly meal outline that includes all food groups is nutrition plan design.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Nutritious Meal Planning
docs.text:
Deciding ahead of time what balanced, healthy foods to include in a meal.

Example: Planning a dinner with vegetables, protein, and whole grains is nutritious meal planning.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Nutritious Snack Choices
docs.text:
Selecting foods for a snack that provide helpful nutrients rather than empty calories.

Example: Choosing an apple with peanut butter instead of candy is a nutritious snack choice.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Online Emergency Response
docs.text:
The correct actions to take when encountering a dangerous, threatening, or emergency situation while using the internet.

Example: Immediately reporting a threat of self-harm seen in an online chat to a trusted adult is an appropriate online emergency response.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Other Substance Short- And Long-Term Effects
docs.text:
The immediate and lasting physical or mental changes caused by using drugs other than nicotine or alcohol.

Example: A short-term effect of a stimulant drug might be a racing heartbeat, while a long-term effect could be heart damage.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Overdose Emergency Response
docs.text:
The steps to take when someone has taken a harmful or excessive amount of a substance, including calling for emergency help.

Example: Calling 911 and staying with the person are key parts of an overdose emergency response.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Ownership Of Health Behaviors
docs.text:
Taking personal responsibility for the choices that affect one's own physical, mental, and social well-being.

Example: Choosing to go to bed on time without being reminded shows ownership of health behaviors.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Ownership Of Personal Health
docs.text:
Taking responsibility for understanding and managing one's own body, habits, and well-being.

Example: Keeping track of your own water intake shows ownership of personal health.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Peer Actions During Emergencies
docs.text:
Helpful steps a friend or classmate can take to support someone during a sudden, urgent health situation.

Example: A classmate calling for a teacher when a friend falls and gets hurt is a peer action during an emergency.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Peer And Media Influence On Health Behavior
docs.text:
The combined effect that friends, classmates, and media messages have on the health choices a person makes.

Example: A student trying a new snack because friends and a social media post both promoted it shows peer and media influence.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Peer Influence On Decisions
docs.text:
The effect that friends or classmates have on the choices a person makes.

Example: Choosing to try a new sport because friends are playing it shows peer influence on decisions.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Peer Pressure
docs.text:
The feeling of being urged by friends or classmates to do something, whether helpful or harmful.

Example: A classmate insisting "everyone is doing it" to convince someone to skip homework is peer pressure.

Used in: Grade 4, Grades 6-8

docs.title: Peer Relationship
docs.text:
A connection between people who are equals, such as classmates or friends of a similar age.

Example: Two classmates who play together at recess have a peer relationship.

Used in: Grade 1, Grade 2

docs.title: Peer Roles In Relationships
docs.text:
The different parts friends or classmates play in supporting, influencing, or interacting with one another.

Example: Being a supportive listener when a friend is upset is one peer role in a relationship.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Permission
docs.text:
Agreement given by a person, often a trusted adult, allowing an action to take place.

Example: Asking a parent's permission before going to a friend's house is an example of seeking permission.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Personal Behaviors And Long-Term Health
docs.text:
The connection between the everyday habits a person practices and their health outcomes later in life.

Example: Exercising regularly as a young person is a personal behavior linked to better long-term health.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Personal Boundaries
docs.text:
The physical, emotional, or social limits a person sets to feel safe and comfortable in interactions with others.

Example: Telling a friend not to read your private messages is setting a personal boundary.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Personal Boundary Communication
docs.text:
Clearly expressing one's limits and needs to another person in a relationship.

Example: Saying "I need some time alone tonight" is personal boundary communication.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Personal Boundary-Setting
docs.text:
The act of deciding and expressing limits for how others may treat or interact with a person.

Example: Telling a friend you are not comfortable sharing personal photos is personal boundary-setting.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Personal Care Practice
docs.text:
A daily habit, such as brushing teeth or bathing, that keeps a person's body clean and healthy.

Example: Brushing your hair each morning is a personal care practice.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1

docs.title: Personal Choices And Wellbeing
docs.text:
The connection between the decisions a person makes and how those decisions affect their overall health and happiness.

Example: Choosing to spend time with supportive friends can improve a person's wellbeing.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Personal Health Goal
docs.text:
A specific health-related target a person sets for themselves to work toward.

Example: Deciding to drink more water each day is a personal health goal.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 3

docs.title: Personal Health Goal Tracking
docs.text:
Recording progress over time toward a specific health-related target.

Example: Marking a calendar each day after completing twenty minutes of exercise is personal health goal tracking.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Personal Health Needs
docs.text:
The things a person's body and mind require to stay healthy, such as food, sleep, and safety.

Example: Getting enough sleep each night meets a personal health need.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Personal Health Wants
docs.text:
Things a person would like to have or do for their health but that are not strictly necessary.

Example: Wanting a new pair of running shoes, though older shoes still work, is a personal health want.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Personal Nutrition Needs Assessment
docs.text:
The process of evaluating an individual's specific dietary requirements based on factors like age, activity level, and health goals.

Example: An athlete calculating how much protein their training requires is conducting a personal nutrition needs assessment.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Personal Protective Equipment
docs.text:
Gear, such as gloves or masks, worn to reduce the risk of injury or exposure to germs.

Example: Wearing gloves while cleaning up a spill is using personal protective equipment.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Personal Space
docs.text:
The physical area around a person's body that they consider their own comfortable distance from others.

Example: Standing an arm's length away from someone while talking respects their personal space.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Personal Stressors
docs.text:
Specific situations, events, or pressures in an individual's own life that trigger a stress response, such as schoolwork, family conflict, or social pressure.

Example: An upcoming exam and a disagreement with a friend are both personal stressors a student might face in the same week.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Physical Activities By Fitness Component
docs.text:
Exercises grouped according to the specific area of fitness they primarily improve, such as strength, endurance, or flexibility.

Example: Jumping rope targets cardiovascular endurance, while stretching targets flexibility, showing physical activities by fitness component.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Physical Activity
docs.text:
Any movement of the body that uses energy, such as walking, running, or playing.

Example: Riding a bike to school is a form of physical activity.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1, Grade 2

docs.title: Physical Activity Access Across Communities
docs.text:
The differences in availability of safe places, programs, or resources for exercise between different neighborhoods or populations.

Example: A community without sidewalks or parks may have limited physical activity access compared to one with many trails.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Playful Interaction
docs.text:
A friendly, fun exchange between people, such as games or joking, that builds positive relationships.

Example: Playing tag with classmates at recess is a playful interaction.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Positive Health Influence
docs.text:
A person, message, or situation that encourages a healthy choice or behavior.

Example: A coach who encourages drinking water during practice is a positive health influence.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Positive Influence
docs.text:
A person, message, or situation that encourages someone toward a healthy or safe choice.

Example: A friend who reminds you to wear a helmet is a positive influence.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Power Dynamics And Consent
docs.text:
The way differences in influence, authority, or control between people can affect whether agreement to an activity is truly free and voluntary.

Example: A supervisor asking an employee for a date raises concerns about power dynamics and consent.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Power Dynamics In Relationships
docs.text:
The way influence, control, or authority can be unevenly distributed between people in a relationship.

Example: An older student having more social influence than a younger one reflects a power dynamic in relationships.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Practicing Emergency Responses
docs.text:
Rehearsing the actions to take during a crisis, such as a fire, severe weather, or lockdown, so the correct steps become automatic when a real emergency happens.

Example: A class walks through the fire drill route and meeting spot before an actual alarm ever sounds.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Practicing Safety Procedures
docs.text:
Repeating the correct steps for staying safe, such as fire drills or seatbelt use, until they can be followed automatically in a real situation.

Example: Practicing how to stop, drop, and roll helps a student react quickly if clothing catches fire.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Prejudice
docs.text:
An unfair opinion or feeling about a person or group formed without enough knowledge or a good reason, often based on group membership rather than the individual.

Example: Assuming a new student isn't good at sports just because of where they moved from is a prejudice.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Preventing Fighting And Violence
docs.text:
Using calm communication, walking away, or getting adult help to stop a conflict from turning physical or harmful.

Example: Telling a teacher about a growing argument before it turns into a fight.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Preventing Pregnancy And STIs Through Boundaries
docs.text:
Setting and communicating personal limits, including abstinence, to reduce the risk of unintended pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Preventing Unintended Pregnancy
docs.text:
Using knowledge, decision-making, and protective behaviors, including abstinence, to avoid a pregnancy that is not planned or wanted.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Priority Response Needs
docs.text:
Identifying which injuries or problems in an emergency require the fastest or most urgent action.

Example: Someone who has stopped breathing needs help before someone with a minor scrape.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Prolonged Sadness
docs.text:
Feeling unhappy for a long stretch of time instead of just a short while, which may be a sign that a child needs extra support.

Example: Feeling sad for many days after a pet dies, instead of just for an afternoon.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Protecting Against STIs
docs.text:
Taking actions, such as abstinence or barrier methods, that lower the chance of getting or spreading a sexually transmitted infection.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Protein
docs.text:
A nutrient found in foods like meat, beans, and eggs that helps build and repair muscles and other body tissues.

Example: Eating chicken or beans after exercising helps muscles recover.

Used in: Grade 3, Grade 4

docs.title: Protein Foods Group
docs.text:
The category of foods, including meat, beans, eggs, and nuts, that give the body protein for growth and repair.

Example: A peanut butter sandwich includes food from the protein foods group.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Puberty
docs.text:
The stage of growth when a child's body starts changing and developing into an adult body.

Example: Growing taller and developing new body hair are changes that happen during puberty.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Puberty Across Cultures
docs.text:
The idea that different cultures view and mark the body changes of puberty in different ways, such as through traditions or celebrations.

Example: Some cultures hold a special ceremony to mark a young person reaching puberty.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Puberty As A Life Stage
docs.text:
Understanding puberty as one part of a person's overall growth and development, coming after childhood and before adulthood.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Public Health Policy Influence
docs.text:
The way that laws and rules made by government or health agencies shape the health choices and habits of a community.

Example: A city rule requiring smoke-free restaurants reduces people's exposure to secondhand smoke.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Public Health Policy Influence On Health Practices
docs.text:
The effect that government and organizational health policies, such as taxes on tobacco or vaccination requirements, have on how people behave and stay healthy.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Reading Medication Labels
docs.text:
Checking the printed information on a medicine container, including dose, warnings, and expiration date, before taking or giving the medicine.

Example: Checking the label to see how many hours must pass before taking another dose.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Recognizing Emergencies
docs.text:
Identifying a situation that is urgent and requires immediate action or help, such as a serious injury or fire.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Recognizing Feelings About Behaviors
docs.text:
Noticing and naming the emotions caused by something someone did, like feeling proud after helping or upset after being left out.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Recognizing Need For Help
docs.text:
Noticing when a problem is too big to solve alone and realizing an adult or other person should be asked for support.

Example: Realizing that a cut is bleeding too much to handle without an adult.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Recognizing Overdose Signs
docs.text:
Identifying physical or behavioral warning signs, such as slowed breathing or unresponsiveness, that indicate someone has taken too much of a substance.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Recognizing Personal Needs
docs.text:
Noticing what a person requires to feel safe, healthy, or comfortable, such as rest, food, or comfort from a friend.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Recognizing Threats
docs.text:
Identifying people, objects, or situations that could cause harm.

Example: Noticing a stranger following you and knowing that is a threat to report.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Recognizing Unsafe Situations
docs.text:
Noticing signs that a place, activity, or interaction could lead to harm.

Example: Seeing ice on a pond and recognizing it is unsafe to walk on.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Reducing Healthcare Barriers
docs.text:
Lowering the obstacles, such as cost, transportation, or lack of information, that make it hard for people to get medical care.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Reflecting On Goal Progress
docs.text:
Thinking back on the steps taken toward a personal goal to decide what is working and what needs to change.

Example: Checking a chart of practiced skills to see how close you are to reaching a reading goal.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Reflecting On Health Message Effectiveness
docs.text:
Evaluating whether a health message, such as an advertisement or public service announcement, successfully informs or persuades its audience.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Refusal Skill
docs.text:
A way of saying no clearly and firmly to something that feels wrong, unsafe, or unwanted.

Example: Saying, "No thanks, I don't want to," when offered something that feels unsafe.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Refusal Skills
docs.text:
Communication strategies used to say no to pressure, such as offering an alternative, walking away, or repeating a firm no.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Refusal Skills Evaluation
docs.text:
Judging how well a refusal strategy worked in a real or practiced situation and identifying ways to improve it.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Relapse
docs.text:
A return to a substance or behavior after a period of stopping or recovery.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Relationship Structures
docs.text:
The different forms that close relationships can take, such as friendships, family bonds, or romantic partnerships, each with its own norms and expectations.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Reliability Of Health Information
docs.text:
How trustworthy and accurate a source of health information is, based on things like who created it and what evidence supports it.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Reliable Health Information
docs.text:
Health information that comes from a trustworthy, accurate, and up-to-date source, such as a doctor or recognized health organization.

Example: A pamphlet from a hospital is more reliable than a random social media post.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Reporting Online Harm
docs.text:
Telling a trusted adult or platform about something dangerous, mean, or upsetting that happened on the internet.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Reporting Safety Concerns
docs.text:
Telling an appropriate adult or authority about a situation that could put someone's safety at risk.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Reporting Unsafe Situations
docs.text:
Telling a trusted adult about a place, activity, or interaction that could cause harm.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Researching Health Topics
docs.text:
Gathering and reviewing information from multiple sources to learn accurate facts about a health issue.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Resilience
docs.text:
The ability to recover from a difficult experience and keep moving forward.

Example: Bouncing back and trying again after losing a game or making a mistake.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Respecting Cultural Differences
docs.text:
Treating people's different traditions, beliefs, and customs with fairness and openness instead of judgment.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Respecting Peer Boundaries
docs.text:
Honoring the personal limits that classmates and friends set about their body, space, or belongings.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Responding To Allergic Reactions
docs.text:
Recognizing signs of an allergic reaction, such as swelling or trouble breathing, and taking appropriate action, such as using medicine or calling for help.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Responding To Bullying
docs.text:
Taking action when bullying is witnessed or experienced, such as telling an adult, supporting the person targeted, or safely intervening.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Responding To Coercion
docs.text:
Recognizing and reacting appropriately when someone is being pressured or forced into doing something against their will.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Responding To Online Threats And Harmful Content
docs.text:
Taking safe and appropriate action, such as reporting or seeking help, when encountering dangerous or upsetting material or messages online.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Responding To Teasing And Exclusion
docs.text:
Choosing a safe and effective way to react when being made fun of or left out, such as calmly speaking up or seeking adult support.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Restorative Self-Management Strategies
docs.text:
Personal methods used to recover from stress and return the body and mind to a calm, balanced state.

Example: Taking slow breaths and resting after a stressful test.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Restorative Stress-Management Practices
docs.text:
Habits and techniques, such as relaxation or physical activity, that help a person recover from and reduce the effects of stress.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Right To Personal Boundaries
docs.text:
The understanding that every person has the right to decide who can touch them or enter their personal space.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Risks Of Sharing Personal Information
docs.text:
The dangers, such as identity theft or unwanted contact, that can come from giving out private details like an address or full name.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Romantic Relationships
docs.text:
Close relationships between people that involve mutual attraction and emotional connection.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Safe Behavior
docs.text:
An action that protects a person from harm or injury.

Example: Wearing a helmet while riding a bike is a safe behavior.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Safe Medication Practices
docs.text:
Habits that reduce the risk of harm when taking medicine, such as following the correct dose and checking with a pharmacist about interactions.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Safe Physical Activity Participation
docs.text:
Taking part in exercise or sports in ways that reduce the risk of injury, such as warming up and using proper equipment.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Safe Place
docs.text:
A location where a person feels protected and free from danger.

Example: A school office is a safe place to go if you feel scared.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Safely Exiting Unsafe Relationships
docs.text:
Taking planned, protective steps to leave a relationship that is harmful, including seeking support from trusted people or organizations.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Safety Drill
docs.text:
A practice exercise, such as a fire or tornado drill, that rehearses what to do in an emergency.

Used in: Grade 1, Grade 2

docs.title: Safety Procedures
docs.text:
The set of steps a person should follow to stay protected from harm in a given situation.
