Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Safety Rules
docs.text:
Guidelines that help keep people safe from injury or harm.

Example: "Look both ways before crossing the street" is a safety rule.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Saying No
docs.text:
Clearly telling someone that you do not want to do something.

Example: Saying "No, I don't want to" when a friend asks you to do something unsafe.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Saying No Or Exiting
docs.text:
Refusing an unwanted request or leaving a situation that feels unsafe or uncomfortable.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Scene Safety Assessment
docs.text:
Checking the surroundings of an emergency for ongoing dangers before helping someone who is hurt.

Example: Making sure a downed power line is not near a car crash before approaching to help.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: School And Community Environment Influence
docs.text:
The effect that the physical and social conditions of a school and neighborhood have on a person's health behaviors and choices.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: School Emergency
docs.text:
An unexpected, urgent situation at school, such as a fire or severe weather, that requires quick and organized action.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1

docs.title: School Safety Actions
docs.text:
Steps students and staff take to prevent or respond to danger at school.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: School Safety Practices Evaluation
docs.text:
Assessing how well a school's safety rules and emergency procedures actually protect students and staff.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: School Shooting Preparedness
docs.text:
Knowledge and practiced actions, such as lockdown procedures, that help students and staff respond safely if an armed intruder enters a school.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: School-Staff Actions During Emergencies
docs.text:
The specific responsibilities and steps school employees carry out to protect students during a crisis.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Seeking Help
docs.text:
Reaching out to another person for support or assistance with a problem.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Seeking Help About Relationships Or Development
docs.text:
Asking a trusted adult or professional for guidance about friendships, family relationships, or body and emotional changes.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Seeking Help For Suicide Or Self-Harm Risk
docs.text:
Reaching out to a trusted adult, counselor, or crisis resource when a person is thinking about harming themselves or ending their life.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Seeking Help For Suicide Risk
docs.text:
Telling a trusted adult or contacting a crisis resource when someone shows signs of thinking about ending their life.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Seeking Support For Relationship Safety
docs.text:
Reaching out to trusted people or services for help when a relationship feels unsafe or harmful.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Seeking Support For Relationships
docs.text:
Asking a trusted adult or friend for advice or help with a friendship or relationship problem.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Self-Advocacy Skills
docs.text:
The ability to speak up for one's own needs, rights, and preferences.

Example: Asking a teacher for extra time when you need it to finish an assignment.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Self-Regulation
docs.text:
The ability to manage one's own emotions, thoughts, and behaviors in different situations.

Example: Taking deep breaths to calm down instead of yelling when frustrated.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Setting Boundaries
docs.text:
Clearly stating personal limits about what a person is and is not comfortable with.

Example: Telling a friend, "Please don't read my texts without asking."

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Sharing Feelings With Trusted Adult
docs.text:
Telling a parent, teacher, or other trusted grown-up about one's emotions in order to get support or advice.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Sharing Information Safely
docs.text:
Deciding what personal details are okay to share and with whom, in order to avoid harm.

Example: Not giving your home address to someone you just met online.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Sharing Messages And Images
docs.text:
Sending texts, pictures, or videos to another person, which can carry risks if the content is private or harmful.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Signs Of Emotional Struggle
docs.text:
Behaviors or feelings, such as withdrawing from friends or frequent crying, that suggest a person is having a hard time emotionally.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Signs Of Substance Use Disorder
docs.text:
Behavioral, physical, or emotional changes, such as losing interest in activities or needing more of a substance to feel the same effect, that suggest someone has a substance use disorder.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Situational Awareness
docs.text:
Paying attention to what is happening around you in order to notice possible dangers or problems.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Situational Feelings
docs.text:
Emotions that come from a specific event or circumstance, such as feeling nervous before a test.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Situations Needing Professional Support
docs.text:
Circumstances, such as ongoing depression or abuse, that are serious enough to require help from a counselor, doctor, or other trained professional.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Situations That Influence Emotions
docs.text:
Events or circumstances, such as a fight with a friend or a big test, that cause a person to feel a certain way.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Sleep And Rest Influences On Health
docs.text:
The ways that the amount and quality of sleep a person gets affect their physical, mental, and emotional well-being.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Sleep And Rest Needs
docs.text:
The amount of sleep and downtime a person's body requires to function and feel well.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Sleep Pattern Influences
docs.text:
Factors, such as screen use or schedule changes, that affect how much and how well a person sleeps.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Sleep Supports Growth And Learning
docs.text:
The idea that getting enough sleep helps the body grow and helps the brain remember and learn new things.

Example: Getting a full night's sleep before a test helps you remember what you studied.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Social Media Effects On Boundaries
docs.text:
The ways that using social media can make it harder or easier to maintain personal limits, such as pressure to overshare or stay constantly connected.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Social Media Harm
docs.text:
Negative effects, such as cyberbullying or unhealthy comparison, that can result from using social media.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Social Norms And Health Practices
docs.text:
The unwritten rules and common behaviors of a group that shape the health choices its members tend to make.

Example: If most classmates bring water instead of soda, that norm can influence others to do the same.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Stages Of Puberty
docs.text:
The different phases of physical and emotional change a body goes through during puberty, occurring in a general order but at different times for each person.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Staying Safe Away From Classroom
docs.text:
Following safety rules while in places like hallways, bathrooms, or the playground where a teacher may not be right beside you.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Stereotypes And Bias Effects On Relationships
docs.text:
The ways that oversimplified beliefs about groups of people can create unfair treatment or misunderstanding within relationships.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: STI Prevention And Treatment
docs.text:
Methods used to avoid getting a sexually transmitted infection and the medical care used to treat one if it occurs.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: STI Signs And Symptoms
docs.text:
Physical changes or discomforts that may indicate a person has a sexually transmitted infection.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: STI Transmission
docs.text:
The ways a sexually transmitted infection can pass from one person to another.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: STI Treatment And Cure
docs.text:
Medical approaches used to manage or eliminate a sexually transmitted infection, noting that some can be cured and others can only be managed.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Stigma Effects On Healthcare Access
docs.text:
The way negative judgment or shame about a health condition can discourage people from seeking medical care.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Stigma Reduction
docs.text:
Actions taken to lessen the shame or negative judgment associated with a health condition or behavior.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Strategies To Identify Health Influences
docs.text:
Methods used to figure out what factors, such as family, media, or culture, are shaping a person's health decisions.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Strong Feelings
docs.text:
Emotions that feel very big or intense, such as anger, excitement, or sadness.

Example: Feeling so excited about a birthday party that you can barely sit still.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Substance Industry Advertising Influence
docs.text:
The effect that marketing from tobacco, alcohol, or other substance companies has on people's attitudes and behaviors toward using those substances.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Substance Marketing And Availability Policy
docs.text:
Laws and regulations that control how substances like tobacco or alcohol can be advertised and where they can be sold.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Substance Use And Injury Risk
docs.text:
The increased chance of accidents or physical harm that comes from using alcohol or other drugs.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Substance Use And Self-Harm Risk
docs.text:
The increased chance that using alcohol or other drugs raises the likelihood of a person hurting themselves.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Substance Use And Sexual Health Risk
docs.text:
The increased chance that using alcohol or other drugs leads to unsafe sexual decisions or situations.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Substance Use And Violence Risk
docs.text:
The increased chance that using alcohol or other drugs leads to aggressive or violent behavior.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Substance Use Disorder
docs.text:
A medical condition in which a person cannot control their use of a substance despite it causing problems in their life.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Substance Use Disorder Treatment And Recovery
docs.text:
The medical and personal support process a person goes through to manage a substance use disorder and rebuild a healthy life.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Substance Use Effects On Decision-Making
docs.text:
The way that alcohol or other drugs can impair a person's judgment and ability to make safe choices.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Substance Use Effects On Mental Health And Brain Function
docs.text:
The ways that alcohol or other drugs can change mood, thinking, and how the brain works, especially in a still-developing brain.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Substance Use Effects On Physiology
docs.text:
The physical changes that alcohol or other drugs cause inside the body's organs and systems.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Substance Use Effects On Relationships School And Work
docs.text:
The ways that alcohol or other drug use can damage friendships, family bonds, school performance, and job responsibilities.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Substance Use Treatment Options
docs.text:
The different types of programs and care, such as counseling or medical treatment, available to help someone stop using a substance.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Substance-Related Health Disparities
docs.text:
Unequal rates of substance use problems or unequal access to treatment that exist between different groups of people.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Sugar In Drinks
docs.text:
The sweet ingredient added to many beverages, which can contribute to health problems like tooth decay when consumed in large amounts.

Example: Regular soda contains far more sugar than plain milk or water.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Suicide And Self-Harm Warning Signs
docs.text:
Behaviors or statements, such as giving away belongings or talking about not wanting to live, that may signal a person is at risk of harming themselves.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Sun And Noise Protection
docs.text:
Actions, such as wearing sunscreen or using ear protection, that guard the body from damage caused by sunlight or loud sound.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Supported Goal-Setting Process
docs.text:
A structured method of setting personal goals with guidance, such as breaking a goal into steps and checking in on progress.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Supporting A Peer In Difficulty
docs.text:
Offering help, comfort, or encouragement to a classmate or friend who is struggling.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Supporting An Elder With Cognitive Impairment
docs.text:
Providing patient, appropriate help to an older person whose memory or thinking ability has declined.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Supporting Others In Reducing Substance Use
docs.text:
Helping a friend or family member who is trying to cut back or stop using alcohol or other drugs.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Supporting Peers In Mental Health Crisis
docs.text:
Recognizing when a friend is in serious emotional distress and helping them connect to appropriate help.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Supporting Yourself In Reducing Substance Use
docs.text:
Using personal strategies and resources to help oneself cut back on or stop using alcohol or other drugs.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Supports And Barriers To Health Decisions
docs.text:
The helpful factors and the obstacles that make it easier or harder for a person to make healthy choices.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Supports For Emotional Distress
docs.text:
Resources and people, such as counselors or hotlines, that can help someone experiencing significant emotional pain.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Systemic Inequity In Health Opportunity
docs.text:
Unequal access to health resources and opportunities that results from the structure of institutions and policies rather than individual choices.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Tailoring Messages To Audiences
docs.text:
Adjusting the content, tone, or format of a health message to fit the needs and characteristics of a specific group of people.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Talking About Feelings
docs.text:
Putting emotions into words and expressing them to another person.

Example: Telling a parent, "I feel sad because my friend moved away."

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Teasing
docs.text:
Making fun of someone in a way that can feel playful or hurtful depending on how it is done and received.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Technology Harm Prevention Strategies
docs.text:
Actions taken to reduce the risk of being hurt, scammed, or exposed to harmful content while using devices or the internet.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Technology Safety
docs.text:
Practices that protect a person from harm while using computers, phones, or other digital devices.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Telling A Trusted Adult
docs.text:
Sharing a problem, concern, or piece of information with a parent, teacher, or other reliable grown-up.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Tracking Health Behaviors
docs.text:
Recording actions related to health, such as exercise or sleep, over time to notice patterns and progress.

Used in: Grade 1, Grade 4

docs.title: Traditional Health Knowledge
docs.text:
Health practices and beliefs that have been passed down within a culture or community over generations.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Traditional Medicine Use Considerations
docs.text:
Factors to think about, such as safety and effectiveness, when using healing practices passed down through cultural tradition.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Traditional Plant Medicine Practices
docs.text:
The use of plants for healing purposes based on knowledge passed down within a culture.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Traditional Tobacco And Plant Medicine Use
docs.text:
The cultural and ceremonial use of tobacco and other plants for spiritual or healing purposes, distinct from recreational or commercial use.

Used in: Grades 6-8, Grades 9-12

docs.title: Tribal Sovereignty In Substance Use Lawmaking
docs.text:
The authority of tribal nations to create and enforce their own laws regarding substance use within their communities.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Trusted Adult
docs.text:
A grown-up, such as a parent, teacher, or relative, who a child can rely on for help, guidance, and safety.

Example: A school nurse is a trusted adult a student can go to if they feel sick.

Used in: Kindergarten, Grade 1, Grade 3, Grade 4, Grade 5, Grades 6-8

docs.title: Trusted Adult Guidance
docs.text:
Advice and support given by a reliable adult to help a young person make safe and healthy decisions.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Types Of Peer Relationships
docs.text:
The different kinds of connections young people can have with classmates and friends, such as close friendships, acquaintances, or group friendships.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Unfair Treatment
docs.text:
Being treated worse than others without a good or just reason.

Example: Being left out of a game because of your skin color is unfair treatment.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Unhealthy Relationship Characteristics
docs.text:
Warning signs, such as control, disrespect, or dishonesty, that indicate a relationship is harmful rather than supportive.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Unhealthy Relationship Recognition
docs.text:
Identifying signs, such as control or disrespect, that show a relationship is not healthy.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Uniqueness
docs.text:
The qualities that make each person different and special from everyone else.

Example: Having a unique way of laughing or a special talent for drawing.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Unkind Behavior
docs.text:
An action that hurts someone's feelings or treats them badly.

Example: Calling someone a mean name is unkind behavior.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Unkindness
docs.text:
Words or actions that hurt someone's feelings or treat them badly.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Unsafe Behavior
docs.text:
An action that could lead to injury or harm.

Example: Running near a pool is an unsafe behavior.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Unsafe Chemicals And Water
docs.text:
Substances such as cleaning products or bodies of water that can cause harm if not handled or approached carefully.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Unsafe Food
docs.text:
Food that could make a person sick because it is spoiled, contaminated, or handled improperly.

Example: Milk that has passed its expiration date and smells sour is unsafe food.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Unsafe Food Handling Practices
docs.text:
Ways of preparing, storing, or serving food that increase the risk of making people sick.

Example: Leaving raw chicken out on the counter for hours before cooking it.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Unsafe Technology Situation
docs.text:
An experience while using a device or the internet, such as talking to a stranger or seeing harmful content, that could put a person at risk.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Unsafe Touch
docs.text:
Physical contact that makes a person feel scared, confused, or hurt, or that touches private parts of the body inappropriately.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Unwanted Touch
docs.text:
Physical contact that a person does not want or has not agreed to.

Used in: Grade 2

docs.title: Using Research For A Position
docs.text:
Gathering facts and evidence to support and explain an opinion or stance on a health topic.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Valid Health Information
docs.text:
Health information that is accurate, evidence-based, and can be trusted as true.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Valid Health Information Sources
docs.text:
Places to find health information, such as government health agencies or medical professionals, that are known to provide accurate, evidence-based content.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Validity And Reliability Of Health Information
docs.text:
The combined measure of whether health information is both accurate and consistently trustworthy across sources and over time.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Validity Of Health Information
docs.text:
Whether a piece of health information is accurate and based on facts or evidence.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Valuing Uniqueness
docs.text:
Appreciating the differences that make each person special instead of judging them.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Variety Of Foods
docs.text:
Eating many different kinds of foods from different food groups instead of the same foods every day.

Example: Eating apples one day and carrots the next instead of always eating the same snack.

Used in: Grade 1, Grade 2

docs.title: Vegetables Group
docs.text:
The category of foods, including carrots, broccoli, and lettuce, that provide vitamins and fiber the body needs.

Example: Carrots and spinach both belong to the vegetables group.

Used in: Kindergarten

docs.title: Verbal And Nonverbal Communication
docs.text:
Sharing messages through spoken or written words as well as through body language, facial expressions, and gestures.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Verbal And Nonverbal Communication Analysis
docs.text:
Examining both spoken words and body language in an interaction to understand the full meaning being communicated.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Verbal Communication
docs.text:
Sharing information or feelings using spoken or written words.

Example: Telling a friend "I'm happy for you" out loud is verbal communication.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Vitamins And Minerals
docs.text:
Nutrients found in foods that the body needs in small amounts to grow, function, and stay healthy.

Example: Vitamin C from oranges helps the body heal cuts.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Warning Sign
docs.text:
A signal that indicates danger or a problem may be present.

Example: A dog growling is a warning sign that it may bite.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Warning Signs Of Emotional Distress
docs.text:
Behaviors or statements that suggest a person is struggling emotionally and may need support.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Water And Hydration
docs.text:
The process of drinking enough water to keep the body's fluid levels healthy and functioning well.

Used in: Grade 4

docs.title: Water As A Drink
docs.text:
Plain water chosen as a beverage instead of sugary or flavored drinks.

Used in: Grade 1

docs.title: Water As The Healthy Drink Choice
docs.text:
The idea that plain water is generally the best beverage option for the body compared to sugary drinks.

Used in: Grade 5

docs.title: Water Versus Sugary Drinks
docs.text:
The comparison between plain water, which has no added sugar, and beverages like soda, which contain large amounts of added sugar.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Who To Talk To
docs.text:
Knowing which trusted people, such as parents, teachers, or counselors, are appropriate to approach for different kinds of help.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Why Germ Prevention Practices Work
docs.text:
The reasons that habits like handwashing and covering coughs stop germs from spreading between people.

Example: Washing hands removes germs before they can be transferred to food or your face.

Used in: Grade 3

docs.title: Withdrawing Consent
docs.text:
Taking back permission that was previously given for an activity, at any point, even after it has started.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.title: Workout Plan Design
docs.text:
Creating a structured schedule of physical activities aimed at meeting specific fitness goals.

Used in: Grades 6-8

docs.title: Youth-Friendly Provider Expectations
docs.text:
The standards young people can expect from healthcare providers, such as confidentiality and respectful, nonjudgmental care.

Used in: Grades 9-12

docs.text: Title Organization Notes Link Health Education Standards (K-12) — landing page Minnesota Department of Education (MDE) Governs K-12 health education requirements in Minnesota. Confirmed requirements include cannabis/substance-use prevention education and mental health instruction, both required starting the 2026-2027 school year. Contact: Brian Rhoads, mde.academic-standards@state.mn.us. https://education.mn.gov/MDE/dse/stds/hpe/ 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards — Commissioner Approved (12/15/25) Minnesota Department of Education (MDE) This is the source used to design this course's age/grade tiers. The proposed standards document, approved by the Commissioner in December 2025 and reviewed at an administrative rulemaking hearing (April 13-14, 2026; public comment closed 2026-05-04). Per the MDE site, locally developed standards remain in effect until formal statewide adoption completes — this document is not yet the legally operative standard, but represents the finalized proposed content. Structure verified: 8 anchor standards (1 knowledge standard + 7 skill standards — analyzing influences, accessing information, communication, decision-making, goal setting, healthy practices, promoting wellbeing), organized into 6 strands (Food & Nutrition K-12; Human Growth & Development K-5 / + Sexual Health 6-12; Mental and Emotional Health K-12; Personal Health and Wellness K-12; Personal Safety and Violence Prevention K-12; Substance Use Awareness and Prevention 6-12). Benchmarks are tabulated individually for grades K, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, then as grade bands 6-8 and 9-12, with each benchmark coded (e.g. 0.1.1.1 for kindergarten, 9.1.1.1 for grades 9-12). docs.title: Course Description — Grade 1
docs.text: This is the Grade 1 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 1.1.1.1) are <grade>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text: Early elementary (beginning independent readers, with read-aloud support still expected). Benchmarks shift from Kindergarten's pure identify/name toward identify and explain why, and toward simple demonstration (e.g., saying "no" to unwanted touch).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 1 students (age ~6-7) and their teachers. Short sentences, high picture-to-text ratio; independent reading is emerging but not assumed for comprehension of nuance.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Kindergarten benchmarks in the same 5 content strands (food groups, recognizing feelings, daily personal-care habits, safety rules, correct body part names) and the Kindergarten skill benchmarks (identifying trusted adults, recognizing influences, naming a personal goal).

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student arriving directly at Grade 1 without the Kindergarten section should be briefly introduced to these ideas before Grade 1 content, since Grade 1 benchmarks build on them without re-teaching them:

  • What a food group is, and that food/water keep the body running.
  • Feelings have names, and it's healthy to talk about them.
  • A trusted adult is someone at home, school, or in the community you can ask for help.
  • Basic hygiene actions (handwashing, covering coughs) stop germs from spreading.
  • Every body part has a correct name, and your body belongs to you.
  • Simple safety rules exist at home, school, and in the community, and there are safe places to go in an emergency.

docs.title: Food and Nutrition
docs.text:
• Why eating a variety of food from all food groups matters (1.1.1.1)
  • Different drink types and their benefits (1.1.1.2)
  • Why breakfast is important (1.1.1.3)
  • Safe practices for storing, preparing, and handling food (1.1.1.4)

docs.title: Human Growth and Development
docs.text: • Characteristics of healthy peer relationships (1.2.1.1)

docs.title: Mental and Emotional Health
docs.text:
• Identifying feelings and why talking about them matters, while honoring cultural practices for support (1.3.1.1)
  • Common signs someone may be struggling emotionally (1.3.1.2)
  • How valuing your own and others' uniqueness strengthens caring relationships (1.3.1.3)
  • How different situations affect the way people feel and respond (1.3.1.4)
  • How kindness and unkindness affect relationships and belonging (1.3.1.5)

docs.title: Personal Health and Wellness
docs.text:
• How daily personal-care practices, cultural traditions, and community practices support health (1.4.1.1)
  • Benefits of regular physical activity for health, learning, and emotions; enjoyable ways to be active daily (1.4.1.2)
  • Common ways germs spread and simple actions to prevent illness (1.4.1.3)

docs.title: Personal Safety and Violence Prevention
docs.text:
• Using technology safely and respectfully, including asking permission to use devices/share information (1.5.1.1)
  • Safe and unsafe behaviors at home, school, and in the community, and knowing when to ask a trusted adult for help (1.5.1.2)
  • Types of school emergencies and how safety drills keep everyone safe (1.5.1.3)
  • Keeping one's body safe; saying "no" to unwanted touch (1.5.1.4)

docs.title: Skill Standards
docs.text:
• How various influences affect health practices and behaviors (1.7.2.1)
  • When and how to seek help from others at home, school, or in the community (1.7.3.1)
  • Recognizing and naming one's own and others' feelings; communicating thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs in healthy ways (1.7.4.1)
  • Recognizing when help is needed and who can support a health-related decision (1.7.5.1)
  • Demonstrating and tracking practices/behaviors that support health and wellbeing (1.7.7.1)
  • Ways to ask for help from others in making safe, health-promoting choices (1.7.8.1)

docs.title: Key Vocabulary
docs.text: food group, breakfast, food safety, peer relationship, uniqueness, belonging, hygiene, germs, physical activity, permission, unsafe touch, safety drill, influence, communication, health decision

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: Outcomes below are grouped by Bloom's Taxonomy level and traced to their source benchmark codes.

docs.title: 1. Remember
docs.text:
By the end of Grade 1, the student will be able to:

  1. Recall different drink types and the benefits they provide (1.1.1.2).
  2. Recall safe practices for storing, preparing, and handling food (1.1.1.4).
  3. Recall common signs that someone may be struggling emotionally (1.3.1.2).
  4. Recall the benefits of regular physical activity for health, learning, and emotions (1.4.1.2).
  5. Recall common ways germs spread (1.4.1.3).
  6. Recall safe and unsafe behaviors at home, school, and in the community (1.5.1.2).
  7. Recall different types of school emergencies (1.5.1.3).
  8. Recall the ways various influences affect health practices and behaviors (1.7.2.1).
  9. Recall when and how to seek help from others at home, school, or in the community (1.7.3.1).
  10. Recall ways to ask for help from others in making safe health-promoting choices (1.7.8.1).

docs.title: 2. Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why eating a variety of food from all food groups is important (1.1.1.1).
  2. Explain why eating breakfast matters (1.1.1.3).
  3. Describe characteristics of healthy peer relationships (1.2.1.1).
  4. Explain why talking about feelings is important, while honoring cultural practices for support (1.3.1.1).
  5. Describe how valuing your own and others' uniqueness strengthens caring relationships (1.3.1.3).
  6. Describe how different situations can affect the way people feel and respond (1.3.1.4).
  7. Explain how kindness and unkindness affect relationships and belonging (1.3.1.5).
  8. Describe how daily personal-care practices, cultural traditions, and community practices contribute to health and wellbeing (1.4.1.1).
  9. Describe simple actions that prevent illness (1.4.1.3).
  10. Explain how to use technology safely and respectfully, including asking permission before using devices or sharing information (1.5.1.1).
  11. Explain how safety drills help keep everyone safe during an emergency (1.5.1.3).
  12. Describe ways to keep one's body safe (1.5.1.4).
  13. Recognize when help is needed and who can support a health-related decision (1.7.5.1).

docs.title: 3. Apply
docs.text:
1. Demonstrate saying "no" to unwanted touch (1.5.1.4).
  2. Demonstrate communicating thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs in healthy ways (1.7.4.1).
  3. Demonstrate and track practices and behaviors that support health and wellbeing (1.7.7.1).

docs.title: 4. Analyze
docs.text:
1. Distinguish safe from unsafe behaviors at home, school, and in the community (1.5.1.2).
  2. Distinguish which people or situations positively or negatively influence a health practice or behavior (1.7.2.1).

docs.title: 5. Evaluate
docs.text: Grade 1 benchmarks do not yet include a compare-options or judge-evidence task. The closest emerging skill is recognizing when a situation calls for outside help (1.7.5.1, listed under Understand above). True evaluative reasoning (comparing choices using evidence) begins at Grade 2-3.

docs.title: 6. Create
docs.text: Grade 1 benchmarks do not yet include a design/construct task. Tracking a practiced behavior over time (1.7.7.1, listed under Apply above) is the closest precursor to the goal-design outcomes that begin at Grade 2.

docs.title: Grade 1 Health Education — Chapters
docs.text:
This section contains 7 chapters that build on each other in order. Each chapter introduces a small set of related ideas and assumes students have already read the chapters before it. Teachers and families can read a chapter aloud together, talk through the pictures and examples, and revisit the "Concepts Covered" list at the end to check understanding before moving on to the next chapter.

  1. Foundations of Health and Safe Habits — Introduces health and the core ideas of trusted adults, permission, safe behavior, influence, and communication that every later chapter builds on.
  2. Food, Drinks, and Staying Safe in the Kitchen — Explores food groups, drink choices, why breakfast matters, and safe food storage and preparation.
  3. Understanding and Talking About Feelings — Helps students name feelings, talk about them, and notice how situations and struggles affect emotions.
  4. Friendship, Uniqueness, and Belonging — Looks at healthy peer relationships, valuing uniqueness, kindness, and belonging.
  5. Healthy Habits, Activity, and Germs — Covers hygiene, personal care, physical activity, and how germs spread and can be prevented.
  6. Staying Safe at Home, School, and Online — Teaches safe technology use, telling safe from unsafe behavior, emergency drills, body safety, and asking a trusted adult for help.
  7. Getting Help and Making Healthy Choices — Brings together influence, communication, and help-seeking skills to support making and tracking healthy decisions.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text: Read the chapters in order, since each one uses ideas from the chapters before it. Start with the Summary to see what the chapter is about, then review the Concepts Covered list together, using the pictures and read-aloud text to talk through new words. There is no need to memorize definitions — the goal is for students to recognize each idea, explain it in their own words, and, where noted, practice it (like saying "no" to an unwanted touch) with the support of a trusted adult or teacher.

docs.title: Foundations of Health and Safe Habits
Summary
docs.text: This opening chapter introduces the big idea of health and six root ideas that later chapters build on: trusted adults, asking permission, safe behavior, influences on our choices, and communication. Students meet these words for the first time so they can recognize them throughout the rest of Grade 1.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Health
  2. Trusted Adult
  3. Permission
  4. Safe Behavior
  5. Influence
  6. Communication

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This is the first chapter in the Grade 1 band. It assumes only the Kindergarten bridging concepts described in the course description: that a trusted adult is someone at home, school, or in the community you can ask for help, and that simple safety rules exist at home, school, and in the community.

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Use This Chapter
docs.text:
This chapter is written for you, the teacher, to read aloud, narrate, and guide from. Grade 1 students are beginning independent readers, but comprehension still depends on your read-aloud support. Use the text below as a script while your class explores the pictures and MicroSims. Every interactive element is designed for a child to click, drag, or point at while you talk them through it.

Hi! I'm Scout.

Welcome to Grade 1 Health Education! I'm Scout, a friendly dog who loves helping kids make healthy choices. I'll be popping up all through this book, but I don't show up just anywhere — I have exactly six jobs, and you can tell which one I'm doing by my pose:

  1. Welcome you at the start of every chapter — that's what I'm doing right now.
  2. Help you think about a big idea, using my thinking pose.
  3. Give you a tip — a small, helpful trick to remember something.
  4. Warn you gently when something needs extra care or a grown-up's help.
  5. Encourage you when an idea feels new or a little tricky.
  6. Celebrate with you when you've learned something great.

That's it — six jobs, six poses. If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. Let's think it through together, friend. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: What Is Health?
docs.text:
Health means how well a person's body and mind are working and feeling. A first grader who is healthy has energy to run, play, and learn. Health also includes feelings — a healthy mind can name how it feels and knows it is okay to talk about those feelings. Health is not just "not being sick" — it also means eating well, moving your body, resting enough, staying safe, and having people you trust to help you.

Talking points for read-aloud:

  • Ask the class: "What does your body and mind need every day to feel your best?"
  • Guide answers toward food, water, sleep, movement, feelings, and safety.
  • Explain that this whole book is really about health, and today's six words will show up again and again.

Big Idea

Health is bigger than just your body. It's your body, your feelings, and the people who help keep you safe — all working together!

The following table previews the six root ideas in this chapter, in the order the class will meet them:

Word One-Sentence Meaning Health How well your body and mind are working and feeling Trusted Adult A grown-up at home, school, or in your community you can go to for help Permission Saying yes before someone does something, like using an item or sharing information Safe Behavior An action that protects you and others from getting hurt Influence Someone or something that affects the choices you make Communication Sharing your thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs with someone else

docs.title: Diagram: Six Big Ideas Concept Map
docs.text:
Six Big Ideas Concept Map

Type: graph-model sim-id: six-big-ideas-map Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: identify, name, recognize

Learning objective: Students identify each of the six root words for this chapter (Health, Trusted Adult, Permission, Safe Behavior, Influence, Communication) and recognize that Health is the central idea connecting the other five.

Purpose: Show Health as a hub node connected to the five supporting ideas, so students see the chapter's whole shape before studying each part.

Node types: 1. Health (center, large yellow circle) - Property: "The big idea — how well your body and mind are working and feeling" 2. Trusted Adult, Permission, Safe Behavior, Influence, Communication (five smaller circles around Health, each a different color: blue, green, orange, purple, teal) - Property: one child-friendly definition sentence per node (matching the table above)

Edge types: 1. CONNECTS_TO (thick gray lines from Health to each of the five outer nodes) - No arrowheads needed; represents "is part of," not direction

Layout: Hierarchical/radial with Health in the center and the five ideas arranged evenly around it like a flower.

Interactive features: - Hover any node: node glows and a caption appears below the graph with that word's one-sentence meaning, read aloud by the teacher - Click any outer node: the connecting edge to Health highlights in yellow, reinforcing "this idea is part of being healthy" - Drag nodes: children can rearrange the circles; they snap gently back into a tidy layout after a few seconds - Zoom: mouse wheel or pinch; Pan: click-and-drag background

Visual styling: Large circular nodes (at least 80px) with big friendly icons (a heart for Health, a handshake for Trusted Adult, a raised hand for Permission, a shield for Safe Behavior, an arrow for Influence, two speech bubbles for Communication). Simple sans-serif labels in large text.

Legend: A small key below the canvas listing each color and its word.

Implementation: vis-network with a fixed hierarchical/radial layout option (not free-floating physics) so the shape stays readable for young students; canvas size approximately 700x450px, responsive to container width.

docs.title: Meeting a Trusted Adult
docs.text:
A trusted adult is a grown-up at home, school, or in your community who you can go to for help — someone who listens, keeps you safe, and helps you solve a problem. Grade 1 students met this idea in Kindergarten. This year, students explain why a person counts as a trusted adult, not just point to one.

A trusted adult is usually someone who:

  1. Listens carefully when you talk to them.
  2. Helps you when something feels wrong, confusing, or scary.
  3. Keeps you safe and does not ask you to keep a secret that feels uncomfortable.
  4. Is available to you at home, at school, or in your neighborhood.

Every child's list of trusted adults may look different — a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, a school nurse, or a neighbor could all count, as long as they meet the qualities above.

Helpful Tip

A good trick: think of three grown-ups you could go to if you needed help right now. If you can name three, you already know how to find a trusted adult!

docs.title: Diagram: Who Is a Trusted Adult?
docs.text:
Who Is a Trusted Adult? MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: trusted-adult-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, classify, justify

Learning objective: Students explain why a person is or is not acting like a trusted adult in a given scene, moving beyond simple identification toward reasoning about the qualities that make someone trustworthy.

Canvas layout: - Top area (150px): One short illustrated scene at a time showing an adult interacting with a child (e.g., a teacher helping a child who is hurt, a stranger offering candy through a car window, a school nurse listening to a worry, a neighbor asking a child to keep a secret from their parents) - Middle area (250px): Two large buttons: "Trusted Adult Behavior" and "Not Trusted Adult Behavior" - Bottom strip (100px): Explanation caption area and "Next Scene" button

Visual elements: - 8 simple scenes cycling one at a time, half showing clear trusted-adult behavior and half showing behavior that does not fit (without depicting anything graphic or frightening — kept calm and matter-of-fact) - Simple, friendly, flat-style illustrations

Interactive controls: - Button: "Trusted Adult Behavior" - Button: "Not Trusted Adult Behavior" - Button: "Next Scene"

Default parameters: - First scene: a teacher helping a student who fell down (clear trusted-adult behavior, to build confidence)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the illustrated scene with no labels Stage 2: After the student answers, show a one-sentence reason ("A trusted adult listens and helps, even with small things.") Stage 3: Reinforce the specific quality shown (listens / keeps you safe / no uncomfortable secrets) so students connect the scene to the four qualities list

Behavior: - Correct answer: scene character gets a warm highlight, gentle chime, and the reason caption appears - Incorrect answer: no harsh feedback; caption gently prompts, "Look again — did this grown-up listen and keep the child safe?"

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level (explain/classify) objective, so the pattern uses step-through scenes with a reason revealed after each answer, rather than continuous animation. Grade 1 benchmarks ask students to explain why, so every scene must surface the underlying reason, not just a right/wrong label.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep all scenes calm, non-graphic, and age-appropriate — the "not trusted adult" examples should feel mildly "off" rather than scary. Captions large enough for read-aloud.

docs.title: Asking Permission
docs.text:
Permission means saying yes before someone does something — like using someone else's belongings, going somewhere new, or sharing a photo or piece of information about someone. Asking permission shows respect for other people and the rules that keep everyone safe. This year, students learn that permission applies to technology too: before using a device or sharing information, a child should ask a trusted adult first.

Everyday moments where asking permission matters:

  • Asking a parent before downloading a game or app.
  • Asking before taking or sharing a picture of a friend.
  • Asking before borrowing a toy, book, or supply that belongs to someone else.
  • Asking a trusted adult before going somewhere that is not the usual routine.

Asking first is never rude — it's respectful. Permission protects you, and it protects other people too.

docs.title: Diagram: Ask First! Permission Scenarios
docs.text:
Ask First! Permission Scenarios MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: ask-first-permission Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, use

Learning objective: Students demonstrate the practice of asking permission before using technology or sharing information by choosing the correct next step in short scenarios.

Canvas layout: - Top area (150px): A short scenario described in one simple sentence plus a picture (e.g., "You want to play a new game on the tablet.") - Middle area (250px): Two large response buttons: "Ask First" and "Just Go Ahead" - Bottom strip (100px): Feedback caption and "Next Scenario" button

Visual elements: - 6 scenarios cycling one at a time: downloading an app, taking a photo of a friend, posting a video, borrowing a classmate's tablet, sharing a home address online, using a parent's phone to call someone

Interactive controls: - Button: "Ask First" - Button: "Just Go Ahead" - Button: "Next Scenario"

Default parameters: - First scenario: downloading a new app (a clear, low-stakes example to build confidence)

Behavior: - Choosing "Ask First": character gives a thumbs-up, gentle chime, and caption explains why asking first was the safe, respectful choice - Choosing "Just Go Ahead": no harsh penalty — a calm caption explains what could go wrong and reminds the student to ask a trusted adult next time - After all 6 scenarios, a summary shows how many the student chose "Ask First" for, with encouragement regardless of score

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (demonstrate/practice) objective, so the MicroSim requires the learner to choose an action in a scenario rather than only recall a definition. Repeated scenario practice builds the habit of pausing to ask permission before acting with technology or shared information.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep tone plainly sincere with no jokes, consistent with the project's rule for personal-safety-adjacent content. Large text and icons for beginning readers; teacher reads scenario text aloud.

docs.title: Choosing Safe Behavior
docs.text:
Safe behavior is an action that protects you and others from getting hurt. The opposite, unsafe behavior, is an action that could cause harm. Safe behavior looks a little different at home, at school, and in the community, but the goal is always the same: keep bodies safe and know when to ask a trusted adult for help.

Grade 1 students are also learning that keeping their own body safe includes the right to say "no" to touch that feels wrong or unwanted, and to tell a trusted adult right away if that happens.

Your Body Belongs to You

If a touch ever feels wrong or makes you uncomfortable, it is always okay to say "no" — loudly and clearly. Then tell a trusted adult right away, even if the person said to keep it a secret.

Examples of safe behavior in three settings:

Setting Safe Behavior Example Home Buckling a seatbelt, staying away from the stove without an adult nearby School Walking in the hallway, lining up during a fire drill Community Holding a grown-up's hand near streets, wearing a helmet while biking

docs.title: Diagram: Safe or Unsafe? School and Community Scenes
docs.text:
Safe or Unsafe? School and Community Scenes MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: safe-or-unsafe-scenes Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: distinguish, examine, differentiate

Learning objective: Students distinguish safe behaviors from unsafe behaviors across home, school, and community settings, and identify when a scene calls for telling a trusted adult.

Canvas layout: - Top area (150px): One illustrated scene at a time (e.g., a child crossing the street holding an adult's hand vs. a child running into the street alone; a child participating calmly in a fire drill vs. a child ignoring the drill) - Middle area (250px): Two large bins: "Safe Behavior" (green) and "Unsafe Behavior" (orange) - Bottom strip (100px): Explanation caption and "Next Scene" button

Visual elements: - 10 paired scenes across home, school, and community settings, each clearly showing one safe and one unsafe version of a similar situation

Interactive controls: - Drag-and-drop or click-to-select: place the scene in the correct bin - Button: "Next Scene" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - First scene: child holding an adult's hand to cross the street (clearly safe, to build confidence)

Behavior: - Correct placement: bin glows green or orange to match, gentle chime, one-sentence explanation appears - Incorrect placement: gentle prompt, "Look again — is anyone in danger of getting hurt here?" - Every 3rd scene, an extra prompt asks: "If this were unsafe, who could you tell?" with the answer always modeling "a trusted adult"

Instructional Rationale: Distinguishing safe from unsafe behavior across multiple settings is an Analyze-level task — it requires comparing visual cues rather than simple recall. Tying the unsafe examples back to "tell a trusted adult" reinforces the connection between Safe Behavior and Trusted Adult introduced earlier in this chapter.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep illustrations calm and non-graphic; no scene should depict actual injury. Maintain a plainly sincere tone in all captions, per the project's safety-content voice rule (no puns).

New Words Can Feel Like a Lot

That's a lot of new words in one chapter! It's okay if they feel new right now — we'll practice them together all year. You've got this!

docs.title: Noticing Influence
docs.text:
An influence is a person or thing that affects the choices you make. Influences can be positive, helping you make healthy choices, or negative, pulling you toward choices that are not as healthy. Friends, family, TV shows, and advertisements can all be influences. Grade 1 students begin telling the difference between a positive influence and a negative influence in simple, everyday examples.

A short list of influences students might notice:

  1. A friend who invites you to play outside (often a positive influence).
  2. A commercial that makes candy look like the best snack ever (often a negative influence).
  3. A family member who reminds you to wear a helmet (a positive influence).
  4. A sibling who dares you to skip washing your hands (a negative influence).

Not every influence is bad, and not every influence is good — the important part is noticing it, and then deciding for yourself what the healthy choice is.

docs.title: Diagram: Positive or Negative Influence?
docs.text:
Positive or Negative Influence? MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: influence-spotter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: distinguish, examine

Learning objective: Students distinguish which people or situations positively or negatively influence a health practice or behavior, using short, everyday examples.

Canvas layout: - Top area (150px): A short scenario sentence plus a picture (e.g., "Your friend says, 'Let's ride bikes with our helmets on!'") - Middle area (250px): Two large buttons: "Positive Influence" and "Negative Influence" - Bottom strip (100px): Explanation caption and "Next Scenario" button

Visual elements: - 8 scenarios cycling one at a time, mixing friends, family, media, and advertising examples

Interactive controls: - Button: "Positive Influence" - Button: "Negative Influence" - Button: "Next Scenario"

Default parameters: - First scenario: friend suggesting bike helmets (clearly positive, to build confidence)

Behavior: - Correct answer: gentle chime, character nods, and a one-sentence explanation appears connecting the choice to health - Incorrect answer: calm caption reframes the example, "Let's think again — does this help your body stay healthy and safe, or not?" - After all scenarios, a wrap-up caption reminds students they get to choose which influences to follow

Instructional Rationale: Judging whether an influence is positive or negative requires comparing the example against a health standard, which is an Analyze-level task. Step-through scenarios with a revealed explanation (rather than animation) keep the focus on the reasoning, matching the Grade 1 benchmark of distinguishing influence direction.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep advertising examples generic (no real brand names or logos). Large text for read-aloud; teacher narrates each scenario.

docs.title: Communicating Thoughts and Feelings
docs.text:
Communication means sharing your thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs with someone else, using words, signs, or pictures. Healthy communication also means listening when someone else shares theirs. Grade 1 students practice naming a feeling out loud and telling another person what they need — a skill they will use in every chapter of this book, from asking for help to saying "no" to unsafe touch.

Simple sentence starters that help young students communicate in healthy ways:

  • "I feel ___ because ___."
  • "I need ___ right now."
  • "Can you help me with ___?"
  • "I don't like ___. Please stop."

When you're not sure what to say, start with "I feel..." Naming your feeling is the first step to getting the help you need.

docs.title: Diagram: Finish the Sentence — Communication Practice
docs.text:
Finish the Sentence — Communication Practice MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: communication-sentence-builder Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, use

Learning objective: Students demonstrate communicating thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs in healthy ways by completing simple sentence-starter scenarios with the best available response.

Canvas layout: - Top area (150px): A short scene showing a child in a situation (e.g., feeling left out at recess, needing help with a zipper, feeling scared during a fire drill) - Middle area (250px): Three large word/phrase tiles the student clicks in order to build a short sentence (e.g., "I feel" + "left out" + "will you play with me?") - Bottom strip (100px): The built sentence displays large on screen; "Next Scene" button

Visual elements: - 6 scenes cycling one at a time, each with 3 tile choices per blank so students assemble a complete, healthy communication sentence

Interactive controls: - Click tiles to build the sentence, in order - Button: "Hear My Sentence" (reads the completed sentence aloud conceptually, i.e., displays it large for teacher read-aloud) - Button: "Next Scene"

Default parameters: - First scene: feeling left out at recess

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scene and the empty sentence frame ("I feel ___ because ___.") Stage 2: Show each tile choice highlighted as the student clicks it Stage 3: Show the complete sentence filled in, large and readable

Behavior: - Once all blanks are filled with a reasonable combination, the character in the scene smiles and a gentle chime plays - No wrong combinations are truly "incorrect" — the MicroSim accepts multiple valid completions, since communication has more than one healthy phrasing, but flags combinations that are unrelated or unkind with a gentle prompt to try again

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (demonstrate/practice) objective, so students build and produce a sentence rather than just recognize one. A tile-based builder scaffolds beginning readers who cannot yet type or write full sentences independently.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep tile text short (2-4 words) and large. Teacher reads the finished sentence aloud with the student.

docs.title: Bringing It All Together
docs.text: Health is the big idea this whole book explores. This chapter introduced five ideas that support it: a trusted adult to help you, permission to ask before you act, safe behavior to protect yourself and others, influence to notice what shapes your choices, and communication to share what you think, feel, need, and want. Every later Grade 1 chapter — food, feelings, friendship, healthy habits, personal safety, and asking for help — will use these six words again.

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, most Grade 1 students should be able to identify and briefly explain each of the six root ideas: Health, Trusted Adult, Permission, Safe Behavior, Influence, and Communication. Several MicroSims in this chapter go beyond simple recall into explaining why and distinguishing examples, matching the Grade 1 shift toward "identify and explain why." No multi-step evaluative reasoning is expected yet — that begins in Grade 2-3.

Chapter Complete!

You made it through the whole chapter, friend! You now know about health, trusted adults, permission, safe behavior, influence, and communication. Keep these six words in your pocket — we'll use every one of them again soon. Healthy choices, happy you!

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "If something felt unsafe, what are the two things you should do?" Then reveal: Say "no" clearly, and tell a trusted adult right away.

docs.title: Food, Drinks, and Staying Safe in the Kitchen
Summary
docs.text: Students explore food groups and why eating a variety of foods matters, learn about different drink types including water, and discover why breakfast helps them learn and feel their best. The chapter closes with simple, age-appropriate rules for storing and preparing food safely.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Food Group
  2. Variety Of Foods
  3. Drink Types
  4. Water As A Drink
  5. Breakfast
  6. Food Safety
  7. Food Storage
  8. Food Preparation Safety

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter builds on the idea of Health introduced in Chapter 1: Foundations of Health and Safe Habits.

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Use This Chapter
docs.text:
This chapter is written for you, the teacher, to read aloud and guide from. Grade 1 students are beginning independent readers, so use the text below as a script while your class explores the pictures and MicroSims together. This chapter shifts from Kindergarten's "name the food group" toward identify and explain why — students should be able to say not just what a food group is, but why eating from several of them matters.

Let's Talk About Food!

Hi again, friend! Today we're exploring food, drinks, and breakfast — and I'll show you how to stay safe in the kitchen too. Let's think it through together. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: What Is a Food Group?
docs.text:
A food group is a set of foods that give our bodies similar kinds of help. Fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods, and dairy are the five food groups most Grade 1 students learn about. Each group helps the body in its own way: fruits and vegetables give vitamins that help the body fight illness, grains give energy for running and thinking, protein foods (like beans, eggs, and meat) help build strong muscles, and dairy foods (like milk and cheese) help build strong bones.

Talking points for read-aloud:

  • Ask the class: "Can you name a food from each of the five groups?"
  • Guide answers toward at least one fruit, one vegetable, one grain, one protein food, and one dairy food.
  • Explain that no single food group can do every job alone — that is why eating from all of them matters.

Big Idea

Each food group has its own special job in your body. Grains give you energy, protein builds your muscles, dairy builds your bones, and fruits and vegetables help your body fight off getting sick!

The following table previews the five food groups students will meet in this chapter:

Food Group Example Foods Main Job in the Body Fruits Apples, bananas, strawberries Vitamins that help fight illness Vegetables Carrots, broccoli, spinach Vitamins and fiber for a healthy body Grains Bread, rice, oatmeal Energy for running, playing, and thinking Protein Foods Beans, eggs, chicken, nuts Building strong muscles Dairy Milk, cheese, yogurt Building strong bones

docs.title: Diagram: Food Group Explorer
docs.text:
Food Group Explorer MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: food-group-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, classify, summarize

Learning objective: Students explain which food group a given food belongs to and summarize what job that food group does in the body, moving beyond simple naming toward reasoning about purpose.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): A large plate illustration divided into five colored sections, one per food group - Right area (150px): A stack of food picture cards to click through, plus an infobox

Visual elements: - Five plate sections labeled Fruits (red), Vegetables (green), Grains (tan), Protein Foods (purple), Dairy (light blue) - 15 food picture cards cycling through (3 per group): apple, banana, strawberry / carrot, broccoli, spinach / bread, rice, oatmeal / beans, egg, chicken / milk, cheese, yogurt

Interactive controls: - Button: "Show Next Food Card" - Click-to-place: student clicks the plate section where they think the food belongs - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - First card: apple (a clear, familiar example to build confidence)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the food card with no label Stage 2: After the student clicks a plate section, show whether it matches Stage 3: Reveal a one-sentence explanation of the food group's job ("Apples are a fruit. Fruits have vitamins that help your body fight getting sick.")

Behavior: - Correct placement: plate section glows, gentle chime, explanation caption appears - Incorrect placement: gentle prompt, "Look again — what job does this food group do?" and the correct section glows softly as a hint

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level (explain/classify) objective, so the MicroSim reveals the food group's purpose after each answer rather than using continuous animation, letting students connect each food to a concrete reason it belongs in that group.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Large, simple, flat-style food illustrations. Teacher reads each food name and explanation aloud.

docs.title: Eating a Variety of Foods
docs.text:
Eating a variety of foods means choosing different foods from different food groups instead of eating the same few foods every day. Grade 1 students are learning to explain why variety matters, not just to name the food groups. No single food — not even a very healthy one — has everything the body needs. A plate with foods from several groups gives the body a fuller set of the vitamins, energy, and building blocks it needs to grow, learn, and play.

Helpful Tip

A good trick: look at your plate before you eat. Can you spot at least three different colors? Different colors often mean different food groups are working together!

Reasons variety matters, in simple terms:

  1. Different food groups give different kinds of help — energy, strong bones, strong muscles, and fighting illness.
  2. Eating the same food every day can mean missing out on a job another food group does.
  3. Trying new foods from each group helps the body get a fuller mix of what it needs.
  4. Variety also makes meals more interesting and fun to eat!

docs.title: Diagram: Build a Balanced Plate
docs.text:
Build a Balanced Plate MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: build-a-balanced-plate Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, use, practice

Learning objective: Students demonstrate building a varied, balanced plate by dragging foods from at least three different food groups onto a plate.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): An empty plate outline - Right area (150px): A tray of 12 draggable food icons (mixed across all five groups) and a "Check My Plate" button

Visual elements: - Empty plate that fills in as foods are dragged onto it - Small counter showing how many different food groups are represented so far

Interactive controls: - Drag-and-drop food icons onto the plate - Button: "Check My Plate" - Button: "Start Over"

Default parameters: - Plate starts empty; student chooses freely

Behavior: - When "Check My Plate" is clicked: if 3 or more different food groups are represented, the plate glows green, a gentle chime plays, and a caption celebrates the variety ("Great mix! You picked foods from four different groups.") - If fewer than 3 groups are represented, a calm caption encourages, "You're off to a good start — can you add a food from a group you haven't tried yet?"

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (demonstrate/use) objective, so students actively build a plate rather than only recognize a definition. Immediate, non-judgmental feedback keeps the focus on practicing variety, matching the Grade 1 shift toward demonstration.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep food icons large, colorful, and simple. Allow unlimited food combinations; do not restrict to one "correct" answer.

docs.title: Drink Types and Why Water Wins
docs.text:
There are many drink types, and each one affects the body differently. Milk gives calcium for strong bones. 100%-juice can offer some vitamins but also has natural sugar. Sports drinks and soda have a lot of added sugar and are not needed for everyday activities. Grade 1 students recall these different drink types and the benefits — or drawbacks — that come with them.

Among all drink types, water as a drink stands out as the best everyday choice. Water has no added sugar, helps the body stay cool, helps muscles and joints work smoothly, and helps the brain stay focused for learning. The body loses water throughout the day through breathing, sweat, and using the bathroom, so it needs to be refilled often — especially after playing or exercising.

A quick comparison of common drink types:

Drink Type Common Benefit Something to Know Water Keeps the body cool and focused, no added sugar Best everyday choice, any time of day Milk Calcium for strong bones Good with meals 100% Fruit Juice Some vitamins Has natural sugar — small amounts are best Soda / Sports Drinks Occasional treat only High in added sugar — not needed daily

Watch the Sugar

Sodas and sports drinks can look fun, but they often have a lot of added sugar. That doesn't mean they're forbidden forever — it means water is the smarter everyday choice.

Type: microsim sim-id: drink-type-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: recall, identify, name

Learning objective: Students recall different drink types and the benefits they provide by sorting drink pictures into "everyday drink" and "occasional treat" bins.

Canvas layout: - Top area (150px): One drink picture card at a time (water, milk, 100% juice, soda, sports drink, flavored milk, water with fruit slices) - Middle area (250px): Two bins: "Everyday Drink" (blue) and "Occasional Treat" (orange) - Bottom strip (100px): Explanation caption and "Next Drink" button

Instructional Rationale: This is a Remember-level (recall/identify) objective, so a simple sort-and-reveal pattern is appropriate — the goal is recognizing each drink type and its basic benefit, not yet analyzing trade-offs.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Large, simple drink illustrations. Teacher reads each drink name and benefit aloud.

Students should notice that water is the one drink that belongs in the "everyday" bin every single time — that repetition is part of the lesson.

docs.title: Why Breakfast Matters
docs.text:
Breakfast is the first meal of the day, and it matters because it gives the body and brain fuel after a long night of sleep without eating. A first grader who eats breakfast often has more energy to play, an easier time paying attention, and a steadier mood throughout the morning. Skipping breakfast can leave a student feeling tired, cranky, or unable to concentrate before lunchtime even arrives.

A healthy breakfast, like a healthy plate, is best when it includes foods from more than one food group — for example, oatmeal (grains) with milk (dairy) and berries (fruit), or scrambled eggs (protein) with whole-grain toast (grains) and orange slices (fruit).

Breakfast is like fuel for a car — without it, the body and brain have to work harder to get going. Eating breakfast helps a student feel ready to learn.

Simple reasons breakfast helps a Grade 1 student's day:

  • Gives energy for morning play and PE class.
  • Helps the brain focus during reading and math time.
  • Helps keep moods steady so mornings feel less cranky.
  • Refuels the body after many hours of sleep with no food.

docs.title: Diagram: Why Breakfast? Cause and Effect

Learning objective: Students explain why eating breakfast is important by comparing two versions of the same student's morning — one with breakfast and one without.

Canvas layout: - Left area (350px): "With Breakfast" morning scene (student playing energetically, focused in class) - Right area (350px): "Without Breakfast" morning scene (student looking tired, distracted) - Bottom strip (100px): Toggle button and explanation caption

Visual elements: - Two side-by-side illustrated scenes of the same cartoon student's morning - Small energy-meter icon above each scene (full vs. low)

Interactive controls: - Button: "Toggle Scene" (switches focus between the two scenes) - Hover or click each scene: reveals a caption explaining what is happening and why

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show both scenes side by side with energy meters Stage 2: Click "With Breakfast" scene — caption explains the fuel/energy connection Stage 3: Click "Without Breakfast" scene — caption explains why the student feels tired and unfocused Stage 4: Summary caption ties both scenes together: "Breakfast fuels your body and brain for the whole morning."

Behavior: - Clicking either scene highlights it and reveals its caption; the energy meter animates filling or draining once, then stays still (no continuous animation)

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level (explain/summarize) objective, so the MicroSim uses a side-by-side comparison with revealed captions rather than continuous animation, letting students infer the cause-and-effect relationship between breakfast and energy/focus at their own pace.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep both scenes calm and simple; avoid making the "without breakfast" student look unwell, just tired and less focused. Teacher reads captions aloud.

You've now learned about food groups, variety, drinks, and breakfast — that's a lot of great health knowledge! Next, let's learn how to stay safe with food in the kitchen.

docs.title: Staying Safe with Food: Food Safety Basics
docs.text:
Food safety means following simple rules so the food we eat keeps us healthy instead of making us feel sick. Food safety is not scary — it is just a set of everyday habits, always done with a trusted adult's help in the kitchen. The most important food safety habit for a Grade 1 student is washing hands before touching or eating food, since hands can carry germs picked up from other things they've touched.

Other simple food safety habits include:

  1. Washing hands with soap and water before eating or helping cook.
  2. Washing fruits and vegetables before eating them.
  3. Never eating food that has fallen on the floor or touched something dirty.
  4. Always asking a trusted adult before tasting or trying a new food, especially anything from the stove, oven, or a hot pan.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep every scene calm and matter-of-fact — frame this as "kitchen rules with a trusted adult," never as scary food-danger content. Large text for read-aloud.

docs.title: Keeping Food Fresh: Food Storage
docs.text:
Food storage means keeping food in the right place so it stays fresh and safe to eat — like the refrigerator, freezer, or a cupboard. Milk, eggs, and leftovers belong in the refrigerator to stay cold and fresh. Bread and canned foods often belong in a cupboard. A trusted adult decides where each food goes, and a Grade 1 student can help by asking, "Where does this belong?"

If you're not sure where a food belongs, that's a perfect question for a trusted adult in the kitchen — asking first keeps everyone's food fresh and safe.

Foods that usually need to stay cold in the refrigerator:

  • Milk and cheese
  • Eggs
  • Leftovers from dinner
  • Fresh fruits and vegetables that spoil quickly

docs.title: Helping Safely: Food Preparation Safety
docs.text:
Food preparation safety means following kitchen rules whenever a Grade 1 student helps get food ready to eat, always alongside a trusted adult. Young students can help with many kitchen jobs, but some jobs are grown-up-only jobs. This is simply a set of practical kitchen rules, not something to feel afraid of — cooking together can be a fun family activity when everyone follows the rules.

Kitchen jobs a Grade 1 student can help with alongside a trusted adult, compared with jobs that stay grown-up-only:

Student Can Help With Grown-Up-Only Job Washing fruits and vegetables Using the stove or oven Stirring a bowl of already-mixed ingredients Cutting with a sharp knife Setting the table Taking hot pans out of the oven Pouring cereal (with supervision) Using the microwave alone

Kitchen Rule

Stoves, ovens, and sharp knives are always a grown-up's job. If you want to help cook, ask a trusted adult what job is safe for you to do together.
