Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scenario card with no label Stage 2: After the student clicks a bin, show whether it matches Stage 3: Reveal a one-sentence explanation of why the action stops or spreads germs

Behavior: - Correct match: bin glows, gentle chime, explanation caption appears - Incorrect match: gentle prompt, "Think about where germs could travel next," correct bin glows softly as a hint

Instructional Rationale: This is an Evaluate-level (judge/assess) objective, so the MicroSim asks students to weigh each action's consequence for germ spread and justify the classification, rather than simply recalling a definition; the concrete explanation after each answer supports that judgment without relying on continuous animation.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep the "Spreads Germs" scenarios realistic and relatable (forgetting, not being careless on purpose) so no character feels blamed. Teacher reads each scenario and explanation aloud.

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text:
This chapter connected nine ideas: hygiene as the big picture of caring for the body, personal care practices as the daily routines that make hygiene happen, community health practices as the cultural traditions families use to stay clean, physical activity and its many benefits, daily active play as the fun way to be active every day, and germs, how they spread, and the illness prevention actions that stop them. By the end of this chapter, most Grade 1 students should be able to name at least two personal care practices, describe one community or family hygiene tradition with respect, explain one benefit of physical activity, name a favorite way to be active daily, and explain at least two illness prevention actions and why they work. Keep the discussion of community health practices warm and non-judgmental — no family's hygiene tradition should ever be presented as more "correct" than another.

Chapter Complete!

Amazing work, friend! You've learned how to care for your body, why moving and playing every day feels great, and how to stop germs before they spread. Healthy choices, happy you!

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "What is one thing you can do today to stop germs from spreading?" Then reveal: Washing your hands with soap, covering a cough or sneeze with your elbow, and not sharing cups or utensils are all illness prevention actions that stop germs from spreading.

docs.title: Staying Safe at Home, School, and Online
Summary
docs.text: Students learn how to use technology safely and respectfully, including asking permission before sharing information, and how to tell safe behaviors from unsafe ones at home, school, and in the community. The chapter also covers school emergency drills, keeping one's body safe, and asking a trusted adult for help when something feels wrong.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Healthy Technology Use
  2. Sharing Information Safely
  3. Unsafe Behavior
  4. School Emergency
  5. Safety Drill
  6. Body Safety
  7. Unsafe Touch
  8. Saying No
  9. Asking A Trusted Adult

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter builds on Permission, Safe Behavior, and Trusted Adult from Chapter 1: Foundations of Health and Safe Habits.

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Use This Chapter
docs.text:
This chapter is written for you, the teacher, to read aloud and guide from. It covers safety topics that matter for every Grade 1 student, including the core child-safety concepts of Body Safety, Unsafe Touch, Saying No, and Asking a Trusted Adult. These are standard, evidence-based parts of K-12 health education. The goal is simple: every student should know that their body belongs to them, that they are allowed to say "no," and that telling a trusted adult is always the right choice — and they will never be in trouble for telling. Please preview this chapter before teaching it, and follow your school's guidance for delivering personal-safety lessons. The tone throughout the second half of this chapter is calm and matter-of-fact, without graphic detail, because that is the tone that helps young children absorb and use this information.

Let's Learn About Staying Safe

Hi, friend. Today we're going to learn about staying safe — with screens, at school, and with our own bodies. Staying safe means knowing the rules that protect you, and knowing exactly who to go to if you ever need help.

docs.title: Healthy Technology Use: Rules for Screens and Devices
docs.text:
Healthy technology use means using phones, tablets, computers, and other devices in ways that are safe, respectful, and approved by a trusted adult. A Grade 1 student is starting to use technology more — for games, videos, or schoolwork — and healthy technology use means always checking with a grown-up first.

Here are the basic rules of healthy technology use for a Grade 1 student:

  1. Ask a trusted adult before using a device you haven't used before.
  2. Only use apps, games, or websites a trusted adult has approved.
  3. Keep screen time balanced with active play, reading, and family time.
  4. Tell a trusted adult right away if something on a screen feels confusing, scary, or makes you feel uncomfortable.

Talking points for read-aloud:

  • Ask the class: "What is one device you use at home or school?"
  • Explain that devices are tools, like a pencil or a ball — helpful when used the right way.
  • Remind students that a trusted adult should always know what apps or games they are using.

docs.title: Sharing Information Safely: Asking Before You Share
docs.text:
Sharing information safely means understanding that personal details — like your name, address, phone number, or a photo of yourself — should never be given out online or to a stranger without asking permission first. This idea connects directly to permission, which students explored in Chapter 1: just as we ask permission before borrowing something, we ask permission before sharing information about ourselves.

A Grade 1 student doesn't need to memorize every kind of personal information. The simple rule is: if you're not sure whether something is safe to share, stop and ask a trusted adult first. A good habit to build: if a screen ever asks for a name, address, or a picture, that's the signal to pause and ask a trusted adult before doing anything else.

docs.title: Diagram: Safe or Ask First? Technology Sorter
docs.text:
Safe or Ask First? Technology Sorter MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: safe-or-ask-first-technology-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, apply

Learning objective: Students apply the rule of asking permission before sharing information by sorting a series of simple scenario cards into "Safe to Do" and "Ask a Trusted Adult First" bins.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): One scenario card at a time (simple flat illustration plus one short sentence) - Right area (150px): Two labeled bins, "Safe to Do" and "Ask a Trusted Adult First," and an infobox

Visual elements: - 8 scenario cards cycling one at a time, such as: "Playing an approved learning game," "Typing in your home address on a pop-up screen," "Watching a video a grown-up picked," "A message asking for your full name and school" - Two friendly labeled bins with icons (a green checkmark for "Safe to Do," a raised hand for "Ask a Trusted Adult First")

Interactive controls: - Click-to-select: student clicks the bin that matches the scenario - Button: "Next Scenario" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - First scenario: "Playing a game a trusted adult downloaded for you" (clearly safe, to build confidence)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scenario card with no label Stage 2: After the student clicks a bin, show whether it matches Stage 3: Reveal a one-sentence explanation of why the scenario is safe or needs an adult's help

Behavior: - Correct match: bin glows softly, gentle chime, explanation caption appears - Incorrect match: gentle prompt, "Take another look — would you need to type in private information?", correct bin glows softly as a hint

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (demonstrate/practice) objective, so the MicroSim has students practice classifying real scenarios rather than only reciting a rule, with concrete feedback after each choice to reinforce the ask-first habit.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep all scenarios age-appropriate and free of any frightening imagery; the goal is building a calm, confident habit, not fear. Teacher reads each scenario aloud and discusses the answer with the class.

You've learned two ways to stay safe with technology: using devices the healthy way, and always asking before sharing information. Now let's look at how to tell safe behaviors from unsafe ones everywhere you go — at home, at school, and in your community.

docs.title: Unsafe Behavior: Actions That Could Cause Harm
docs.text:
Students already learned about safe behavior in Chapter 1 — actions that protect people from harm, like wearing a seatbelt or looking both ways before crossing a street. Unsafe behavior is the opposite: an action that could hurt yourself or someone else, whether at home, at school, or out in the community.

Recognizing unsafe behavior is an important skill. Some unsafe behaviors are easy to spot, like running near a swimming pool. Others are less obvious, like following someone you don't know or playing with matches. A Grade 1 student is learning to notice unsafe behavior and to know when it's time to ask a trusted adult for help.

Here are examples of safe and unsafe behaviors side by side:

Situation Safe Behavior Unsafe Behavior Crossing the street Looking both ways and crossing with an adult Running into the street without looking Riding in a car Wearing a seatbelt Unbuckling the seatbelt while the car is moving At the playground Waiting your turn on the slide Climbing up the slide the wrong way Meeting someone new Staying near a trusted adult Walking away with someone you don't know Around the kitchen Asking an adult before using the stove Touching a hot stove or sharp knife alone

Big Idea

Safe behavior protects you and others. Unsafe behavior could cause harm. Learning to notice the difference — and asking a trusted adult when you're not sure — keeps everyone safer.

docs.title: Diagram: Safe and Unsafe Behavior Explorer
docs.text:
Safe and Unsafe Behavior Explorer Infographic

Type: infographic sim-id: safe-and-unsafe-behavior-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: distinguish, examine, differentiate

Learning objective: Students distinguish safe from unsafe behaviors across three settings — home, school, and community — by exploring an illustrated scene of each setting.

Purpose: Help students examine three familiar settings and differentiate between behaviors that are safe and behaviors that are unsafe within each one

Layout: Three tabs across the top labeled "Home," "School," and "Community." Each tab opens a simple illustrated scene with 4-5 clickable hotspots showing children doing different things.

Scenes to show: - Home: a child washing hands before dinner (safe), a child playing near an unlocked cleaning-supply cabinet (unsafe), a child wearing a helmet while biking in the driveway (safe), a child playing with a lighter found on a table (unsafe) - School: a child walking in the hallway (safe), a child pushing others near the stairs (unsafe), a child raising a hand to leave the room (safe), a child opening an exterior door for a stranger (unsafe) - Community: a child holding an adult's hand crossing the street (safe), a child wandering away from the group at the park (unsafe), a child wearing a helmet while scootering (safe), a child accepting a ride from someone the family doesn't know (unsafe)

Interactive elements: - Click each hotspot to reveal a label: "Safe Behavior" or "Unsafe Behavior," plus a one-sentence explanation - A running tally at the top shows how many safe and unsafe behaviors the student has identified in the current scene

Visual style: Bright, simple flat-style illustrations with diverse characters; unsafe hotspots glow gently amber when revealed (never anything frightening), safe hotspots glow green Color scheme: Green for safe, amber for unsafe, neutral warm background

Implementation: p5.js with clickable regions mapped to label-and-caption reveals; tabs implemented as simple buttons that swap the displayed scene

docs.title: School Emergency: When Something Unexpected Happens at School
docs.text:
A school emergency is an unexpected event at school — like a fire, severe weather, or another situation — that requires everyone to follow a special safety plan. School emergencies don't happen often, but schools prepare for them so that every student and adult knows exactly what to do to stay safe.

Common types of school emergencies a Grade 1 student may practice for include:

  • Fire (requiring students to leave the building)
  • Severe weather, like a tornado (requiring students to move to a safe indoor spot)
  • A situation requiring students to stay quietly in their classroom

Talking points for read-aloud:

  • Ask the class: "Has our school ever practiced what to do during a fire drill?"
  • Explain that adults at school have a plan for every kind of emergency, and the plan is practiced so it becomes easy to remember.
  • Reassure students that the calm, orderly practice is what keeps everyone safe — there is no need to feel scared during a drill.

docs.title: Safety Drill: Practicing What to Do
docs.text:
A safety drill is a planned practice of what to do during a specific type of school emergency, done regularly so that everyone knows the steps by heart before a real emergency ever happens. Just like practicing a fire drill helps students walk calmly to a safe spot, practicing other drills helps students know exactly where to go and what to do.

Before we look at how a safety drill works step by step, let's define the key term: a cue is the signal — like an alarm sound or a teacher's instruction — that tells everyone a drill (or a real emergency) is starting.

docs.title: Diagram: Fire Drill Steps Walkthrough
docs.text:
Fire Drill Steps Walkthrough MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: fire-drill-steps-walkthrough Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, describe, summarize

Learning objective: Students explain the steps of a school fire drill in order, using a step-through walkthrough with concrete classroom scenes at each stage.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): One classroom scene per step, shown one at a time - Right area (150px): "Next Step" and "Previous Step" buttons, a step counter ("Step 2 of 5"), and an infobox

Visual elements: - Step 1: Alarm cue sounds, shown as a simple sound-wave icon above the classroom - Step 2: Students line up calmly at the door - Step 3: Teacher leads the line out of the classroom - Step 4: Class walks to the designated safe spot outside - Step 5: Teacher checks that every student is present

Interactive controls: - Button: "Next Step" (advances to the next classroom scene) - Button: "Previous Step" (returns to the prior scene) - Step counter always visible

Default parameters: - Starts at Step 1 (alarm cue)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the alarm cue and a caption: "The alarm is the cue that a drill or emergency is starting." Stage 2: Show students lining up and a caption: "Everyone lines up calmly — no running." Stage 3: Show the teacher leading the line with a caption: "Students follow the teacher's directions." Stage 4: Show the walk to the safe spot with a caption: "The class walks to the same safe spot every time." Stage 5: Show the attendance check with a caption: "The teacher checks that everyone made it out safely."

Behavior: - Each click of "Next Step" reveals the next scene and caption; "Previous Step" allows review - A final summary caption appears after Step 5: "Practicing these steps means everyone knows exactly what to do, so a real emergency feels calm and familiar."

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level (explain/describe) objective, so the MicroSim uses a step-through walkthrough with concrete scenes and captions rather than continuous animation, letting students trace each step of the process in order and in their own time.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep every scene calm and orderly — no depictions of fire, smoke, or danger, only the organized practice behavior. Teacher can pause on any step to connect it to the school's real drill procedure.

docs.title: Body Safety: Your Body Belongs to You
docs.text:
The rest of this chapter covers body safety — one of the most important safety topics a Grade 1 student will learn. Please read this section carefully before teaching it, and keep the tone calm, warm, and matter-of-fact.

Body safety means understanding that your own body belongs to you, and that you have the right to say how, when, and by whom your body is touched. This idea builds directly on something students already learned: every body part has a correct name, and a person's body belongs to them.

Three simple ideas make up body safety for a Grade 1 student:

  1. Your body belongs to you.
  2. Most touches are safe and welcome — like a hug from a family member or a high-five from a friend — but you always get to decide what feels okay for your own body.
  3. If a touch ever feels wrong, confusing, or makes you uncomfortable, you can say "no," and you should always tell a trusted adult about it, right away.

Big Idea

Your body belongs to you. That means you always have the right to say "no" to a touch that doesn't feel right, no matter who is asking.

docs.title: Unsafe Touch: When Something Doesn't Feel Right
docs.text:
An unsafe touch is any touch that makes a person feel confused, scared, or uncomfortable, or that involves the private parts of the body covered by a swimsuit. This definition stays simple and clear for a Grade 1 student, without graphic detail: an unsafe touch is one that feels wrong, and a student's feelings about their own body are always worth listening to.

It helps to know that an unsafe touch can come from anyone — even someone the student knows and normally trusts, like a family member, neighbor, or older student. This is why the rule stays the same no matter who is involved: if a touch feels wrong, it's an unsafe touch, and it should always be reported to a trusted adult.

A simple way to help students hold onto this idea is the "uh-oh feeling" — the uncomfortable feeling in your stomach or chest that shows up when something isn't right. Students already have practice naming feelings from earlier chapters; body safety asks them to notice that same "uh-oh feeling" specifically in connection with touch, and to act on it by telling a trusted adult.

docs.title: Diagram: Body Safety Rules Interactive Guide
docs.text:
Body Safety Rules Interactive Guide

Type: infographic sim-id: body-safety-rules-interactive-guide Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, describe, recognize

Learning objective: Students explain the three core body-safety rules (my body belongs to me, I can say no, I always tell a trusted adult) by exploring a calm, simple interactive guide.

Purpose: Reinforce the three body-safety rules in a warm, non-frightening way that a Grade 1 student and teacher can revisit together

Layout: Three large, friendly panels arranged side by side, each with a simple icon: a heart over a body outline ("My body belongs to me"), a raised hand ("I can say no"), and a trusted adult figure with a speech bubble ("I always tell a trusted adult")

Interactive elements: - Click each panel to reveal one calm sentence explaining the rule in simple words - Click a fourth "What if?" panel to reveal: "If a touch ever feels confusing or wrong, remember: it is never your fault, and telling a trusted adult is always the right choice — you will not be in trouble for telling." - No panel contains frightening imagery; all illustrations are calm, warm, and reassuring

Visual style: Soft, warm color palette; simple flat-style icons; generously spaced panels so the page never feels crowded or intense Color scheme: Soft blue and green tones throughout, avoiding any alarming colors like harsh red

Implementation: p5.js or HTML/CSS with click-to-reveal panels; each reveal is text-only, no animation, to keep the tone calm and steady

Implementation notes: This infographic must be reviewed for tone before publishing — every sentence should sound reassuring and empowering, never frightening. Teachers may want to pause on the "What if?" panel and read it aloud slowly.

docs.title: Saying No: Your Right to Refuse an Unsafe Touch
docs.text:
Saying no is the clear, direct way a student can refuse an unsafe touch or an unsafe situation. A Grade 1 student is old enough to practice saying "no" firmly, even to an adult, and even to someone they know well. This is an important shift from earlier grades: students are now expected to actually demonstrate this skill, not just talk about it.

Saying no can look like:

  • Saying the word "No" in a clear, firm voice
  • Saying "Stop, I don't like that" while stepping away
  • Simply walking away and going straight to a trusted adult

A student never needs a perfect reason to say no to a touch that doesn't feel right — feeling uncomfortable is reason enough. Practicing this skill out loud, in a safe classroom setting, helps a student feel ready to use it in real life.

You Can Practice This

Saying "no" in a strong, clear voice can feel hard to practice at first — that's normal. The more you practice it here, in a safe place, the easier it becomes to use when you really need it.

docs.title: Diagram: Practice Saying No Role-Play Simulator
docs.text:
Practice Saying No Role-Play Simulator

Type: microsim sim-id: practice-saying-no-role-play-simulator Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, apply

Learning objective: Students demonstrate saying "no" to an unsafe or uncomfortable touch by selecting and practicing a firm refusal phrase in response to simple, non-graphic scenario prompts, matching the Grade 1 benchmark that calls for demonstration of this skill.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): One calm scenario prompt at a time, shown as a short sentence with a simple, non-graphic illustration (e.g., "Someone wants to hug you but you don't want a hug right now.") - Right area (150px): Three response-choice buttons showing firm, calm refusal phrases, plus an infobox

Visual elements: - A simple illustrated scene with two friendly characters, never depicting distress or danger, only an everyday moment where a choice is needed - Three phrase-choice buttons per scenario, such as: "No, thank you," "Stop, I don't like that," "I need to go find [trusted adult]"

Interactive controls: - Click-to-select: student selects a phrase in response to the prompt - Button: "Try Saying It" (optional — pairs with the text-to-speech skill to play the chosen phrase aloud in a calm, confident voice, letting the student hear it modeled) - Button: "Next Scenario" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - First scenario is a low-stakes, everyday example (an unwanted tickle from a sibling) to build comfort with the practice before any more serious scenario

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scenario prompt and three phrase choices, no feedback yet Stage 2: After a choice is selected, show a caption affirming that all three phrases are strong, acceptable ways to say no Stage 3: Reveal a closing caption for every scenario: "Any of these responses is okay. What matters most is telling a trusted adult afterward."

Behavior: - All three response choices are treated as correct and strong — there is no "wrong" phrase, since the goal is building confidence, not testing for a single right answer - Every scenario ends with the same reinforcing message about telling a trusted adult

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (demonstrate/practice) objective, so the MicroSim has students actively choose and rehearse a refusal phrase rather than passively reading about the idea, directly matching the Grade 1 benchmark's call for demonstration; keeping every scenario low-stakes and non-graphic protects the calm, empowering tone required for this topic.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Every scenario must be reviewed to ensure it is age-appropriate, non-graphic, and never depicts a specific perpetrator or frightening imagery. Teacher should introduce and debrief this activity rather than leaving students to use it fully independently.

docs.title: Asking A Trusted Adult: The Most Important Step
docs.text:
Every idea in this chapter leads to the same final step: asking a trusted adult for help. Students met the idea of a trusted adult in Chapter 1 — someone at home, at school, or in the community who a student can go to for help. In body safety, asking a trusted adult is not optional or just one choice among many — it is the step that must always happen, every single time a touch feels unsafe or confusing.

Three things are true every time a student tells a trusted adult about an unsafe touch, and these are worth repeating often:

  • It is never the student's fault.
  • The student will not be in trouble for telling.
  • The trusted adult's job is to listen, believe the student, and help keep them safe.

If the first trusted adult a student tells doesn't help, the student should keep telling other trusted adults until someone helps. This is an important backup rule: telling is always the right choice, and a student should never stop at just one try.

docs.title: Diagram: Who Are My Trusted Adults? Web Builder
docs.text:
Who Are My Trusted Adults? Web Builder MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: who-are-my-trusted-adults-web-builder Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: apply, identify, construct

Learning objective: Students apply their understanding of trusted adults by building a personal web of at least three trusted adults from home, school, and the community, reinforcing that there is always more than one person to tell.

Canvas layout: - Center node: a friendly icon labeled "Me" - Surrounding candidate nodes arranged in a ring: family members (parent, grandparent, aunt/uncle), school adults (teacher, school counselor, principal), and community adults (coach, doctor, family friend) - Right-side panel (150px): instructions and a running count of trusted adults added

Visual elements: - Center "Me" node in a warm color - Candidate adult nodes shown as simple labeled circles grouped by setting (home, school, community), each a different soft color - Connecting lines that appear once a node is selected, linking "Me" to that trusted adult

Interactive controls: - Click a candidate node to add it to "My Trusted Adults" web (line connects it to "Me") - Click again to remove it - Button: "Show My Web" (highlights all connected trusted adults) - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - No adults connected at start; all candidate nodes visible and unselected

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the empty web with "Me" in the center and all candidate adults around it Stage 2: As each adult is clicked, show the connecting line appear and the counter increase Stage 3: Once 3 or more trusted adults are connected, show a caption: "You have more than one trusted adult! If one person can't help right away, you can always go to another."

Behavior: - The MicroSim accepts any combination of at least one adult from each setting (home, school, community) as a complete answer, since every family's trusted adults are different - A gentle prompt appears if only one adult is selected, encouraging the student to think of at least one more

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (identify/construct) objective, so the MicroSim has students actively build their own personal network rather than only reading a list, reinforcing the crucial backup rule that there is always more than one trusted adult to ask.

Implementation notes: Use vis-network for the node-and-line web, styled with soft rounded nodes and gentle colors. Teacher should discuss real trusted adults from the students' own lives after the activity, since the MicroSim uses generic role labels rather than actual names.

Remember This

If a touch ever feels wrong, it is never your fault, and you will not be in trouble for telling. Always tell a trusted adult — and if the first person doesn't help, tell another trusted adult.

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text:
This chapter connected nine ideas across two themes. The first theme covered everyday safety skills: healthy technology use, sharing information safely by asking permission first, telling safe behavior from unsafe behavior, and understanding school emergencies and the safety drills that prepare everyone for them. The second theme, body safety, is the most important part of this chapter: every student's body belongs to them, an unsafe touch is any touch that feels wrong, saying "no" is always allowed, and asking a trusted adult is the step that must always happen. By the end of this chapter, most Grade 1 students should be able to demonstrate saying "no" to an unwanted touch, name at least three trusted adults they could tell, and explain that telling a trusted adult is never something they'll get in trouble for. Please revisit these ideas throughout the year in short, calm check-ins rather than treating this as a one-time lesson.

Chapter Complete

You've done important work today, friend. You've learned how to stay safe with technology, how to spot unsafe behavior, what to do during a safety drill, and — most importantly — that your body belongs to you, you can say "no," and a trusted adult is always there to help.

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "If a touch ever feels wrong, what should you do?" Then reveal: Say "no" in a clear voice if you can, then tell a trusted adult right away. It is never your fault, and you will not be in trouble for telling.

docs.title: Getting Help and Making Healthy Choices
Summary
docs.text: This closing chapter shows how influences can be positive or negative, how communicating feelings and needs helps people get what they need, and how recognizing when help is needed leads to better health decisions. Students also practice tracking healthy behaviors and asking for help with choices.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Positive Influence
  2. Negative Influence
  3. Seeking Help
  4. Communicating Feelings
  5. Communicating Needs
  6. Recognizing Need For Help
  7. Health Decision

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter builds on Influence and Communication from Chapter 1: Foundations of Health and Safe Habits, Feelings from Chapter 3: Understanding and Talking About Feelings, Personal Care Practice and Physical Activity from Chapter 5: Healthy Habits, Activity, and Germs, and Asking A Trusted Adult from Chapter 6: Staying Safe at Home, School, and Online.

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Use This Chapter
docs.text:
This is the final chapter of the Grade 1 book, and it ties together many of the skills students have practiced all year. It covers how outside influences shape health choices, how to communicate feelings and needs clearly, when and how to ask for help, and how to make and track healthy decisions. None of these ideas require the same careful tone as the personal-safety content in Chapter 6, but they do build directly on it — recognizing when you need help and knowing how to ask for it are the same muscles students practiced when learning to tell a trusted adult. Read each section aloud, pause for the discussion prompts, and let students use the MicroSims described below as guided or independent practice, depending on your classroom's technology access.

Let's Learn About Getting Help and Making Choices

Hi, friend! Today we're going to learn about the people and things that influence our choices, how to share our feelings and needs with words, and how to know when it's time to ask for help. These skills will help you make healthy choices for the rest of your life.

docs.title: Positive Influence: People and Things That Help You Choose Well
docs.text:
Back in Chapter 1, students learned that an influence is a person, thing, or idea that affects how someone thinks or acts. Now it's time to look more closely at two kinds of influence a Grade 1 student meets every day.

A positive influence is a person, thing, or idea that helps someone make a healthy choice. A positive influence might be a family member who packs a lunch full of fruits and vegetables, a friend who invites you to play outside, or a coach who reminds the team to drink water. Positive influences make it easier, not harder, to take care of your body and feelings.

Talking points for read-aloud:

  • Ask the class: "Who is someone in your life who helps you make healthy choices?"
  • Explain that a positive influence isn't always a person — a favorite park, a song that makes you want to dance, or a family rule about bedtime can all be positive influences too.
  • Point out that the same influence (like a friend) can be positive in one moment and negative in another, which is why noticing influences is a skill worth practicing.

docs.title: Negative Influence: People and Things That Make Healthy Choices Harder
docs.text:
A negative influence is a person, thing, or idea that makes it harder to make a healthy choice, or that encourages an unhealthy or unsafe one. A negative influence might be an advertisement for sugary snacks, a friend who dares someone to skip washing their hands, or a show that makes staying up too late look exciting.

Recognizing a negative influence does not mean the person or thing is "bad" — it means noticing that, in this one moment, it is pulling a choice in an unhealthy direction. A Grade 1 student is learning to pause and think, "Is this helping me make a healthy choice, or making it harder?"

Before the diagram below, let's define one more term: to distinguish means to tell two things apart by noticing what makes them different.

docs.title: Diagram: Positive or Negative? Influence Sorter
docs.text:
Positive or Negative? Influence Sorter MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: positive-or-negative-influence-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: distinguish, examine, differentiate

Learning objective: Students distinguish positive influences from negative influences by sorting simple, everyday scenario cards into two labeled bins, matching the Grade 1 benchmark on which people or situations positively or negatively influence a health behavior.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): One scenario card at a time, shown as a short sentence with a simple flat illustration - Right area (150px): Two labeled bins, "Positive Influence" and "Negative Influence," plus an infobox

Visual elements: - 8 scenario cards cycling one at a time, such as: "A grandparent packs apple slices in your lunch," "A commercial makes candy look like the best snack ever," "A friend invites you to ride bikes after school," "A show makes staying up past bedtime look fun," "A coach reminds the team to drink water," "A friend dares you to skip washing your hands" - Two friendly labeled bins with icons (a sun for "Positive Influence," a cloud for "Negative Influence")

Interactive controls: - Click-to-select: student clicks the bin that matches the scenario - Button: "Next Scenario" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - First scenario: "A grandparent packs apple slices in your lunch" (clearly positive, to build confidence)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scenario card with no label Stage 2: After the student clicks a bin, show whether it matches Stage 3: Reveal a one-sentence explanation of why the scenario is a positive or negative influence

Behavior: - Correct match: bin glows softly, gentle chime, explanation caption appears - Incorrect match: gentle prompt, "Take another look — does this make a healthy choice easier or harder?", correct bin glows softly as a hint

Instructional Rationale: This is an Analyze-level (distinguish/examine) objective, so the MicroSim has students actively sort concrete examples into two categories rather than only reciting definitions, building the pattern-recognition skill needed to notice influences in real life.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep all scenarios everyday and age-appropriate — no mention of substances or mature themes, since this Grade 1 skill focuses on everyday choices like food, activity, sleep, and hygiene.

Big Idea

Influences are all around you every day. A positive influence makes a healthy choice easier. A negative influence makes it harder. Noticing which is which helps you choose well.

docs.title: Communicating Feelings: Using Words to Share How You Feel
docs.text:
You've learned to notice influences on your choices. Next, let's look at a skill that helps with almost every part of health: communicating clearly. Students explored feelings in Chapter 3 — feelings are the emotions we experience, like happy, sad, worried, or excited. Communicating feelings means using words, and sometimes gestures or pictures, to tell another person how you feel inside.

Communicating feelings matters because other people cannot see what's happening inside you. A trusted adult or friend can only help once they know how you feel. Saying "I feel worried about the spelling test" or "I feel happy that you shared your crayons with me" gives other people the information they need to respond in a caring way.

Here are simple sentence starters a Grade 1 student can use to communicate feelings:

  • "I feel _ because ___."
  • "Right now I am feeling _____."
  • "That made me feel _____."

docs.title: Communicating Needs: Using Words to Ask for What You Need
docs.text:
Closely related to communicating feelings is communicating needs — using words to tell another person what you need, such as help, rest, food, or space. A need is different from a feeling: a feeling is how you feel inside, while a need is something that would help you feel better or stay healthy.

For example, a student who feels tired (a feeling) might communicate the need by saying, "I need to rest for a few minutes" (a need). A student who feels hungry might say, "I need a snack." Communicating needs clearly — instead of just acting upset or frustrated — helps other people understand exactly how to help.

Here is how feelings and needs work together, using a few common Grade 1 examples:

Situation Feeling Communicating the Need Missed recess because of rain Disappointed "I need to move my body — can we do an indoor activity?" Loud, crowded classroom Overwhelmed "I need a quiet moment, please." Difficult math problem Frustrated "I need help with this problem." Left out of a game Sad "I need a friend to play with."

docs.title: Diagram: Feelings and Needs Communication Coach
docs.text:
Feelings and Needs Communication Coach MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: feelings-and-needs-communication-coach Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, apply

Learning objective: Students demonstrate communicating thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs in healthy ways by building a complete sentence from a picture prompt, matching the Grade 1 benchmark on communicating thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs in healthy ways.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): One picture-prompt scene at a time (e.g., a child looking left out at recess) - Right area (150px): Word-bank buttons for feelings and needs, plus a sentence-building strip and an infobox

Visual elements: - 6 scenes showing a Grade 1 student in a common school or home situation (rained-out recess, loud classroom, hard homework problem, left out of a game, tired after lunch, excited about a good grade) - A sentence strip at the bottom that fills in as the student taps word-bank buttons: "I feel ___ because . I need ." - Word-bank buttons grouped by feeling words (happy, sad, tired, frustrated, worried, excited) and need words (help, rest, a friend, quiet, a snack, a turn)

Interactive controls: - Click-to-select: student taps a feeling word and a need word to complete the sentence strip - Button: "Try Saying It" (pairs with the text-to-speech skill to read the finished sentence aloud in a warm, encouraging voice) - Button: "Next Scene" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - First scene: rained-out recess, to model a low-stakes, relatable example

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the picture prompt with an empty sentence strip Stage 2: Show the sentence strip fill in as each word is selected Stage 3: Reveal a caption once the sentence is complete: "Great! You just told someone exactly how you feel and what you need."

Behavior: - Multiple feeling-and-need combinations are accepted as correct for each scene, since more than one honest answer can fit a situation - Completed sentence appears in a speech bubble above the character in the scene

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (demonstrate/practice) objective, so the MicroSim has students actively construct their own feeling-and-need sentences from a word bank rather than only reading examples, directly rehearsing the healthy-communication skill the benchmark calls for.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep all scenes warm and everyday; avoid any scenario resembling the personal-safety content from Chapter 6, since this MicroSim focuses on everyday emotional and physical needs, not unsafe situations.

You now know two important communication skills: sharing feelings and sharing needs. Sometimes, though, sharing a feeling or a need isn't quite enough on its own — sometimes what's needed is help from another person. Let's look at that next.

docs.title: Seeking Help: Reaching Out When You Need Support
docs.text:
Seeking help means reaching out to another person — often a trusted adult — when you need support with a problem, a task, or a feeling. Students already practiced asking a trusted adult in Chapter 6 in the context of safety. Seeking help is the broader skill underneath that: knowing that it is always okay, and often the smart choice, to ask for support rather than struggling alone.

Seeking help can happen for all kinds of reasons — not just emergencies. A student might seek help to open a stubborn juice box, to understand a confusing homework question, to find a bandage for a scraped knee, or to talk through a disagreement with a friend. There is no situation too small to ask for help with, and there is no situation so big that asking for help is the wrong choice.

Helpful Tip

Asking for help is not a sign of weakness — it's a smart, healthy habit. The people who care about you want to know when you need support.

docs.title: Recognizing Need For Help: Noticing When It's Time to Ask
docs.text:
Before a student can seek help, they need a skill that comes first: recognizing need for help, which means noticing the signs that a situation calls for support from someone else. This might mean noticing that a task feels too hard to finish alone, that a feeling is too big to handle by yourself, or that a friend seems to be struggling and could use a helper too.

Recognizing the need for help is like the "uh-oh feeling" students learned about in Chapter 6, but broader: it's the moment of noticing "I can't quite do this by myself" or "This doesn't feel right," and understanding that the very next step is to seek help.

Here are common signs that it's time to ask for help:

  1. A task keeps feeling too hard, even after trying more than once.
  2. A feeling is very big — like very sad, very worried, or very angry — and it isn't going away.
  3. Something feels unsafe, confusing, or wrong.
  4. A friend or classmate seems to need support too.

docs.title: Diagram: Time to Ask? Recognizing the Signs
docs.text:
Time to Ask? Recognizing the Signs Infographic

Type: infographic sim-id: time-to-ask-recognizing-the-signs Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: recognize, describe, explain

Learning objective: Students recognize when help is needed and who can support a health-related decision by exploring everyday scenes and identifying the signal that it's time to seek help.

Purpose: Help students connect a feeling or situation to the recognition that help is needed, reinforcing the Grade 1 benchmark on recognizing when help is needed and who can support a decision

Layout: A single friendly scene with four clickable characters, each showing a different situation (a student stuck on a shoe tying, a student with a very big worried feeling before a test, a student who can't reach a high shelf, a student who notices a friend sitting alone and looking sad)

Interactive elements: - Click each character to reveal a caption naming the sign ("This task feels too hard alone," "This feeling is very big," "I can't do this safely by myself," "My friend might need help too") and a matching helper suggestion (family member, teacher, school staff, trusted friend) - A summary panel lists all four signs after all characters have been clicked

Visual style: Warm, everyday classroom and home scenes in flat illustration style; no distressing imagery, just relatable Grade 1 moments Color scheme: Soft, warm palette consistent with the rest of the book

Implementation: p5.js with clickable character hotspots mapped to caption reveals; a simple counter tracks how many of the four signs have been explored

docs.title: Health Decision: Choosing an Action That Supports Your Wellbeing
docs.text:
All the skills covered so far — noticing influences, communicating feelings and needs, recognizing when to ask for help, and seeking that help — come together in one important idea: the health decision. A health decision is a choice a person makes that affects their health or safety, such as choosing a snack, deciding how to spend free time, or deciding whether to tell a trusted adult about a problem.

Some health decisions are easy and can be made alone, like choosing water instead of soda. Other health decisions are harder and benefit from asking a trusted adult for support — especially when a positive or negative influence is involved, or when the student isn't sure what to do.

Let's connect this to something students already know: a positive influence made a health decision easier, while a negative influence made it harder. A student who recognizes a negative influence (like a friend daring them to skip handwashing) can use that recognition to make a healthier decision (washing their hands anyway, and telling a trusted adult if the dare continues).

docs.title: Diagram: Making a Healthy Choice Decision Path
docs.text:
Making a Healthy Choice Decision Path MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: making-a-healthy-choice-decision-path Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, describe, summarize

Learning objective: Students explain the steps of making a health decision — noticing the influence, thinking about the choice, and asking for help if needed — using a step-through walkthrough with a concrete, relatable scenario.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): One decision-path scene per step, shown one at a time - Right area (150px): "Next Step" and "Previous Step" buttons, a step counter ("Step 2 of 4"), and an infobox

Visual elements: - Step 1: A student is offered a sugary snack by a friend at lunch (the influence) - Step 2: A thought bubble shows the student asking, "Is this a positive or negative influence on my choice right now?" - Step 3: A thought bubble shows the student deciding, "I can choose the fruit instead," or "I'm not sure — I could ask a trusted adult." - Step 4: The student makes the healthy choice and feels proud

Interactive controls: - Button: "Next Step" (advances to the next scene) - Button: "Previous Step" (returns to the prior scene) - Step counter always visible

Default parameters: - Starts at Step 1 (the influence is introduced)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the snack offer and caption: "A friend offers you a sugary snack every day at lunch." Stage 2: Show the thinking step and caption: "Notice the influence — is it helping or making the choice harder?" Stage 3: Show the decision step and caption: "Decide what to do, or ask a trusted adult if you're not sure." Stage 4: Show the outcome and caption: "You made a health decision that supports your body."

Behavior: - Each click of "Next Step" reveals the next scene and caption; "Previous Step" allows review - A closing caption after Step 4 reads: "Every health decision follows this same path: notice the influence, think it through, ask for help if you need it, then choose."

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level (explain/describe) objective, so the MicroSim uses a step-through walkthrough with a concrete scenario rather than continuous animation, letting students trace the full decision path in order and connect it back to the influence and help-seeking concepts already taught in this chapter.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep the scenario everyday and low-stakes (food choice), since Grade 1 health decisions should stay concrete and relatable rather than abstract.

Big Idea

A health decision is a choice that affects your health or safety. Notice the influence, think it through, and remember — asking a trusted adult for help is always part of making a good choice.

docs.title: Tracking Health Behaviors: Watching Your Healthy Habits Over Time
docs.text:
Making one good health decision is a great start, but health also grows from tracking health behaviors — watching and recording healthy practices over time, like brushing teeth, being active, or eating a variety of foods. Tracking connects directly to personal care practice and physical activity from Chapter 5: those are the habits, and tracking is how a student notices whether the habits are actually happening regularly.

Tracking doesn't need to be complicated. A Grade 1 student might use a simple chart with a box to check off each day they brush their teeth, drink water, or play actively outside. Seeing the checked boxes build up over a week helps a student feel proud of their healthy habits and notice patterns, like which days are harder to be active.

Here are simple ways a Grade 1 student can track health behaviors:

  • A weekly chart with a box to check for each healthy habit completed
  • Stickers placed on a calendar for each day a habit happens
  • A short conversation with a family member each night about the day's healthy choices

docs.title: Diagram: My Healthy Habits Tracker
docs.text:
My Healthy Habits Tracker MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: my-healthy-habits-tracker Library: Chart.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, track

Learning objective: Students demonstrate and track practices and behaviors that support health and wellbeing by checking off a simple weekly habit tracker and watching a bar chart grow, matching the Grade 1 benchmark on demonstrating and tracking health-supporting practices.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): A 7-day-by-4-habit checklist grid (rows: "Brushed Teeth," "Drank Water," "Active Play," "Ate a Fruit or Vegetable"; columns: Monday through Sunday) - Right area (150px): A live-updating bar chart showing total check marks per habit, plus an infobox

Visual elements: - Checklist grid with clickable checkboxes for each day/habit cell - A bar chart with one bar per habit, height matching how many days that habit was checked this week - A friendly weekly total counter ("You tracked 18 healthy habits this week!")

Interactive controls: - Click-to-toggle: student clicks a checkbox to mark a habit complete for a day - Button: "New Week" (clears the grid to start tracking again) - Hover on any bar to see the exact count and which days were checked

Default parameters: - All checkboxes start unchecked - Chart updates immediately as boxes are checked

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the empty checklist grid and a bar chart with all bars at zero Stage 2: Show a bar grow immediately each time a checkbox is clicked Stage 3: Show the weekly total counter update with each new check mark

Behavior: - Every checkbox click immediately updates the corresponding bar in the chart, giving instant visible feedback - Hovering a bar shows a tooltip with the exact number of days checked, reinforcing that hovering reveals more detail

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (demonstrate/track) objective, so the MicroSim has students actively practice the real skill of tracking — checking boxes and watching a chart respond — rather than only reading about the idea of tracking, which directly rehearses the benchmark's call for demonstration.

Implementation notes: Use Chart.js for the live bar chart paired with a simple HTML/CSS checklist grid. Teacher can use this as a model before students start a paper or take-home version of the same weekly tracker.

docs.title: Asking For Help With Choices: Bringing It All Together
docs.text:
The final concept in this chapter — and in the whole Grade 1 book — is asking for help with choices: reaching out to a trusted adult or another trusted person specifically to help think through a health decision. This brings together everything from this chapter: recognizing when help is needed, and using that recognition to make a better health decision.

Asking for help with a choice does not mean someone else makes the decision instead of the student. It means the student shares the situation, listens to ideas, and then makes a more informed choice. For example, a student unsure whether a snack is a healthy choice might ask, "Can you help me decide what to eat before my game?" A trusted adult can offer information the student didn't have, making the final decision easier and healthier.

Here are simple phrases a Grade 1 student can use to ask for help with a choice:

  1. "I'm not sure what to do — can you help me think about it?"
  2. "Can you help me decide between these two things?"
  3. "What would you do if you were me?"

You Can Do This

Asking for help with a hard choice can feel a little scary at first — that's okay. The more you practice asking, the easier and more natural it becomes, and you'll always have people ready to help you think it through.

docs.title: Diagram: Ask for Help With a Choice — Practice Scenarios
docs.text:
Ask for Help With a Choice — Practice Scenarios MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: ask-for-help-with-a-choice-practice-scenarios Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, apply

Learning objective: Students demonstrate asking for help from others in making safe, health-promoting choices by selecting an appropriate help-seeking phrase in response to everyday decision scenarios, matching the Grade 1 benchmark on ways to ask for help in making safe, health-promoting choices.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): One decision scenario at a time (e.g., "You're not sure if you should play outside or rest because you feel a little sick.") - Right area (150px): Three phrase-choice buttons and an infobox

Visual elements: - 6 scenario cards covering food, activity, rest, and hygiene decisions - Three phrase-choice buttons per scenario, drawn from the sentence starters taught in this section

Interactive controls: - Click-to-select: student selects the phrase they would use to ask for help - Button: "Try Saying It" (pairs with the text-to-speech skill to play the chosen phrase aloud) - Button: "Next Scenario" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - First scenario: deciding between playing outside and resting when feeling a little tired, a low-stakes and relatable example

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scenario and three phrase choices, no feedback yet Stage 2: After a choice is selected, show a caption affirming that asking for help was the right move Stage 3: Reveal a closing caption: "Asking for help with a choice means you get to think it through with someone who cares about you."

Behavior: - All three phrase choices are treated as correct, since the goal is building the habit of asking, not testing for one exact phrase - Every scenario ends with the same reinforcing message about the value of asking for help

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (demonstrate/practice) objective, so the MicroSim has students rehearse real help-seeking language across several everyday decisions, directly matching the benchmark's call for demonstrating ways to ask for help with health-promoting choices.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep every scenario everyday and low-stakes, reinforcing that asking for help is for big and small choices alike.

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text:
This chapter, and the Grade 1 book, close by connecting nine ideas into one habit of mind: notice the influence, communicate the feeling or need, recognize when help is needed, seek that help, and use it to make and track a healthy decision. By the end of this chapter, most Grade 1 students should be able to tell a positive influence from a negative one, use a simple sentence to communicate a feeling or need, name a sign that it's time to ask for help, and describe at least one way to track a healthy habit. These are lifelong skills — please continue to revisit them in short check-ins throughout Grade 1 and beyond, connecting them back to the food, feelings, friendship, healthy habits, and safety topics from earlier chapters.

You Finished the Whole Book!

Congratulations, friend! You made it through the whole Grade 1 book — from food and feelings to friendship, healthy habits, safety, and now getting help and making good choices. You've built so many healthy habits this year. Healthy choices, happy you!

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "If you're not sure whether a choice is healthy, what can you do?" Then reveal: You can ask a trusted adult to help you think it through — asking for help is always a smart, healthy choice.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 1
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 1 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than a general-purpose graph — 55 concepts rather than 200 — because Grade 1 health benchmarks are identify-and-explain-level content for 6-7 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Kindergarten band's 45-concept graph and uses the same 7-category taxonomy for cross-band comparability.

docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 1 course description is a well-structured, standards-traceable document derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards. It enumerates 24 benchmark-coded topics across five content strands (Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) plus a cross-cutting Skill Standards group, and organizes learning outcomes using the 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze — with Evaluate and Create deliberately thin/absent per the developmental design of the K-12 standards, and this is explicitly documented in the text rather than an oversight).

Because this is a Grade 1 (early elementary, beginning-reader) band, the topic set is intentionally narrow — identify/explain-level content and simple demonstration tasks rather than multi-step reasoning or design tasks. This assessment therefore evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 50-55 concepts, not the skill's generic 200-concept default, which would force invented content not grounded in the standards.

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Every topic traces to a specific MDE benchmark code, giving the learning graph strong provenance.

  • Clear five-strand + Skill Standards structure maps cleanly onto a taxonomy consistent with the Kindergarten band's scheme.

  • Key Vocabulary section (14 terms) gives ready-made concept candidates.

  • Explicit "Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band" section clarifies which Kindergarten-level ideas are assumed but not re-taught.

  • Explicit, documented rationale for the thinness of Evaluate- and Create-level content avoids the false impression of an oversight and matches the developmental progression described in the standards.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
• No dedicated "Topics Excluded" section (partial credit given based on related context elsewhere in the document).

  • Apply and Analyze outcomes are present but modest in count, reflecting the developmental level of the band (early elementary, identify/explain plus simple demonstration) rather than a document defect.

  • Evaluate- and Create-level outcomes are explicitly deferred to Grade 2-3, which is appropriate for this band but caps rubric points under a generic scoring template designed for adult/higher-ed courses.

docs.title: Concept Count Guidance
docs.text: Per explicit run-level override, this band targets approximately 50-55 concepts (not 200), built only from the 24 enumerated benchmarks, the 14 key vocabulary terms, and a small number of clearly-implied bridging concepts. This is appropriate given the identify/explain-level scope of Grade 1 health standards, and keeps the graph comparable in density to the Kindergarten band's 45-concept graph.

docs.title: Course Description — Grade 2
docs.text: This is the Grade 2 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 2.1.1.1) are <grade>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text: Early elementary, independent reading of short passages expected. Benchmarks introduce comparison ("compare the sugar and caffeine in various drinks") and simple cause-effect explanation, alongside continued identify/describe work.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 2 students (age ~7-8) and their teachers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Grade 1 benchmarks across all 5 content strands, plus the Grade 1 skill benchmarks (identifying influences, seeking help, communicating feelings, recognizing decision points, tracking a health practice).

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student arriving directly at Grade 2 without the K-1 sections should be briefly introduced to these ideas first:

  • Food groups exist and different foods serve different purposes; some drinks are healthier choices than others.
  • Feelings can be talked about, and different situations affect how people feel.
  • Trusted adults can be asked for help, and simple I-statements ("I feel...") are one way to share a feeling.
  • Basic hygiene habits (handwashing, covering coughs) prevent germs from spreading.
  • Technology use has safety rules, including asking permission.
  • "No" is an acceptable response to unwanted or unsafe touch, and there are known safe places and routines for school emergencies.

docs.title: Food and Nutrition
docs.text:
• What each food group does for the body; how trying varied foods supports growth (2.1.1.1)
  • Comparing sugar/caffeine across drinks and their health impact (2.1.1.2)
  • How food provides energy and supports growth (2.1.1.3)
  • Why safe practices matter for storing, preparing, and handling food (2.1.1.4)

docs.title: Human Growth and Development
docs.text: • Different types of peer relationships (2.2.1.1)

docs.title: Mental and Emotional Health
docs.text:
• Coping strategies and cultural practices (e.g., storytelling, ceremony) for well-being (2.3.1.1)
  • Recognizing needs helps understand personal space and boundaries (2.3.1.2)
  • Healthy ways to handle conflict, manage/express struggling emotions or stress, and share feelings with trusted adults (2.3.1.3)
  • Playful and kind interaction; how different types of teasing affect feelings and community (2.3.1.4)

docs.title: Personal Health and Wellness
docs.text:
• Protecting the body from environmental health risks: sun exposure, loud noise, unsafe chemicals, unsafe water (2.4.1.1)
  • Types of physical activity, including cultural/traditional games or dances, and how they support health (2.4.1.2)
  • How germs spread through air, food, water, and personal contact; illness prevention through hygiene, clean environments, and cultural traditions (2.4.1.3)

docs.title: Personal Safety and Violence Prevention
docs.text:
• Unsafe or uncomfortable technology situations and getting help from a trusted adult (2.5.1.1)
  • Encouraging others toward safe choices, drawing on community values and cultural traditions (2.5.1.2)
  • Strategies for staying safe during drills away from the classroom/teacher (2.5.1.3)
  • Saying no or exiting a situation involving inappropriate touch (2.5.1.4)

docs.title: Skill Standards
docs.text:
• How family, school, and media/technology influence health practices and behaviors (2.7.2.1)
  • How to locate and use school and community health helpers (2.7.3.1)
  • Using simple I-statements to share feelings (2.7.4.1)
  • Demonstrating active listening in a variety of situations (2.7.4.2)
  • Describing options and potential outcomes for a health-related decision (2.7.5.1)
  • Determining actions that support a personal health-related goal and reflecting on results (2.7.6.1)
  • Recognizing how current practices/behaviors make you feel (2.7.7.1)
  • Modeling positive health choices for others (2.7.8.1)

docs.title: Key Vocabulary
docs.text: food group, energy, food safety, peer relationship, coping, personal space, boundary, conflict, teasing, environmental health risk, physical activity, germs, hygiene, technology safety, active listening, I-statement, goal setting

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: Outcomes below are grouped by Bloom's Taxonomy level and traced to their source benchmark codes.

docs.title: 1. Remember
docs.text:
By the end of Grade 2, the student will be able to:

  1. Recall different types of peer relationships (2.2.1.1).
  2. Recall ways to protect the body from environmental health risks such as sun exposure, loud noise, unsafe chemicals, and unsafe water (2.4.1.1).
  3. Recall unsafe or uncomfortable technology situations (2.5.1.1).
  4. Recall strategies for staying safe during drills away from the classroom (2.5.1.3).

docs.title: 2. Understand
docs.text:
1. Describe what each food group does for the body and how trying a variety of foods supports growth (2.1.1.1).
  2. Explain how food gives energy and helps the body grow (2.1.1.3).
  3. Describe why safe practices matter for storing, preparing, and handling food (2.1.1.4).
  4. Describe strategies to cope with challenges, including cultural practices such as storytelling and ceremony (2.3.1.1).
  5. Explain how recognizing your needs helps you understand personal space and boundaries (2.3.1.2).
  6. Describe healthy ways to handle conflict and manage or express struggling emotions (2.3.1.3).
  7. Describe playful, kind ways to interact and how different types of teasing affect feelings and community (2.3.1.4).
  8. Describe types of physical activity, including cultural/traditional games or dances, and how they support health (2.4.1.2).
  9. Describe how germs spread through air, food, water, and personal contact, and ways to prevent illness (2.4.1.3).
  10. Describe ways to encourage others toward safe choices, drawing on community values and cultural traditions (2.5.1.2).
  11. Explain how family, school, and media/technology influence health practices and behaviors (2.7.2.1).
  12. Explain how to locate and use school and community health helpers (2.7.3.1).
  13. Describe options and potential outcomes for a health-related decision (2.7.5.1).
  14. Recognize how current practices and behaviors make you feel (2.7.7.1).

docs.title: 3. Apply
docs.text:
1. Demonstrate saying no or exiting a situation involving inappropriate touch (2.5.1.4).
  2. Use simple I-statements to share feelings with others (2.7.4.1).
  3. Demonstrate active listening skills in a variety of situations (2.7.4.2).
  4. Model positive health choices to encourage the health, safety, and wellbeing of others (2.7.8.1).

docs.title: 4. Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare the sugar and caffeine content of various drinks and analyze their impact on health (2.1.1.2).
  2. Determine actions that support achieving a personal health-related goal (2.7.6.1).

docs.title: 5. Evaluate
docs.text: 1. Reflect on the results of working toward a personal health-related goal (2.7.6.1).

docs.title: 6. Create
docs.text: Grade 2 benchmarks do not yet include a design/construct task. Determining actions toward a goal (2.7.6.1, listed under Analyze above) is the closest precursor — true goal-plan construction (resources, barriers, progress-tracking) begins at Grade 4.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This Grade 2 section of the textbook is organized into 7 chapters covering 55 concepts from the Grade 2 learning graph.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Health Basics, Friendships, and Feelings - Introduces the idea of health itself, peer relationships, and early emotional-health tools like coping strategies, personal space, boundaries, and I-statements.
  2. Food, Energy, and Safe Eating - Explores what food groups do for the body, how variety and energy support growth, and why safe storage, preparation, and handling of food matter.
  3. Handling Conflict and Kind Play - Builds on early emotional-health tools to address conflict resolution, managing strong emotions, playful interaction, and the effects of teasing.
  4. Staying Healthy in Our Environment - Covers protecting the body from environmental health risks, the value of physical activity, and how germs spread and can be prevented.
  5. Technology, Community, and Emergency Safety - Addresses safe technology use, encouraging safe choices through community values, staying safe during drills, and finding health helpers.
  6. Body Safety and Speaking Up - A focused chapter on recognizing unwanted touch and practicing how to say no or exit an unsafe situation.
  7. Influences, Decisions, and Personal Goals - Ties the band together with how family, school, and media influence health behaviors, how to weigh decisions, and how to set and reflect on personal health goals.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Work through the chapters in order — each one builds on concepts introduced earlier, so completing chapters 1 through 6 will prepare students for the decision-making and goal-setting skills in Chapter 7. Teachers may revisit Chapter 6 (Body Safety and Speaking Up) as a standalone lesson whenever a sensitive-topics refresher is needed, since it does not depend on chapters after it.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This opening chapter introduces the concept of health itself as the foundation for everything else in the Grade 2 band. Students learn about the different kinds of peer relationships they experience at school and in their community, and they build a first toolkit for emotional well-being: coping strategies (including cultural practices such as storytelling and ceremony), personal space, boundaries, and simple I-statements for sharing feelings. After completing this chapter, students will be able to name a coping strategy, describe a boundary, and use an I-statement to express a feeling.
