docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Use This Chapter
docs.text:
This chapter is written for you, the teacher, to read aloud, narrate, and guide from. Grade 2 students are gaining independence as readers, but full comprehension of these ideas still depends on your read-aloud support and classroom discussion. Use the text below as a script while your class explores the pictures and MicroSims. Every interactive element is designed for a child to click, drag, or point at while you talk them through it.

Hi! I'm Scout.

Welcome to Grade 2 Health Education! I'm Scout, a friendly dog who loves helping kids make healthy choices. I'll be popping up all through this book, but I don't show up just anywhere — I have exactly six jobs, and you can tell which one I'm doing by my pose:

  1. Welcome you at the start of every chapter — that's what I'm doing right now.
  2. Help you think about a big idea, using my thinking pose.
  3. Give you a tip — a small, helpful trick to remember something.
  4. Warn you gently when something needs extra care or a grown-up's help.
  5. Encourage you when an idea feels new or a little tricky.
  6. Celebrate with you when you've learned something great.

That's it — six jobs, six poses. If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. Let's think it through together, friend. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: What Is Health?
docs.text:
Health means how well a person's body and mind are working and feeling. A second grader who is healthy has energy to run, play, and learn, and also has ways to notice and share how they feel inside. Health is not just "not being sick." It includes eating well, moving your body, resting enough, staying safe, and — just as important this year — understanding your feelings, your friendships, and the space around your body.

Talking points for read-aloud:

  • Ask the class: "Besides food and sleep, what else does a healthy person need?"
  • Guide answers toward friends, feelings, calm-down strategies, and personal space.
  • Explain that this chapter is about the people and feelings parts of health — the friends we make and the tools we use when big feelings show up.

Big Idea

Health isn't only about your body. It's also about your friendships and your feelings — and knowing what to do when either one needs some care.

docs.title: Meeting Peer Relationships
docs.text:
A peer relationship is a connection you have with someone your own age — a classmate, a teammate, a neighbor kid, a cousin close to your age. Peers are different from the trusted adults in your life because peers are equals: you are learning and growing together, side by side.

Not every peer relationship looks the same. That is where types of peer relationships come in. Comparing them helps students notice that different peers play different roles in daily life.

Here are common types of peer relationships a second grader might notice:

Type of Peer Relationship What It Looks Like Classmate Someone who shares your classroom and daily activities Friend Someone you choose to spend time with and trust Teammate Someone you work with toward a shared goal, like a game or project Neighbor or Cousin Someone close in age you see outside of school

Comparing these types matters: a classmate might not be a close friend yet, and that is perfectly normal. A good teammate might become a friend over time. Noticing the differences helps students understand why some relationships feel closer than others — try comparing two peer relationships from your own life to see how they are alike and how they differ.

docs.title: Diagram: Sort the Peer Relationship
docs.text:
Sort the Peer Relationship MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: peer-relationship-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: classify, compare, contrast

Learning objective: Students classify short everyday scenes into the correct type of peer relationship (classmate, friend, teammate, neighbor/cousin) and compare what makes each type similar or different.

Canvas layout: - Top area (150px): One short illustrated scene at a time (e.g., two children sharing a reading table, two children building a blanket fort together, a soccer team huddled before a game, two cousins playing at a family picnic) - Middle area (250px): Four labeled bins: "Classmate," "Friend," "Teammate," "Neighbor/Cousin" - Bottom strip (100px): Explanation caption and "Next Scene" button

Visual elements: - 8 simple scenes cycling one at a time, flat friendly illustration style, evenly covering all four relationship types

Interactive controls: - Click or drag the scene into the matching bin - Button: "Next Scene" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - First scene: two children sharing a classroom reading table (clear "Classmate" example, to build confidence)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scene with no label Stage 2: After the student picks a bin, show the correct label and a one-sentence reason Stage 3: Show a short compare line such as "A classmate shares your room. A friend is someone you also choose to be with."

Behavior: - Correct placement: bin glows, gentle chime, reason caption appears - Incorrect placement: calm prompt, "Look again — where do these two children usually spend time together?" - After all scenes, a summary caption reminds students that one person can be more than one type of peer at the same time (a teammate can also be a friend)

Instructional Rationale: Classifying and comparing types of peer relationships is an Understand-level task, so the pattern uses step-through scenes with a revealed reason and comparison line rather than animation. This matches the Grade 2 benchmark shift toward comparison, not just naming a single peer relationship.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep scenes warm and inclusive of different family and cultural configurations (cousins, multigenerational households, blended families). Large text for read-aloud.

docs.title: Coping Strategies: Tools for Big Feelings
docs.text:
Everyone — kids and grown-ups alike — has moments with big feelings: frustration, worry, sadness, excitement that feels like too much. A coping strategy is something a person does on purpose to feel better or calmer when a feeling gets big. Coping strategies are not about making a feeling disappear — they are tools that help a person move through the feeling safely.

Some common coping strategies for second graders:

  1. Taking slow, deep breaths.
  2. Counting to ten, or counting backward from ten.
  3. Drawing or writing about the feeling.
  4. Asking for a hug or quiet time.
  5. Moving the body — stretching, walking, or squeezing a soft object.
  6. Talking to a trusted adult about what happened.

Helpful Tip

A coping strategy works best when you practice it on a calm day first. Try one right now — take three slow breaths together as a class — so it's ready to use when a big feeling shows up!

docs.title: Cultural Coping Practices
docs.text:
Coping strategies are not only breathing and counting. Families and communities around the world have practiced cultural coping practices for generations — traditions that help people feel calm, connected, and supported during hard times or big feelings. These practices are just as real and just as valuable as any other coping strategy, and they connect a person to their family's and community's history.

Examples of cultural coping practices from different traditions:

  • Storytelling — sharing a family story, legend, or teaching tale to make sense of a hard moment or pass down wisdom.
  • Ceremony — a gathering, song, prayer, or ritual that marks an important moment or brings a community together for comfort.
  • Music and dance — singing a family song or dancing a traditional dance to release feelings and feel connected to others.
  • Shared meals — cooking or eating a familiar food together as a way of comforting one another.

Every student's family may practice coping in its own way, and there is no single "right" cultural practice — the goal is for students to recognize that coping can look different across families and still be healthy and valuable. Maybe your family tells stories at bedtime, sings a special song, or has a favorite gathering — all of these can be healthy ways of coping.

docs.title: Diagram: Coping Strategies Around the World
docs.text:
Coping Strategies Around the World Infographic

Type: infographic sim-id: coping-strategies-map Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, exemplify, explain

Learning objective: Students describe a range of coping strategies, including cultural practices such as storytelling and ceremony, and explain how each one helps a person feel calmer or more supported.

Purpose: Show a warm, inclusive gallery of coping strategies — both everyday strategies (breathing, drawing) and cultural practices (storytelling, ceremony, music, shared meals) — so students see coping as a wide, respected toolkit rather than one narrow method.

Layout: A grid or gentle circle of 8 labeled picture-cards, each representing one coping strategy or cultural practice.

Cards to include: 1. Deep Breathing 2. Counting Calmly 3. Drawing Feelings 4. Quiet Hug Time 5. Family Storytelling 6. Community Ceremony 7. Traditional Music and Dance 8. Sharing a Meal Together

Interactive elements: - Hover or tap a card: card enlarges slightly and an infobox appears explaining what the practice is and how it helps - Click a card: the infobox stays open with a simple explanation a teacher can read aloud, plus one example sentence ("Some families gather for a ceremony to feel connected and supported.") - "Show Me Another Family's Way" button cycles an optional second example for the cultural cards, reinforcing that many traditions exist

Visual style: Warm, flat illustration style with diverse families and settings represented respectfully; no single culture singled out or stereotyped.

Color scheme: Soft, calming colors (light blue, warm yellow, soft green) rather than bright primary colors, to reinforce a calm mood.

Responsive behavior: Grid reflows from 4 columns to 2 columns on narrow screens; cards remain tappable at all sizes.

Implementation: p5.js with an object array of card data (label, description, example) driving hover/click infobox display.

docs.title: Recognizing Personal Needs
docs.text:
Before a person can ask for help or set a boundary, they first need to notice what they are feeling and what they need. Recognizing personal needs means paying attention to signals from your own body and mind — like feeling crowded, tired, hungry, or overwhelmed — and understanding what would help.

This skill connects directly to the next two ideas in this chapter: personal space and boundaries. A student who can say "I need some quiet space right now" is using recognizing personal needs, personal space, and communication all at once.

Simple signals that can help students recognize a need:

  • A tight or fluttery feeling in the stomach may mean worry or nervousness.
  • Wanting to move away from a crowd may mean a need for quiet or personal space.
  • Feeling grumpy or tired may mean a need for rest or food.
  • Feeling left out may mean a need for connection or to talk to someone.

Noticing Takes Practice

Noticing your own feelings and needs is a brand-new skill, and it can feel tricky at first. That's completely normal — the more you practice pausing and asking "What do I need right now?", the easier it gets. You've got this!

docs.title: Personal Space and Boundaries
docs.text:
Personal space is the area around a person's body that feels comfortable and safe to them. Everyone's personal space is a little different, and it can even change depending on the day or the situation. Recognizing your own needs helps you notice when your personal space feels crowded or uncomfortable.

A boundary is a limit a person sets to protect their personal space, body, feelings, or belongings. A boundary tells other people what is okay and what is not okay. Boundaries are healthy — they are not unfriendly. Good friends and family respect each other's boundaries.

Examples of healthy boundaries a second grader might set:

  1. "Please knock before you come into my room."
  2. "I don't want a hug right now, but a high-five is okay."
  3. "Please ask before you borrow my things."
  4. "I need quiet time before I want to talk about my day."

Your Space, Your Choice

Personal space is like an invisible bubble around your body. You get to decide who comes close and how — and it's okay to say so out loud!

docs.title: Diagram: My Personal Space Bubble
docs.text:
My Personal Space Bubble MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: personal-space-bubble Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, apply

Learning objective: Students apply the idea of personal space and boundaries by adjusting a visible "bubble" around a character and practicing a boundary sentence for different situations.

Canvas layout: - Left/center area (450px): A friendly cartoon child character in the middle of the canvas with a circular "bubble" drawn around them showing personal space - Right/control area (150px): Slider and scenario buttons

Visual elements: - Character in the center with a soft, translucent circle (the "bubble") around them - A second character figure that can be dragged closer or farther away - Scenario labels above (e.g., "A classmate you just met," "Your best friend," "Someone offering a high-five")

Interactive controls: - Slider: "Bubble Size" (small, medium, large) representing that personal space can change based on comfort - Draggable second figure: moving it closer shows the bubble highlighting yellow when "crowded," green when comfortable - Button: "Try a Boundary Sentence" — reveals one of the four example boundary sentences from the text, matched to the scenario - Button: "Next Scenario"

Default parameters: - Default bubble size: medium - First scenario: "A classmate you just met" approaching

Behavior: - When the second figure enters the bubble and turns yellow, a caption prompts: "This might feel crowded. What boundary sentence could you use?" - Clicking "Try a Boundary Sentence" shows an example sentence appropriate to the scenario, read aloud by the teacher - Resetting returns the second figure to a comfortable distance and the bubble to green

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (demonstrate/practice) objective, so the MicroSim requires the learner to actively adjust the scene and select/practice a boundary sentence rather than passively watch an animation. Direct manipulation of the "bubble" builds concrete understanding that personal space is real, visible, and adjustable.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep character designs simple and neutral so any student can see themselves in the scene. Maintain a warm, non-alarming tone — this is about everyday comfort, not danger.

docs.title: Sharing Feelings with an I-Statement
docs.text:
Once a student recognizes a need or a boundary, the next step is sharing it out loud in a healthy way. An I-statement is a simple sentence that starts with "I" and shares a feeling, need, or boundary without blaming or accusing anyone else. I-statements work well because they focus on your own feeling, which is easier for another person to hear and understand.

A simple I-statement pattern:

"I feel ___ when , and I need ."

Example I-statements a second grader might use:

  • "I feel frustrated when my blocks get knocked down, and I need us to build carefully."
  • "I feel happy when you share the swing with me."
  • "I feel crowded when you sit so close, and I need a little more space."
  • "I feel left out when I'm not picked for a game, and I need a turn next time."

I-statements connect every idea in this chapter: they use recognizing personal needs (noticing the feeling), they can express a boundary (saying what you need), and they help peer relationships stay respectful and kind.

docs.title: Diagram: Build Your Own I-Statement
docs.text:
Build Your Own I-Statement MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: i-statement-builder Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: use, demonstrate, practice

Learning objective: Students use the "I feel ___ when , and I need " sentence pattern to build I-statements that share a feeling or boundary in a healthy way, applying the pattern to new scenarios.

Canvas layout: - Top area (150px): A short scene showing a situation between two peers (e.g., someone cutting in line, someone sharing a toy nicely, someone sitting too close, someone including a classmate in a game) - Middle area (250px): Three tile columns the student clicks in order — "I feel ," "when ," and "I need ___" — each with 3-4 short word/phrase options - Bottom strip (100px): The assembled I-statement displays large; "Next Scene" button

Visual elements: - 6 scenes cycling one at a time, mixing situations that need a boundary (crowding, interrupting) and situations that celebrate a peer relationship (sharing, including)

Interactive controls: - Click tiles in order to build the sentence - Button: "Hear My I-Statement" (displays the completed sentence large for teacher read-aloud) - Button: "Next Scene"

Default parameters: - First scene: someone sitting too close during story time (clear personal-space example, to build confidence)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scene and the empty sentence frame ("I feel ___ when , and I need .") Stage 2: Show each tile choice highlighted as the student clicks it Stage 3: Show the complete I-statement filled in, large and readable, with the peer character responding warmly

Behavior: - Once all three blanks are filled with a reasonable combination, the peer character in the scene nods and a gentle chime plays - Multiple valid combinations are accepted, since more than one honest I-statement can fit a scene; combinations that are unrelated or unkind receive a gentle prompt to try again

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level (use/demonstrate) objective, so students must construct and produce an I-statement rather than merely recognize one. A tile-based builder scaffolds students who are still developing independent writing while keeping the focus on applying the sentence pattern to new situations.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep tile text short (2-5 words) and large. Teacher reads the finished I-statement aloud with the student and discusses how the peer in the scene might respond.

docs.title: Bringing It All Together
docs.text:
Health is the big idea this whole book explores, and this chapter connected it to the people around us and the feelings inside us. Peer relationships come in different types — classmates, friends, teammates, neighbors and cousins — and comparing them helps students understand their own social world. When big feelings show up, coping strategies (including cultural practices like storytelling and ceremony) give students real tools to feel calmer. Recognizing personal needs leads directly to personal space and boundaries, and an I-statement is the healthy way to share all of it out loud.

Every later Grade 2 chapter — food, physical activity, safety, and asking for help — will build on these same words: health, peer relationships, coping, personal space, boundaries, and I-statements.

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, most Grade 2 students should be able to name a coping strategy (including a cultural example), compare two types of peer relationships, describe what a personal space boundary is, and use an I-statement pattern to share a feeling. The MicroSims in this chapter move from simple classification (peer relationship sorter) to applied practice (personal space bubble, I-statement builder), matching the Grade 2 shift toward comparison and cause-effect explanation described in the course description.

Chapter Complete!

You made it through the whole chapter, friend! You now know about health, peer relationships, coping strategies, personal space, boundaries, and I-statements. Keep these ideas close — we'll use every one of them again soon. Healthy choices, happy you!

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "What are the three parts of an I-statement?" Then reveal: "I feel ___ when , and I need ."

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter explores what each food group does for the body and why trying a variety of foods supports growth. Students compare the sugar and caffeine content of different drinks to understand how drink choices affect health, and they learn why safe practices for storing, preparing, and handling food matter. After completing this chapter, students will be able to explain how food provides energy, compare drink choices, and describe a food-safety practice.

This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Health Basics, Friendships, and Feelings

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Use This Chapter
docs.text:
This chapter is written for you, the teacher, to read aloud, narrate, and guide from. Grade 2 students are building independent reading skills, but full comprehension of food-safety rules and drink comparisons still depends on your read-aloud support and classroom discussion. Use the text below as a script while your class explores the pictures and MicroSims.

Let's Talk About Food!

Hi again, friend! Today we're going to explore food groups, find out where our energy comes from, compare some drinks, and learn how to keep food safe. Let's think it through together. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: What Food Groups Do for the Body
docs.text:
Every food we eat belongs to a food group, and each food group has a special job to do inside the body. Food group function means understanding what each group of foods actually does for you — it is not enough to just name the groups, we want to know why they matter.

Talking points for read-aloud:

  • Ask the class: "What do you think happens inside your body after you eat breakfast?"
  • Guide answers toward growing, moving, healing, and thinking.
  • Explain that different food groups do different jobs, just like different tools in a toolbox.

Here is what each major food group does for the body:

Food Group What It Does for the Body Example Foods Grains Gives quick, lasting energy for the whole day Bread, rice, oatmeal Vegetables Helps the body fight germs and stay strong Carrots, broccoli, spinach Fruits Gives vitamins and helps the body heal and stay healthy Apples, oranges, berries Protein (meat, beans, eggs, nuts) Builds and repairs muscles and body parts Chicken, beans, eggs Dairy Builds strong bones and teeth Milk, cheese, yogurt

Big Idea

Food groups aren't just a list to memorize — each one has a real job. Grains give you energy, protein builds muscle, dairy builds bones, and fruits and vegetables help you stay well.

docs.title: Diagram: What Each Food Group Does
docs.text:
What Each Food Group Does MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: food-group-function-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, describe, classify

Learning objective: Students explain what each food group does for the body by clicking on a food group icon and seeing its job and example foods.

Canvas layout: - Left area (450px): Five large tappable food-group icons arranged in a row or wheel (Grains, Vegetables, Fruits, Protein, Dairy) - Right area (150px): Infobox panel showing the selected group's job and example foods

Visual elements: - Flat, friendly icons for each food group (a wheat stalk, a carrot, an apple, a drumstick/bean pod, a milk carton) - A simple cartoon child character in the center who "reacts" (stretches, flexes, smiles) based on which group is selected

Interactive controls: - Click a food-group icon to select it - Button: "Show Me a Meal" — displays a simple plate containing one example from each group

Default parameters: - No group selected at start; instructions read "Tap a food group to see its job!"

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show five icons with no explanation Stage 2: On click, show the group name and its one-sentence job ("Grains give you energy to run and play!") Stage 3: Show 2-3 example foods for that group Stage 4: The character animation matches the job (flexes for protein, stretches for grains)

Behavior: - Clicking a new icon updates the infobox and character animation immediately - "Show Me a Meal" button highlights one food from each group on a plate graphic to reinforce that a healthy meal uses several groups together

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level (explain/describe) objective, so the design uses direct click-to-reveal information rather than animation for its own sake. Concrete text and example foods are visible at every stage so a teacher can read them aloud.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep icons large and simple for read-aloud pointing. Ensure text is large enough to read from the front of a classroom.

docs.title: Trying a Variety of Foods
docs.text:
No single food group can do every job by itself. That is why variety of foods matters: eating different foods from different groups — and different foods within each group — helps the body get everything it needs to grow.

Think of it this way: if a student only ate bread every day, their body would have plenty of energy but would be missing the vitamins from fruits and vegetables and the muscle-building power of protein. Trying new foods, including foods from different cultures and family traditions, is one of the best ways to make sure the body gets a full set of tools for growing.

Some ways to try more variety:

  1. Add one new fruit or vegetable to a plate each week.
  2. Try a food from a classmate's or neighbor's family tradition.
  3. Choose a different grain, like brown rice or whole wheat bread, instead of the same one every day.
  4. Notice the colors on your plate — different colors often mean different vitamins.

Helpful Tip

A fun way to remember variety is to "eat the rainbow" — try to get a few different colors of fruits and vegetables on your plate each day!

docs.title: Food Energy: Fuel for Growing and Playing
docs.text:
Food energy is the power that food gives your body to move, grow, think, and even just breathe and stay warm. Every single thing your body does — running at recess, solving a math problem, healing a scraped knee — uses energy that came from food you ate earlier.

A simple cause-and-effect way to think about it: when you eat, your body breaks the food down and turns it into energy; when you use that energy all day, you start to feel hungry again, which is your body's signal that it needs more fuel.

  • Eating breakfast gives you energy to focus in the morning.
  • Running out of food energy can make a person feel tired, cranky, or unable to concentrate.
  • Growing bodies need food energy not just to move, but to build new bone, muscle, and skin as they grow taller.

Ever feel grumpy or tired before lunchtime? That's a totally normal signal that your body needs more food energy — noticing that feeling is a great health skill.

docs.title: Diagram: Where Does Your Energy Come From?
docs.text:
Where Does Your Energy Come From? MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: food-energy-cause-effect Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, interpret

Learning objective: Students explain the cause-and-effect relationship between eating food and having energy to grow, move, and think, using a step-through scenario of a school day.

Canvas layout: - Top area (150px): A timeline strip showing four moments in a school day (Breakfast, Morning Class, Recess, Afternoon Snack) - Middle area (250px): A character whose "energy meter" (a simple bar or battery icon) rises and falls at each moment - Bottom strip (100px): Step-through "Next" and "Back" buttons with a caption

Visual elements: - Energy meter styled like a friendly battery icon (empty to full) - Character shown running, thinking, or yawning depending on energy level

Interactive controls: - Button: "Next" advances to the next moment in the day - Button: "Back" returns to the previous moment - Click the energy meter at any time to see a caption explaining the current energy level

Default parameters: - Starts at "Breakfast" with a full energy meter

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show "Breakfast" — energy meter fills up, caption: "Food gives the body energy to start the day." Stage 2: Show "Morning Class" — energy meter slightly lower, caption: "The body uses energy to think and pay attention." Stage 3: Show "Recess" — energy meter drops more, caption: "Running and playing use up energy fast!" Stage 4: Show "Afternoon Snack" — energy meter refills, caption: "Eating again gives the body more energy to finish the day."

Behavior: - Each step change animates the energy meter rising or falling and updates the caption - If the student clicks "Next" repeatedly past snack, the cycle can loop back to show energy needs happen all day, every day

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level (explain) objective focused on cause and effect, so the design uses a step-through timeline with visible energy-level data at each stage rather than continuous animation, letting students trace the cause (eating) to the effect (energy available) explicitly.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep the energy meter large and simple, like a battery icon. Captions should be large enough for read-aloud.

docs.title: Comparing Drink Choices: Sugar and Caffeine
docs.text:
Not all drinks are the same, and comparing them is an important health skill. Two things to look for and compare in a drink are sugar in drinks and caffeine in drinks.

Sugar in drinks means the extra sweet stuff added to many juices, sodas, and flavored drinks. A little sugar occasionally is not harmful, but drinks with a lot of added sugar, especially every day, can lead to problems like tooth decay and feeling tired after a sugar "crash."

Caffeine in drinks is a substance found in some sodas, some teas, and energy drinks that can make a person's heart beat faster and make it harder to fall asleep at night. Caffeine is generally not recommended for children, so recognizing which drinks contain it is an important skill.

Read the Label

Some drinks that taste fruity or fun might still have caffeine or a lot of added sugar hiding inside. It's always smart to ask a trusted adult to help read the label before trying a new drink.

Comparing drink choices means looking at two or more drinks side by side and deciding which one is the healthier choice based on what is inside them. This is a genuine comparison skill for Grade 2 — not just naming what is in one drink, but weighing several drinks against each other.

Here is a side-by-side comparison of common drinks:

Drink Sugar Level Caffeine? Healthiest Everyday Choice? Water None No Yes — best everyday choice Plain milk Low (natural) No Yes — good everyday choice Fruit juice High No Occasional treat, not every day Soda Very high Often yes Not a good everyday choice Sports drink High No Only needed after long, hard exercise Sweetened iced tea High Often yes Not a good everyday choice

Comparing this table row by row shows a clear pattern: the drinks with the least sugar and no caffeine — water and plain milk — are the best everyday choices, while drinks high in sugar or caffeine are better saved for special occasions.

docs.title: Chart: Comparing Sugar and Caffeine in Drinks

  1. Caffeine Level (blue bars):
  2. Water: 0
  3. Plain Milk: 0
  4. Fruit Juice: 0
  5. Soda: 3
  6. Sports Drink: 0
  7. Sweetened Iced Tea: 3

Title: "Comparing Sugar and Caffeine in Common Drinks" Legend: Top-right, showing gold = sugar level, blue = caffeine level

Interactive elements: - Hover over any bar to see a tooltip with the exact drink name, the level, and a one-sentence explanation ("Soda has the highest sugar level and often contains caffeine too.") - Toggle buttons: "Show Sugar Only," "Show Caffeine Only," "Show Both" to let students focus the comparison - Click a drink name on the x-axis to highlight both of its bars and show a caption: "This drink is [not a good everyday choice / a good everyday choice] because..."

Annotations: - A dashed horizontal line at level 1 labeled "Best Everyday Zone" so students can visually see which drinks fall below it

Implementation: Chart.js grouped bar chart with a button group wired to dataset visibility toggling and an onHover tooltip callback.

Comparing drinks is like being a detective — look at the sugar, look at the caffeine, and then decide which drink is the better everyday choice for every day.

docs.title: Why Food Safety Matters
docs.text:
Choosing healthy foods and drinks is only part of the picture — keeping food safe is just as important. Food that is not stored, prepared, or handled safely can make people sick, even if the food itself is healthy.

There are three parts to food safety that second graders should know about: storing food, preparing food, and handling food. Each one happens at a different point before food reaches your plate.

Big Idea

Food safety isn't just one rule — it's three steps working together: keeping food stored right, preparing it carefully, and handling it with clean hands.

docs.title: Food Storage Safety
docs.text:
Food storage safety means keeping food at the right temperature and in the right place so it does not spoil or grow harmful germs. Some foods need to stay cold in the refrigerator, some need to stay frozen, and some are safe at room temperature in a sealed container.

Simple food storage safety rules:

  1. Put milk, eggs, and meat in the refrigerator right away.
  2. Keep the refrigerator door closed as much as possible to stay cold.
  3. Check that leftovers go into the fridge soon after a meal, not left out for hours.
  4. Store raw meat on a lower shelf so its juices cannot drip onto other foods.

docs.title: Food Preparation Safety
docs.text:
Food preparation safety means using safe practices while food is being cooked or made ready to eat — like washing fruits and vegetables, cooking meat thoroughly, and keeping raw and cooked foods separate.

Simple food preparation safety rules:

  1. Wash fruits and vegetables under running water before eating them.
  2. Use a different cutting board for raw meat than for vegetables.
  3. Make sure meat is cooked all the way through, not left raw or pink inside.
  4. Keep pets and pests away from food preparation areas.

docs.title: Food Handling Safety
docs.text:
Food handling safety means the everyday habits a person uses whenever they touch food — this is the part every second grader can practice themselves, every day.

Simple food handling safety rules:

  1. Wash your hands with soap before touching or eating food.
  2. Use clean utensils and plates, not ones that touched raw meat.
  3. Do not share drinks or food that has already touched someone else's mouth.
  4. Tell a trusted adult if food smells strange, looks moldy, or seems spoiled.

docs.title: Workflow: From Store to Plate — Keeping Food Safe
docs.text:
From Store to Plate — Keeping Food Safe Workflow

Type: workflow sim-id: food-safety-workflow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, explain, classify

Learning objective: Students describe why safe practices matter at each stage food travels through — storage, preparation, and handling — by clicking each step to reveal its safety rule.

Purpose: Show the journey of food from the store to the plate, with a safety habit attached to each stage, so students see storage, preparation, and handling as three connected but distinct steps.

Visual style: Left-to-right Mermaid flowchart with four boxes and arrows between them

Steps: 1. Box: "Food Arrives Home" (storage stage) Click text: "Food Storage Safety: Put cold foods like milk and meat in the refrigerator right away so they don't spoil."

  1. Box: "Food Gets Prepared" (preparation stage) Click text: "Food Preparation Safety: Wash fruits and vegetables, cook meat fully, and use separate cutting boards for meat and produce."

  2. Box: "Food Is Handled" (handling stage) Click text: "Food Handling Safety: Wash your hands before eating and use clean plates and utensils."

  3. Box: "Food Is Enjoyed Safely" (outcome) Click text: "When all three safety steps are followed, food is much less likely to make someone sick!"

Color coding: - Blue: Storage stage - Green: Preparation stage - Orange: Handling stage - Gold: Final safe-to-eat outcome

Interactive features: Every node in the Mermaid diagram has a click NodeId call showInfo("nodeName") handler that opens an infobox with the safety rule text above, matching the glossary definition for that concept.

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart syntax with click directives bound to a small JavaScript showInfo() function that displays the infobox panel beneath the diagram.

Chapter Complete!

Great work, friend! You now know what each food group does, why trying variety matters, where your energy comes from, how to compare sugar and caffeine in drinks, and the three parts of food safety. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, most Grade 2 students should be able to name what one food group does for the body, explain that food gives energy, compare two drinks and say which is the healthier everyday choice, and name at least one food-safety rule for storage, preparation, or handling. The MicroSims in this chapter move from simple click-to-reveal exploration (food group function, food energy) to genuine comparison (the sugar/caffeine drink chart), matching the Grade 2 shift toward comparison and cause-effect explanation described in the course description.

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "Which drink is the best everyday choice — water or soda — and why?" Then reveal: "Water is the best everyday choice because it has no added sugar and no caffeine."

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Building on the coping strategies and emotional-health foundations from Chapter 1, this chapter addresses healthy ways to handle conflict and manage or express strong emotions, including sharing feelings with a trusted adult. Students also examine playful interaction and how different types of teasing affect feelings and community. After completing this chapter, students will be able to describe a healthy conflict-resolution step and explain how teasing can affect others.

docs.title: Prerequisites

This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Health Basics, Friendships, and Feelings

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Use This Chapter
docs.text:
This chapter is written for you, the teacher, to read aloud, narrate, and guide from. Grade 2 students are building independent reading skills, but full understanding of conflict, strong emotions, and teasing still depends on your read-aloud support and classroom discussion. Use the text below as a script while your class explores the pictures and MicroSims. Two sections in this chapter — Teasing and Effects Of Teasing — touch on peer conflict and emotional harm, so the tone there stays plainly sincere rather than playful.

Getting Along and Playing Kindly

Hi again, friend! Today we're going to talk about what happens when people disagree, how to handle big feelings, and how to play in ways that feel good to everyone. Let's think it through together. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: What Is Conflict?
docs.text:
Conflict happens whenever two or more people want different things, disagree, or have a problem to work out together. Conflict is a normal part of life — it happens between friends, between brothers and sisters, and even between grown-ups. Having a conflict does not mean two people are bad friends; it just means they need to find a way to solve a problem.

Conflict can look like:

  • Two friends both wanting to be first in line.
  • Two students disagreeing about the rules of a game at recess.
  • A brother and sister both wanting the same toy at the same time.
  • A group project where classmates have different ideas about what to do.

Big Idea

Conflict is not the same as a fight. Conflict is just a disagreement — what matters most is how people choose to handle it.

docs.title: Healthy Conflict Resolution
docs.text:
Healthy conflict resolution means using calm, respectful steps to solve a disagreement so that everyone involved feels heard and the problem gets better instead of worse. Second graders can learn a simple, repeatable set of steps to use whenever a conflict comes up, whether it is at school, at home, or on the playground.

Here is a simple four-step process students can practice:

  1. Stop and take a breath. Pause before reacting so you can think clearly.
  2. Say how you feel using an "I-statement." For example, "I feel frustrated when we can't agree on the game."
  3. Listen to the other person's side. Let them explain what they want and why.
  4. Find a solution together. Try taking turns, compromising, or asking an adult to help if you get stuck.

Before we look at the diagram below, notice that these four steps always happen in the same order: calm down first, then talk, then listen, then solve. Skipping a step — like trying to "solve" before anyone has calmed down — usually makes the conflict harder to fix.

docs.title: Diagram: Four Steps to Solve a Conflict
docs.text:
Four Steps to Solve a Conflict MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: conflict-resolution-steps Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, use, practice

Learning objective: Students apply the four-step healthy conflict resolution process to a simple playground scenario by choosing what to do at each step.

Canvas layout: - Top area (100px): A short scenario banner describing a conflict (e.g., "Two friends both want to use the only jump rope at recess.") - Middle area (300px): Four large numbered step cards (Stop and Breathe, Say How You Feel, Listen, Find a Solution) arranged left to right - Bottom area (100px): An infobox that shows feedback text

Visual elements: - Four step cards, each with a simple icon (a hand for "stop," a speech bubble for "say how you feel," an ear for "listen," a handshake for "find a solution") - Two simple cartoon children shown at the top holding a jump rope

Interactive controls: - Click each step card in order to reveal what that step looks like in this scenario - Button: "Try a New Scenario" — swaps in one of three preset conflict scenarios (jump rope, board game turn, group project idea) - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - Scenario 1 (jump rope) selected at start - No steps revealed yet; instructions read "Click Step 1 to begin!"

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scenario banner and four unrevealed step cards Stage 2: Click Step 1 -- show caption "Both friends stop and take a deep breath instead of grabbing the rope." Stage 3: Click Step 2 -- show caption "One friend says, 'I feel left out when I don't get a turn.'" Stage 4: Click Step 3 -- show caption "The other friend listens and says, 'I didn't know you felt that way.'" Stage 5: Click Step 4 -- show caption "They agree to take turns every five minutes."

Behavior: - Steps must be revealed in order; clicking a later step before an earlier one shows a gentle reminder to go in order - After all four steps are revealed, a checkmark appears over the scenario banner and the infobox reads "Conflict solved calmly!" - "Try a New Scenario" resets all four steps to unrevealed and loads new scenario text

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level objective, so the design lets students practice choosing and sequencing the four steps in a concrete scenario rather than just watching an animation. Requiring steps in order reinforces that healthy conflict resolution is a repeatable process, not a random set of options.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep text large enough for read-aloud. Icons should be simple and flat, matching the mascot's friendly visual style.

Helpful Tip

A trusted adult can always help if a conflict feels too big to solve alone. Asking for help is part of solving the problem, not giving up on it.

docs.title: Managing Strong Emotions
docs.text:
Sometimes a conflict — or something else entirely — brings up feelings that feel very big, like anger, frustration, or sadness. Managing strong emotions means noticing when a feeling is big and using a calming strategy before acting on it, instead of letting the feeling take over.

Big feelings are not bad. Everyone has them. What matters is what a person does next. Here are some strategies Grade 2 students can use to manage strong emotions:

  • Take three slow, deep breaths.
  • Count slowly to ten.
  • Squeeze a stress ball or hug a stuffed animal.
  • Walk away from the situation for a moment to cool down.
  • Draw or write about the feeling.
  • Ask for a hug or quiet moment with a trusted adult.

Managing a strong emotion is different from ignoring it. Ignoring a feeling means pretending it is not there; managing a feeling means noticing it, naming it, and choosing a calm way to work through it.

docs.title: Diagram: Cooling Down a Big Feeling
docs.text:
Cooling Down a Big Feeling MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: managing-strong-emotions-cooldown Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, describe

Learning objective: Students explain how a calming strategy lowers a strong emotion over time by stepping through a "feelings thermometer" scenario.

Canvas layout: - Left area (200px): A vertical "feelings thermometer" showing emotion intensity from calm (bottom, blue) to very upset (top, red) - Right area (400px): A step-through scene with a character and a caption box, plus Next/Back buttons

Visual elements: - Thermometer with a marker that moves up or down - A simple cartoon character whose face changes expression (frustrated, calming, calm) at each stage - Caption box below the character

Interactive controls: - Button: "Next" advances to the next stage of the scenario - Button: "Back" returns to the previous stage - Dropdown: Choose which calming strategy the character tries (deep breaths, counting to ten, walking away)

Default parameters: - Thermometer starts near the top (very upset) after a conflict scenario is described - Default strategy: "deep breaths"

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show thermometer high (red) with caption "A friend took the last turn on the swing. This character feels really upset!" Stage 2: Show the chosen calming strategy happening, thermometer marker begins moving down, caption names the strategy: "Taking three deep breaths..." Stage 3: Show thermometer lower (yellow), caption "The feeling is getting smaller." Stage 4: Show thermometer near bottom (blue/calm), caption "Now the character feels calm enough to talk about what happened."

Behavior: - Changing the strategy dropdown resets the scenario and shows a slightly different caption for each strategy, so students see that different strategies can all work - The thermometer marker animates smoothly between stages when Next/Back is clicked

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level (explain) objective about a cause-and-effect process, so the design uses a step-through thermometer with visible stages rather than continuous animation, letting students trace how a calming strategy causes the emotion to shrink over time.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep the thermometer large and simple. Facial expressions should be easy to read from across a classroom.

You've Got This!

Big feelings can feel scary at first, but they always get smaller with time and a calming strategy. You've got this!

docs.title: Sharing Feelings With a Trusted Adult
docs.text:
Sometimes a feeling is too big to manage alone, or a conflict is too hard to solve without help. Sharing feelings with a trusted adult means telling a parent, teacher, or other safe grown-up what happened and how it made you feel, so they can help.

A trusted adult is someone a student and their family already know is safe and caring — often a parent, teacher, school counselor, or another caregiver. Sharing feelings with a trusted adult is not "tattling" — it is a healthy skill that helps solve problems that feel too big to handle alone.

A simple way to share a feeling with a trusted adult is to use an I-statement, the same skill from Chapter 1:

"I feel ___ when ___ happens."

For example: "I feel sad when my friend teases me about my drawing."

Recall from Chapter 1 that active listening — giving full attention, making eye contact, and reflecting back what you heard — is also something a trusted adult uses when a student shares a feeling with them.

docs.title: Playful Interaction
docs.text:
Not every moment with friends involves conflict — most of the time, being with friends means playful interaction: joking, laughing, and having fun together in ways that feel good to everyone involved. Playful interaction is a big part of healthy friendships and healthy communities.

Kind, playful interaction usually shares a few features:

Feature of Kind Play What It Looks Like Everyone is laughing together No one feels left out or made fun of Playing stops if someone says "stop" Friends respect when a game or joke needs to end Turns and rules are fair Everyone gets a chance to play or lead Words build people up Jokes are about silly situations, not about a person's body, family, or abilities

This table sums up a pattern worth remembering: kind, playful interaction always leaves everyone feeling included, not just some of the people involved. Playful interaction is meant to bring people closer together — if a "joke" pushes someone away or makes them feel small, it has stopped being playful.

docs.title: Teasing
docs.text:
Teasing is when someone makes a joking remark, often about another person, that can feel funny to one person but hurtful to another. Teasing sits right on the edge between playful interaction and something that can cause real harm, which is why it is important to understand it carefully.

There are different types of teasing, and they do not all feel the same:

  • Playful teasing between friends who both agree it is funny — for example, gently joking about a shared inside joke that both people laugh about.
  • Teasing that targets something a person cannot easily change — like their name, their family, how they look, or something they are working hard to learn.
  • Repeated teasing that continues after someone has asked it to stop.

The second and third types of teasing are not healthy play, even if the person doing the teasing says "I was just joking." A joke that only one person finds funny is not truly playful — it is something else, and it deserves a caring, honest look rather than a light one.

An Important Difference

If a joke keeps happening after someone has said "please stop" or shown they are hurt, it is not playful teasing anymore — it needs a trusted adult's help.

docs.title: Effects of Teasing
docs.text:
Effects of teasing refers to how teasing changes the way a person feels — about themselves, about the person teasing them, and about being part of the group. Understanding these effects helps students recognize when a joke has crossed the line from fun into harm, in themselves and in others.

Teasing that is unwanted can lead to feelings like:

  1. Embarrassment or shame, even about something that is not actually a problem.
  2. Sadness or loneliness, especially if the teasing happens in front of others.
  3. Anger or frustration at being made fun of.
  4. Worry about being teased again, which can make a person avoid places or people.

These effects do not stay only with one person. When teasing happens in a classroom or on a playground, it can change how safe the whole group feels — some students may start to worry they could be teased next, which can make a classroom or community feel less kind overall.

docs.title: Diagram: How Teasing Can Ripple Through a Group
docs.text:
How Teasing Can Ripple Through a Group MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: effects-of-teasing-ripple Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, distinguish, compare

Learning objective: Students examine how one instance of unwanted teasing can affect not only the person teased but also the feelings of others who witness it, distinguishing this from playful interaction that everyone enjoys.

Canvas layout: - Center area (300px): A simple classroom or playground scene with five small cartoon children arranged in a loose circle - Right area (300px): An infobox panel that displays feeling-word text for whichever character is clicked

Visual elements: - Five simple, calm cartoon children figures, each a neutral color at the start - A toggle switch at the top labeled "Kind Joke" / "Unwanted Teasing"

Interactive controls: - Toggle: Switch between "Kind Joke" scenario and "Unwanted Teasing" scenario - Click any child figure to reveal how that character likely feels in the current scenario, shown in the infobox

Default parameters: - Toggle starts on "Kind Joke" - No character selected at start; instructions read "Click a character to see how they feel."

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1 (Kind Joke toggle): All five figures shown smiling; clicking any one shows infobox text such as "This friend is laughing along -- everyone agreed the joke was funny." Stage 2 (Unwanted Teasing toggle): The figure representing the teased child turns a muted color with a downturned expression; clicking it shows infobox text "This student feels embarrassed and left out." Stage 3 (Unwanted Teasing toggle): Clicking one of the four onlooker figures shows infobox text such as "This classmate feels uneasy watching -- they wonder if it could happen to them next."

Behavior: - Switching the toggle immediately redraws all five figures' expressions and colors to match the selected scenario - Every character is clickable in both scenarios, so students can compare how the same group of children feels differently depending on whether the interaction was a kind joke or unwanted teasing

Instructional Rationale: This is an Analyze-level objective requiring students to distinguish between two situations and examine effects on multiple people, so the design uses a compare-toggle with clickable figures rather than a single animation, letting students directly contrast how kind play and unwanted teasing ripple differently through a group.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep facial expressions simple, clear, and non-exaggerated so the emotional contrast is easy to read without being upsetting. Maintain a calm, caring visual tone throughout -- avoid cartoonish exaggeration of sadness.

docs.title: Recognizing Feelings About Behaviors
docs.text:
The last skill in this chapter ties everything together. Recognizing feelings about behaviors means noticing and naming how a specific action — your own or someone else's — makes you or others feel, so you can decide what to do next.

This skill applies to everything covered in this chapter:

  • Recognizing that a conflict is making you feel frustrated is the first step toward using healthy conflict resolution.
  • Recognizing that a feeling is getting too big is the first step toward managing strong emotions.
  • Recognizing that a joke made a friend feel small — even if it was meant to be funny — is the first step toward understanding the effects of teasing.

A simple habit for practicing this skill is to pause after any interaction and ask: "How did that make me feel? How might it have made the other person feel?" Comparing your own reaction to how someone else might have reacted is exactly the kind of comparison skill Grade 2 students are building this year. Try asking that question after playtime, a disagreement, or a joke — noticing your own feelings is a skill that gets stronger every time you practice it.

Here is a quick summary connecting each concept in this chapter to the skill it builds:

Concept Skill It Builds Conflict Recognizing that a disagreement is happening Healthy Conflict Resolution Solving a disagreement calmly, step by step Managing Strong Emotions Calming down before reacting Sharing Feelings With Trusted Adult Asking for help with a feeling or problem Playful Interaction Having fun together in ways that include everyone Teasing Telling the difference between a joke everyone enjoys and one that hurts Effects Of Teasing Understanding how teasing changes feelings for a person and a group Recognizing Feelings About Behaviors Naming feelings caused by an action, in yourself and others Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "Your friend teases you about tripping in the hallway, and you feel embarrassed even after you ask them to stop. What is the healthiest next step?" Then reveal: "Share the feeling with a trusted adult, since the teasing continued after being asked to stop — that is no longer playful teasing."

Chapter Complete!

Wonderful work, friend! You now know how to handle conflict calmly, manage big feelings, share feelings with a trusted adult, play kindly, and recognize how teasing affects everyone. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text: By the end of this chapter, most Grade 2 students should be able to describe at least one step of healthy conflict resolution and explain how teasing can affect the person being teased as well as others who see it happen. The MicroSims in this chapter move from an Apply-level step-through of the conflict-resolution process, to an Understand-level cooldown scenario for strong emotions, to an Analyze-level comparison of kind play versus unwanted teasing — matching the Grade 2 emphasis on comparison and cause-effect explanation. Because the Teasing and Effects Of Teasing sections touch on peer conflict and emotional harm, consider pairing this chapter with a class discussion norm (for example, "we can disagree about a game, but we don't make fun of who someone is") before moving on to Chapter 4.

docs.text: This chapter introduces environmental health risks such as sun exposure, loud noise, unsafe chemicals, and unsafe water, and how to protect the body from them. Students learn about the value of physical activity, including cultural and traditional games or dances, and explore how germs spread through air, food, water, and personal contact along with the hygiene practices that prevent illness. After completing this chapter, students will be able to describe an environmental health risk, name a form of physical activity, and explain how illness prevention works.

docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 8 concepts from the learning graph:

  1. Environmental Health Risk

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Health Basics, Friendships, and Feelings

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Use This Chapter
docs.text:
This chapter is written for you, the teacher, to read aloud, narrate, and guide from. Grade 2 students are building independent reading skills, but full understanding of environmental risks and disease prevention still depends on your read-aloud support and classroom discussion. Use the text below as a script while your class explores the pictures and MicroSims. The tone throughout stays warm and encouraging, since this chapter focuses on everyday protective habits rather than sensitive personal-safety content.

Taking Care of Our Bodies and Our World

Hi again, friend! Today we're exploring how our bodies and the world around us work together. We'll look at things in our environment that can hurt us, how to protect ourselves, why moving our bodies feels great, and how tiny germs spread — and how we stop them. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: What Is an Environmental Health Risk?
docs.text:
An environmental health risk is anything in the world around us — in the air, water, ground, or nearby objects — that could hurt our bodies if we are not careful. Environmental health risks are different from germs or foods; they come from the environment itself, like the sun overhead, a loud sound, a bottle of cleaning spray, or water that is not safe to drink.

Second graders encounter environmental health risks almost every day, often without noticing them. Understanding what they are is the first step toward protecting the body. Common environmental health risks include:

  • Strong sunlight that can burn skin.
  • Loud noises that can hurt ears.
  • Chemicals, such as cleaning products or medicines, that are unsafe to touch, smell, or taste.
  • Water that has not been made safe to drink.

Notice that these four risks come from very different places — the sky, a sound, a bottle, and a faucet — but they share one thing in common: each one can hurt the body if a person does not know how to protect against it. None of these things are "bad" on their own — the sun helps plants grow, and cleaning products keep our homes healthy! The risk only appears when we don't protect ourselves the right way.

docs.title: Sun and Noise Protection
docs.text:
Sun and noise protection means using specific habits and tools to keep sunlight and loud sounds from damaging the skin and ears. These two risks are grouped together because both come from everyday parts of life — being outside and hearing sounds — that become safer with simple protective steps.

Protecting skin from the sun:

  1. Wear sunscreen on skin that will be in the sun.
  2. Wear a hat that shades the face and neck.
  3. Wear sunglasses that block bright light.
  4. Sit in shade during the sunniest part of the day.

Protecting ears from loud noise:

  1. Cover ears or wear ear protection near very loud sounds, like fireworks or power tools.
  2. Move away from a sound that hurts your ears.
  3. Keep headphone volume at a level where you can still hear someone talking next to you.

Before trying the diagram below, think about this: sun protection and noise protection use different tools (sunscreen versus earmuffs), but they follow the exact same pattern — notice the risk, then choose a protection step before damage happens, not after.

docs.title: Diagram: Match the Protection to the Risk
docs.text:
Match the Protection to the Risk MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: sun-noise-protection-match Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: use, demonstrate, practice

Learning objective: Students apply the correct protective action to a sun-risk or noise-risk scenario by matching protection tools/habits to the situation shown.

Canvas layout: - Top area (100px): A scenario banner showing a picture and short caption (e.g., "It's a sunny day at the park.") - Middle area (300px): Four draggable/clickable protection icons (sunscreen bottle, sun hat, ear muffs, "move away" arrow) - Bottom area (100px): Infobox showing feedback text

Visual elements: - Six preset scenario cards that cycle through: sunny playground, loud fireworks show, sunny beach, noisy construction site, cloudy park (no risk), quiet library (no risk) - Four protection icons that can be clicked to "apply" to the current scenario

Interactive controls: - Button: "Next Scenario" cycles to the next of six scenario cards - Click a protection icon to apply it to the current scenario - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - Scenario 1: sunny playground - No protection icon selected yet

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show scenario image and caption for "sunny playground" Stage 2: Student clicks sunscreen or sun hat icon -- infobox shows "Correct! Sunscreen protects skin from sunburn on a sunny day." Stage 3: Student clicks ear muffs icon on the same sunny scenario -- infobox shows "Ear protection isn't needed here -- there's no loud noise in this scene. Try a sun-protection icon instead." Stage 4: Student advances to "loud fireworks" scenario and clicks ear muffs -- infobox shows "Correct! Ear protection keeps loud fireworks sounds from hurting your ears."

Behavior: - Each scenario has one or two correct protection icons; clicking a correct icon highlights it green and shows a matching explanation - Clicking an icon that does not match the current risk shows a gentle correction explaining why, without a red "wrong" buzzer sound - "Cloudy park" and "quiet library" scenarios teach that not every situation needs sun or noise protection

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level objective, so students practice choosing and using the correct protective action for a specific situation rather than only reading a list. Including two "no risk needed" scenarios helps students discriminate between situations that need protection and situations that do not, avoiding the misconception that protection is always required everywhere.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep icons large, simple, and high-contrast for young readers. Use encouraging tones in all feedback text.

Helpful Tip

A good habit is to put on sunscreen and a hat before going outside to play, not after your skin already feels hot. Protecting first is always easier than fixing later!

docs.title: Unsafe Chemicals and Water
docs.text:
Unsafe chemicals and water refers to substances that look harmless — or even inviting — but can make a person very sick if touched, tasted, or swallowed. This includes cleaning products, medicines that belong to someone else, and water that has not been made safe to drink.

Some important safety rules:

  • Never touch, smell, or taste a cleaning product, spray, or medicine without a trusted adult.
  • Many unsafe chemicals are kept in bottles that look like drinks or candy — always check with an adult first.
  • Not all water is safe to drink. Water from a pond, puddle, or unfamiliar source may contain unsafe chemicals or germs.
  • Only drink water that a trusted adult says is safe, such as from a home tap, a water fountain, or a sealed bottle.

Comparing safe and unsafe water sources helps make this idea concrete:

Water Source Usually Safe to Drink? Why Home kitchen tap Yes Treated and tested by the water system School water fountain Yes Treated and tested, checked by adults Sealed bottled water Yes Sealed and tested before sale Puddle or pond No Not treated; may carry germs or chemicals Unlabeled bottle found outside No Could contain an unsafe chemical, not water

This table shows a pattern worth remembering: a water source is safe when a trusted adult and a water system have checked it — never based only on how the water looks.

An Important Rule

If you find a bottle, spray, or container you don't recognize, don't touch it, smell it, or taste it. Go tell a trusted adult right away.

docs.title: Physical Activity
docs.text:
Physical activity is any movement of the body that uses energy and helps a person stay healthy and strong — running, jumping, dancing, swimming, biking, and playing active games all count. Physical activity supports the body in many ways at once.

Regular physical activity helps the body by:

  • Building strong muscles and bones.
  • Keeping the heart and lungs strong.
  • Helping the body use energy from food (connecting back to what students learned about food and energy).
  • Improving mood and helping manage strong emotions (connecting back to Chapter 3).
  • Helping the body rest better at night.

Physical activity does not have to mean a formal sport. Climbing on playground equipment, playing tag, riding a scooter, and dancing to a favorite song are all physical activity too.

docs.title: Diagram: How Physical Activity Helps the Body
docs.text:

Type: infographic sim-id: physical-activity-body-benefits Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Learning objective: Students describe how physical activity benefits different parts and functions of the body by exploring a labeled body diagram.

Canvas layout: - Left area (300px): A simple, friendly outline of a child's body with four labeled hotspot zones (heart/chest, legs, head/brain, whole-body outline) - Right area (300px): Infobox panel showing benefit text for whichever zone is clicked

Visual elements: - Simple front-facing cartoon body outline, non-gendered, flat style matching the mascot - Four glowing hotspot dots at chest, legs, head, and a "whole body" dot near the center

Interactive controls: - Click each hotspot to reveal a benefit in the infobox - Button: "Show All" reveals all four benefits at once for review

Default parameters: - No hotspot selected at start; instructions read "Click a glowing dot to learn how activity helps that part of you."

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show body outline with four unselected hotspots Stage 2: Click chest hotspot -- infobox shows "Physical activity makes your heart and lungs stronger, so they can send energy all over your body." Stage 3: Click legs hotspot -- infobox shows "Movement builds strong muscles and bones in your legs and the rest of your body." Stage 4: Click head hotspot -- infobox shows "Being active can help your brain feel calmer and help you sleep better at night." Stage 5: Click whole-body hotspot -- infobox shows "Your whole body uses energy from food when you move -- that's why eating well and staying active go together."

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level (explain/describe) objective, so the design uses a labeled, clickable diagram with concrete benefit statements at each hotspot rather than a continuous animation, letting students explore body-benefit connections at their own pace and revisit any zone.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep the body outline simple and inclusive of different body types. Use warm, encouraging language in every infobox message.

However you like to move — running, dancing, biking, or playing tag — your body benefits every time. Now let's look at some of the many ways different cultures move and play.

docs.title: Cultural Physical Activity
docs.text:
Cultural physical activity means active games, dances, and traditions that come from a specific culture or community and have often been passed down for generations. These activities are physical activity and a way that communities share stories, celebrations, and belonging.

Communities around the world have wonderful traditions of active play. A few examples:

  • Jump-rope games with rhymes and chants, played in many communities across generations.
  • Tinikling, a dance from the Philippines where dancers step between long bamboo poles in rhythm.
  • Powwow dancing, practiced by many Indigenous nations in North America, with regalia, drumming, and specific dance styles passed down through families.
  • Line dances and circle dances, found in many cultures, where a whole group moves together in patterns.
  • Traditional ball and tag games, played by children in cultures all over the world, each with its own rules and rhymes.

No single tradition here is more "normal" than another — every culture has its own active games and dances, and all of them count as physical activity that also carries meaning and history for the people who practice them. Learning about these traditions helps us move our bodies and respect where they come from.

docs.title: Diagram: Active Games and Dances Around the World

Geographic scope: World map with five marked regions

Purpose: Show that active, traditional games and dances exist in communities all over the world, each with its own history

Locations and markers: - Philippines: Tinikling dance marker - North American Indigenous nations (general region marker, respectfully labeled by nation where possible): Powwow dance marker - West Africa: traditional circle-dance marker - Caribbean: jump-rope game marker (Double Dutch origins) - General "your community" marker inviting students to think of a local tradition

Interactive features: - Click each marker to open an infobox with: name of the activity, a simple description, and one sentence on why it is physically active - All markers presented with equally respectful, neutral description style -- no marker described as more "unusual" than another - Button: "Show My Community" prompts students (via teacher discussion) to name a local tradition to add to the discussion
