Concept Tested: Dressing For Weather

docs.title: 7. What are "cultural germ prevention practices"?
docs.text:
1. Rules that only apply in hospitals
  2. New inventions made by scientists last year
  3. Games played only in gym class
  4. Customs and habits communities use to reduce the spread of illness-causing germs
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Cultural germ prevention practices are customs and habits that different communities use to reduce the spread of illness-causing germs, often built into daily routines, greetings, or shared meals.

Concept Tested: Cultural Germ Prevention Practices

docs.title: 8. Removing shoes before entering a home mainly blocks which path that germs use to travel?
docs.text:
1. The path from one person's hands directly to another's
  2. The path from outdoor dirt on shoes to indoor floors
  3. The path through the air from a cough
  4. The path from food to a plate
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Removing shoes blocks the path from outdoor dirt on shoes to indoor floors and hands, keeping outdoor germs from spreading onto floors where people sit, eat, and play.

Concept Tested: Why Germ Prevention Practices Work

docs.title: 9. Why do many cultures teach covering a cough or sneeze with an elbow instead of a bare hand?
docs.text:
1. It looks more polite in photographs
  2. It keeps clothing cleaner
  3. It blocks droplets from spreading into the air or onto hands
  4. It makes the cough quieter
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Covering a cough or sneeze with an elbow or cloth blocks droplets from spreading into the air or onto hands, protecting both the sneezer and the people around them.

Concept Tested: Cultural Germ Prevention Practices

docs.title: 10. Why do germ prevention practices, like hand washing or removing shoes, actually work?
docs.text:
1. Germs cannot travel on their own, so blocking their path (hands, air, surfaces) stops them from spreading
  2. They make rooms smell better
  3. They are simply old traditions with no real reason
  4. They only work in cold weather
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Germs cannot travel on their own — they need to be carried by hands, droplets in the air, or surfaces people touch. Each cultural practice blocks a different path germs use to spread between people.

Concept Tested: Why Germ Prevention Practices Work

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Students learn to recognize hunger and fullness signals, understand carbohydrates, protein, and fats on nutrition labels, and see why limiting caffeinated and sugary drinks matters while choosing beverages that support physical activity. The chapter also covers food safety practices and preparation methods that promote healthy eating.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Hunger And Fullness Signals
  2. Carbohydrates
  3. Protein
  4. Fats
  5. Nutrition Label
  6. Limiting Caffeinated Drinks
  7. Limiting Sugary Drinks
  8. Beverages For Physical Activity
  9. Food Safety Practices
  10. Food Preparation Methods

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on the foundational ideas about health introduced in Chapter 1: Foundations Of Health and the physical activity concepts in Chapter 3: Wellness And Activity.

Listening to Your Body, Reading the Label

Hi, friend! This chapter is all about food and drinks — how our bodies tell us when to eat and when to stop, what's really inside our food, and how to keep food safe. Let's think it through together. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Hunger and Fullness Signals
docs.text:
Every body comes with its own built-in messenger system. Long before a stomach growls loudly, the body sends small signals asking for fuel — and later, sends different signals saying "that's enough for now." Learning to notice these signals is the first step toward a healthy, comfortable relationship with food.

Hunger and fullness signals are the body's natural feelings that tell a person when it needs food for energy (hunger) and when it has had enough food to feel satisfied (fullness). These signals are not about counting or measuring — they are about paying attention to how the body actually feels.

Hunger signals can include:

  • A rumbling or empty feeling in the stomach
  • Feeling low on energy or a little cranky
  • Trouble focusing on schoolwork or play
  • Thinking about food more than usual

Fullness signals can include:

  • The stomach feeling comfortably full, not stretched or tight
  • Energy returning and focus feeling steadier
  • Food starting to taste less exciting than the first few bites
  • A natural slowing down while eating

Big Idea

Hunger and fullness signals are about energy and comfort, never about weight or how a body looks. Every body's signals are a little different, and that is completely normal.

docs.title: Diagram: Reading Your Body's Signals
docs.text:
Reading Your Body's Signals MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: hunger-fullness-signal-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: recall, identify, recognize

Learning objective: Students recall and identify body signals for hunger and fullness by matching feeling-cards to a labeled body figure.

Canvas layout: - Left side (400px): A simple, friendly body figure with a highlighted stomach/belly zone - Right side (200px): A stack of clickable feeling-cards (e.g., "rumbling tummy," "hard to focus," "comfortably full," "food tastes less exciting")

Visual elements: - Body figure with a gentle glow around the belly area - Feeling-cards in two color groups: hunger cards (light orange) and fullness cards (light green) - A simple two-column sorting area labeled "Hungry" and "Full"

Interactive controls: - Click and drag (or click to select, then click a column) each feeling-card into the "Hungry" or "Full" column - Button: "Check My Answers" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - All feeling-cards start in a shuffled pile above the two columns

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the shuffled pile of feeling-cards above two empty columns Stage 2: As each card is sorted, show it snap into the chosen column Stage 3: When "Check My Answers" is clicked, show a checkmark or gentle "try again" cue on each card, with the correct column highlighted for any that were misplaced

Behavior: - Correctly sorted cards get a small checkmark and the body figure smiles - Incorrectly sorted cards get a gentle nudge with a one-sentence explanation of which signal group they belong to - A "You found them all!" caption appears once every card is correctly sorted

Instructional Rationale: This is a Remember-level objective (recall, identify), so the design uses a flashcard-style sorting activity rather than a complex simulation — students need to recognize and recall signals, which a simple sort-and-check pattern supports directly.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep the body figure simple and gender-neutral. Because this is a K-3 band, this MicroSim is the direct student-facing practice activity; the surrounding body text remains teacher-facing read-aloud material.

Paying attention to hunger and fullness signals helps a person eat in a way that feels good — not too little, not too much — and builds trust in the body's own wisdom. This same body awareness becomes even more useful once students start learning what is actually inside their food, which is where nutrition labels come in.

docs.title: Carbohydrates, Protein, and Fats
docs.text:
Food is more than just something that tastes good — it is made of building blocks that give the body energy, help it grow, and keep it running. Three of the most important building blocks are carbohydrates, protein, and fats, and all three show up on the nutrition labels found on packaged food.

Carbohydrates are a nutrient found in foods like bread, rice, pasta, fruit, and vegetables that give the body its main, fastest source of energy. Carbohydrates are like the body's quick fuel — the first energy source used for running, playing, and thinking.

Protein is a nutrient found in foods like beans, eggs, meat, fish, and dairy that helps build and repair the body's muscles and other tissues. Protein is especially important for growing bodies, since Grade 3 students are actively building muscle, bone, and other tissue every day.

Fats are a nutrient found in foods like nuts, seeds, avocados, and oils that provide a longer-lasting energy source and help the body absorb certain vitamins. Fats have an unfair reputation — in reality, the body needs a reasonable amount of healthy fats every day to work properly.

Nutrient Example Foods Main Job in the Body Carbohydrates Bread, rice, fruit, vegetables Quick, ready energy Protein Beans, eggs, fish, dairy Building and repairing muscle Fats Nuts, seeds, avocado, oil Long-lasting energy, helps absorb vitamins

Carbohydrates, protein, and fats are not "good" or "bad" foods fighting each other — they are teammates. Each one has a different job that helps a growing body do its best work.

docs.title: Diagram: Meet the Three Nutrient Teammates
docs.text:
Meet the Three Nutrient Teammates MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: nutrient-teammates-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, classify, exemplify

Learning objective: Students explain how carbohydrates, protein, and fats help the body grow by classifying example foods under the correct nutrient and reading a one-sentence explanation of its job.

Canvas layout: - Left side (400px): Three labeled bins — "Carbohydrates," "Protein," "Fats" — each with a small icon (lightning bolt for quick energy, muscle for repair, battery for long-lasting energy) - Right side (200px): A row of clickable food icons (bread, rice, apple, beans, egg, fish, nuts, avocado, oil)

Visual elements: - Three nutrient bins with distinct colors (gold for carbohydrates, red for protein, blue for fats) - Food icons that can be clicked or dragged into a bin

Interactive controls: - Click or drag a food icon into the bin where it belongs - Button: "Check My Answers" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - All nine food icons begin in a shuffled row above the three bins

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the shuffled food icons and three empty labeled bins Stage 2: As each food is sorted, show it snap into the chosen bin Stage 3: When "Check My Answers" is clicked, reveal a one-sentence explanation under each bin (e.g., "Carbohydrates give your body quick energy for running and playing.")

Behavior: - Correct placements get a checkmark; incorrect ones get a gentle explanation of the correct bin - Once all nine foods are sorted correctly, a "Nutrient Expert!" caption appears

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level objective (explain, classify), so the design uses a classify-and-reveal pattern with concrete example foods and short text explanations, rather than animation, so students can see the specific reasoning behind each nutrient's job.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep icons simple, flat, and easy to tell apart. This MicroSim is the direct student practice activity for this K-3 chapter.

docs.title: Reading a Nutrition Label
docs.text:
Once students know what carbohydrates, protein, and fats do, the next skill is finding them on a real food package. Nearly every packaged food and drink sold in a store has a Nutrition Facts label printed somewhere on it, and learning to read one is a practical, lifelong skill.

A nutrition label is the printed information on a food package that lists the amount of carbohydrates, protein, fats, and other nutrients in one serving of that food. Nutrition labels also show the serving size — the amount the rest of the label is describing — which is an important detail, since a package can contain more than one serving.

A simple nutrition label reading routine for Grade 3 students:

  1. Find the serving size at the top of the label.
  2. Look for the carbohydrates line and notice the grams listed.
  3. Look for the protein line and notice the grams listed.
  4. Look for the fats line and notice the grams listed.
  5. Compare two labels side by side to see which food has more of a certain nutrient.

Helpful Tip

Reading a nutrition label is like reading a mini fact sheet about your food — it's not about "good" or "bad" foods, just about knowing what's inside.

docs.title: Diagram: Explore a Nutrition Label
docs.text:
Explore a Nutrition Label MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: nutrition-label-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: use, demonstrate, practice

Learning objective: Students practice reading a real-style nutrition label by clicking each section to reveal what it means, then apply that skill by comparing two sample labels.

Canvas layout: - Left side (350px): A large, simplified Nutrition Facts label graphic with clickable rows (serving size, carbohydrates, protein, fats) - Right side (250px): An infobox panel and a "Compare Labels" toggle showing a second sample label (e.g., plain crackers vs. a granola bar)

Visual elements: - Clickable label rows highlighted with a soft outline - Two sample food labels available for comparison mode

Interactive controls: - Click any row on the label to reveal its meaning in the infobox - Toggle: "Compare with a Second Label" - Dropdown: choose which second food to compare (granola bar, crackers, yogurt) - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - Sample food: granola bar; no row selected at start

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the blank-highlighted label with all rows visible but unexplained Stage 2: Clicking a row shows its grams/amount and a one-sentence plain-language meaning (e.g., "Protein: 4 grams — this food has some protein to help build and repair muscles.") Stage 3: In compare mode, show both labels side by side with the same row highlighted on each, so students can directly compare grams of the same nutrient

Behavior: - Clicking a row updates the infobox instantly - Compare mode re-renders both labels whenever a new food is chosen from the dropdown - A short prompt asks, "Which food has more protein?" with an optional reveal button

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level objective (use, demonstrate, practice), so the design lets students actively interact with real label data and compare concrete values, rather than simply viewing a static picture of a label.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Use realistic but simplified label formatting so it transfers to real packages students see at home. This MicroSim is the direct student practice activity for this K-3 chapter.

Carbohydrates, protein, fats, and the nutrition label that lists them are the foundation for understanding food — but drinks matter just as much as food, which is where the chapter turns next.

docs.title: Limiting Caffeinated Drinks
docs.text:
Not everything a body drinks affects it the same way, and one ingredient that Grade 3 students should start to recognize is caffeine. Caffeine is found in coffee, many energy drinks, and some sodas and teas, and it is not recommended for children.

Limiting caffeinated drinks means choosing to avoid or reduce drinks containing caffeine, because caffeine can interfere with a growing body's sleep, heart rate, and mood regulation. A child's body is more sensitive to caffeine than an adult's body, so even small amounts can cause jitters, a racing heart, or trouble falling asleep.

Reasons children benefit from limiting caffeinated drinks:

  • Caffeine can make it harder to fall asleep or stay asleep, and growing bodies need consistent, quality sleep.
  • Caffeine can cause a racing heartbeat or jittery, anxious feelings in a child's more sensitive body.
  • Caffeine can mask normal tiredness, making it harder to notice the body's real fullness and rest signals.

Don't Skip This Step

Energy drinks and many sodas contain caffeine, even when it isn't obvious. Checking a drink label for "caffeine" is a smart habit before trying something new.

docs.title: Limiting Sugary Drinks
docs.text:
Alongside caffeine, another ingredient worth paying attention to is added sugar. Many popular drinks — sodas, sports drinks, sweetened juices, and flavored waters — contain much more sugar than most people realize.

Limiting sugary drinks means choosing to avoid or reduce drinks with large amounts of added sugar, because these drinks can cause quick energy spikes followed by tired crashes, and they can fill a person up without providing lasting nutrition. This is framed around energy and feeling good, not about weight — a sugary drink simply isn't an efficient way to fuel the body for the whole day.

Water and milk are two simple, everyday choices that support the body well without the sugar crash pattern.

docs.title: Diagram: Sugar Crash Story
docs.text:
Sugar Crash Story Chart

Type: chart sim-id: sugar-crash-line-chart Library: Chart.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, explain, interpret

Learning objective: Students describe why limiting caffeinated and sugary drinks matters by interpreting a simple energy-over-time line chart comparing a sugary drink to water.

Chart type: Line chart

Purpose: Show how energy level changes over the two hours after drinking a sugary soda compared to drinking water, illustrating the "quick spike, then crash" pattern.

X-axis: Time after drinking (0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120 minutes) Y-axis: Felt energy level (Low, Medium, High — simple 3-point scale)

Data series: 1. Sugary drink (orange line): - 0 min: Medium - 15 min: High - 30 min: High - 45 min: Medium - 60 min: Low - 90 min: Low - 120 min: Medium

  1. Water (blue line):
  2. 0 min: Medium
  3. 15 min: Medium
  4. 30 min: Medium
  5. 45 min: Medium
  6. 60 min: Medium
  7. 90 min: Medium
  8. 120 min: Medium

Title: "Energy After a Sugary Drink vs. Water" Legend: Position top-right

Interactive features: Hovering any point on either line reveals the exact energy level and a one-sentence caption (e.g., "30 minutes: sugary drinks often cause a quick burst of energy that doesn't last."); a toggle button lets students show or hide each line to compare them one at a time

Annotations: - Callout near the orange line's peak: "Quick spike!" - Callout near the orange line's dip: "Energy crash" - Callout on the blue line: "Steady, no crash"

Implementation: Chart.js line chart with point hover tooltips and a toggle-series legend

You've Got This

It can be tricky to say no to a sweet drink, especially when friends are having one. Remember — choosing water most of the time is a strong, healthy habit, and treats can still have their place once in a while.

docs.title: Beverages for Physical Activity
docs.text:
Not all drinks are something to limit — some drinks are genuinely helpful, especially around physical activity. Knowing which beverages support energy, strength, and recovery helps students make smart choices before, during, and after being active.

Beverages for physical activity are drinks that help supply energy, prevent dehydration, and support the body's recovery during and after exercise — with plain water being the best choice for most everyday activity. For most kids doing typical recess, gym class, or sports practice, water is enough to replace what the body loses through sweat.

Situation Best Beverage Choice Why Regular recess or gym class Water Replaces fluid lost through normal sweating Long or very intense exercise (over an hour, hot weather) Water, sometimes milk after Supports hydration and recovery After activity, feeling hungry and thirsty Milk or water with a snack Milk provides protein for muscle repair plus fluids Any time Sports drinks, soda, energy drinks Usually unnecessary for kids and often high in sugar or caffeine

For almost all kids' activities, plain water is the champion beverage. Sports drinks are built for adult athletes doing very long, intense exercise — not for a typical recess game.

docs.title: Diagram: Choose the Right Drink
docs.text:
Choose the Right Drink MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: activity-beverage-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: apply, demonstrate, practice

Learning objective: Students apply knowledge of beverages for physical activity by matching drink choices to activity scenarios (recess, long practice, after activity, everyday).

Canvas layout: - Left side (400px): Four scenario cards shown one at a time (recess/gym class, long hot-weather practice, after activity feeling hungry, just relaxing at home) - Right side (200px): Row of drink icons (water bottle, milk carton, sports drink, soda, energy drink)

Visual elements: - Scenario illustration changes with each card - Drink icons remain constant across scenarios

Interactive controls: - Click the drink icon that best matches the current scenario - Button: "Next Scenario" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - Starts on the "recess or gym class" scenario

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scenario illustration and all drink icon options Stage 2: After a choice is made, reveal whether it was the best choice and a one-sentence reason (e.g., "Water is the best choice for regular recess — your body just needs its fluids back.") Stage 3: Advancing to the next scenario resets the choice and shows a new situation

Behavior: - Best-choice selections get a checkmark and a short reason - Less ideal choices get a gentle explanation of why water (or milk, after activity) is usually better - After all four scenarios are complete, a "Hydration Helper!" caption appears

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level objective (apply, demonstrate), so the design uses a scenario-matching pattern where students actively apply the water-first principle to new situations, rather than just reading a rule.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep scenario art simple and recognizable. This MicroSim is the direct student practice activity for this K-3 chapter.

docs.title: Food Safety Practices
docs.text:
Choosing the right foods and drinks matters, but so does keeping food safe to eat in the first place. Food safety practices are the habits that keep food free from harmful germs, such as washing hands before eating, keeping raw and cooked foods separate, and storing food at the right temperature.

Key food safety habits for students to know:

  • Wash hands with soap and water before touching or eating food.
  • Keep raw meat separate from other foods, including using separate cutting boards.
  • Keep cold foods cold (in the refrigerator) and hot foods hot until eating.
  • Never eat food that smells wrong, looks moldy, or has passed its date without an adult checking first.
  • Wash fruits and vegetables before eating them.

Food that sits out too long — especially meat, eggs, or dairy — can grow germs you can't see or smell. When in doubt, ask a trusted adult before eating something that seems questionable.

docs.title: Diagram: Kitchen Safety Checklist
docs.text:
Kitchen Safety Checklist Workflow

Type: workflow sim-id: kitchen-safety-workflow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, explain, summarize

Learning objective: Students describe food safety practices that promote healthy eating by exploring each step of a simple kitchen safety sequence and why it matters.

Purpose: Show the sequence of food safety habits from before cooking to after eating, with an explanation of why each step prevents illness.

Visual style: Simple linear flowchart with six steps in sequence

Steps (every node must have a Mermaid click directive opening an infobox): 1. "Wash Hands Before Cooking" — Hover text: "Hands pick up germs all day; washing them removes germs before they can get onto food." 2. "Wash Fruits and Vegetables" — Hover text: "Produce can carry dirt and germs from the farm or store, so rinsing it removes them before eating." 3. "Keep Raw Meat Separate" — Hover text: "Raw meat can carry germs that spread to other foods if they touch the same cutting board or utensils." 4. "Cook Food to a Safe Temperature" — Hover text: "Heat kills most harmful germs living in raw food." 5. "Keep Hot Foods Hot, Cold Foods Cold" — Hover text: "Germs grow fastest at room temperature, so foods are stored hot or cold to slow that growth." 6. "Wash Hands Again Before Eating" — Hover text: "A final hand wash removes any germs picked up while cooking or setting the table."

Color coding: - Blue: Hand-washing steps - Green: Food preparation steps - Orange: Temperature-control steps

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart with click directive on every node calling an infobox function that displays the hover text above; linear top-to-bottom sequence.

docs.title: Food Preparation Methods
docs.text:
Food safety and food preparation go hand in hand. Food preparation methods are the different ways food can be cooked or prepared — such as baking, boiling, steaming, grilling, or eating raw — and each method affects both safety and the nutrients in the food.

Some general patterns worth knowing:

  1. Baking, boiling, steaming, and grilling all use heat to kill harmful germs that might be in raw food.
  2. Steaming tends to keep more vitamins in vegetables compared to boiling, since fewer nutrients dissolve away into water.
  3. Raw fruits and vegetables that are safe to eat uncooked still need thorough washing first.
  4. Frying adds extra fat to food, which isn't harmful occasionally, but isn't the best everyday choice.

Trying foods prepared in different ways — steamed broccoli one night, roasted the next — is a fun way to discover new favorite flavors while keeping meals safe and healthy.

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "Why do we keep raw meat separate from other foods in the kitchen?" Then reveal: "Raw meat can carry germs that spread to other foods if they touch the same cutting board, plate, or utensils — keeping them separate blocks that path."

Chapter Complete!

Great job, friend! You now know how to notice hunger and fullness signals, what carbohydrates, protein, and fats do for a growing body, how to read a nutrition label, why water beats sugary and caffeinated drinks, and how to keep food safe and well prepared. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text: By the end of this chapter, most Grade 3 students should be able to recall at least three hunger and fullness signals (3.1.1.1); explain how carbohydrates, protein, and fats each help the body grow and locate them on a nutrition label (3.1.1.2); describe why limiting caffeinated and sugary drinks matters and identify water as the best everyday choice for physical activity (3.1.1.3); and describe at least two food safety practices and two food preparation methods that promote healthy eating (3.1.1.4). The MicroSims progress from a Remember-level signal-sorting activity, through Understand-level nutrient classification and a sugar-crash chart, to Apply-level label-reading and beverage-scenario simulators, matching the Remember/Understand/Apply mix of benchmarks in this content strand. Because this is a K-3 band, keep the body text as teacher-facing read-aloud material and treat the MicroSims as the direct hands-on practice for students. Keep all discussion of hunger, fullness, and food choices body-positive and centered on energy and feeling good — never on weight, dieting, or restriction.

docs.title: Quiz: Food And Nutrition
docs.text: Test your understanding of hunger and fullness signals, nutrients, nutrition labels, drinks, and food safety with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which of these is an example of a hunger signal?
docs.text:
1. A rumbling or empty feeling in the stomach
  2. The stomach feeling comfortably full
  3. Food tasting less exciting than the first bite
  4. Energy returning and focus feeling steady
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A rumbling or empty feeling in the stomach is a hunger signal — the body's way of asking for fuel. Fullness signals, like feeling comfortably full, are different and mean the body has had enough for now.

Concept Tested: Hunger And Fullness Signals

docs.title: 2. Which of these is an example of a fullness signal?
docs.text:
1. Feeling low on energy or a little cranky
  2. Thinking about food more than usual
  3. Trouble focusing on schoolwork
  4. The stomach feeling comfortably full, not stretched or tight
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The stomach feeling comfortably full, not stretched or tight, is a fullness signal. It tells the body it has had enough food to feel satisfied.

Concept Tested: Hunger And Fullness Signals

docs.title: 3. What is the main job of carbohydrates in the body?
docs.text:
1. Building and repairing muscle
  2. Helping the body absorb certain vitamins
  3. Giving the body its quick, main source of energy
  4. Making bones stronger
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Carbohydrates are found in foods like bread, rice, pasta, fruit, and vegetables, and they give the body its main, fastest source of energy — like the body's quick fuel for running and playing.

Concept Tested: Carbohydrates

docs.title: 4. What is the main job of protein in the body?
docs.text:
1. Helping build and repair muscles and other tissues
  2. Giving the fastest burst of energy
  3. Making food taste sweet
  4. Helping the body absorb vitamins
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Protein is found in foods like beans, eggs, meat, fish, and dairy, and it helps build and repair the body's muscles and other tissues — especially important for growing bodies.

Concept Tested: Protein

docs.title: 5. On a nutrition label, what does the "serving size" tell you?
docs.text:
1. How the food should be cooked
  2. The amount the rest of the label is describing
  3. The price of the food
  4. Where the food was grown
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The serving size is the amount the rest of the nutrition label is describing. This matters because a package can contain more than one serving.

Concept Tested: Nutrition Label

docs.title: 6. Why should children limit caffeinated drinks?
docs.text:
1. Caffeine can interfere with sleep, heart rate, and mood in a growing body
  2. Caffeine makes food taste better
  3. Caffeine helps children grow taller
  4. Caffeine has no effect on children at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A child's body is more sensitive to caffeine than an adult's body, so even small amounts can cause jitters, a racing heart, or trouble falling asleep, which is why limiting caffeinated drinks matters.

Concept Tested: Limiting Caffeinated Drinks

docs.title: 7. What is the best beverage choice for a typical recess or gym class?
docs.text:
1. An energy drink
  2. Soda
  3. Water
  4. A sports drink
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. For most kids doing typical recess, gym class, or sports practice, water is enough to replace what the body loses through sweat. Sports drinks are built for very long, intense adult exercise, not everyday activity.

Concept Tested: Beverages For Physical Activity

docs.title: 8. Why do sugary drinks often lead to a "crash" after a burst of energy?
docs.text:
1. They contain protein that builds muscle slowly
  2. They give a quick energy spike that isn't followed by lasting nutrition
  3. They make the body feel hungry right away
  4. They contain no ingredients at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Sugary drinks can cause quick energy spikes followed by tired crashes, and they can fill a person up without providing lasting nutrition — unlike water, which supports steady energy.

Concept Tested: Limiting Sugary Drinks

docs.title: 9. Which of these is a good food safety practice?
docs.text:
1. Using the same cutting board for raw meat and vegetables
  2. Leaving cooked food out at room temperature all day
  3. Eating food that smells wrong without checking with an adult
  4. Washing hands with soap and water before touching or eating food
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Washing hands with soap and water before touching or eating food is a key food safety habit that helps keep food free from harmful germs.

Concept Tested: Food Safety Practices

docs.title: 10. Compared to boiling, why does steaming vegetables tend to keep more vitamins in the food?
docs.text:
1. Steaming takes much longer than boiling
  2. Steaming uses more salt than boiling
  3. Fewer nutrients dissolve away into water during steaming
  4. Steaming cooks food at a colder temperature than boiling
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Steaming tends to keep more vitamins in vegetables compared to boiling, since fewer nutrients dissolve away into the water during the steaming process.

Concept Tested: Food Preparation Methods

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter examines the roles family members and peers play in healthy relationships, the right to personal boundaries, and how teasing, exclusion, or bullying affects individuals and the community. Students learn why treating all people of all abilities with kindness and respect matters.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Family Member Roles
  2. Peer Roles In Relationships
  3. Healthy Relationships
  4. Bullying
  5. Exclusion
  6. Effects Of Bullying And Exclusion
  7. Right To Personal Boundaries

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on the foundational ideas about health introduced in Chapter 1: Foundations Of Health.

Family, Friends, and Fairness

Hi, friend! This chapter is about the people in our lives — the roles families and friends play, what makes a relationship healthy, and how everyone deserves kindness and respect. Let's think it through together. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Family Member Roles
docs.text:
Every student belongs to a family, and every family looks a little different. Some families are large with grandparents and cousins nearby; some are small; some include stepparents, foster parents, or guardians. What all healthy families share is that each member plays a role in helping the family work well together.

Family member roles are the different jobs and responsibilities that people in a family take on to keep each other safe, cared for, and supported, such as providing food and shelter, teaching new skills, or offering comfort during hard times. Grown-ups in a family often provide safety, rules, and guidance, while children contribute by helping with chores, following family routines, and treating others in the home with respect.

Common family member roles include:

  • Caregiving — feeding, clothing, and looking after health needs
  • Teaching — showing a child how to do new things, from tying shoes to handling emotions
  • Providing safety — setting rules and routines that keep everyone secure
  • Emotional support — listening, comforting, and celebrating good news together
  • Contributing — even young family members can help through chores and cooperation

No two families divide these roles in exactly the same way, and that variety is normal. What matters most is that the roles add up to a home where people feel cared for.

docs.title: Diagram: Who Does What in a Family
docs.text:
Who Does What in a Family MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: family-roles-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, classify, exemplify

Learning objective: Students describe the roles of family members in healthy relationships by matching everyday family actions to the role category they represent.

Canvas layout: - Left side (400px): Five labeled role bins — "Caregiving," "Teaching," "Providing Safety," "Emotional Support," "Contributing" — each with a simple icon - Right side (200px): A stack of clickable action cards (e.g., "Packing a lunch," "Showing how to ride a bike," "Setting a bedtime," "Giving a hug after a hard day," "Setting the table")

Visual elements: - Five colorful role bins arranged in a row - Action cards in a shuffled pile above the bins - A friendly house illustration in the background

Interactive controls: - Click or drag each action card into the role bin where it belongs - Button: "Check My Answers" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - All action cards begin shuffled above the five bins

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the shuffled action cards and five empty labeled bins Stage 2: As each card is sorted, show it snap into the chosen bin Stage 3: When "Check My Answers" is clicked, reveal a one-sentence explanation for each card (e.g., "Showing how to ride a bike is teaching — helping someone learn a new skill.")

Behavior: - Correctly sorted cards get a checkmark - Incorrectly sorted cards get a gentle nudge explaining the correct role bin - A "Family Roles Expert!" caption appears once every card is sorted correctly

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level objective (describe, classify), so the design uses a classify-and-reveal pattern with concrete family examples, letting students see the reasoning behind each role rather than only memorizing a list.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep family illustrations diverse and simple so many family structures feel represented. This MicroSim is the direct student-facing practice activity; the surrounding text remains teacher-facing read-aloud material for this K-3 band.

Family roles give students their first experience of relationships, but family is not the only place students practice being a good relationship partner — school and neighborhood friendships matter just as much.

docs.title: Peer Roles In Relationships
docs.text:
A peer is someone close to a student's own age, such as a classmate, teammate, or neighborhood friend. Just like family members, peers take on roles that shape how a friendship or classroom relationship feels.

Peer roles in relationships are the different ways classmates and friends act toward one another — such as including others, sharing, cooperating, and offering support — that build trust between people who are growing up together. A student can be a good peer by inviting someone to join a game, sharing supplies, listening when a friend is upset, or working well as part of a team.

Big Idea

Peers can be a source of learning too — friends teach each other new games, new words, and new ways of solving problems. Good peer relationships go both directions: giving support and receiving it.

Peer roles usually fall into a few familiar patterns:

Peer Role What It Looks Like Why It Builds Trust Including others Inviting a classmate to join a game or group project Nobody feels left out Sharing Offering a pencil, snack, or supplies Shows generosity and fairness Cooperating Taking turns and following game or group rules Makes teamwork possible Listening and supporting Paying attention when a friend needs to talk Builds emotional safety

Family roles and peer roles work together — the caregiving and teaching a student experiences at home often becomes the model for how that student treats friends at school.

docs.title: Healthy Relationships
docs.text:
With family roles and peer roles in mind, students are ready for the bigger question: what makes any relationship — with a parent, sibling, friend, or classmate — a healthy one?

A healthy relationship is a connection between people built on trust, respect, honesty, and kindness, where both people feel safe, valued, and free to be themselves. In a healthy relationship, disagreements can still happen, but people work through them without hurting each other physically or with unkind words.

Signs of a healthy relationship include:

  1. Both people listen to each other, even when they disagree.
  2. People tell the truth, even when it's hard.
  3. Mistakes are followed by an apology and a chance to make things right.
  4. Each person supports the other's interests and feelings.
  5. Both people feel physically and emotionally safe.

By contrast, an unhealthy relationship might involve one person often feeling scared, controlled, put down, or unsafe. Recognizing the difference helps students notice when a relationship needs a trusted adult's help.

docs.title: Diagram: Healthy or Needs Help?
docs.text:
Healthy or Needs Help? Scenario Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: healthy-relationship-scenario-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, interpret, classify

Learning objective: Students describe the roles of family members and peers in healthy relationships by reading short scenarios and identifying the healthy relationship signs present.

Canvas layout: - Left side (400px): One scenario card at a time, shown as simple illustrated text (e.g., "Maya's brother helps her with homework and says sorry when he snaps at her.") - Right side (200px): Four checkbox-style options representing healthy relationship signs (listening, honesty, apology and repair, support) plus a "Show Answer" button

Visual elements: - Scenario illustration with two simple characters - Checkboxes that light up green when correctly identified

Interactive controls: - Click the checkboxes that apply to the current scenario - Button: "Show Answer" - Button: "Next Scenario"

Default parameters: - Begins on scenario 1 of 5 with no checkboxes selected

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scenario text/illustration and four unmarked checkboxes Stage 2: After the student selects checkboxes and clicks "Show Answer," reveal which signs truly applied with a one-sentence explanation for each Stage 3: "Next Scenario" loads a new short scenario, resetting the checkboxes

Behavior: - Correct selections turn green with a brief explanation - Missed or incorrect selections are gently highlighted with the correct reasoning - After all five scenarios, a "Relationship Detective!" caption appears

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level objective (describe, interpret), so the design uses short worked scenarios with concrete, visible reasoning rather than an animated simulation, helping students connect the abstract "signs of healthy relationships" list to real situations.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep scenarios warm, age-appropriate, and free of any physical danger content — this MicroSim addresses everyday friendship and family situations, not abuse or crisis situations. This MicroSim is the direct student-facing practice activity for this K-3 band.

You now know how family and peer roles build healthy relationships. Next, this chapter looks honestly at what happens when relationships go wrong — through bullying and exclusion — so students can recognize it and know how to respond.

docs.title: Bullying
docs.text:
Not every relationship stays healthy, and one of the most serious ways a relationship can go wrong is through bullying.

Bullying is repeated, unwanted, and harmful behavior — physical, verbal, or online — by one person or group toward another person, usually where there is a real or perceived difference in power. Bullying can look like hitting or shoving, name-calling, spreading rumors, or repeatedly leaving hurtful comments online or in messages.

Three features usually present in bullying:

  • It is repeated, not a single one-time conflict.
  • It is intentional, meant to hurt, control, or frighten someone.
  • There is a power difference, whether from size, popularity, group numbers, or other advantage.

It is important for students to know the difference between bullying and an ordinary disagreement or conflict between friends, since not every unkind moment is bullying — but any repeated pattern of harm deserves a trusted adult's attention.

A Serious Topic

Bullying is a serious topic, and every student deserves to feel safe at school and online. If bullying is happening to you or someone you know, telling a trusted adult is always the right step.

docs.title: Diagram: What Counts as Bullying?
docs.text:
What Counts as Bullying? Identification Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: bullying-identification-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, distinguish, classify

Learning objective: Students describe how bullying affects individuals and distinguish bullying situations from one-time disagreements by sorting short scenario cards into two categories.

Canvas layout: - Left side (400px): Two labeled columns — "Bullying" and "One-Time Disagreement" - Right side (200px): A stack of short scenario cards read aloud by the teacher (e.g., "A classmate calls someone a mean name every day at lunch" vs. "Two friends argue once about which game to play")

Visual elements: - Two calm, non-graphic columns with simple icons - Scenario cards presented as plain text, no depictions of physical harm

Interactive controls: - Click each scenario card and place it in the correct column - Button: "Check My Answers" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - Six scenario cards begin shuffled above the two columns

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the shuffled scenario cards above the two empty columns Stage 2: As each card is placed, show it snap into the chosen column Stage 3: When "Check My Answers" is clicked, reveal a calm, factual one-sentence explanation for each card, noting whether it was repeated, intentional, and involved a power difference

Behavior: - Correct placements get a checkmark - Incorrect placements get a brief, factual explanation of the three bullying features - A closing message reminds students: "If you see or experience bullying, tell a trusted adult."

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level objective (describe, distinguish), so the design uses a calm sorting-and-explanation pattern with plain, factual language rather than any dramatized animation, keeping the tone serious and supportive rather than sensational.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep all scenario text mild, non-graphic, and free of any names resembling real students. Always end the activity with a visible reminder to talk to a trusted adult. This MicroSim is the direct student-facing practice activity for this K-3 band.

docs.title: Exclusion
docs.text:
Bullying is not the only way people can be hurt in a group. Sometimes the harm is quieter — being left out altogether.

Exclusion is the act of deliberately leaving someone out of a group, activity, or conversation, such as refusing to let a classmate join a game, forming a group specifically to keep someone out, or ignoring someone on purpose. Exclusion can happen without a single unkind word being said, which sometimes makes it harder for adults to notice — but it can hurt just as much as name-calling.

Exclusion can show up in ordinary school moments:

  • Saving seats so a particular classmate cannot sit with the group
  • Whispering so someone nearby is obviously left out of a conversation
  • Choosing teams in a way designed to leave one person out or picked last on purpose
  • Leaving one classmate out of a group message or invitation on purpose

Everyone, regardless of ability, background, or how they look or communicate, deserves to be included. Exclusion does not always look dramatic — noticing who is not included in a game or conversation is just as important as noticing unkind words, and it is a first step toward stopping it.

docs.title: Effects of Bullying and Exclusion
docs.text:
Bullying and exclusion are not small, forgettable events — they leave real effects on the people involved and on the whole community around them.

Effects of bullying and exclusion are the emotional, social, and physical consequences experienced by a person who is bullied or excluded, which can include sadness, anxiety, loneliness, trouble sleeping, physical complaints like stomachaches, and lower confidence at school. These effects do not stay contained to just the person targeted — a classroom or school community where bullying or exclusion is common becomes a less safe, less trusting place for everyone.

Effects can include:

Who Is Affected Possible Effects The person targeted Sadness, fear, loneliness, trouble sleeping, stomachaches, avoiding school Bystanders who witness it Feeling unsafe, guilt, uncertainty about what to do The person doing the bullying or excluding Difficulty forming healthy relationships, ongoing behavior patterns without help The whole classroom or community Lower trust, less willingness to speak up, an unwelcoming environment

This is exactly why treating all people — of every ability, background, and way of communicating — with kindness and respect matters so much. A classroom where everyone is included is a classroom where everyone can focus, learn, and feel safe.

docs.title: Diagram: The Ripple Effect
docs.text:
The Ripple Effect of Bullying and Exclusion

Type: infographic sim-id: bullying-ripple-effect-diagram Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, summarize, interpret

Learning objective: Students explain how teasing, exclusion, or bullying affects individuals and the community by exploring an infographic showing effects that ripple outward from one person to the whole classroom.

Purpose: Show, in a calm and factual way, how the effects of bullying and exclusion extend beyond the person targeted to bystanders and the whole classroom community.

Layout: Concentric-circle infographic — a center circle labeled "Person Targeted," surrounded by a ring labeled "Bystanders," surrounded by an outer ring labeled "Whole Classroom/Community"

Interactive elements: - Click the center circle to reveal effects on the person targeted (sadness, fear, loneliness, trouble sleeping, stomachaches) - Click the middle ring to reveal effects on bystanders (feeling unsafe, guilt, not knowing what to do) - Click the outer ring to reveal effects on the whole community (lower trust, less willingness to speak up) - A calm "What Helps" button reveals three supportive actions: telling a trusted adult, including others, and treating everyone with kindness and respect

Visual style: Soft, non-alarming concentric circles; muted, calm color palette (blues and greens) rather than harsh reds

Color scheme: Center circle in soft blue, middle ring in soft teal, outer ring in soft green; the "What Helps" button in warm gold

Implementation: p5.js infographic with click-to-reveal infobox panels for each ring; ends every path with the reminder that trusted adults can help.

You've Got This

Learning about the effects of bullying and exclusion can feel heavy, but understanding them is exactly what helps students choose kindness and know when to ask a trusted adult for help.

docs.title: Right to Personal Boundaries
docs.text:
Every person — regardless of age — has the right to decide who can be close to them, what kind of touch feels okay, and what personal information they choose to share.

The right to personal boundaries means every person has the right to say what feels comfortable for their own body, space, and belongings, and to have that boundary respected by others, including family members, peers, and adults. A boundary might be as simple as "please don't touch my things without asking" or "I don't want a hug right now, but a high-five is okay."

Boundaries matter because they help a person feel safe, respected, and in control of their own choices. A few key facts about personal boundaries for Grade 3 students:

  • A person's boundary should be respected even if others don't understand it or think it's unusual.
  • Saying "no" to unwanted touch or attention is allowed, even with familiar people.
  • If someone's boundary is not being respected, telling a trusted adult is the right next step — asking for help is a strength, not a weakness.
  • Respecting other people's boundaries, even when a student disagrees with them, is part of being a good friend and family member.

Helpful Tip

A clear, calm sentence works well for setting a boundary: "I don't like that, please stop," or "I'd rather not, thank you." Practicing these words ahead of time makes them easier to use in the moment.

docs.title: Diagram: Practice Setting a Boundary
docs.text:
Practice Setting a Boundary MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: personal-boundary-practice-simulator Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: use, demonstrate, practice

Learning objective: Students practice using clear boundary-setting language by choosing the best response in short, everyday scenarios involving personal space or belongings.

Canvas layout: - Left side (400px): One scenario at a time (e.g., "A cousin wants to borrow your favorite toy without asking" or "A friend keeps tickling you after you asked them to stop") - Right side (200px): Three response choice buttons (a clear boundary statement, a silent/no-response option, an unkind response) plus a "Show What Happens" button

Visual elements: - Simple scenario illustration with two friendly characters - Three response buttons with plain text

Interactive controls: - Click the response the student would choose - Button: "Show What Happens" - Button: "Next Scenario"

Default parameters: - Begins on scenario 1 of 4 with no response chosen

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scenario and three response choices Stage 2: After a choice and clicking "Show What Happens," reveal a short, calm outcome and explanation (e.g., "Saying 'Please stop, I don't like that' is clear and respectful — it tells your friend exactly what you need.") Stage 3: "Next Scenario" loads a new situation, resetting the choices

Behavior: - The clear boundary statement is affirmed as the strongest choice, with a one-sentence reason - Other choices receive a gentle, non-judgmental explanation of why a clear boundary statement usually works better - After all four scenarios, a "Boundary-Setting Star!" caption appears, along with a reminder that a trusted adult can always help if a boundary is not respected

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level objective (use, demonstrate, practice), so the design lets students actively choose and test boundary-setting language in realistic scenarios, rather than only reading about the concept, which builds a practical skill they can use in real situations.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep every scenario mild and age-appropriate (toys, personal space, tickling, hugs) — never depict abuse or unsafe situations. Every scenario path should end supportively. This MicroSim is the direct student-facing practice activity for this K-3 band.

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "If a friend keeps doing something that makes you uncomfortable, even after you've asked them to stop, what should you do?" Then reveal: "Tell a trusted adult. Everyone has the right to have their personal boundaries respected, and asking for help is always okay."

Chapter Complete!

Wonderful work, friend! You now understand the roles family members and peers play in healthy relationships, what bullying and exclusion look like and why they matter, and your own right to personal boundaries. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text: By the end of this chapter, most Grade 3 students should be able to describe the roles of family members and peers in healthy relationships (3.2.1.1) and explain how teasing, exclusion, or bullying impacts individuals and the community, including why treating all people of all abilities with kindness and respect matters (3.3.1.6), as well as describe the right to personal boundaries (3.5.1.4). The MicroSims progress from Understand-level classification and scenario-interpretation activities (family and peer roles, healthy relationships, recognizing bullying, understanding ripple effects) to an Apply-level boundary-practice simulator, matching the Understand/Apply mix of benchmarks in this content strand. Because this is a K-3 band, keep the body text as teacher-facing read-aloud material and treat the MicroSims as the direct hands-on practice for students. Keep the tone plainly sincere — without puns or light dog-themed phrasing — specifically in the Bullying, Exclusion, and Effects of Bullying and Exclusion sections, since these are violence-prevention-adjacent topics; the mascot may still appear there warmly, but only in its neutral or encouraging voice. Always close any bullying, exclusion, or boundary discussion with a clear reminder that trusted adults are available to help.

docs.title: Quiz: Relationships And Respect
docs.text: Test your understanding of family and peer roles, healthy relationships, bullying, exclusion, and personal boundaries with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. "Showing a younger sibling how to ride a bike" is an example of which family member role?
docs.text:
1. Providing safety
  2. Emotional support
  3. Contributing
  4. Teaching
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Teaching means showing someone how to do new things, from tying shoes to riding a bike. Showing a sibling how to ride a bike fits the teaching role described in the chapter.

Concept Tested: Family Member Roles

docs.title: 2. What is a "peer"?
docs.text:
1. Someone close to a student's own age, like a classmate or teammate
  2. A student's parent or guardian
  3. A family pet
  4. A teacher or school principal
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A peer is someone close to a student's own age, such as a classmate, teammate, or neighborhood friend. Peers take on roles that shape how a friendship or classroom relationship feels.

Concept Tested: Peer Roles In Relationships

docs.title: 3. Which of these is a sign of a healthy relationship?
docs.text:
1. One person always decides everything alone
  2. Mistakes are never mentioned again
  3. People never disagree about anything
  4. Both people listen to each other, even when they disagree
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In a healthy relationship, both people listen to each other, even when they disagree, and work through disagreements without hurting each other with unkind words or actions.

Concept Tested: Healthy Relationships

docs.title: 4. What is "bullying"?
docs.text:
1. Repeated, unwanted, and harmful behavior toward someone, usually involving a power difference
  2. Any single disagreement between two friends
  3. A game played at recess
  4. Choosing not to play a certain game
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Bullying is repeated, unwanted, and harmful behavior — physical, verbal, or online — by one person or group toward another, usually where there is a real or perceived difference in power.

Concept Tested: Bullying

docs.title: 5. Two friends argue once about which game to play, then make up and move on. Is this bullying?
docs.text:
1. Yes, any disagreement counts as bullying
  2. Yes, because someone felt upset
  3. No, because bullying is repeated and intentional, not a single disagreement
  4. No, because friends can never disagree
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Bullying is repeated and intentional, with a power difference involved. Not every unkind moment is bullying — a single disagreement between friends who make up afterward is different from a repeated pattern of harm.

Concept Tested: Bullying

docs.title: 6. A group of classmates always saves seats so one particular classmate can never sit with them. What is this an example of?
docs.text:
1. A healthy relationship
  2. Exclusion
  3. Active listening
  4. A personal boundary
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Exclusion is the act of deliberately leaving someone out of a group, activity, or conversation. Saving seats so a classmate can never sit with the group is a real example of exclusion given in the chapter.

Concept Tested: Exclusion

docs.title: 7. According to the chapter, who can be affected when bullying or exclusion happens in a classroom?
docs.text:
1. Only the person who is bullying or excluding someone
  2. No one except the person who is bullied
  3. Only the teacher
  4. The person targeted, bystanders, and the whole classroom community
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The effects of bullying and exclusion reach beyond the person targeted — bystanders can feel unsafe or guilty, and the whole classroom or community can become less trusting and less welcoming.

Concept Tested: Effects Of Bullying And Exclusion

docs.title: 8. Why does the chapter describe the effects of bullying as a "ripple effect" across a whole classroom?
docs.text:
1. Because only water activities are affected
  2. Because bullying only affects the exact moment it happens
  3. Because the harm spreads outward, affecting the person targeted, bystanders, and the whole community's trust
  4. Because ripples make a classroom quieter
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Like a ripple spreading outward from a center point, the effects of bullying and exclusion start with the person targeted but extend to bystanders and lower the trust and safety of the whole classroom community.

Concept Tested: Effects Of Bullying And Exclusion

docs.title: 9. What does the "right to personal boundaries" mean?
docs.text:
1. Only adults are allowed to say no to unwanted touch
  2. Every person has the right to say what feels comfortable for their own body, space, and belongings
  3. Boundaries only apply to strangers, never to family
  4. A person must always explain why they set a boundary
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Every person has the right to decide what feels comfortable for their own body, space, and belongings, and to have that boundary respected by others, including family members, peers, and adults.

Concept Tested: Right To Personal Boundaries

docs.title: 10. A friend keeps tickling a student after being asked to stop. What is the best response?
docs.text:
1. Say clearly, "Please stop, I don't like that," and tell a trusted adult if it continues
  2. Tickle the friend back even harder
  3. Say nothing and hope it stops on its own
  4. Stop being friends with them immediately without saying anything
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A clear, calm sentence like "Please stop, I don't like that" is the strongest way to set a boundary. If the boundary is still not respected, telling a trusted adult is always the right next step.

Concept Tested: Right To Personal Boundaries

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Students are introduced to puberty and its stages, and learn how to ask a trusted adult for help managing physical and emotional changes during this time of growth.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Puberty
  2. Stages Of Puberty
  3. Asking For Help With Body Changes
  4. Identifying Trusted Adults

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on the trusted-adult and safety-procedure concepts from Chapter 2: Safety And Trusted Adults.

Every Body Grows and Changes

Hi, friend. This chapter is about something that happens to every single person as they grow up: their body starts to change in new ways. It's called puberty, and it's a normal and healthy part of growing older. Let's think it through together.

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Introduce This Chapter
docs.text: This chapter is written to be read aloud and facilitated by a teacher, parent, or other trusted adult, not read independently by an 8- or 9-year-old student. It is the first time the curriculum names puberty directly, so the goal for this grade band is narrow and specific: help students understand that puberty is a normal, healthy stage of growth that happens to every human body, that it happens at different times for different people, and that a trusted adult is always available to answer questions. This is an introduction, not a detailed anatomy lesson — later grades will build on this foundation with more depth. Consider previewing this chapter with families before class, and be ready to pause for questions. There are no wrong questions in this chapter.

docs.title: Puberty
docs.text:
Every person who has ever lived has gone through the same basic stage of growth: a time when the body changes from a child's body into a more grown-up body. This stage has a name.

Puberty is the normal, healthy stage of growth when a child's body gradually begins changing into a more adult body, including growing taller, developing new body shapes, and experiencing new feelings. Puberty happens to every human body eventually — it is not something that happens to only some people or that can be avoided. It is simply part of being human, the same way that learning to walk or losing baby teeth was part of growing up earlier in life.

One of the most important facts about puberty is timing: it does not start on the same day, month, or even year for everyone. Some classmates will begin noticing changes while they are still in elementary school; others will not notice changes until they are in middle school. Both are completely normal. There is no "correct" age for puberty to begin, and starting earlier or later than a friend does not mean anything is wrong.

Big Idea

Puberty happens at a different pace for every person — even between identical twins. That means there is no "right" time for it to start. Every timeline is a normal timeline.

During puberty, a young person's body and feelings change in a few general ways:

  • Growth spurts — growing taller and heavier faster than in earlier years
  • Body shape changes — the body gradually beginning to take on a more adult shape
  • Skin changes — skin may become oilier, and some young people notice more sweat or body odor
  • Emotional changes — feelings can feel stronger, more mixed-up, or more sudden than before

Puberty is guided by natural chemical messengers inside the body called hormones, but a young person doesn't need to memorize the science to understand the big picture: this is a normal, healthy stage of growth, and every body goes through it in its own way and its own time.

It is also completely normal to feel a mix of emotions about puberty — some students feel excited about growing up, some feel nervous, some feel confused, and many feel several of these feelings on the very same day. None of those feelings are wrong.

All Feelings Are Okay

Feeling excited, nervous, confused, or all of those at once about growing up is completely normal. There is no wrong way to feel about puberty — and talking about those feelings with a trusted adult can help.

docs.title: Diagram: Everyone's Timeline Looks Different
docs.text:
Everyone's Timeline Looks Different MicroSim

Type: timeline sim-id: puberty-timeline-explorer Library: vis-timeline Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, explain, interpret

Learning objective: Students describe that puberty is a normal, healthy stage of growth that happens to every person at a different time, by exploring several sample timelines side by side.

Purpose: Normalize the wide range of ages at which puberty can begin, without showing any anatomical detail — the focus is entirely on the idea of timing variety and reassurance.

Visual style: Four to five simple horizontal timeline bars, one per sample young person (labeled "Person A," "Person B," "Person C," etc. — no depicted bodies or images of children), each spanning roughly ages 8 through 14, with a single marker showing "changes begin noticeably" at a different point on each bar

Data shown (age ranges only, no names or images): - Person A: changes begin around age 9 - Person B: changes begin around age 11 - Person C: changes begin around age 13 - Person D: changes begin around age 10 - Person E: changes begin around age 12

Interactive features: - Clicking any timeline marker reveals an infobox: "This is just one example. There is no 'right' age for puberty to begin — every person's timeline is different, and that's normal." - A "Where's the same age for everyone?" button reveals the message: "There isn't one! That's the whole point — every body has its own timeline."

Color scheme: Soft, warm, non-clinical colors (light green, light blue, soft yellow) for each timeline bar; no skin tones or body imagery of any kind

Implementation notes: Absolutely no anatomical imagery — this is an abstract timeline of labeled bars and markers only, similar to a project-planning timeline. The purpose is purely to teach the concept "different people, different timing, all normal." Use vis-timeline or an equivalent bar-based rendering.

Now that puberty itself makes sense as a normal, healthy stage of growth, it helps to know that this stage usually unfolds in a general order, rather than all at once.

docs.title: Stages Of Puberty
docs.text:
Puberty is not a single moment — it is a gradual process that unfolds over several years. Thinking about it in simple stages can help students understand what "going through puberty" actually means.

Stages of puberty are the general, simplified phases young people move through during this stage of growth: a time before changes start, a time when changes are just beginning, and a time when changes continue and become more noticeable. These stages are not exact ages and do not look identical for every person — they are simply a helpful way to describe the general order that growth tends to follow.

A simple way to think about the three general stages:

  1. Before changes start — the body is still growing the way it has throughout childhood, without puberty changes yet.
  2. Changes beginning — a young person may start noticing small changes, such as growing a bit faster or new feelings that seem stronger than before.
  3. Changes continuing — changes become more noticeable over time, such as continued growth spurts and body shape changes, as the body continues moving toward its adult form.

It's worth repeating an important point from the first section: no two people move through these three general stages at exactly the same age. A student might be in the "changes beginning" stage while a same-age classmate is still in "before changes start," and both are exactly where they should be.

Helpful Tip

Instead of asking "Am I ahead or behind?", it helps to ask "What stage am I noticing right now?" There is no race, and no finish line to beat anyone to.

docs.title: Diagram: Sort the Stage
docs.text:
Sort the Stage MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: puberty-stage-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, classify, sequence

Learning objective: Students recognize the general stages of puberty by sorting plain, non-anatomical statements into the correct simplified stage: Before Changes Start, Changes Beginning, or Changes Continuing.

Canvas layout: - Left side (400px): Three labeled stage bins in order — "Before Changes Start," "Changes Beginning," "Changes Continuing" - Right side (200px): A stack of plain statement cards (e.g., "Growing the same steady way I always have," "Noticing I grow a little faster than last year," "Having stronger feelings some days," "My body shape is changing more than before")

Visual elements: - Three calm, evenly spaced bins with simple growth-arrow icons (small, medium, large arrow) rather than any body imagery - Statement cards in plain text only

Interactive controls: - Click or drag each statement card into the stage bin where it belongs - Button: "Check My Answers" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - All statement cards begin shuffled above the three bins

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the shuffled statement cards and three empty labeled bins Stage 2: As each card is sorted, show it snap into the chosen bin Stage 3: When "Check My Answers" is clicked, reveal a calm one-sentence explanation for each card's correct stage

Behavior: - Correctly sorted cards get a checkmark - Incorrectly sorted cards get a gentle, factual explanation of why the statement fits a different stage - A reassuring closing message appears once every card is sorted: "Remember — everyone reaches these stages at a different age. That's normal!"

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level objective (describe, classify), so the design uses a calm sorting-and-explanation pattern with plain, non-anatomical statements, keeping the focus on the general idea of ordered stages rather than any physical detail.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. No anatomical imagery or body silhouettes of any kind — use only arrow-size icons and plain text. Keep tone entirely reassuring and never suggest any stage is "better" or "worse."

Knowing that puberty happens in a general order is useful, but the most important skill in this whole chapter isn't a fact to memorize — it's knowing exactly what to do when a body change feels confusing, and who to turn to.

docs.title: Asking For Help With Body Changes
docs.text:
With so many new changes happening, it is completely normal for a young person to have questions — and just as normal to feel a little unsure about how to ask them.

Asking for help with body changes means telling a trusted adult about a physical or emotional change, or a question about growing up, so that adult can explain what is happening and offer support. This is a skill, just like asking for help with a hard math problem or a scraped knee — the more a student practices it, the easier it becomes.

There is no such thing as a silly question about growing up. A trusted adult would always rather answer a question — even one asked more than once — than have a student worry alone. Some examples of the kinds of things a student might ask a trusted adult:

  • "Is it normal that I feel like crying for no reason some days?"
  • "My friend already started changing and I haven't — is something wrong with me?"
  • "I noticed my body doing something new. Is that normal?"
  • "I feel nervous about growing up. Is that okay?"

The answer to every single one of these questions is: yes, that's normal, and a trusted adult can talk it through.

A Normal Part of Growing Up

Puberty can bring up big questions, and that is completely expected. Trusted adults have answered these same questions for children for as long as people have grown up — a student is never the first person to wonder about it.

docs.title: Diagram: Who Can I Ask?
docs.text:
Who Can I Ask? Support Network Diagram

Type: graph-model sim-id: who-can-i-ask-support-network Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: use, identify, demonstrate

Learning objective: Students identify trusted adults and practice using the skill of asking for help with body changes by exploring a support-network map centered on themselves.

Purpose: Show students a visual "map" of the trusted adults available to them for body-change questions, reinforcing that help is close by and that asking is always the right move.

Node types: 1. Center node: "Me" (soft yellow circle) 2. Trusted adult nodes (soft blue circles) connected directly to "Me": Parent/Guardian, School Nurse, Teacher, Counselor, Doctor, Another Trusted Family Member

Edge types: - Single line connecting "Me" to each trusted adult, labeled with how that adult can help (e.g., "Can answer questions at home," "Can help at school," "Knows about bodies and health")

Layout: Radial/hub layout with "Me" in the center and trusted adult nodes arranged around it

Interactive features: - Click any trusted adult node to reveal an infobox: who this person is, and one example question a student could ask them about body changes - Click the center "Me" node to reveal the reminder: "You can ask more than one trusted adult, and you can ask the same question more than once." - Drag nodes to rearrange the network; zoom and pan supported

Visual styling: Warm, friendly color palette (soft yellow center, soft blue trusted-adult nodes); simple circle shapes, no realistic depictions of people

Legend: Explains that the yellow center node represents the student, and blue nodes represent trusted adults who can help with questions about growing up

Implementation: vis-network with click-to-reveal infobox panels; no anatomical content anywhere in this diagram — it is purely a support-network map.

Practicing how to start the conversation can make it much easier when a real question comes up. Here are a few simple sentence starters students can use:

  1. "Can I ask you something about my body?"
  2. "Something is changing and I have a question."
  3. "I feel kind of nervous about growing up. Can we talk?"
  4. "Is it normal if...?"

Any of these openers works well, and a trusted adult will recognize exactly what is being asked and will want to help.

docs.title: Identifying Trusted Adults
docs.text:
Asking for help only works if a student first knows who counts as a trusted adult for this kind of question. This chapter builds directly on the trusted-adult idea from Chapter 2, and applies it specifically to body changes and growing up.

Identifying trusted adults means recognizing which grown-ups in a student's life are safe, caring, and appropriate to go to with questions or concerns about body changes and growing up — such as a parent or guardian, another close family member, a school nurse, a teacher, or a doctor. A trusted adult for this topic is someone who listens without making a student feel embarrassed, answers honestly, and keeps the conversation calm and supportive.

A few signs that someone is a good trusted adult to ask about body changes:

Sign What It Looks Like Listens fully Gives full attention instead of rushing the conversation Answers honestly Gives calm, truthful answers instead of avoiding the topic Keeps students comfortable Never teases or makes a student feel embarrassed for asking Is available Can be reached at home, at school, or at a doctor's visit

Every student's list of trusted adults may look a little different, and that is completely fine — the important thing is that every student has at least one adult they feel comfortable asking. If the very first trusted adult a student asks seems busy or the moment doesn't feel right, that's okay — trying a different trusted adult, or trying again later, is a perfectly good next step.

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "If you noticed a body change and felt confused or worried about it, what could you do?" Then reveal: "Tell a trusted adult, like a parent, guardian, school nurse, teacher, or doctor. Puberty is a normal, healthy part of growing up, and trusted adults are there to help answer questions — no question is too small or too silly to ask."

Chapter Complete!

Well done, friend. You now understand that puberty is a normal, healthy stage of growth that happens to every person at a different time, that it unfolds in general stages, and that trusted adults are always available to help answer questions about body changes.

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text: By the end of this chapter, most Grade 3 students should be able to recognize the general stages of puberty (3.2.1.2, Remember level) and demonstrate asking for help to manage physical and emotional changes during puberty (3.2.1.2, Apply level). The MicroSims move from an Understand-level timeline exploration and stage-sorting activity to an Apply-level support-network exercise that has students practice identifying and reaching out to a trusted adult, matching the Remember-to-Apply span of the underlying benchmark. Because this is a K-3 band, the body text is written as teacher-facing read-aloud material, and the MicroSims are the direct hands-on practice for students.
