This entire chapter — not just one section — is intentionally plainly sincere throughout: there are no puns, no catchphrase, and no light dog-themed phrasing anywhere in this content, since puberty is this band's most sensitive topic and the tone should stay warm but serious. Every diagram in this chapter deliberately avoids anatomical imagery, focusing instead on timelines, stage-sorting, and a support-network map. Preview this chapter with families ahead of instruction, and be ready to answer follow-up questions calmly — remind students throughout that every timeline is different, and that trusted adults are always available to help.

docs.title: Quiz: Growth And Puberty
docs.text: Test your understanding of puberty as a normal stage of growth, its general stages, and asking trusted adults for help with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is "puberty"?
docs.text:
1. The normal, healthy stage of growth when a child's body gradually changes into a more adult body
  2. A sickness that only some people get
  3. Something that can be avoided if a person tries hard enough
  4. A test students take in school
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Puberty is the normal, healthy stage of growth when a child's body gradually begins changing into a more adult body, including growing taller and experiencing new feelings. It happens to every human body eventually.

Concept Tested: Puberty

docs.title: 2. Why is there no "right" age for puberty to begin?
docs.text:
1. Because puberty never actually begins
  2. Because only some people go through puberty
  3. Because scientists have not studied it yet
  4. Because puberty happens at a different pace for every person, and every timeline is normal
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Puberty happens at a different pace for every person — even between identical twins. That means there is no "correct" age for it to begin, and every timeline is a normal timeline.

Concept Tested: Puberty

docs.title: 3. Which of these is listed as a general body change during puberty?
docs.text:
1. Growth spurts — growing taller and heavier faster than before
  2. Losing the ability to walk
  3. Becoming much shorter
  4. Losing all baby teeth at once
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Growth spurts, meaning growing taller and heavier faster than in earlier years, are one of the general body changes described during puberty, along with body shape changes, skin changes, and emotional changes.

Concept Tested: Stages Of Puberty

docs.title: 4. In the "changes beginning" stage of puberty, what might a young person start to notice?
docs.text:
1. No changes of any kind, ever
  2. That puberty is completely finished
  3. Small changes, like growing a bit faster or feelings that seem stronger than before
  4. That their body has stopped growing completely
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. During the "changes beginning" stage, a young person may start noticing small changes, such as growing a bit faster or new feelings that seem stronger than before.

Concept Tested: Stages Of Puberty

docs.title: 5. What is the general order of the three simplified stages of puberty described in the chapter?
docs.text:
1. Changes continuing, changes beginning, before changes start
  2. Before changes start, changes beginning, changes continuing
  3. Changes beginning, before changes start, changes continuing
  4. There is no order at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The three general stages move in this order: before changes start, changes beginning, and changes continuing — though the exact age this happens is different for every person.

Concept Tested: Stages Of Puberty

docs.title: 6. A student notices a new body change and feels unsure if it's normal. What is the best thing to do?
docs.text:
1. Keep it a secret from everyone forever
  2. Assume something is wrong without asking anyone
  3. Compare their body to every classmate's body
  4. Tell a trusted adult, since asking questions about growing up is always okay
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Asking for help with body changes means telling a trusted adult about a physical or emotional change or a question about growing up. There is no such thing as a silly question about growing up.

Concept Tested: Asking For Help With Body Changes

docs.title: 7. Why is it normal to feel a mix of excited, nervous, and confused feelings about puberty, sometimes all on the same day?
docs.text:
1. Because those feelings mean something is wrong
  2. Because only some students are allowed to feel that way
  3. Because growing up is a big change, and many students feel several emotions about it at once
  4. Because puberty does not involve any feelings at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. It is completely normal to feel a mix of emotions about puberty — excited, nervous, confused, or several of these on the same day. None of those feelings are wrong.

Concept Tested: Puberty

docs.title: 8. Which sentence starter could a student use to begin a conversation with a trusted adult about body changes?
docs.text:
1. "I don't want to talk about anything, ever."
  2. "Can I ask you something about my body?"
  3. "This topic is too embarrassing to mention."
  4. "I already know everything, so never mind."
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. "Can I ask you something about my body?" is one of the sentence starters suggested in the chapter to help a student begin a conversation with a trusted adult about growing up.

Concept Tested: Asking For Help With Body Changes

docs.title: 9. Which of these is a trusted adult a student could go to with questions about body changes?
docs.text:
1. A school nurse, parent, guardian, or doctor
  2. A stranger online who seems friendly
  3. Any classmate the student has never spoken to
  4. A cartoon character
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Trusted adults for questions about body changes and growing up include a parent or guardian, another close family member, a school nurse, a teacher, or a doctor.

Concept Tested: Identifying Trusted Adults

docs.title: 10. A student asks two different adults about a body change. One rushes through the answer and seems annoyed; the other listens fully and answers honestly. Which one better matches the chapter's description of a good trusted adult for this topic?
docs.text:
1. Neither adult, because no one should ever be asked
  2. The one who rushes through the answer
  3. Both are equally good, since any adult will do
  4. The one who listens fully and answers honestly
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A good trusted adult for body-change questions listens fully, answers honestly, keeps the student comfortable, and is available — not one who rushes or seems annoyed by the question.

Concept Tested: Identifying Trusted Adults

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter explores resilience and how personal choices affect mental and emotional wellbeing, ways to cope with challenging situations and who to talk to, and what mental health challenges are and how they affect people. Students also build empathy and examine how emotions influence and are expressed through behavior.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Resilience
  2. Personal Choices And Wellbeing
  3. Coping With Challenges
  4. Who To Talk To
  5. Mental Health Challenge
  6. Effects Of Mental Health Challenges
  7. Empathy
  8. Empathy In Friendships
  9. Emotions Influence Behavior
  10. Expressing Emotions
  11. Kindness And Respect For All Abilities

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on the foundational ideas about health in Chapter 1: Foundations Of Health, the trusted-adult concept from Chapter 2: Safety And Trusted Adults, and the relationships and bullying concepts from Chapter 5: Relationships And Respect.

Feelings Are Part of Being Healthy Too

Hi, friend. So far this book has talked about food, bodies, and relationships. This chapter is about something just as important: the mind and the feelings inside it. We'll talk about bouncing back from hard days, who to turn to when things feel tough, and how to treat everyone — including ourselves — with kindness. Let's think it through together.

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Introduce This Chapter
docs.text: This chapter is written to be read aloud and facilitated by a teacher, parent, or other trusted adult. Two sections — Mental Health Challenge and Effects Of Mental Health Challenges — introduce the idea that some people experience ongoing struggles with their thoughts, feelings, or behavior, and that this is a normal part of some people's lives, not something shameful or scary. Keep the tone in those two sections calm, plain, and factual, exactly like a lesson about a broken arm needing a cast: something can be hard, and there is help for it. Preview this chapter with families, and be ready to name your own building's specific trusted adults (counselor, school psychologist, nurse) during discussion.

docs.title: Resilience
docs.text:
Every person has hard days — a friend might move away, a pet might get sick, or a test might not go the way a student hoped. What matters most is not whether hard things happen, since they happen to everyone, but what a person does next.

Resilience is the ability to recover from a hard day, a disappointment, or a difficult situation, and keep going in a healthy way. Resilience does not mean never feeling sad, mad, or discouraged — it means feeling those feelings and then finding a path forward instead of staying stuck. Resilience is a skill that grows stronger with practice.

A student building resilience might:

  • Notice and name the hard feeling ("I feel disappointed that I didn't make the team.")
  • Remind themselves that one hard moment does not erase all the good things in their life
  • Try again, ask for help, or try a different approach
  • Give themselves credit for trying, even when the outcome wasn't perfect

Big Idea

Resilience isn't about ignoring hard feelings — it's about moving through them. Bending like a tree in the wind is strong. Trying never to feel the wind at all isn't possible for anyone.

Resilience connects directly to the everyday choices a student makes, which is the next idea in this chapter.

docs.title: Personal Choices And Wellbeing
docs.text:
Some parts of mental and emotional wellbeing are outside a student's control, like whether a big change happens in their family. But many parts are shaped by small, everyday choices.

Personal choices and wellbeing describes the connection between the decisions a person makes each day — such as how much sleep they get, how they move their body, who they spend time with, and how they talk to themselves — and how healthy their mind and emotions feel over time. "Wellbeing" simply means an overall sense of feeling okay, physically, mentally, and emotionally, most days, and choices that support it don't have to be complicated.

Here is a look at how everyday choices tend to affect wellbeing:

Choice Effect on Wellbeing Getting enough sleep Improves mood, focus, and patience with others Being physically active Releases feelings of stress and boosts mood Spending time with caring people Builds a sense of belonging and support Talking about feelings instead of bottling them up Prevents feelings from building into bigger problems Taking quiet breaks from screens Gives the brain time to rest and reset

A student cannot control every event in their life, but small choices, repeated daily, add up to a big difference in how someone feels.

docs.title: Diagram: Choice and Wellbeing Explorer
docs.text:
Choice and Wellbeing Explorer MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: choice-and-wellbeing-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, describe, interpret

Learning objective: Students explain how everyday personal choices affect mental and emotional wellbeing by adjusting sliders for common daily choices and observing a simple wellbeing meter respond.

Canvas layout: Left side (350px) has four labeled sliders — Hours of Sleep (4-10), Time Being Active (0-60 min), Time Talking With Someone Caring (0-30 min), Quiet Screen-Free Time (0-30 min). Right side (250px) shows a semicircle "Wellbeing Meter" gauge with a needle moving from "Running on Empty" (red) to "Feeling Good" (green), plus a short explanation text box.

Interactive controls: Four draggable sliders; a "Reset to Example Day" button.

Default parameters: Sleep 7 hours, Active 20 min, Talking 10 min, Quiet time 10 min — meter starts in the middle "Okay" zone.

Data Visibility Requirements: As a student drags any slider up, the needle moves toward green and a one-sentence plain-language reason appears (e.g., "More sleep helps your brain rest and reset."). Dragging down moves the needle toward red with a matching reason. No single slider can max the meter alone, reinforcing that wellbeing comes from combined healthy choices.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level objective, so the design favors direct manipulation with immediate, concrete feedback over any competitive or scored element.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep reasons short, reassuring, and non-judgmental.

Even with excellent daily choices, hard situations still happen sometimes. That's exactly what the next section is about.

docs.title: Coping With Challenges
docs.text:
A challenging situation is any moment that brings up strong or uncomfortable feelings — frustration over a hard homework problem, sadness about an argument with a friend, or worry about a change at home. Facing challenges is normal, and there are healthy ways to move through them.

Coping with challenges means using healthy strategies to manage the strong feelings that come with a difficult situation, instead of letting those feelings take over or ignoring them completely.

Some healthy coping strategies a student can try:

  1. Take slow, deep breaths and count to ten
  2. Name the feeling out loud or write it down
  3. Go for a walk, stretch, or move the body
  4. Draw, write, or make something
  5. Talk to someone who cares

Helpful Tip

Coping strategies work best when practiced before a hard moment happens — like a fire drill. Trying a few strategies out on an ordinary day makes them easier to remember on a hard one.

Coping strategies help in the moment, but knowing who to bring bigger feelings to is just as important a skill.

docs.title: Who To Talk To
docs.text:
Some feelings are light enough to handle with a quick coping strategy. Others are heavier and work best when shared with someone else — and that is not a sign of weakness. It is one of the healthiest things a person can do.

Who to talk to refers to identifying the trusted people in a student's life — such as a parent or guardian, another family member, a teacher, a school counselor, or a school nurse — who can be told about a hard feeling so they can help. This builds directly on the trusted-adult idea from earlier in this book: the same people who help with safety questions can also help with feelings. A good person to talk to about feelings listens without judging, takes the feeling seriously, and helps figure out a next step.

docs.title: Diagram: Who Can I Talk To About My Feelings?
docs.text:
Who Can I Talk To About My Feelings? Diagram

Type: graph-model sim-id: who-to-talk-to-feelings-map Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: identify, recall, recognize

Learning objective: Students identify trusted people they can talk to about hard feelings by exploring a support-network map centered on themselves.

Purpose: Reinforce that help for emotional struggles is close by, using the same hub-and-spoke pattern as the trusted-adult map from Chapter 2, now applied specifically to feelings.

Node types: Center node "Me" (soft yellow circle); trusted-person nodes (soft blue circles) connected to "Me" — Parent/Guardian, Teacher, School Counselor, School Nurse, Another Trusted Family Member, Close Friend.

Edge types: A line connecting "Me" to each trusted person, labeled with the kind of help offered (e.g., "Helps me think it through," "Knows calming strategies," "Listens without judging").

Layout: Radial/hub layout with "Me" in the center.

Interactive features: Click any trusted-person node to reveal an infobox naming who they are and an example thing to say to them. Click the center "Me" node to reveal: "You can talk to more than one person, more than once." Drag, zoom, and pan supported.

Visual styling: Warm palette, simple circle shapes, no realistic depictions of people.

Implementation: vis-network with click-to-reveal infobox panels.

Practicing what to say can make starting the conversation much easier. A few sentence starters a student can use:

  • "Can I talk to you about something that's bothering me?"
  • "I've been feeling really [sad/worried/frustrated] lately."
  • "Something happened and I don't know how to feel about it."

Any trusted adult who hears one of these openers will know exactly how to help. Sometimes, though, a hard feeling isn't just a single tough day — it can last longer and need a different kind of understanding, which is what the next two sections explain.

docs.title: Mental Health Challenge
docs.text:
Just like some people have ongoing physical health needs — such as needing glasses to see clearly, or medicine to manage allergies — some people have ongoing needs related to their thoughts, feelings, or behavior.

A mental health challenge is an ongoing difficulty with thoughts, feelings, or behavior that affects how a person feels or acts in daily life, and that can be helped by talking with trusted adults or health professionals. Examples students may have heard of include feeling worried much of the time (anxiety) or feeling very sad for a long stretch of time (depression). A mental health challenge is not something a person chooses, and a person cannot simply decide to stop having one, just like a person cannot decide to stop needing glasses.

A few important, plain facts about mental health challenges:

  • They are common. Many people — children and adults — experience a mental health challenge at some point in their lives.
  • They are not anyone's fault. A person does not cause their own mental health challenge, and nothing is "wrong" with someone who has one.
  • They can be helped. Talking with a trusted adult, a school counselor, or a doctor is the first step, and there are many ways professionals can help.
  • They are private and personal. A person gets to decide how much to share about their own experience, and everyone deserves privacy and respect around this topic.

Having a mental health challenge is a normal part of some people's lives, the same way needing help with reading or needing a cast for a broken arm is normal. It is nothing to feel ashamed of, and trusted adults and health professionals are there to help.

docs.title: Effects Of Mental Health Challenges
docs.text:
Effects of mental health challenges are the ways an ongoing difficulty with thoughts, feelings, or behavior can show up in a person's daily life, such as trouble concentrating in class, changes in sleep or appetite, pulling away from friends, or feeling tired even after resting. These effects look different from person to person, and can also affect the people who care about that person. A classmate showing one of these signs is not choosing to act that way, and deserves the same patience a student would want if they were struggling with something hard.

What It Might Look Like What It Does Not Mean Trouble focusing on schoolwork The person isn't trying hard enough Pulling away from friends The person doesn't like their friends anymore Seeming tired, sad, or worried often The person is being dramatic Changes in eating or sleeping The person is doing it on purpose

The most helpful response to a classmate, friend, or family member showing these signs is the same skill from earlier in this chapter: encouraging them to talk to a trusted adult, and being a caring, non-judgmental friend while they get support. Trusted adults and health professionals, such as school counselors, doctors, and therapists, are specially trained to help people manage mental health challenges, and asking for that help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "If a mental health challenge is a normal part of some people's lives, what is the most helpful thing a friend can do?" Then reveal: "Be patient and kind, and encourage them to talk to a trusted adult or health professional. Mental health challenges are common, they are nobody's fault, and they can be helped."

With a clear, caring understanding of mental health challenges in place, this chapter now turns to a skill that supports every relationship a student will ever have: empathy.

docs.title: Empathy
docs.text:
Understanding what someone else might be feeling, especially a feeling a student has never personally experienced, is one of the most valuable skills a person can build.

Empathy is the ability to notice, understand, and care about what another person is feeling, even when that feeling is different from what the student is feeling in that moment. Empathy is different from simply feeling sorry for someone; it means genuinely trying to imagine the situation from the other person's point of view.

Empathy can be practiced in small, everyday moments:

  • Noticing when a classmate looks upset and checking in on them
  • Imagining how a new student might feel on their first day
  • Pausing before reacting to ask, "What might they be feeling right now?"

Empathy Takes Practice

Empathy can feel hard at first, especially for feelings a student hasn't experienced themselves. That's completely okay — empathy is a muscle that gets stronger every time it's used.

Once a student understands empathy in general, it becomes easier to see exactly how it shows up in one of the most important parts of their daily life: friendship.

docs.title: Empathy In Friendships
docs.text:
Friendships are built and strengthened through many small moments of noticing and caring about a friend's feelings.

Empathy in friendships means using empathy specifically to support and care for friends — noticing when a friend is struggling, celebrating with a friend who is excited, and responding to a friend's feelings with kindness rather than dismissing them. Empathy is one of the biggest reasons some friendships feel warm and supportive while others feel one-sided.

docs.title: Diagram: Spot the Empathetic Response
docs.text:
Spot the Empathetic Response MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: spot-the-empathetic-response Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, apply, practice

Learning objective: Students demonstrate recognition of empathetic responses in friendships by choosing the most empathetic reply to a friend's statement from several options.

Canvas layout: Top (100px) shows a speech-bubble box with a friend's statement (e.g., "I didn't make the team," "I got a new puppy!", "I'm nervous about the test"). Middle (300px) shows three response-choice buttons — one empathetic, one dismissive, one self-centered. Bottom (100px) is a feedback panel.

Interactive controls: Click a response choice; "Next Scenario" and "Reset" buttons.

Default parameters: Starts on scenario 1 of 5 prepared scenarios.

Behavior: Clicking a response reveals whether it was the most empathetic choice and explains why in one or two sentences before advancing.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level objective, so realistic scenario choices with immediate explanatory feedback replace passive viewing.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep scenarios everyday friendship moments only — no bullying or mental-health-challenge content here.

Empathy inside friendships doesn't just help the other person — it connects directly to how a student's own emotions show up in their actions, the focus of the next section.

docs.title: Emotions Influence Behavior
docs.text:
Feelings and actions are closely linked. Recognizing that link is one of the most useful things a student can understand about themselves.

Emotions influence behavior describes the way a person's feelings shape what they do next — for example, frustration might lead to snapping at someone, while excitement might lead to talking very fast or wanting to share good news right away. Noticing this connection gives a student the power to pause and choose a helpful action instead of letting a strong feeling take over automatically.

A simple way to picture the link: Feeling → Noticing the feeling → Choosing a response → Action. For example: feeling frustrated → noticing "I'm getting frustrated" → deciding to take a breath instead of yelling → calmly asking for help. That pause between noticing a feeling and choosing an action is exactly where resilience and coping strategies from earlier in this chapter come into play.

docs.title: Expressing Emotions
docs.text:
Once a student notices a feeling, the next skill is deciding how to share it with others in a way that helps rather than hurts.

Expressing emotions means communicating feelings to others in healthy ways — through words, tone of voice, facial expressions, or body language — instead of bottling feelings up or letting them come out as hurtful words or actions. Healthy expression names the feeling calmly and clearly; unhealthy expression either hides the feeling completely or lets it explode onto someone else.

Feeling Unhealthy Expression Healthy Expression Frustration Yelling or slamming things "I feel frustrated because this is hard for me." Sadness Hiding it and pretending to be fine "I feel sad about what happened today." Excitement Interrupting everyone to talk only about it "I'm so excited — can I tell you something?" Jealousy Saying mean things about the other person "I feel jealous, and I want to talk about why."

docs.title: Diagram: Healthy vs. Unhealthy Expression Sorter
docs.text:
Healthy vs. Unhealthy Expression Sorter MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: expression-style-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: differentiate, examine, distinguish

Learning objective: Students differentiate between healthy and unhealthy ways of expressing emotions by sorting example statements and actions into the correct category.

Canvas layout: Left side (400px) has two labeled bins, "Healthy Expression" (speech-bubble-with-heart icon) and "Unhealthy Expression" (stormy-cloud icon). Right side (200px) holds a stack of shuffled example cards, such as "I feel left out, can we talk?", "Slamming the door and refusing to speak", "I'm nervous about the game, wish me luck", "Yelling mean names when losing a game."

Interactive controls: Click or drag each card into a bin; "Check My Answers" and "Reset" buttons.

Data Visibility Requirements: As each card is sorted it snaps into the chosen bin; clicking "Check My Answers" reveals a one-sentence explanation for every card, and incorrectly sorted cards get a gentle explanation of why they fit the other category.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level objective requiring students to distinguish categories by shared features, so sorting-with-explanation is appropriate.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep tone non-judgmental toward the "unhealthy" category — frame it as practice noticing the difference, not as labeling a student.

Everything this chapter has covered so far — resilience, coping, talking to trusted people, empathy, and healthy expression — comes together in one final, essential idea: treating every single person with kindness and respect, no matter how their mind or body works.

docs.title: Kindness And Respect For All Abilities
docs.text:
Every classroom is full of people whose minds and bodies work in different ways. Some students learn to read at a different pace than others, some use a wheelchair, hearing aid, or other tool, and some think, focus, or process the world differently — sometimes called being neurodivergent, which includes differences like ADHD, autism, or dyslexia. None of these differences make a person less valuable, less capable, or less deserving of friendship.

Kindness and respect for all abilities means treating every person with care and fairness regardless of how their body or mind works, recognizing that different does not mean less — it simply means different. This includes both physical disabilities and differences in how a person's brain processes information, learns, or focuses.

A few ways students can show this kind of respect every day:

  • Ask a classmate how they'd like to be helped, instead of assuming
  • Include classmates with disabilities or differences in games and group work
  • Never tease, exclude, or mock the way someone talks, moves, learns, or focuses
  • Remember that a tool someone uses — like a wheelchair, hearing aid, or fidget tool — is just a tool, the same way glasses are a tool
  • Speak directly to the classmate, not just to their helper or aide

Different, Not Less

Every brain and body works a little differently, and every single one of them deserves kindness. A classroom full of different kinds of minds is a classroom full of different kinds of strengths.

docs.title: Diagram: Kindness for Every Ability Explorer
docs.text:
Kindness for Every Ability Explorer Infographic

Type: infographic sim-id: kindness-for-every-ability-explorer Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, describe, exemplify

Learning objective: Students explain how to show kindness and respect to classmates of all abilities by exploring a set of clickable classmate icons representing different physical and neurological differences.

Purpose: Build genuine, concrete understanding of inclusion through specific, respectful examples rather than abstract statements.

Layout: A row of six simple, friendly cartoon classmate icons (no realistic depictions), arranged left to right, none visually marked as more "different" than another.

Icons and content: (1) Uses a wheelchair — click reveals: "Alex uses a wheelchair to get around. Ask how to include them, like choosing a game area that's easy to reach." (2) Uses a hearing aid — click reveals: "Jordan uses a hearing aid. Facing Jordan when you talk helps them hear and understand you." (3) Is autistic — click reveals: "Sam's brain processes the world a little differently and may need quiet breaks — that's a strength of knowing what helps, not a weakness." (4) Has ADHD — click reveals: "Riley has ADHD, which can make sitting still or focusing harder some days. Riley isn't being lazy on purpose." (5) Has dyslexia — click reveals: "Priya has dyslexia, which makes reading take more effort. Priya is just as smart as any classmate." (6) No visible difference — click reveals: "Not every difference can be seen. Being kind to everyone, always, is the right choice."

Interactive features: Click any icon to reveal its infobox. A "What's the same for everyone?" button reveals: "Everyone wants to be included, respected, and treated kindly."

Implementation: vis-network or a clickable icon grid with infobox panels; responsive layout that reflows on narrow screens.

Kindness for all abilities is what resilience, empathy, and healthy emotional expression look like in practice, with every classmate, every day.

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "If a classmate learns, moves, or focuses differently than you do, what should that change about how you treat them?" Then reveal: "Nothing about your kindness or respect should change. Different does not mean less — everyone deserves to be included and treated with care."

Chapter Complete!

Great work, friend. You now understand resilience, healthy coping, who to talk to, what mental health challenges are, empathy, and how to show kindness and respect to every classmate. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text: By chapter's end, most Grade 3 students should describe resilience and how personal choices affect wellbeing, recall coping strategies and who to talk to (3.3.1.2), describe mental health challenges and their effects (3.3.1.3), describe empathy and its role in friendships (3.3.1.4), and explain how emotions influence and are expressed through behavior (3.3.1.5). The MicroSims progress from Remember-level identification through Understand-level exploration to Apply-level practice and Analyze-level differentiation. As directed, the Mental Health Challenge and Effects Of Mental Health Challenges sections use a plainly sincere register with no puns or catchphrase, framing challenges as common, nobody's fault, private, and helped by trusted adults and professionals. The closing Kindness And Respect For All Abilities section is genuinely inclusive of physical disabilities and neurodivergence (ADHD, autism, dyslexia), and deliberately avoids re-covering the bullying mechanics already taught in Chapter 5. Preview the mental health sections with families, and have your building's support contacts (counselor, school psychologist, nurse) ready to share with students.

docs.title: Quiz: Mental And Emotional Health
docs.text: Test your understanding of resilience, coping, mental health challenges, empathy, and kindness for all abilities with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is "resilience"?
docs.text:
1. Never feeling sad, mad, or discouraged
  2. The ability to recover from a hard day or disappointment and keep going in a healthy way
  3. Winning every game or contest
  4. Avoiding hard situations completely
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Resilience is the ability to recover from a hard day, a disappointment, or a difficult situation, and keep going in a healthy way. It does not mean never feeling sad or discouraged.

Concept Tested: Resilience

docs.title: 2. Which everyday choice is described as helping a person's mental and emotional wellbeing?
docs.text:
1. Skipping sleep as often as possible
  2. Getting enough sleep
  3. Avoiding all physical activity
  4. Never talking about feelings
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Getting enough sleep improves mood, focus, and patience with others. The chapter describes several everyday choices, including sleep, activity, caring relationships, and talking about feelings, that support wellbeing over time.

Concept Tested: Personal Choices And Wellbeing

docs.title: 3. A student feels frustrated after a hard homework problem. Which is a healthy coping strategy?
docs.text:
1. Taking slow, deep breaths and counting to ten
  2. Yelling at a family member
  3. Ignoring the feeling completely and never mentioning it
  4. Giving up on all homework forever
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Taking slow, deep breaths and counting to ten is one of the healthy coping strategies listed in the chapter for managing strong feelings during a difficult moment.

Concept Tested: Coping With Challenges

docs.title: 4. Which of these is an example of "who to talk to" about a hard feeling?
docs.text:
1. Ignoring the feeling until it goes away
  2. A stranger online
  3. No one, because feelings should stay private
  4. A parent, teacher, school counselor, or school nurse
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Who to talk to refers to trusted people in a student's life — such as a parent or guardian, teacher, school counselor, or school nurse — who can help when a feeling is heavy or hard to carry alone.

Concept Tested: Who To Talk To

docs.title: 5. Which statement best describes a "mental health challenge"?
docs.text:
1. Something a person chooses and can decide to stop having
  2. An ongoing difficulty with thoughts, feelings, or behavior that can be helped by trusted adults or professionals
  3. Something only a few people in the whole world ever experience
  4. Something shameful that should never be mentioned
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A mental health challenge is an ongoing difficulty with thoughts, feelings, or behavior that affects daily life, and it can be helped by talking with trusted adults or health professionals. It is common and not anyone's fault.

Concept Tested: Mental Health Challenge

docs.title: 6. A classmate seems tired and pulls away from friends for a while. What does this NOT mean, according to the chapter?
docs.text:
1. That something might be affecting how they feel or act
  2. That patience and kindness could help
  3. That the classmate is being dramatic on purpose
  4. That a trusted adult could help figure out what's going on
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter is clear that signs like pulling away from friends or seeming tired do not mean a person is being dramatic or choosing to act that way — they may be effects of a mental health challenge that deserve patience, not judgment.

Concept Tested: Effects Of Mental Health Challenges

docs.title: 7. What is "empathy"?
docs.text:
1. The ability to notice, understand, and care about what another person is feeling
  2. Feeling sorry for someone without trying to understand them
  3. Only caring about your own feelings
  4. Avoiding people who feel differently than you
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Empathy is the ability to notice, understand, and care about what another person is feeling, even when that feeling is different from what the student is feeling. It is different from just feeling sorry for someone.

Concept Tested: Empathy

docs.title: 8. A friend says, "I didn't make the team." Which response shows the most empathy?
docs.text:
1. "That's too bad, anyway, guess what happened to me today?"
  2. "You probably didn't try hard enough."
  3. "I get it, no big deal, let's move on."
  4. "That sounds really disappointing. Do you want to talk about it?"
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. An empathetic response notices and cares about the friend's feeling, like disappointment, and invites them to share more, rather than dismissing the feeling or making it about someone else.

Concept Tested: Empathy In Friendships

docs.title: 9. Which pair correctly matches an unhealthy expression of frustration with a healthy expression of the same feeling?
docs.text:
1. Unhealthy: "I feel frustrated because this is hard." Healthy: yelling and slamming things
  2. Unhealthy: staying calm. Healthy: yelling
  3. Unhealthy: yelling and slamming things. Healthy: "I feel frustrated because this is hard for me."
  4. Both yelling and calm words are equally healthy
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Yelling or slamming things is an unhealthy way to express frustration, while calmly saying "I feel frustrated because this is hard for me" names the feeling clearly — a healthy expression of the same emotion.

Concept Tested: Expressing Emotions

docs.title: 10. A classmate uses a wheelchair to get around the classroom. What is the most respectful way to include them in a game?
docs.text:
1. Leave them out so they don't have to worry about it
  2. Only speak to their helper or aide instead of them
  3. Assume they don't want to play at all
  4. Ask them how they'd like to be included, and choose a game area that works for everyone
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Kindness and respect for all abilities means asking a classmate how they'd like to be helped or included, instead of assuming, and choosing activities that work for everyone rather than leaving anyone out.

Concept Tested: Kindness And Respect For All Abilities

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Students practice verbal and nonverbal communication, active listening, and using I-statements to express thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs, including in decision-making situations. The chapter closes with setting a personal health goal, judging whether help is needed, and identifying health topics that matter most.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on the foundational ideas about health in Chapter 1: Foundations Of Health, the coping and who-to-talk-to concepts from Chapter 7: Mental And Emotional Health, and the physical activity concepts from Chapter 3: Wellness And Activity.

Using Your Words (and More Than Words)

Hi, friend! Every idea, feeling, and need a person has only helps them — and helps others — once it gets communicated clearly. This chapter is about talking, listening, and body language, and it ends with something exciting: setting a real health goal of your own. Let's think it through together.

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Introduce This Chapter
docs.text: This is the final chapter of the Grade 3 book, and it shifts from understanding health topics to practicing skills students will use for the rest of their lives: communicating clearly, listening well, and setting goals. Model each communication skill out loud before asking students to try it — Grade 3 students learn these behaviors best through demonstration and guided practice, not description alone. The closing goal-setting sections are meant to be done collaboratively, with the teacher or a trusted adult helping the student pick something realistic and small.

docs.title: Verbal Communication
docs.text:
Every day, students share thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs with the people around them. The words a person chooses, and how those words are said, make a big difference in whether the message is understood.

Verbal communication means using spoken or written words to share thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs with another person. It includes not just what is said, but how it is said — the tone of voice, the volume, and the speed of speaking all shape how a message lands.

A student using strong verbal communication:

  • Uses clear, specific words instead of vague ones ("I don't understand the third math problem" instead of just "This is hard")
  • Speaks in a calm, steady voice, even when a feeling is strong
  • Waits for a good moment to speak, rather than interrupting
  • Says thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs directly, instead of hinting

Big Idea

Clear words help other people understand exactly what's going on inside a person's head — and that's the first step to getting help, working things out, or sharing good news.

Words are only part of the story, though. The very next section explores the messages people send without saying a single word.

docs.title: Nonverbal Communication
docs.text:
Long before a person finishes a sentence, their face, posture, and hands are already sending a message.

Nonverbal communication means sharing thoughts and feelings through facial expressions, body language, gestures, eye contact, and posture, without using words at all. Nonverbal messages can support spoken words, or they can accidentally contradict them — like saying "I'm fine" while frowning and crossing arms.

docs.title: Diagram: Match the Body Language
docs.text:
Match the Body Language MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: match-the-body-language Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: identify, recognize, name

Learning objective: Students identify the feeling behind common nonverbal cues by matching simple cartoon body-language poses to the feeling they most likely show.

Canvas layout: Left side (350px) shows one large cartoon figure at a time in a clear pose (arms crossed and frowning, shoulders slumped and looking down, wide smile with open arms, tense shoulders with clenched fists). Right side (250px) shows four feeling-word buttons (e.g., "Frustrated," "Sad," "Happy," "Angry") plus a feedback box.

Interactive controls: Click a feeling-word button to answer; "Next Pose" and "Reset" buttons.

Default parameters: Starts on pose 1 of 6 prepared poses, presented in random order each reset.

Behavior: Clicking a feeling reveals whether it matches the pose and a one-sentence explanation of the specific cue (e.g., "Crossed arms and a frown often mean someone feels frustrated or closed off.").

Instructional Rationale: Remember-level objective calling for straightforward recognition, so simple matching with immediate feedback is appropriate — no timer or scoring pressure.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js with simple flat cartoon figures, no realistic faces. Keep the tone neutral; note that body language is a clue, not a certainty, since people can feel one way and look another.

Because nonverbal cues can be misread, it helps to notice both a person's words and their body language together, rather than relying on just one.

Helpful Tip

If someone's words and body language don't match, it's okay to gently ask, "Are you really okay?" Checking in shows you're paying attention to more than just words.

Sending clear messages, verbal and nonverbal, is only half of communication. The other half is just as important: truly hearing what someone else is sending back.

docs.title: Active Listening
docs.text:
Good communication is a two-way street. A student can speak clearly and read body language well, and still miss the point if they aren't truly listening.

Active listening means fully paying attention to a speaker — with eyes, body, and mind — instead of just waiting for a turn to talk. Active listening includes making eye contact, nodding, staying quiet while the other person speaks, and checking understanding by repeating back what was heard.

Here is a comparison of active listening and its opposite:

Active Listening Looks Like Not Listening Looks Like Facing the speaker and making eye contact Looking at a screen or elsewhere Waiting for a pause before responding Interrupting mid-sentence Nodding or saying "I hear you" Staring blankly or looking bored Asking a follow-up question Changing the subject right away Repeating back the main idea to check Assuming you already know what they'll say

docs.title: Diagram: Active Listening Checklist Builder
docs.text:
Active Listening Checklist Builder MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: active-listening-checklist-builder Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, apply

Learning objective: Students demonstrate active listening behaviors by selecting the actions an active listener would take during a short animated conversation scenario.

Canvas layout: Top (150px) shows a simple two-character comic-style scene with a speech bubble describing what one character is saying (e.g., "I'm nervous about my soccer game tomorrow"). Middle (250px) shows six behavior-choice cards a listener could do (e.g., "Look at my phone," "Make eye contact," "Interrupt to talk about myself," "Nod and say 'that makes sense'," "Change the subject," "Ask 'What are you nervous about?'"). Bottom (100px) is a feedback panel.

Interactive controls: Click each card to mark it "Active Listening" or "Not Listening"; "Check My Answers" and "Next Scenario" buttons.

Default parameters: Starts on scenario 1 of 4 prepared conversation scenarios.

Data Visibility Requirements: After clicking "Check My Answers," each card reveals a check mark or an X plus a one-sentence reason (e.g., "Interrupting takes the focus away from the speaker's feelings.").

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level objective requiring students to practice choosing correct behaviors in a realistic scenario, so scenario-based selection with explanatory feedback is appropriate.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js with simple flat character illustrations. Keep scenarios everyday and low-stakes (sports, school, friendship), not emotionally heavy.

Verbal communication, nonverbal communication, and active listening work together as a full toolkit — and that toolkit becomes especially useful in a specific kind of moment: making a decision.

docs.title: Communication In Decision-Making
docs.text:
Many decisions involve more than one person — choosing a group project topic, deciding what game to play at recess, or figuring out a plan with a family member. Communication skills make those moments go much more smoothly.

Communication in decision-making means using verbal communication, nonverbal communication, and active listening together to share opinions, hear other people's opinions, and reach a decision that works for everyone involved. This might mean explaining a preference clearly, listening to someone else's reason, and being willing to compromise.

A simple process for communicating well during a group decision:

  1. Say what you think or want, clearly and calmly
  2. Actively listen to what others think or want
  3. Notice everyone's nonverbal cues (excited? unsure? frustrated?)
  4. Look for an option that respects as many people's needs as possible
  5. Agree on a decision together, or ask a trusted adult to help if the group is stuck

Big Idea

Good decision-making with others isn't about who talks the loudest — it's about everyone getting a real turn to speak and be heard.

Sharing an opinion clearly during a decision works best with one particular sentence pattern, which is exactly what the next section teaches.

docs.title: I-Statement
docs.text:
Sometimes a person needs to share a feeling or a need in a moment that already feels a little tense — like when a friend borrowed something without asking, or a sibling turned off a TV show mid-episode. The words chosen in that moment matter enormously.

An I-statement is a way of expressing a thought, feeling, want, or need that starts with "I" and focuses on the speaker's own experience, rather than blaming or accusing the other person. A typical pattern is: "I feel [feeling] when [situation happens], because [reason]. Could you [request]?" I-statements tend to keep conversations calm, because they describe an experience instead of attacking a person.

Here is a comparison of blaming statements and I-statements:

Blaming Statement (Y0u-Statement) I-Statement "You always take my stuff without asking!" "I feel frustrated when my things are borrowed without asking. Could you ask me first next time?" "You never listen to me!" "I feel unheard when I'm interrupted. Could I finish my thought?" "You ruined the game!" "I feel disappointed that the game ended early. Can we plan a rule for next time?"

docs.title: Diagram: I-Statement Builder
docs.text:
I-Statement Builder MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: i-statement-builder Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: use, construct, practice

Learning objective: Students practice constructing I-statements by assembling a feeling, a situation, and a request from a scenario prompt using the "I feel ___ when , because . Could you ___?" frame.

Canvas layout: Top (100px) shows a short scenario prompt (e.g., "Your friend keeps interrupting you at lunch"). Middle (300px) shows four fill-in-the-blank dropdown menus matching the I-statement frame, each pre-populated with a few word/phrase choices, one clearly best. Bottom (100px) shows the assembled sentence building live as choices are made, plus a "Check My Statement" button.

Interactive controls: Four dropdown selectors; "Check My Statement," "Next Scenario," and "Reset" buttons.

Default parameters: Starts on scenario 1 of 5 prepared everyday scenarios (borrowing without asking, interrupting, excluding from a game, teasing about a mistake, not listening).

Data Visibility Requirements: As each dropdown is filled, the growing sentence appears in a speech bubble in real time so students see the full I-statement take shape. Clicking "Check My Statement" reveals whether the choice keeps the statement calm and focused on feelings rather than blame, with a one-sentence explanation.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level objective requiring learners to construct a correctly formed sentence, so guided assembly with a visible live sentence supports practice better than passive multiple choice alone.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep every scenario a mild, everyday friend/family conflict — nothing involving unsafe situations, which belong in the Personal Safety chapters instead.

Starting with "I feel..." instead of "You always..." is a small change that makes a big difference in how a conversation goes.

With verbal communication, nonverbal communication, active listening, decision-making, and I-statements all in place, this chapter now turns to something these skills make possible: setting and reaching a personal health goal.

docs.title: Personal Health Goal
docs.text:
Everything communicated clearly — a feeling, a need, a decision — can also be aimed at something bigger: a goal a student sets for their own health.

A personal health goal is a specific, health-related behavior a student chooses to work on, such as drinking more water, going to bed earlier, or trying a new fruit or vegetable each week. A strong personal health goal is specific (naming exactly what will change), realistic (something the student can actually do), and personal (chosen because it matters to that student, not just assigned by someone else).

Examples of well-formed personal health goals:

  • "I will drink a full glass of water with breakfast, lunch, and dinner this week."
  • "I will go to bed 15 minutes earlier on school nights."
  • "I will practice one deep-breathing coping strategy when I feel frustrated."
  • "I will try one new vegetable at dinner this week."

docs.title: Diagram: My Health Goal Planner
docs.text:
My Health Goal Planner MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: my-health-goal-planner Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, organize, distinguish

Learning objective: Students examine candidate goal statements and distinguish specific, realistic, personal goals from vague or unrealistic ones, then build their own goal statement.

Canvas layout: Left side (350px) shows five example goal cards to sort into two bins: "Strong Goal" and "Needs Work" (e.g., "Be healthier" vs. "Drink a glass of water with lunch each day"). Right side (250px) holds a simple goal-builder form: a text input for "My goal is..." plus three checkboxes the student self-checks — "Specific," "Realistic," "Matters to me."

Interactive controls: Drag or click to sort cards; text input field; three checkboxes; "Save My Goal" button.

Data Visibility Requirements: Sorting a card reveals a one-sentence reason it is strong or needs work (e.g., "'Be healthier' doesn't say exactly what will change."). After typing a goal and checking all three boxes, "Save My Goal" displays the finished goal statement in a printable-looking card.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level objective requiring students to examine goal statements against criteria, so a sort-then-build design lets students apply the criteria to examples before applying them to their own goal.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js and a real HTML text input for the goal so it is easy to read and edit. This MicroSim is intended for guided, individual student use with a teacher or family member nearby to help, consistent with K-3 practice.

Choosing a goal is an exciting first step — but not every goal can be reached alone, which is exactly what the next section helps a student figure out.

docs.title: Determining Need For Assistance
docs.text:
Some goals are easy to work on independently, like remembering to drink more water. Others go much better with someone else's help, like changing a bedtime routine that depends on the whole family's schedule.

Determining need for assistance means thinking honestly about a personal health goal and deciding whether it can be reached alone, or whether it would go better with help or collaboration from a parent, teacher, coach, or other trusted adult. Recognizing when help is useful is not a weakness — it is a smart, realistic part of goal-setting.

Questions a student can ask to figure this out:

  • Does reaching this goal depend on someone else's schedule or decisions (like bedtime or meals)?
  • Would it help to have someone check in and remind me?
  • Is there a part of this goal I don't know how to do yet?
  • Would celebrating progress with someone else keep me motivated?

If the answer to any of these is "yes," asking for assistance is a great next step.

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "If a student's goal is to go to bed 15 minutes earlier, who might they need help from, and why?" Then reveal: "A parent or guardian, because bedtime often depends on the whole family's evening routine — asking for their help makes the goal much more realistic."

With a goal chosen and a clear sense of whether help is needed, the last two sections zoom back out to the bigger picture of health-supporting practices and topics.

docs.title: Examining Health-Supporting Practices
docs.text:
A single goal is a great start, but it helps to first take a wider look at all the everyday practices that support health, before narrowing in on just one.

Examining health-supporting practices means looking closely at the everyday behaviors that support a person's physical, mental, and emotional health, in order to notice which practices are already going well and which ones might need attention. This connects nearly every topic from this entire book — food choices, physical activity, sleep, safety habits, communication, and coping skills all count as health-supporting practices.

docs.title: Diagram: Health Practices Self-Check
docs.text:
Health Practices Self-Check MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: health-practices-self-check Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, organize, compare

Learning objective: Students examine a set of everyday health-supporting practices across multiple health categories and identify which ones they already do well and which they might want to improve.

Canvas layout: A grid of eight practice cards spanning categories from across the book (Eating balanced meals, Staying active, Getting enough sleep, Washing hands, Using safety gear, Talking about feelings, Being kind to others, Following family safety plans). Each card has a simple three-option selector: "Going Well," "Could Improve," "Not Sure."

Interactive controls: Click a rating on each card; a "See My Summary" button.

Data Visibility Requirements: After all eight cards are rated, "See My Summary" displays a simple non-graded summary such as "You marked 5 practices as Going Well and 2 as Could Improve," and highlights the "Could Improve" cards as candidates for a personal health goal.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level objective requiring students to organize and compare their own practices across categories, so a self-rating grid with a reflective summary is appropriate — this is a private reflection tool, not a scored quiz.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep the tone entirely non-judgmental; there is no "wrong" self-rating. This tool works well paired directly with the My Health Goal Planner MicroSim above.

Every Practice Counts

Nobody has every single health practice perfectly figured out, and that's completely normal. Noticing one small thing to work on is already a big win.

Looking across all these practices naturally raises one more question: out of everything covered in this book, which topics matter most to a student right now?

docs.title: Identifying Relevant Health Topics
docs.text:
Not every health topic feels equally important to every student at every moment — and that's expected. Part of taking charge of one's own health is noticing which topics feel most relevant right now.

Identifying relevant health topics means recognizing which health topics feel most meaningful or useful to a student and the people around them at this point in their life, so that attention and effort can be focused where they matter most. A topic that feels very relevant to one student, like managing nervousness before a big event, might feel less urgent to another student focused on building a new sleep routine.

docs.title: Diagram: What Matters Most to Me Right Now
docs.text:
What Matters Most to Me Right Now MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: what-matters-most-right-now Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Evaluate (L5) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: prioritize, judge, justify

Learning objective: Students prioritize which health topics from across the book feel most personally relevant right now and justify their choice in a short reflection.

Purpose: Give students a concrete way to connect the whole book's topics back to their own life and choose where to focus next, tying together every strand covered this year.

Layout: A radial node map with "Me" in the center and eight surrounding topic nodes drawn from the book's strands — Food Choices, Growth and Changing Bodies, Feelings and Coping, Physical Activity, Safety Habits, Friendships and Respect, Communication Skills, Personal Health Goals.

Interactive features: Drag any topic node closer to "Me" to mark it as more relevant right now, or farther away to mark it as less relevant currently. Clicking a node reveals a one-sentence reminder of what that topic covers. A "Save My Top Choice" button lets the student type a short reason their closest topic matters most right now.

Visual styling: Warm, friendly palette matching earlier chapter diagrams; simple circular icons, no realistic depictions of people.

Implementation: vis-network with draggable nodes and a simple text-reflection field; responsive layout for narrower screens.

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "Why might two students pick different 'most relevant' health topics, even though they read the same book?" Then reveal: "Every student's life, body, and feelings are a little different, so the topics that matter most right now can be different too — and that's perfectly normal."

You Finished the Whole Grade 3 Book!

What an incredible journey, friend! You've explored the foundations of health, safety, wellness, food, relationships, growing bodies, feelings, and now communication and goals. You've grown so much as a healthy, caring person this year. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text: By chapter's end, most Grade 3 students should demonstrate verbal and nonverbal communication skills, including in decision-making situations (3.7.4.1), express thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs using I-statements with support (3.7.4.2), identify a personal health-related behavior to set a goal and determine whether assistance is needed (3.7.6.1), examine practices and behaviors that support health and wellbeing (3.7.7.1), and identify health topics relevant and meaningful to themselves and others (3.7.8.1). The MicroSims progress from Remember-level recognition (body language matching) through Apply-level practice (active listening, I-statements) to Analyze-level examination (goal quality, health-practice self-check) and Evaluate-level prioritization (relevant topics), matching Grade 3's introduction of genuine evaluative benchmarks. The goal-setting MicroSims are designed for guided, individual use with a teacher or family member nearby, consistent with this band's teacher-as-primary-audience approach. As the closing chapter of the Grade 3 book, consider pairing this chapter with a brief family take-home reflection on the student's chosen personal health goal.

docs.title: Quiz: Communication And Goals
docs.text: Test your understanding of verbal and nonverbal communication, active listening, I-statements, and personal health goals with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is "verbal communication"?
docs.text:
1. Sending a message using only facial expressions
  2. Sharing thoughts through posture and gestures
  3. Using spoken or written words to share thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs
  4. Never speaking at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Verbal communication means using spoken or written words to share thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs with another person. It includes not just what is said, but how it is said.

Concept Tested: Verbal Communication

docs.title: 2. What is "nonverbal communication"?
docs.text:
1. Sharing thoughts and feelings through facial expressions, body language, and posture, without words
  2. Writing a letter to a friend
  3. Speaking loudly on purpose
  4. Reading a book out loud
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Nonverbal communication means sharing thoughts and feelings through facial expressions, body language, gestures, eye contact, and posture, without using words at all.

Concept Tested: Nonverbal Communication

docs.title: 3. Which of these is an example of active listening?
docs.text:
1. Looking at a screen while someone talks
  2. Interrupting to change the subject
  3. Facing the speaker, making eye contact, and asking a follow-up question
  4. Assuming you already know what the person will say
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Active listening means fully paying attention to a speaker with eyes, body, and mind, including making eye contact, staying quiet while they speak, and asking a follow-up question to show you're listening.

Concept Tested: Active Listening

docs.title: 4. A friend says, "I'm nervous about my soccer game tomorrow." Which response shows active listening?
docs.text:
1. Looking at a phone instead of responding
  2. Changing the subject to talk about something else
  3. Interrupting to talk about your own day
  4. Making eye contact and saying, "What are you nervous about?"
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Making eye contact and asking a follow-up question, like "What are you nervous about?", shows the speaker that you are fully paying attention and care about what they said.

Concept Tested: Active Listening

docs.title: 5. When a group is deciding what game to play at recess, which step comes first in communicating well during that decision?
docs.text:
1. Refusing to talk about it at all
  2. Saying what you think or want, clearly and calmly
  3. Picking without asking anyone else
  4. Waiting for someone else to decide everything
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's process for communicating well during a group decision starts with saying what you think or want, clearly and calmly, before listening to others and looking for an option that works for everyone.

Concept Tested: Communication In Decision-Making

docs.title: 6. Which of these is an example of an "I-statement"?
docs.text:
1. "You always take my stuff without asking!"
  2. "I feel frustrated when my things are borrowed without asking. Could you ask me first next time?"
  3. "You ruined everything!"
  4. "You never listen to me!"
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An I-statement starts with "I" and focuses on the speaker's own feeling and experience, rather than blaming the other person. This keeps the conversation calm instead of accusing someone.

Concept Tested: I-Statement

docs.title: 7. What makes a "personal health goal" strong, according to the chapter?
docs.text:
1. It is vague, so it can mean anything
  2. It is picked by someone else, not the student
  3. It is specific, realistic, and personally chosen
  4. It is impossible to actually do
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A strong personal health goal is specific (naming exactly what will change), realistic (something the student can actually do), and personal (chosen because it matters to that student).

Concept Tested: Personal Health Goal

docs.title: 8. Which of these two goals is the "stronger" goal, and why: "Be healthier" versus "Drink a glass of water with lunch each day"?
docs.text:
1. "Be healthier" is stronger because it covers more topics
  2. Neither goal is useful for a student
  3. Both goals are equally strong
  4. "Drink a glass of water with lunch each day" is stronger because it is specific and realistic
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. "Be healthier" doesn't say exactly what will change, so it's vague. "Drink a glass of water with lunch each day" names a specific, realistic action, which makes it a stronger personal health goal.

Concept Tested: Examining Health-Supporting Practices

docs.title: 9. A student's goal is to go to bed 15 minutes earlier. Why might they need a parent's help with this goal?
docs.text:
1. Bedtime often depends on the whole family's evening routine and schedule
  2. Parents are not allowed to help with health goals
  3. The goal has nothing to do with anyone else
  4. Asking for help means the goal was a bad choice
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Determining need for assistance means recognizing when a goal depends on someone else's schedule or decisions. Bedtime often depends on the whole family's evening routine, so a parent's help makes the goal more realistic.

Concept Tested: Determining Need For Assistance

docs.title: 10. Two students read the same chapter but pick different "most important" health topics to work on. Why might this happen?
docs.text:
1. One of the students must be wrong
  2. Every student's life, body, and feelings are a little different, so relevant topics can differ too
  3. Only one topic is ever allowed to matter
  4. Health topics are the same for every single person
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Identifying relevant health topics means recognizing which topics feel most meaningful to a student right now. Because every student's life and feelings are different, the topics that matter most can be different too — and that's normal.

Concept Tested: Identifying Relevant Health Topics

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 3
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 3 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than a general-purpose graph — 57 concepts rather than 200 — because Grade 3 health benchmarks are describe/explain-level content, with the first genuine evaluate-level reasoning and the first explicit puberty topic, for 8-9 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Kindergarten (45-concept), Grade 1 (55-concept), and Grade 2 (55-concept) bands' graphs and uses the same 7-category taxonomy for cross-band comparability.

docs.title: Explore the Interactive Learning Graph
docs.text:
Use the interactive viewer to explore this band's concepts and their dependencies. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, and click a concept to highlight its connections. The viewer opens with the Grade 3 graph loaded; you can switch to any other grade band from the dropdown.

Open the Grade 3 Learning Graph Viewer

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating a right-sized concept set for this band
  • Compares course description against similar bands
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement

View the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 1 entry point (Health)
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier. This band uses 7 categories, seeded from its five content strands plus a cross-cutting Skill Standards group — the same scheme used for Kindergarten, Grade 1, and Grade 2.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with 7 categories
  • Category organization - foundational elements first
  • Balanced categories (1.8% - 24.6% each)
  • All categories under the 30% threshold
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in the CSV file

View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This report shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds a reasonable number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.title: Concept List — Grade 3
docs.text:

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 3 course description is a well-structured, standards-traceable document derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards. It enumerates 27 benchmark-coded topics across five content strands (Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) plus a cross-cutting Skill Standards group, and organizes learning outcomes using the 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate — with Create still deliberately thin/absent per the developmental design of the K-12 standards, explicitly documented in the text rather than an oversight).

Grade 3 is a meaningful developmental step up from Grade 2: it introduces the first genuine Evaluate-level benchmarks (evaluating personal behaviors to prevent injuries; determining validity/reliability of health information) and the first explicit mention of puberty as a body-change topic. This assessment evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 55-60 concepts, not the skill's generic 200-concept default, which would force invented content not grounded in the standards.

• Every topic traces to a specific MDE benchmark code, giving the learning graph strong provenance.

  • Clear five-strand + Skill Standards structure maps cleanly onto the same taxonomy scheme used for Kindergarten, Grade 1, and Grade 2, supporting cross-band comparability.
