Purpose: Show a respectful sample of cultural self-regulation traditions across regions, reinforcing that no single tradition is the "correct" way to self-regulate.

Geographic scope: World map with six marked regions/communities

Locations and examples: - South/East Asia: mindfulness meditation traditions - West Africa: music and drumming for releasing tension - Northern Plains and other Indigenous nations of North America: storytelling and connection to nature - Latin America and the Pacific Islands: dance and movement traditions - Middle East, South Asia, and worldwide faith communities: prayer and quiet reflection - A general "worldwide" marker: family-specific blended practices

Legend: A marker icon for each region labeled with the practice name

Interactive features: - Click any marker to open an infobox with two to three respectful, factual sentences about that practice and how it helps calm strong emotions - A closing note visible after clicking any two markers: "There are many more traditions than shown here. What matters is finding a calming practice that fits you and your family."

Color scheme: Warm, neutral marker colors (soft teal and gold) with no stereotyped imagery

Implementation: Leaflet map with custom markers and click-to-open infobox panels; content reviewed for respectful, non-stereotyping language before publication.

docs.title: Mental Health Benefits Of Culture
docs.text:
Cultural self-regulation practices do more than calm a single tough moment — over time, staying connected to culture can support mental health in an ongoing way.

Mental health benefits of culture refers to the ways that cultural traditions, community connection, and shared identity can support a person's overall emotional well-being, not just in a single stressful moment but across a person's whole life. Feeling connected to family traditions, community celebrations, language, music, and shared history can build a steady sense of belonging — and that sense of belonging is closely tied to good mental health.

Researchers and health professionals have found that people who feel connected to their culture and community often have:

  1. A stronger sense of identity and belonging
  2. More people to turn to for support during hard times
  3. Traditional coping practices that have been refined across generations
  4. A feeling of being part of something larger than themselves

None of this means culture is the only thing that supports mental health, or that everyone experiences their culture the same way — but it does mean that cultural connection is a real, valuable resource, worth understanding and respecting in yourself and in others.

This is one reason why community celebrations, family holidays, and cultural clubs at school are not just fun extras — they genuinely support students' emotional well-being. A student who feels disconnected from their cultural background, perhaps because they moved to a new place or attend a school where few people share their traditions, can still build these same benefits by staying in touch with family, seeking out a community group, or learning more about their own family's history and stories.

Belonging Matters

Feeling connected to your family's traditions and community is not just nice — it is genuinely good for your mental health.

docs.title: Emotions Influence Behavior
docs.text:
Now that you have some tools for calming strong feelings, it helps to understand exactly why those tools matter: emotions do not stay quietly inside — they shape what you actually do.

Emotions influence behavior describes the way feelings — like anger, excitement, fear, or sadness — often lead directly to actions, whether those actions are helpful or unhelpful. For example, frustration might lead one student to slam a book down, while it leads another student to ask for help. The emotion is the same; the behavior it leads to is a choice.

Recognizing this connection is powerful because it means behavior is not automatic — noticing an emotion early gives you a chance to choose your next action instead of reacting without thinking.

docs.title: Diagram: Emotion-to-Behavior Pathway Map
docs.text:
Emotion-to-Behavior Pathway Map

Type: graph-model sim-id: emotion-behavior-pathway-map Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, differentiate, distinguish

Learning objective: Students analyze how a single emotion can branch into either a helpful or unhelpful behavior, distinguishing between the feeling itself and the choice made in response to it.

Purpose: Show that emotions are not "good" or "bad," but the behaviors that follow them can be more or less helpful, and that a person can choose which path to take.

Node types: 1. Emotion nodes (circle, gold): Frustration, Excitement, Fear, Sadness, Embarrassment 2. Behavior nodes (square): each emotion connects to one helpful behavior (green square) and one unhelpful behavior (gray square)

Edge types: - LEADS TO (arrow from emotion to behavior), labeled with a short connecting phrase

Sample data: - Frustration → LEADS TO → "Ask a trusted adult for help" (helpful, green) or "Slam materials down" (unhelpful, gray) - Excitement → LEADS TO → "Channel energy into the activity" (helpful) or "Interrupt others without noticing" (unhelpful) - Fear → LEADS TO → "Tell someone what is scary" (helpful) or "Avoid the situation without explaining why" (unhelpful) - Sadness → LEADS TO → "Talk to a friend or trusted adult" (helpful) or "Withdraw from everyone silently" (unhelpful) - Embarrassment → LEADS TO → "Laugh it off and move on" (helpful) or "Snap at whoever is nearby" (unhelpful)

Layout: Force-directed, with emotion nodes in a center column and behavior nodes branching left (unhelpful) and right (helpful)

Interactive features: - Hover an emotion node: highlights both of its behavior branches - Click a behavior node: opens an infobox explaining why that behavior is helpful or unhelpful, and what a self-regulation strategy from earlier in the chapter could do at that moment - Drag, zoom, and pan supported

Visual styling: Green nodes for helpful behaviors, neutral gray for unhelpful behaviors, gold for emotions; edge labels describe the link (e.g., "can lead to")

Legend: Node shape/color key explaining emotion vs. helpful behavior vs. unhelpful behavior

Implementation: vis-network JavaScript library, force-directed layout, click-to-open side panel Canvas size: responsive, minimum 700x450px

Feeling an emotion and choosing a behavior are two different steps. You cannot always control the feeling, but you can practice choosing the behavior.

docs.title: Managing Emotions
docs.text:
Recognizing that emotions influence behavior naturally leads to the next question: what are the actual, healthy strategies for managing those emotions well?

Managing emotions means using specific, healthy strategies to handle a strong feeling so it leads to a helpful behavior rather than an unhelpful one. This builds directly on self-regulation, but focuses on concrete steps you can use in the moment a feeling shows up.

Healthy strategies for managing emotions include:

  • Naming the feeling out loud or in your head ("I feel frustrated right now")
  • Using a self-regulation strategy, like slow breathing or a short break
  • Talking to a trusted adult or friend about what happened
  • Writing or drawing about the feeling
  • Moving your body — a walk, a stretch, or shooting hoops
  • Waiting until the strong feeling has settled before making a decision or saying something you might regret

Unhealthy patterns to watch for include bottling feelings up until they explode, taking feelings out on other people, or pretending a strong feeling does not exist. Noticing these patterns in yourself is the first step toward changing them.

Managing emotions well does not mean you will always get it right on the first try. Even adults are still practicing this skill. What matters is building the habit of pausing to notice a feeling before it turns into a behavior you might regret, and trying again next time if a strategy does not work as well as you hoped.

A useful habit to remember: name it, tame it, then act. Name the feeling, use a calming strategy to tame it, then choose your next action.

Quick Check — Click to expand

Question: A student feels embarrassed after tripping in the hallway and other students laugh. Name one healthy way to manage that feeling.

Answer: Several healthy options work, including taking a slow breath, reminding yourself that everyone trips sometimes, laughing along if it feels okay, or talking to a friend or trusted adult about how it felt. Snapping at classmates or hiding for the rest of the day would not help the feeling pass in a healthy way.

docs.title: Bias
docs.text:
So far, this chapter has focused on your own feelings and behaviors. The next two ideas — bias and prejudice — describe patterns that can affect how people treat each other, and understanding them helps you recognize unfairness and respond to it.

Bias is an unfair leaning toward or against a person or group, often without even realizing it, usually based on limited or incomplete information. Everyone can develop biases, often without meaning to, because the brain naturally looks for patterns — but a pattern based on very little information can lead to an unfair assumption about a whole group of people.

For example, assuming a new student who speaks a different language at home will not be good at math, without any actual evidence, is a bias. Recognizing bias in yourself and others is not about blame — it is about noticing the assumption, questioning whether it is fair, and choosing to judge people by who they actually are instead.

docs.title: Diagram: Recognizing Bias in Everyday Scenarios
docs.text:
Recognizing Bias in Everyday Scenarios MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: recognizing-bias-scenario-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, distinguish, differentiate

Learning objective: Students analyze short, realistic classroom scenarios to distinguish between a fair, evidence-based judgment and a biased assumption made with limited information.

Canvas layout: - Top (400px): A scenario card describing a short classroom situation - Bottom (150px): Two labeled zones, "Fair Judgment" and "Biased Assumption," and one scenario card that the student drags to the correct zone

Visual elements: - Neutral scenario icons only (no depictions of specific people's appearance) - A calm color scheme: blue for "Fair Judgment" zone, soft amber for "Biased Assumption" zone (avoid red/wrong-answer coding, since the goal is reflection, not scorekeeping)

Interactive controls: - Drag-and-drop scenario card into one of the two zones - Button: "Next Scenario" - Button: "Why?" to reveal an explanation after sorting

Default parameters: - 8 scenario cards total, presented one at a time in random order

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the full scenario text Stage 2: Show the two sorting zones Stage 3: After sorting, show a calm explanation of why the scenario is a fair judgment (based on direct evidence) or a biased assumption (based on a stereotype or limited information) Final: Show how many scenarios were correctly identified, with an option to review any missed ones

Behavior: - Correct sort: brief affirming message plus the explanation - Incorrect sort: gentle correction plus the same explanation, framed as a learning moment rather than a failure

Instructional Rationale: This is an Analyze-level objective requiring learners to examine scenarios and distinguish evidence-based judgments from biased assumptions. A sorting interaction with reflection-based feedback (rather than a scored quiz) keeps the tone appropriate for this sensitive topic.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep all scenario text realistic, respectful, and focused on assumptions about ability, interests, or behavior rather than physical appearance or protected characteristics, to keep content classroom-appropriate for this age group.

docs.title: Prejudice
docs.text:
Bias describes an unfair leaning in someone's thinking. Prejudice describes what can happen when that unfair thinking becomes a fixed judgment.

Prejudice is a negative opinion or feeling about a person or group formed before knowing the facts, and held onto even when evidence shows it is not true. While bias can be a quick, sometimes unnoticed assumption, prejudice is a stronger, more fixed belief — and it is more likely to lead to treating someone unfairly.

Prejudice can be aimed at people because of their race, religion, culture, language, family background, ability, appearance, or many other things that make people different from one another. Left unchallenged, prejudice can lead to teasing, exclusion, or bullying — the topics covered later in this chapter.

The following table compares bias and prejudice so the difference stays clear:

Bias Prejudice What it is An unfair leaning, often unnoticed A fixed, negative opinion How strong it is Can be mild and quickly corrected Usually stronger and harder to change Awareness Person may not realize they have it Person may be aware but hold onto it anyway What helps Noticing the pattern and questioning it Seeking real information and getting to know the person or group directly

Recognizing bias and prejudice in the world, and sometimes in ourselves, is part of learning to treat every person fairly.

docs.title: Mental Health Changes Over Time
docs.text:
Just like physical health, mental health is not fixed — it moves up and down over the course of a life, and even over the course of a single week.

Mental health changes over time means that a person's emotional well-being can shift due to life events, growth, stress, relationships, and many other factors — sometimes getting stronger, sometimes becoming more difficult, much like physical health can improve or decline. A person who is doing well emotionally this month might go through a harder stretch next month, perhaps after a move, a loss, a change in friendships, or simply a stressful season — and that does not mean anything is permanently wrong with them.

This is an important idea to hold onto: struggling with your mental health sometimes is a normal part of being human, not a personal failure. Just as you would see a doctor for a physical illness that is not improving, it is appropriate and healthy to seek help when mental health struggles last a while or feel too big to manage alone.

docs.title: Diagram: Mental Health Over Time — Interactive Timeline
docs.text:
Mental Health Over Time — Interactive Timeline

Type: timeline sim-id: mental-health-over-time-timeline Library: vis-timeline Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, explain, interpret

Learning objective: Students describe how mental health can rise and fall over time in response to life events, just as physical health does, and explain that seeking help during a harder stretch is a normal, healthy response.

Purpose: Normalize the idea that mental health is dynamic, not fixed, using a relatable one-year example timeline.

Time period: A single representative school year (September through June)

Orientation: Horizontal, with a wavy line showing a "mental health level" rising and falling across the months

Events plotted along the wavy line: - September: Starting a new school year (steady) - November: A stressful stretch after losing a pet (dip) - December: Time with family during a break (rise) - February: A harder stretch after a friendship conflict (dip) - March: Talking to a school counselor and feeling supported (rise begins) - June: Feeling steady again at the end of the year (steady, higher than the February dip)

Visual style: A smooth wavy line graph with a calm color gradient; no numeric "score," just relative up/down movement, to avoid implying mental health is measured like a test grade

Color coding: Cool blue for dips, warm gold for rises, neutral gray for steady periods

Interactive features: - Click any point on the line to open an infobox describing that life event and how it might affect mental health - Click the March point specifically to reveal: "Reaching out for help during a harder stretch is one of the healthiest things a person can do — it's exactly like seeing a doctor for a physical illness." - A closing note after exploring three or more points: "Notice that the line goes back up. Mental health can improve again after a harder stretch, especially with support."

Implementation: vis-timeline with a custom-rendered wavy overlay line and click-to-reveal infobox panels.

Ups and Downs Are Normal

If you're going through a harder stretch right now, that does not mean something is wrong with you forever. Mental health moves up and down for everyone, and it is okay to ask for support while you wait for things to get better.

docs.title: Culturally Appropriate Help
docs.text:
Knowing that mental health changes over time naturally raises a question: where can a student actually turn for help, especially help that respects their own background?

Culturally appropriate help means mental health support that respects a person's cultural background, language, family structure, and community practices, rather than expecting everyone to seek help in exactly the same way. Some students may feel most comfortable talking to a school counselor; others may prefer talking with a family elder, a religious or spiritual leader, a community health worker, or a trusted adult who shares their cultural background and language.

All of these are valid paths to support. What matters most is that the help offered actually respects who the student is — their language, their family's beliefs, and their community's practices — rather than requiring the student to set those things aside to get help.

If the first person a student talks to does not feel like the right fit, that is okay — it does not mean help is unavailable. It simply means it is worth trying a different trusted adult or community resource until the support feels respectful and helpful.

Some examples of culturally appropriate help available to students include:

  1. A school counselor or school psychologist trained to work with students from many backgrounds
  2. A trusted family member or community elder
  3. A religious or spiritual leader or advisor, if that fits the family's beliefs
  4. A community health worker who speaks the family's home language
  5. A trusted teacher, nurse, or coach who has earned the student's trust

There is no single "right" person to talk to about a hard feeling. The right person is whoever helps you feel heard, safe, and respected.

docs.title: Responding To Teasing And Exclusion
docs.text:
Understanding bias, prejudice, and culturally respectful help gives you a foundation for one of the most practical skills in this chapter: knowing what to do when teasing or exclusion happens to you or someone nearby.

Responding to teasing and exclusion means using safe, healthy strategies when you are teased, left out, or treated unfairly, or when you see it happening to someone else. Teasing and exclusion can happen because of bias or prejudice, or simply because of a disagreement — but the response strategies below apply either way.

Here are healthy, safe steps for responding to teasing and exclusion:

  1. Use a calm, clear voice to say how it made you feel. "I feel left out when I'm not invited. Can I join?"
  2. Walk away and find another group or activity if the teasing continues.
  3. Tell a trusted adult, especially if it keeps happening or feels unfair.
  4. If you see it happening to someone else, consider including that person, or calmly telling an adult what you noticed.

No student is ever responsible for teasing or exclusion aimed at them — the responsibility always belongs to the person doing the teasing or excluding. Asking for help is always the right choice, and it never means someone has failed to handle it "on their own."

docs.title: Diagram: Responding to Teasing and Exclusion — Decision Path
docs.text:
Responding to Teasing and Exclusion — Decision Path

Type: workflow sim-id: teasing-exclusion-response-workflow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, use, practice

Learning objective: Students demonstrate the correct sequence of safe, healthy responses when experiencing or witnessing teasing or exclusion.

Purpose: Give a clear, memorable decision path for responding to teasing or exclusion, whether experienced directly or witnessed.

Visual style: Mermaid flowchart with decision diamonds and process rectangles; every node has a click handler opening an infobox

Steps: 1. Start: "Teasing or exclusion happens (to you or someone else)" Hover/click text: "This could be being left out of a game, called a hurtful name, or excluded from a group." 2. Decision: "Is it happening to you, or are you seeing it happen to someone else?" Click text: "The response is a little different depending on which one it is." 3a. Process (to you): "Say calmly how it made you feel" Click text: "Example: 'I feel left out when I'm not invited. Can I join?'" 4a. Decision: "Did it stop?" Click text: "Sometimes a calm, clear statement is enough to resolve it." 5a. Process (if no): "Walk away and tell a trusted adult" Click text: "Continuing unfair treatment should always be reported to a trusted adult." 3b. Process (witnessed): "Consider including the person or calmly telling an adult" Click text: "You do not have to solve it yourself — noticing and including someone, or getting an adult involved, both help." 6. End: "Situation reported or resolved safely" Click text: "Whether resolved by a calm conversation or with an adult's help, asking for support is always a safe, correct choice."

Color coding: Blue for the "experienced it" branch, green for the "witnessed it" branch, gold for decision diamonds

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart syntax with click directives on every node calling a JavaScript function that opens an infobox with the hover/click text above.

If someone teases you or leaves you out, that is about their choice, not about your worth. You deserve to be treated with respect, and telling a trusted adult is always okay.

docs.title: Responding To Bullying
docs.text:
Teasing and exclusion can sometimes be occasional or accidental. Bullying is different, and it calls for its own clear response plan.

Responding to bullying means recognizing bullying — repeated, intentional unfair or hurtful behavior where one person has more power than the other — and using safe strategies to respond, whether it is happening to you or to someone you see. Bullying can be physical, verbal, or happen online, and it is never something a student is expected to handle entirely alone.

The most important response steps for bullying are:

  1. Stay as calm as possible and avoid fighting back physically.
  2. Get to a safe place or safe group of people.
  3. Tell a trusted adult right away — a parent, teacher, counselor, or school staff member. Bullying should always be reported, even if it has already stopped.
  4. If you witness bullying, do not join in. If it is safe to do so, calmly support the person being bullied, and always tell a trusted adult what you saw.
  5. Keep telling adults until it stops. If one adult does not help enough, tell another one.

Bullying is different from a single disagreement or moment of teasing because it is repeated and involves an imbalance of power. Recognizing that difference helps you know when the stronger, more urgent steps above are needed.

Teasing / Exclusion Bullying Pattern Can be a single incident Repeated over time Power Roughly equal between students One person has more power over the other First response Calm statement of feelings often helps Get to safety and tell a trusted adult right away Reporting Tell an adult if it continues Always tell a trusted adult, every time

Chapter Complete!

Great work, friend! You now understand self-regulation and the many cultural traditions that support it, how emotions influence behavior and how to manage them in healthy ways, how to recognize bias and prejudice, and how to respond safely to teasing and bullying. You also know that mental health changes over time and that culturally respectful help is always available. Healthy choices, happy you!

Quick Check — Click to expand

Question: What is the difference between bias and prejudice, and what is one safe first step if you are being bullied?

Answer: Bias is an unfair leaning toward or against a person or group, often without realizing it, based on limited information. Prejudice is a stronger, fixed negative opinion held even when evidence shows it is untrue. If you are being bullied, a safe first step is to get to a safe place or group of people and tell a trusted adult right away — bullying should always be reported.

docs.title: Quiz: Mental and Emotional Health
docs.text: Test your understanding of self-regulation, emotions, bias, and responding safely to teasing and bullying with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is self-regulation?
docs.text:
1. The ability to notice a strong feeling and choose how to respond to it
  2. Hiding your feelings so nobody notices them
  3. A rule that says you can never feel upset
  4. Letting a strong feeling control what you do next
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Self-regulation is not about hiding feelings or never feeling upset — it means noticing what you feel, naming it, and picking a helpful next step instead of letting the feeling take over.

Concept Tested: Self-Regulation

docs.title: 2. Why does mental health change over time?
docs.text:
1. Because it is fixed forever once a person is born
  2. Because only physical health can change, not mental health
  3. Because life events, growth, stress, and relationships can shift emotional well-being up or down, just like physical health
  4. Because mental health only changes if a person does something wrong
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Just like physical health, mental health moves up and down over time due to life events, stress, and relationships. A harder stretch does not mean something is permanently wrong with a person.

Concept Tested: Mental Health Changes Over Time

docs.title: 3. What is the purpose of cultural self-regulation practices like mindfulness meditation, prayer, or storytelling?
docs.text:
1. They are only for adults, not students
  2. They are traditional methods that help people calm strong emotions and find balance
  3. They replace the need for trusted adults entirely
  4. They only work if a person's whole family uses the same one
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Cultural self-regulation practices are traditional methods passed down through a culture or community that help calm strong emotions. No single tradition is more "correct" than another — they are different paths to the same goal of steadiness.

Concept Tested: Cultural Self-Regulation Practices

docs.title: 4. How can feeling connected to your culture and community support your mental health?
docs.text:
1. It can build a sense of belonging and give you more people to turn to for support
  2. It guarantees a person will never feel sad
  3. It only matters for adults, not students
  4. It replaces the need for any other kind of support
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. People who feel connected to their culture and community often have a stronger sense of identity, more people to turn to for support, and traditional coping practices refined across generations, all of which support mental health.

Concept Tested: Mental Health Benefits Of Culture

docs.title: 5. Why is it important to remember that emotions influence behavior?
docs.text:
1. Because behavior is always automatic and cannot be changed
  2. Because only negative emotions lead to behavior
  3. Because it means feelings and actions are exactly the same thing
  4. Because noticing an emotion early gives you a chance to choose your next action instead of reacting without thinking
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Emotions often lead to actions, but the emotion and the behavior are two different steps. Noticing a feeling early, like frustration, gives you the chance to choose a helpful behavior, like asking for help, instead of reacting without thinking.

Concept Tested: Emotions Influence Behavior

docs.title: 6. Malik feels embarrassed after tripping in the hallway, and a few classmates laugh. Which response shows healthy management of that emotion?
docs.text:
1. Snapping angrily at the nearest classmate
  2. Pretending the embarrassment never happened and never thinking about it again
  3. Taking a slow breath, reminding himself that everyone trips sometimes, and moving on
  4. Avoiding the hallway completely for the rest of the school year
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Healthy strategies for managing emotions include naming the feeling, using a calming strategy like slow breathing, and giving yourself a moment before deciding how to act. This helps the feeling pass without leading to an unhelpful behavior.

Concept Tested: Managing Emotions

docs.title: 7. What is bias?
docs.text:
1. A fixed, negative opinion a person refuses to change even with new evidence
  2. An unfair leaning toward or against a person or group, often based on limited information
  3. A type of bullying that happens online
  4. A healthy way to manage strong emotions
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Bias is an unfair leaning toward or against a person or group, often without even realizing it, usually based on limited or incomplete information. Everyone can develop biases, and noticing them is the first step toward being fair.

Concept Tested: Bias

docs.title: 8. A teacher assumes a new student won't be good at math just because the student speaks a different language at home, and keeps thinking this even after the student does very well on several tests. How is this different from a quick, unnoticed bias?
docs.text:
1. It isn't different at all — bias and prejudice always mean the exact same thing
  2. It is less serious because the teacher is an adult
  3. It is only a problem if the student finds out about it
  4. It has become prejudice, because the negative opinion is being held onto even when evidence proves it wrong
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Bias can be a quick, sometimes unnoticed assumption, but prejudice is a stronger, fixed belief that persists even when evidence shows it is untrue. Holding onto the unfair opinion despite proof it's wrong is what makes this prejudice rather than simple bias.

Concept Tested: Prejudice

docs.title: 9. Sofia notices that a group of classmates has been leaving her out of games at recess for the past few days. What is the best first step for Sofia to try?
docs.text:
1. Leave the school grounds without telling anyone
  2. Yell at the classmates in front of the whole class
  3. Calmly say how it made her feel, like "I feel left out when I'm not invited. Can I join?"
  4. Assume nothing can be done and stop going to recess
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A calm, clear statement about how the situation made you feel is often a good first step for teasing or exclusion. If it continues, walking away and telling a trusted adult are the next safe steps. No student is responsible for exclusion aimed at them.

Concept Tested: Responding To Teasing And Exclusion

docs.title: 10. Which resource is an example of culturally appropriate help for a student's mental health?
docs.text:
1. A community health worker who speaks the family's home language, or a school counselor trained to work with students from many backgrounds
  2. Only ever talking to a stranger online
  3. A rule that everyone must talk to the exact same type of person
  4. Ignoring the problem until it goes away on its own
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Culturally appropriate help means support that respects a person's cultural background, language, and family practices. This can include a school counselor, a family elder, a religious leader, or a community health worker — whoever helps a student feel heard, safe, and respected.

Concept Tested: Culturally Appropriate Help

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter examines how family, peers, culture, and media/technology influence behavior, including harmful technology use. Students build situational awareness, learn to recognize warning signs and exit unsafe situations, set personal boundaries, and practice refusal skills for resisting peer pressure.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Influences On Health Behavior
  2. Media And Technology Influence
  3. Harmful Technology Behavior
  4. Situational Awareness
  5. Exiting Unsafe Situations
  6. Personal Boundaries
  7. Setting Boundaries
  8. Warning Sign
  9. Peer Pressure
  10. Refusal Skill
  11. Demonstrating Refusal Skills

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on Chapter 3: Mental and Emotional Health, which establishes emotional self-regulation skills that support recognizing and responding to unsafe or pressured situations.

Building Your Safety Skills

Hi, friend! This chapter is about staying safe — noticing what is influencing your choices, paying attention to your surroundings, and practicing exactly what to say when something feels wrong. Let's think it through together.

docs.title: Influences On Health Behavior
docs.text:
Every day, you make choices about how to act, what to eat, how to spend your time, and how to treat other people. Very few of those choices happen in a vacuum — most are shaped by people and forces around you, whether or not you notice it.

Influences on health behavior are the people, groups, and forces — including family, peers, culture, and media/technology — that shape the choices someone makes about their health and safety. Your family teaches you habits from a young age, like how to brush your teeth or how to talk about feelings. Your friends can encourage you to try a new sport or, sometimes, pressure you toward a choice you are not sure about. Your culture shapes what foods feel familiar and what traditions feel comforting. Media and technology — shows, apps, games, and social platforms — show you images and ideas that can shape what you think is normal or expected.

None of these influences are automatically good or bad. Recognizing that an influence exists is the first step toward deciding, on purpose, whether to follow it.

The following table organizes the four major influences this chapter focuses on, along with one example of each:

Influence Example Family A parent who models washing hands before meals Peers A friend who invites you to join a walking club at recess Culture A community tradition that shapes favorite foods or celebrations Media/technology A video or app that shows a certain way of talking or acting as "normal"

Notice the Source

A helpful habit: when you notice yourself wanting to do something, ask "Where did this idea come from?" Naming the source helps you decide if it is a healthy choice for you.

docs.title: Media And Technology Influence
docs.text:
Media and technology deserve their own closer look, because they reach students constantly and in ways that are easy to miss.

Media and technology influence is the way that shows, videos, games, apps, advertisements, and social media shape a person's ideas, habits, and behavior — sometimes without the person even realizing it is happening. An advertisement might make a sugary snack look exciting. A video game might make staying up late feel normal. A social media post might make an unhealthy habit look like something "everyone" does, even when that is not true.

Media and technology are not automatically harmful — many shows, games, and apps are entertaining, educational, or help people stay connected to friends and family. The goal is not to avoid all media and technology, but to notice its influence and think critically about it.

Here are questions that help you think critically about media and technology influence:

  • Is this trying to sell me something?
  • Does this show a healthy choice, or just an exciting one?
  • Would a trusted adult agree this is a good idea?
  • Does this make an unhealthy or unsafe choice look normal?

docs.title: Diagram: Media Message Detective
docs.text:
Media Message Detective MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: media-message-detective Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, distinguish, differentiate

Learning objective: Students analyze short, realistic media examples (an ad, a game scene, a social post) to identify what the media is trying to influence and whether the influence supports or works against a healthy choice.

Canvas layout: - Top (350px): A card showing a short text description of a media example (no real brand names or images, all fictional/generic) - Bottom (200px): Two labeled zones, "Healthy Influence" and "Watch Out For This," plus a "Why?" button

Visual elements: - Simple icon representing the media type (TV screen, phone, game controller) - Calm color scheme: teal for "Healthy Influence," soft amber for "Watch Out For This"

Interactive controls: - Drag-and-drop the example card into one of the two zones - Button: "Why?" reveals a short explanation after sorting - Button: "Next Example"

Default parameters: - 8 example cards, shown one at a time in random order

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the media example text in full Stage 2: Show the two sorting zones Stage 3: After sorting, show a short explanation of what the media example was trying to influence and why it fits that zone Final: Show how many examples were sorted, with an option to revisit any of them

Behavior: - Every sort (correct or not) is followed by the explanation, framed as a learning moment rather than a scored test - Examples include: an ad making candy look exciting, a show where a character asks a trusted adult for advice, a game that encourages taking a break every hour, a post that makes staying up very late look "normal" and fun

Instructional Rationale: This is an Analyze-level objective requiring learners to examine media examples and distinguish healthy influence from influence that undermines healthy choices. A sorting activity with an explanation for every answer keeps the focus on reasoning rather than memorized rules.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep every example fictional and generic (no real brand, show, or platform names) so the activity stays evergreen and appropriate for classroom use.

docs.title: Harmful Technology Behavior
docs.text:
Media and technology can also be used in ways that directly hurt someone's safety or emotional well-being. This next idea is more serious, so it deserves careful, direct attention.

Harmful technology behavior is any use of a phone, app, game, or the internet that hurts someone's safety or mental health — including cyberbullying, sharing someone's photos or information without permission, or a stranger online trying to get personal information or arrange to meet in person. This kind of behavior can happen through texting, gaming chat, social media, or any app that lets people communicate.

Some warning signs that a technology situation may be harmful include:

  1. Someone online asks for your address, your school's name, or a photo they should not need
  2. A person online asks you to keep a conversation secret from your parents or another trusted adult
  3. Messages or posts are being used to embarrass, threaten, or exclude someone repeatedly
  4. Someone asks to meet in person after only talking online
  5. A message or image makes you feel confused, scared, or uneasy in your stomach

If any of these things happen to you or a friend, the response is always the same, no matter which situation it is: stop responding, do not delete the message, and tell a trusted adult right away. You will never be in trouble for reporting something that felt wrong online — telling an adult is always the safe and correct choice.

Tell a Trusted Adult, Always

If anything online ever makes you feel unsafe, confused, or asked to keep a secret from your family, tell a trusted adult right away. This is true every single time, with no exceptions.

Recognizing harmful technology behavior connects directly to the next set of skills in this chapter: noticing when something is wrong in the moment, whether online or in person, and knowing exactly what to do about it.

docs.title: Situational Awareness
docs.text:
Just as you can learn to notice a harmful pattern online, you can also learn to notice safety clues in the physical world around you.

Situational awareness means paying attention to your surroundings, the people nearby, and how a situation is unfolding, so you can notice early if something feels unsafe. It is not about being afraid all the time — it is a calm habit of checking in with your surroundings, similar to looking both ways before crossing a street.

Building situational awareness includes noticing things like:

  • Who else is around, and whether a trusted adult is nearby
  • Whether you know a safe way out of the area you are in
  • Whether the mood of a situation is calm or is starting to feel tense
  • Whether your own body is giving you a signal, like a nervous stomach or a strong urge to leave

docs.title: Diagram: Situational Awareness Scene Explorer
docs.text:
Situational Awareness Scene Explorer MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: situational-awareness-scene-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, identify, interpret

Learning objective: Students describe and identify situational-awareness clues (people nearby, exits, mood, body signals) present in a still scene, building the habit of scanning surroundings calmly.

Canvas layout: - Left (450px): A simple, calm, illustrated scene (e.g., a park, a school hallway, a store) with four clickable hotspots - Right (250px): An infobox panel and a running checklist of clues found

Visual elements: - Illustrated scene with hotspots marked by small circles: "People Nearby," "Exit/Way Out," "Mood of the Room," "How My Body Feels" - Checklist panel that fills in as hotspots are clicked

Interactive controls: - Click each hotspot to reveal its clue in the infobox - Button: "New Scene" loads a different illustrated setting - Button: "Reset Checklist"

Default parameters: - Scene 1: a school hallway between classes, all four hotspots present and calm/neutral

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the full illustrated scene with all four hotspots visible Stage 2: Show the clue text for each hotspot once clicked Stage 3: Show the running checklist update after each click Final: Show a short summary message once all four hotspots are found: "You just practiced situational awareness — noticing people, exits, mood, and your own feelings."

Behavior: - Each hotspot always reveals its clue when clicked, regardless of order - Scenes rotate between calm, everyday settings (classroom, park, bus stop, cafeteria); none depict danger directly — the sim teaches the scanning habit, not threat scenarios

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level objective, so the design uses concrete, step-through exploration of a static scene rather than animation, letting students see and name each clue at their own pace before applying the skill to real situations.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js with simple flat illustrations. Keep all scenes ordinary and non-threatening; the goal is building the observation habit, not simulating danger.

Situational awareness is a skill you can practice anywhere — at school, at a park, or at a family gathering. The more you practice noticing these clues in calm moments, the more naturally you will notice them if a situation ever starts to feel unsafe.

docs.title: Exiting Unsafe Situations
docs.text:
Noticing a warning clue only helps if you also know what to do next. That is exactly what this next skill covers.

Exiting unsafe situations means having a clear, practiced plan for leaving a place, conversation, or group as soon as something feels unsafe or wrong, without waiting to see if it gets worse. Trusting that uneasy feeling in your stomach, and acting on it right away, is one of the most important safety skills a person can build.

A simple plan for exiting an unsafe situation includes these steps:

  1. Notice the feeling. Your body often signals unsafe before your mind fully understands why.
  2. State that you are leaving, if it is safe to speak. "I have to go now" is enough — you do not owe anyone a detailed explanation.
  3. Move toward people or a place you know is safe — a trusted adult, a public area, or home.
  4. Tell a trusted adult what happened, even if you are not fully sure it was actually unsafe. It is always okay to check.

You never need a "good enough" reason to leave a situation that feels wrong. Trusting your own instinct is reason enough.

Practice Makes It Automatic

Try saying "I have to go now" out loud a few times at home. Practicing the words ahead of time makes them much easier to use for real, if you ever need them.

docs.title: Personal Boundaries
docs.text:
Exiting an unsafe situation is one way of protecting yourself. Setting a boundary before things go that far is another — and it is worth understanding clearly.

Personal boundaries are the limits a person sets about what they are comfortable with regarding their body, their belongings, their time, and their information. Boundaries are personal — what feels comfortable for one person may not feel comfortable for another, and that is completely normal. Everyone has the right to their own boundaries, and everyone has a responsibility to respect other people's boundaries too.

Boundaries can apply to many parts of life, including:

Type of Boundary Example Physical Deciding who can hug you or how close someone can stand Belongings Deciding whether to lend an item to someone Time Deciding whether to join an activity right now or later Information Deciding what personal details to share, and with whom

A boundary is not rude or unfriendly — it is a normal, healthy part of every relationship, including friendships and family relationships.

docs.title: Setting Boundaries
docs.text:
Understanding that boundaries exist is the first step. Actually stating one, clearly and respectfully, is the practical skill that follows.

Setting boundaries means clearly and respectfully telling another person what you are, or are not, comfortable with. A boundary does not need to be angry or dramatic — it can be calm, short, and direct.

Here are example phrases for setting a boundary in different situations:

  • "Please ask before you borrow my things."
  • "I'm not ready to talk about that yet."
  • "Please don't touch my hair without asking."
  • "I need some quiet time right now."

Setting a boundary sometimes feels uncomfortable at first, especially with a friend or family member, but a boundary stated calmly and respectfully is one of the healthiest things you can do for a relationship — it helps both people understand each other better. Setting your own boundaries matters, and so does respecting someone else's boundary the moment they state it, even if you don't fully understand why they set it.

docs.title: Diagram: Personal Boundaries Interactive Map
docs.text:
Personal Boundaries Interactive Map

Type: infographic sim-id: personal-boundaries-interactive-map Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, exemplify, classify

Learning objective: Students explain and classify examples of personal boundaries across four categories (physical, belongings, time, information) and connect each to an example boundary-setting phrase.

Purpose: Reinforce the four boundary categories from the chapter and show a matching respectful phrase for each.

Layout: A central circle labeled "Personal Boundaries" with four surrounding petal shapes labeled Physical, Belongings, Time, and Information

Interactive elements: - Hover or click a petal to reveal: a one-sentence definition of that boundary type, one everyday example, and one example phrase for setting that boundary - Clicking the center circle reveals a summary: "You have the right to set boundaries, and you also have the responsibility to respect other people's boundaries."

Data to display per petal: - Physical: "Your body and personal space." Example: someone standing too close. Phrase: "Please give me a little more space." - Belongings: "Your things." Example: a classmate grabbing your pencil. Phrase: "Please ask before you borrow my things." - Time: "How you spend your time." Example: being pressured to stay longer at an activity. Phrase: "I need to head home now." - Information: "What you share about yourself." Example: being asked personal questions by someone you don't know well. Phrase: "I'd rather not share that."

Color coding: Each petal a distinct calm color (blue, green, purple, gold); center circle in warm neutral gray

Responsive behavior: Petals rearrange into a vertical stack on narrow screens while keeping click/hover functionality

Implementation: p5.js with clickable petal shapes and a text infobox panel that updates on interaction.

docs.title: Warning Sign
docs.text:
Personal boundaries and situational awareness both depend on noticing clues. This next concept names exactly what those clues look like when a person or a situation is unsafe.

A warning sign is a behavior or detail that signals a person or situation might be unsafe or dangerous. Warning signs do not guarantee danger, but they are a signal to slow down, pay closer attention, and consider getting help from a trusted adult.

Warning signs can appear in people's words, actions, or requests. Examples include:

  1. Asking you to keep a secret from your parents or another trusted adult
  2. Ignoring you when you say no or ask them to stop
  3. Offering gifts, favors, or special attention that feels like it comes with a hidden expectation
  4. Trying to get you alone, away from other people
  5. Making you feel confused about whether something is okay, when your gut says it isn't

Noticing one warning sign does not always mean danger is certain, but it always means it is time to pay closer attention and consider telling a trusted adult about what you noticed.

Quick Check — Click to expand

Question: An adult you don't know very well asks you to keep a secret from your parents about a gift they gave you. Is this a warning sign, and what should you do?

Answer: Yes, this is a warning sign — asking a child to keep a secret from a trusted adult is one of the clearest warning signs there is. The safe response is to tell a trusted adult about the gift and the request to keep it secret, right away.

docs.title: Peer Pressure
docs.text:
Not every unsafe situation involves a stranger or a clear danger. Sometimes the pressure comes from someone you already know — even a friend — and it can be much harder to notice.

Peer pressure is the feeling of being pushed, directly or indirectly, by people your own age to do something you might not otherwise choose to do. Peer pressure is not always loud or obvious — sometimes it is a comment like "everyone else is doing it," and sometimes it is simply the discomfort of being the only person who says no.

Peer pressure can push someone toward a harmless choice, like trying a new food, or toward an unsafe or unhealthy choice, like skipping a safety rule, being unkind to someone else, or trying something that could hurt them. Recognizing which kind of pressure you are feeling is an important first step.

docs.title: Diagram: Peer Pressure Situation Sorter
docs.text:
Peer Pressure Situation Sorter MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: peer-pressure-situation-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: examine, distinguish, differentiate

Learning objective: Students analyze short peer-pressure scenarios to distinguish low-risk social pressure from pressure toward an unsafe or unhealthy choice, preparing them to decide when a refusal skill is needed.

Canvas layout: - Top (350px): A scenario card describing peer pressure in a short, realistic situation - Bottom (200px): Two zones, "Low-Risk Choice" and "Needs a Refusal Skill," and a "Why?" button

Visual elements: - Neutral scenario icons (two speech bubbles representing friends talking) - Calm colors: green for "Low-Risk Choice," amber for "Needs a Refusal Skill"

Interactive controls: - Drag-and-drop scenario card into a zone - Button: "Why?" reveals explanation - Button: "Next Scenario"

Default parameters: - 8 scenarios presented one at a time in random order, mixing low-risk (trying a new snack, joining a new game) and higher-risk (skipping a bike helmet, going somewhere without telling an adult, being pressured to exclude a classmate) examples

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the full scenario text Stage 2: Show the two sorting zones Stage 3: After sorting, show a short explanation and, for "Needs a Refusal Skill" scenarios, a reminder that the next section teaches exactly what to say Final: Show how many scenarios were sorted, with an option to review any of them

Behavior: - Every sort is followed by an explanation regardless of correctness, framed as learning rather than scoring - "Needs a Refusal Skill" scenarios link thematically forward to the Refusal Skill and Demonstrating Refusal Skills sections

Instructional Rationale: This is an Analyze-level objective requiring learners to examine scenarios and distinguish types of peer pressure. Sorting with full explanations builds the judgment needed before practicing refusal scripts in the next sections.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep all scenarios realistic and age-appropriate, focused on situations like activity choices, dares, and social exclusion rather than substance use, which is covered in a later band.

Peer pressure is a normal part of having friends and being part of a group — it happens to everyone, including adults. What matters is having a plan ready for the moments when the pressure pushes toward something unsafe, unkind, or against your own values.

docs.title: Refusal Skill
docs.text:
This is exactly the plan you need: a clear, practiced way to say no and mean it.

A refusal skill is a specific, practiced way of saying no to pressure, clearly and confidently, so that your choice is respected. A refusal skill is not the same as simply hoping you will know what to say in the moment — it is a script, practiced ahead of time, so the words are ready when you need them.

Here are refusal skill scripts you can practice right now, out loud, so they become automatic:

  • The direct no: "No thanks, I'm not doing that." Then walk away.
  • The broken record: Repeat the same short refusal calmly, no matter what the other person says. "No thanks." "No thanks." "No thanks." You do not need a new excuse each time — repeating the same short phrase is often the most effective response.
  • Suggest something else: "No thanks, let's play basketball instead." Offering an alternative can redirect the group without an argument.
  • Blame a rule or trusted adult: "I can't, my mom said I need to be home by five." Using a family rule as the reason takes the pressure off of you personally.
  • Walk away: Leaving the situation entirely, especially if the pressure continues after you have said no.

A refusal skill does not require an explanation, an apology, or a debate. "No thanks" is a complete sentence.

Saying No Gets Easier

Saying no to a friend can feel hard at first, even when you know it's the right choice. That feeling gets smaller every time you practice — and a true friend will respect your no.

docs.title: Demonstrating Refusal Skills
docs.text:
Knowing a refusal script and actually being able to use it in the moment are two different things. This final section is about practicing until the script feels natural.

Demonstrating refusal skills means actually using a refusal script out loud, in a realistic situation, until it feels natural and confident rather than awkward or forced. Just like practicing a fire drill helps you react quickly in a real emergency, practicing refusal scripts with a trusted adult, family member, or classmate helps you use them confidently when you actually need them.

The following role-play MicroSim lets you branch through a realistic peer-pressure scenario and choose your own refusal response at each step, seeing how the conversation could unfold.

docs.title: Diagram: Refusal Skills Role-Play Branching Scenario
docs.text:
Refusal Skills Role-Play Branching Scenario MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: refusal-skills-role-play Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, use

Learning objective: Students apply refusal-skill scripts (direct no, broken record, suggest an alternative, blame a rule, walk away) by choosing responses in a branching dialogue scenario and observing realistic, respectful outcomes.

Canvas layout: - Top (300px): A comic-style dialogue panel showing a peer character's speech bubble and a short scene description - Bottom (250px): Four to five response buttons, each showing one refusal-skill script type by name and example phrase

Visual elements: - Two simple flat-illustration characters: "You" and "Friend," speech bubbles for dialogue - A small progress tracker showing how many rounds of pressure have been navigated - A calm color palette (no threatening imagery); the peer character is drawn as an ordinary classmate, not a menacing figure

Interactive controls: - Button per response option (e.g., "Direct No," "Broken Record," "Suggest Alternative," "Blame a Rule," "Walk Away") - Button: "Start Over" - Button: "Try a Different Scenario" (cycles between 3 preset scenarios: being pressured to skip wearing a helmet, being pressured to exclude a classmate from a game, being pressured to go somewhere without telling an adult)

Default parameters: - Scenario 1: "Come on, take off your helmet, it looks silly" loads first - Every scenario is resolved within 2-3 rounds of dialogue

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the scene and the friend's pressuring line Stage 2: Show the available refusal-script response options with their exact wording Stage 3: After a choice, show the friend's realistic reply (sometimes pressure continues once, sometimes it stops) and whether the chosen script type worked in this round Stage 4: If pressure continues, show a follow-up choice (repeat the script, escalate to "walk away," or "tell a trusted adult") Final: Show a short recap of which refusal scripts were used and a confirming message that any of the scripts, used calmly and repeated if needed, is an effective and respectful choice

Behavior: - All response options are treated as valid strategies; the sim never penalizes a choice, but shows that persistence (repeating a script or walking away) is sometimes needed if the first attempt does not work - Every scenario resolves safely within the branching paths — there is no "losing" ending, only different realistic paths to a safe resolution - The "tell a trusted adult" option is always available as a branch and always leads to a supportive, resolved ending

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level objective requiring learners to practice using refusal scripts in a realistic, low-stakes context before needing them in real life. Branching dialogue with guaranteed safe resolutions lets students rehearse language and build confidence without anxiety about "failing" the scenario.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js with a simple state-machine structure for dialogue branches. Store each scenario as a small tree of nodes (prompt, response options, follow-up nodes). Keep all peer characters, settings, and pressure scenarios ordinary and age-appropriate (helmets, group games, telling an adult where you're going) rather than involving strangers or graphic danger, which are covered elsewhere in this chapter.

Practicing refusal skills, even when nothing is currently wrong, is like a fire drill: it builds the habit before you ever need it for real. The more you say these scripts out loud — at home, with a trusted adult, or even alone in your room — the more naturally they will come out when you actually need them.

The table below reviews all five refusal-skill scripts from this chapter together, so you can pick the one that fits a situation:

Script What You Say When It Works Well Direct no "No thanks, I'm not doing that." Quick, clear situations Broken record Repeat the same short no calmly Someone keeps pushing after the first no Suggest alternative "No thanks, let's do ___ instead." You want to keep the friendship moving forward Blame a rule "I can't, my family's rule is ___." Taking the pressure off yourself personally Walk away Leave the situation Pressure continues or you feel unsafe

You're Building Real Safety Skills

Great work, friend! You now understand how family, peers, culture, and media/technology influence behavior, how to recognize harmful technology behavior, how to build situational awareness and exit unsafe situations, how to set personal boundaries, and how to recognize warning signs and peer pressure. Most importantly, you've practiced real refusal skill scripts you can actually use. Healthy choices, happy you!

Quick Check — Click to expand

Question: A friend keeps asking you to skip a safety rule after you already said no once. Name two refusal skills you could use next.

Answer: Several options work well together, including the broken record (calmly repeating "No thanks" again), suggesting an alternative activity, blaming a family rule, or simply walking away if the pressure continues. Telling a trusted adult afterward is also always a safe and correct choice.

docs.title: Quiz: Personal Safety and Refusal Skills
docs.text: Test your understanding of influences, safety awareness, boundaries, and refusal skills with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which four things does this chapter identify as major influences on health behavior?
docs.text:
1. Weather, homework, sports, and pets
  2. Family, peers, culture, and media/technology
  3. Money, grades, distance, and time
  4. Teachers, buses, lunch, and recess
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Family, peers, culture, and media/technology are the four major influences that shape the choices a person makes about health and safety. None of these influences are automatically good or bad — recognizing them is the first step toward deciding, on purpose, whether to follow them.

Concept Tested: Influences On Health Behavior

docs.title: 2. Someone online asks a student to keep a conversation secret from their parents and asks for the student's home address. What should this signal to the student?
docs.text:
1. That the person online must be a family friend
  2. That it is fine as long as the student does not share a photo too
  3. That the student should wait a few days before deciding what to do
  4. That this is harmful technology behavior, and the student should stop responding and tell a trusted adult
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Asking for personal information and asking to keep a secret from a trusted adult are classic warning signs of harmful technology behavior. The response is always the same: stop responding, do not delete the message, and tell a trusted adult right away.

Concept Tested: Harmful Technology Behavior

docs.title: 3. What is situational awareness?
docs.text:
1. Paying attention to your surroundings, the people nearby, and how a situation is unfolding
  2. Being afraid of every new place you visit
  3. A rule that says you must always have an adult with you
  4. Ignoring your surroundings so you can focus on one thing
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Situational awareness is a calm habit of checking in with your surroundings — noticing who is nearby, whether you know a safe way out, and how the mood of a situation feels — similar to looking both ways before crossing a street.

Concept Tested: Situational Awareness

docs.title: 4. What is the recommended first step when exiting an unsafe situation?
docs.text:
1. Wait to see if the situation gets worse before doing anything
  2. Argue until the other person agrees with you
  3. Notice the uneasy feeling in your body and trust it
  4. Ask everyone nearby whether they think it's actually unsafe
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A simple plan for exiting an unsafe situation starts with noticing the feeling — your body often signals unsafe before your mind fully understands why. You never need a "good enough" reason to leave; trusting your instinct is reason enough.

Concept Tested: Exiting Unsafe Situations

docs.title: 5. Which of these is an example of a personal boundary?
docs.text:
1. A rule that everyone must have exactly the same comfort level about everything
  2. Deciding whether to lend a favorite item to a classmate
  3. A grade a teacher gives on a test
  4. The weather forecast for the weekend
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Personal boundaries are the limits a person sets about what they are comfortable with regarding their body, belongings, time, and information. Deciding whether to lend an item is a boundary about belongings, and everyone's comfort level can be different.

Concept Tested: Personal Boundaries

docs.title: 6. A cousin keeps touching Amara's hair without asking, and it makes her uncomfortable. Which is the best example of setting a boundary?
docs.text:
1. Never speaking to that cousin again
  2. Quietly avoiding the cousin at every family event without saying anything
  3. Yelling at the cousin in front of the whole family
  4. Calmly saying, "Please don't touch my hair without asking."
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Setting a boundary means clearly and respectfully telling another person what you are, or are not, comfortable with. A boundary does not need to be angry or dramatic — it can be calm, short, and direct, like "Please don't touch my hair without asking."

Concept Tested: Setting Boundaries

docs.title: 7. What is a warning sign?
docs.text:
1. A behavior or detail that signals a person or situation might be unsafe
  2. A grade that is lower than expected
  3. A rule about how to line up for recess
  4. A type of nutrition label
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A warning sign is a behavior or detail, like being asked to keep a secret from a trusted adult or being asked to go somewhere alone, that signals a person or situation might be unsafe. It is a signal to slow down and consider getting help.

Concept Tested: Warning Sign

docs.title: 8. A classmate tells Devon, "Everyone else is skipping the safety rule, so you should too." What is happening here?
docs.text:
1. Devon is reading a nutrition label
  2. Devon is demonstrating situational awareness
  3. Devon is experiencing peer pressure
  4. Devon is being taught a new skill by a teacher
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Peer pressure is the feeling of being pushed, directly or indirectly, by people your own age to do something you might not otherwise choose to do. "Everyone else is doing it" is a very common peer-pressure comment.

Concept Tested: Peer Pressure

docs.title: 9. One classmate suggests trying a new snack at lunch. Another classmate pressures a friend to skip wearing a bike helmet "because it looks silly." How are these two situations different?
docs.text:
1. They are not different at all — both need the exact same response
  2. The snack suggestion is low-risk, while skipping a helmet is pressure toward an unsafe choice that calls for a refusal skill
  3. The helmet situation is actually the safer one of the two
  4. Neither situation is an example of peer pressure
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Peer pressure can push someone toward a harmless choice, like trying a new food, or toward an unsafe choice, like skipping a safety rule. Recognizing which kind of pressure you are feeling helps you decide whether a refusal skill is needed.

Concept Tested: Peer Pressure

docs.title: 10. A friend keeps asking Priya to skip wearing her helmet, even after she already said no once. Which refusal skill is Priya using if she calmly repeats, "No thanks. No thanks. No thanks."?
docs.text:
1. Blaming a rule
  2. Suggesting an alternative
  3. Walking away
  4. The broken record
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The broken record refusal skill means repeating the same short, calm refusal no matter what the other person says. You do not need a new excuse each time — repeating the same phrase is often the most effective response to continued pressure.

Concept Tested: Refusal Skill

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers common causes of allergic reactions and prevention strategies, and how cultural traditions such as dance and community sports provide physical activity benefits for the body and mood. Students also distinguish infectious from non-infectious disease, learn how germs spread, and study prevention strategies alongside cultural perspectives on wellness and caregiving.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Allergy
  2. Allergy Prevention And Management
  3. Cultural Physical Activity Traditions
  4. Benefits Of Physical Activity On Mood
  5. Infectious Disease
  6. Non-Infectious Disease
  7. How Germs Spread
  8. Disease Prevention Strategies
  9. Cultural Wellness Perspectives

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on Chapter 2: Growth and Development Across Cultures, which introduces respecting cultural differences, a concept this chapter's discussion of cultural physical-activity traditions and wellness perspectives depends on.

Keeping Your Body Well

Hi, friend! This chapter is about staying well — recognizing allergies, moving your body in ways that also lift your mood, and understanding how diseases start and how to prevent them. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Allergy
docs.text:
Some bodies react strongly to things that don't bother most people at all — a certain food, a bee sting, or even pollen in the air. Understanding why this happens is the first step toward staying safe.

An allergy is the body's immune system overreacting to a substance that is usually harmless, called an allergen, and treating it like a threat. Common allergens include foods (peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, shellfish), insect stings (bees, wasps), pollen, pet dander, and certain medicines. When a person with an allergy is exposed to their allergen, their immune system releases chemicals that cause symptoms.

Allergic reaction symptoms can range from mild to very serious. Recognizing them quickly matters:

  • Itchy, watery eyes or a runny, stuffy nose
  • Hives (red, itchy bumps) or a skin rash
  • Swelling of the lips, face, or tongue
  • Coughing, wheezing, or trouble breathing
  • Stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting (often with food allergies)

Most allergic reactions are mild and uncomfortable rather than dangerous. However, a small number of people can have a severe, fast-moving reaction called anaphylaxis, which affects breathing and requires emergency medical help right away.

Serious Symptoms Need Fast Action

Swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, or feeling like your throat is closing up are emergency signs. Tell a trusted adult immediately — these symptoms should never be ignored or wait.

docs.title: Allergy Prevention And Management
docs.text:
Knowing that allergies exist is useful, but the practical skill is knowing what to do about one — either your own or someone else's.

Allergy prevention and management means the everyday practices that reduce the chance of an allergic reaction and the steps to take if one happens anyway. Prevention starts with knowing your own allergens (or a classmate's) and avoiding them on purpose. Management means having a plan ready in case exposure happens despite your best efforts.

The table below organizes prevention and response strategies students can actually use:

Situation What To Do You know your own allergen Read food labels carefully; ask what's in a food before eating it at a party or friend's house A classmate has a known allergy Don't share food with them without checking; take their allergy seriously, even if you don't understand it Mild symptoms appear Tell a trusted adult right away, even if you're not fully sure it's a reaction Severe symptoms appear (swelling, trouble breathing) This is a medical emergency — get an adult immediately; some people carry emergency medicine (an epinephrine auto-injector) for exactly this situation

Many schools have clear allergy plans, such as peanut-free tables in the cafeteria. These plans are not overreactions — they exist because for some students, exposure to even a small amount of an allergen can be dangerous. Respecting these plans is one concrete way you support a classmate's safety.

docs.title: Diagram: Allergy Response Decision Guide
docs.text:
Allergy Response Decision Guide MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: allergy-response-decision-guide Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, use, practice

Learning objective: Students apply allergy prevention and response knowledge by working through short scenarios and choosing the correct next step, reinforcing when a symptom requires telling an adult versus when it is a medical emergency.

Canvas layout: - Top (300px): A scenario card describing a short, realistic situation involving a possible allergic reaction - Bottom (250px): Three response buttons: "Keep Watching," "Tell a Trusted Adult," "This Is an Emergency — Get Help Now"

Visual elements: - Simple flat-illustration icons (a food item, an insect, a person with mild symptoms) matched to each scenario - Color-coded feedback: green for correct match, soft amber for "close, but let's look again," with the correct answer always shown afterward

Interactive controls: - Button per response option - Button: "Next Scenario" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - 6 scenarios cycling in random order, ranging from mild (itchy eyes after petting a friend's cat) to severe (swelling face and trouble breathing after a bee sting)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the full scenario text and a simple icon Stage 2: Show the three response options Stage 3: After a choice, show whether it matches the recommended response and a short explanation of why Final: Show a summary of all scenarios reviewed, with the emergency-level ones flagged clearly

Behavior: - Every choice reveals an explanation; the sim never simply marks an answer "wrong" without teaching the reasoning - Emergency-level scenarios always confirm that "get help now" is correct, reinforcing that these symptoms cannot wait

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level objective requiring learners to use allergy knowledge in realistic situations rather than just recall facts. Scenario-based decision practice builds the quick judgment needed in a real reaction, while guaranteed explanations keep the tone supportive rather than high-stakes.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep all scenarios realistic and age-appropriate; never depict a resolved outcome for the emergency scenarios other than "get an adult now," since this chapter's goal is building the correct fast response, not diagnosing.

docs.title: Cultural Physical Activity Traditions
docs.text:
Bodies are built to move, and every culture around the world has developed its own joyful ways of doing that. Recognizing these traditions helps you see physical activity as something richer than just "exercise."

Cultural physical activity traditions are forms of movement — dances, games, and community sports — that come from a culture's history and are practiced and passed down as part of that community's identity. These are not simply exercise routines; they carry meaning, stories, and connection to family and community.

Examples from around the world include:

  • Traditional dances performed at celebrations, such as powwow dances practiced in many Indigenous nations, Irish step dancing, or West African dance traditions
  • Community sports like lacrosse, which originated with Indigenous nations in North America and is still played today
  • Martial arts traditions, such as Tai Chi or Capoeira, which combine movement, rhythm, and cultural history
  • Community games passed down through generations, like jump-rope games with traditional rhymes, or traditional wrestling styles practiced in different countries

These traditions are valid, valuable forms of physical activity — not just "extra" or "optional" activities. They belong in the same conversation as organized sports and gym class, and they often carry the added benefit of connecting a person to their family history and community.

Movement Looks Different Everywhere

What is a physical activity tradition in your own family or community? It might be a dance, a game, or a sport passed down from someone who taught you. That counts as real, meaningful physical activity.

docs.title: Diagram: World Traditions of Movement Map

docs.title: Benefits Of Physical Activity On Mood
docs.text:
Physical activity does more than build strong muscles and a healthy heart — it changes how a person feels, often within minutes.

Benefits of physical activity on mood refers to the way movement — including dance, sports, and active play — improves how a person feels emotionally, not just physically. When you move your body, your brain releases chemicals that can reduce stress, ease worry, and boost feelings of happiness. Physical activity can also improve focus and energy for learning afterward.

Consider these mood-related benefits that regular physical activity provides:

  1. Reduces stress — Moving your body can help release tension built up from a hard day.
  2. Improves mood — Many people feel happier and calmer after being active.
  3. Boosts energy for learning — A short burst of movement can help you focus better afterward, not just tire you out.
  4. Builds confidence — Getting better at a dance, game, or sport over time builds a sense of accomplishment.
  5. Strengthens connection — Group activities like community dances or team sports build friendships and a sense of belonging.

Cultural physical activity traditions offer all of these same mood benefits, plus something extra: a connection to family history, community identity, and celebration. Dancing at a family celebration or playing a traditional community game delivers the same mood-lifting chemistry as any other physical activity, while also strengthening cultural belonging.
